articles.title: Roblox agrees on child-safety measures with PH gov’t
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines — Roblox has agreed to integrate stricter safeguards and child protection into its user verification in a bid to prevent the presence of online groomers, the Cybercrime…

blocks.caption: This illustration photo shows a child playing a video game on a tablet using Roblox, an online gaming and game-creation platform, in Terville, northeastern France, on March 11, 2026. —Photo by Jean-Christophe Verhaegen/Agence France-Presse

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — Roblox has agreed on integrating stricter safeguards and child protection on its user verification in a bid to prevent the presence of online groomers, the Cybercrime Investigation and Coordinating Center (CICC) said on Friday.

At a meeting with Philippine officials and Roblox’s executives in Singapore, Roblox committed to incorporating the Philippine National Identification Systems into its user verification process, CICC said.
Meanwhile, stricter safeguards on its messaging features for children will also be developed, which will ensure minors can only communicate within their age group.

“We are pleased with the direction of our discussions with Roblox and the willingness they have shown to work with the Philippine government. This is an important beginning, and we want to build on it to create a safer gaming environment for our children,” CICC Executive Director Undersecretary Renato Paraiso said.

According to the CICC, Roblox has also implemented an Artificial Intelligence age verification. Users who fail to undergo an age check will have their chat function disabled and will also be restricted to the platform’s kids’ catalog.
It added that Roblox is set to establish an office space in the country by October for a more coordinated response regarding online safety concerns and other matters on its regulations.
A liaison officer will also be designated to directly coordinate with the authorities, including with the National Bureau of Investigation.

“Regulations work best when we understand how these platforms actually operate. We want to hear from the developers, learn what they are seeing on the ground, and use those insights to build safety measures that have teeth, practical, and responsive to new risks,” he expressed.

Meanwhile, Meta has also expressed its support in coordinating with the Philippine government in integrating child protection features and formulating a framework for heightened security measures against online risks.

“The commitments made today are a starting point. The responsibility now is to turn them into action and to ensure that online threats are addressed before they become real-world harm,” Department of Information and Communications Technology (DICT) Secretary Henry Aguda, who was also present at the meeting, said.
The efforts came amid urgent calls for online safeguards for children following the Zamboanga school shooting last Aug. 18.
The Department of Interior and Local Government alleged that the junior high school perpetrator may have been influenced by the game platform after he was found using Roblox. /cb

articles.title: Greenland says findings on genocide allegation not final
articles.summary: Experts examined the use of forced contraception on the Inuit community during the 1960s and 70s.

blocks.text: Greenland's justice minister has said the government cannot conclude whether genocide was committed against the Inuit community after experts examined the use of forced contraception in the 1960s and 70s.
"We cannot say, on behalf of the government, whether there was genocide," Marianne Paviasen told reporters. "This is something we can continue to debate."
Two reports on the practice were released on Friday, a year after Denmark apologised for the treatment of Inuit women and girls in its autonomous territory.
Greenlandic Prime Minister Jens-Frederik Nielsen said a "reconciliation commission" would be set up while Danish PM Mette Frederiksen promised the governments would work together.
Denmark has passed a compensation law to pay 300,000 Danish crowns (£34,404; $46,800) to each woman affected by the policy.

Records from the national archives show that, between 1966 and 1970, 4,500 Greenlandic women and girls, some as young as 13, had an intra-uterine device (IUD) implanted under a birth-control programme administered by Danish doctors.
In recent years, many women came forward to say they had been fitted with an IUD without their knowledge or consent.
Use of the birth control was so widespread that Greenland's population growth severely slowed.
Frederiksen issued an apology last August to Greenlandic women and their families affected by "systematic discrimination".
In 2024, a former prime minister of Greenland, Mute B Egede, described the practice as "genocide".

Under the UN Convention on the Prevention and Punishment of the Crime of Genocide, external, one definition of genocide is "imposing measures intended to prevent births" within a "national, ethnical, racial or religious group".
The territory tasked a panel of four experts with establishing whether human rights had been violated and whether such violations met the definition of genocide.
However, the panel split, with two members resigning and producing a separate report.

The two experts who remained, Alaskan lawyer Dalee Sambo Dorough and University of Copenhagen law professor Miriam Cullen, found in their report that the rights of Inuit women in Greenland had been violated.
But they said that they could not conclude that genocide had taken place "on the basis of contraceptive practices alone".

They added that genocidal intent by Denmark remained a "possible inference" that a court might establish, based on evidence that fell outside the scope of their report, such as the removal of Inuit children to be raised by Danish families.

The rival report, produced by Jonas Christoffersen, former head of the Danish Institute for Human Rights, and Jensine Nedergaard, a psychologist who had worked in Greenland, accepted that women had been wronged but could not establish the extent of their mistreatment.
They found no evidence "any authority or health professional at any time had any intention of destroying the Greenlandic population".
Reacting on Friday, Greenland's justice minister said the two reports were so different that one "says there was no genocide at all" while the other "says there could have been".

One woman affected by the forced contraception policy, Henriette Berthelsen, told news agency AFP before the reports were presented that their conclusions had been skewed from the start because no Greenlandic Inuits had been appointed as experts.
"For me, this is not just about history or politics. It's my body, my life and my right to self-determination," she said.
"And once again, I see that it is others who will investigate and define what was done to me and to other Inuit women."
Another woman, Inger Platou, 70, told Reuters that she remembered waking up from what she had been told was a minor operation to discover an IUD had been inserted without her consent.
"It turns out we were treated like animals," she said. "Without consent, they just wanted to stop women from giving birth or having children. It was a very inhumane act."
A doctor, she added, later told her complications from the coil had left her unable to become pregnant. She went on to adopt two children from Colombia.
"We are very deferential to authority because we are colonial children," she said.

Reacting to the reports on Friday, Frederiksen said: "We will handle the political process together with the government of Greenland. The most important thing for me is that we find the right path together."
Greenland was a Danish colony until 1953 and did not gain home rule until 1979. Copenhagen continued to oversee its healthcare system until 1992.
The Inuit, or mixed Danish and Inuit, make up nearly 90% of the island's population of 56,000.

The birth-control campaign was designed to control the territory's population, which had ballooned since the 1950s, aided by modernisation and better healthcare. This growth, in addition to an increasing rate of teenage pregnancies, had alarmed the Danish authorities.

In 1970, the campaign was considered a "success" as fertility rates had fallen sharply, though the rate continued to fall for some time after that. In the eight years from the campaign's inception in 1966 until 1974 when it levelled off, Greenland's fertility rate plunged from seven children per woman to 2.3.

articles.title: Rob Reiner's son Jake on his parents' killings: 'I will never understand why this happened'
articles.summary: Jake Reiner this week gave his first sit-down interview since the killing of his parents, filmmaker Rob Reiner and Michele Singer Reiner, in California in December. He told KABC-TV about the shock he…

image.caption: Jake Reiner appears in this screenshot from an interview on KABC-TV — his first interview since his parents, Hollywood filmmaker Rob Reiner and photographer Michele Singer Reiner, were killed on Dec. 14. (ABC7/YouTube)

blocks.text: Entertainment·New

Jake Reiner this week gave his first sit-down interview since the killing of his parents, filmmaker Rob Reiner and Michele Singer Reiner, in California in December. He told KABC-TV about the shock he felt after being told his parents were dead and the complicated feelings he has for his younger brother, Nick, who's currently facing murder charges in the killings.
Jake Reiner gives his first interview since the deaths of his parents 8 months ago

blocks.caption: Jake Reiner appears in this screenshot from an interview on KABC-TV — his first interview since his parents, Hollywood filmmaker Rob Reiner and photographer Michele Singer Reiner, were killed on Dec. 14. (ABC7/YouTube)

blocks.text: For Jake Reiner, ever since Dec. 14, 2025, time has moved both excruciatingly slowly and impossibly fast.

"It's been eight months. It feels like eight years at the same time, and it also feels like eight minutes," he told KABC-TV's Mark Cota-Robles in his first sit-down interview since his parents, Rob Reiner and Michele Singer Reiner, were found fatally stabbed in their Los Angeles home that Sunday afternoon. Hours later, the couple's 32-year-old son, Nick Reiner, was arrested and later charged with murder in their deaths.

items: Rob Reiner, dead at 78, remembered as Hollywood legend in his own right after following father's footsteps

blocks.text: "Every moment that I wake up, I'm reminded of my reality and you're living through that every single day," Jake said.
In the interview, which was released on Thursday, he recalled getting a call that day from his younger sister, Romy, who had made the discovery.
"Romy told me that our dad was dead and then she said, I can't find mom," he told Cota-Robles in the hour-long interview. "I immediately went into shock."

items: What we know about Nick Reiner, in custody following his parents' deaths

blocks.text: Nick was formally indicted on July 20 on two counts of first-degree murder in connection with the deaths of Rob Reiner, a prolific Hollywood filmmaker, actor and political activist, and his wife, Michele, a photographer and producer. He pleaded not guilty.

In the indictment, unsealed on Aug. 12, the LA County grand jury alleged that Nick, who had a long documented history of mental health challenges and struggles with addiction, was lying in wait before attacking his parents.

In 2016, Rob and Nick Reiner released a film they worked on together called Being Charlie, inspired by Nick's struggles with addiction. The film tells the story of a rebellious, drug-addicted teenage son of an actor-turned-politician father, who falls in love with a fellow addict.
At the time, Rob told the media that the film was "by far the most personal thing that I've ever done," and that filming the movie brought him closer to his son.

items: Indictment alleges Nick Reiner lay in wait before killing his parents, Rob Reiner and Michele Singer Reiner

blocks.text: In Thursday's interview, when asked about previously describing the aftermath of the killings as losing half of his family — including Nick — Jake doubled down, while seemingly struggling to find the right words.
"I mean he's in jail so, you know it's — it's like I physically lost my parents and then Nick was arrested and it's like, no it's just me and Romy," he said.
He also addressed the complicated feelings he now has toward his younger brother, saying he will "never understand why this happened."

"For me, it manifests into anger, it manifests into rage, into how unfair this was, how I didn't get a say in what happened," he said. "I didn't get to stop it from happening. I had no choice in the matter, and I just have to accept the reality of it. And to me, that's one of the most infuriating parts of all of this."
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Kayla McLean is a web journalist with CBC News in Toronto. She grew up in Brampton, Ont., and received her bachelor of arts in media production at Toronto Metropolitan University. Before joining CBC in 2024, she worked as a breaking news reporter at Global News Toronto — covering everything from crime, sports, festivals and politics. She also reported for Global News's current affairs show, The New Reality, covering stories with a focus on racial equality and climate justice. She also previously held positions as a chase producer and writer for CTV News Channel.

articles.title: Right-wing commentator Milo Yiannopoulos detained by ICE
articles.summary: The British citizen, who lives and works in the US, has supported Trump and ICE agents in the past.

blocks.text: British right-wing political commentator Milo Yiannopoulos has apparently been detained by Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), according to the agency's records.
Yiannopoulos, 41, a former editor of Breitbart News and a onetime employee of rapper Kanye West, appears to be held in Louisiana, according to a search of ICE's inmate registry.
The self-styled provocateur has called himself the "most fabulous supervillain on the internet". His critics call him a purveyor of hate speech.
Neither ICE nor Yiannopoulos has responded to the BBC's request for comment, but his name and British origins appear in a search of detainees nationwide.
Yiannopoulos, who grew up in Kent in the south of England, currently resides in the US. The circumstances around his apparent detention are still unclear.

He was an early supporter of Donald Trump during the 2016 election, headlining an event called Gays for Trump during the Republican National Convention that year, and has backed Trump's tighter immigration restrictions in the US.

But he had a bitter fallout with Trump's movement. While Yiannopoulos continues to voice support for the Republican president's agenda, he posted in March this year on X that Trump "has lost his way, bought off by foreign interests".

Yiannopoulos has been widely criticised for his comments about transgender people, Muslims, Black Lives Matter, feminists and gay people, even though he himself identified as gay. Yiannopoulos now calls himself an "ex-gay".
He has written columns titled "Birth Control Makes Women Unattractive and Crazy" and "Would You Rather Your Child Had Feminism or Cancer?"

In 2017, Yiannopoulos was uninvited from speaking at CPAC, a US conservative conference that also hosted Trump, after footage emerged of him appearing to condone paedophilia. He also later apologised and resigned from Breitbart.
He denied the allegations, and said he had been speaking about his own experiences as a child.

Yiannopoulos was once regularly linked with the alt-right, a disparate group that is outspoken against so-called political correctness and feminism and which includes neo-Nazis and white supremacists.
He has said he does not consider himself part of the alt-right, although he has called it "energising and exciting".

articles.title: Norway mourns King Harald as Haakon VIII ascends throne
articles.summary: Mourners gather outside the palace as royals, politicians and citizens remember a beloved king, whose son has adopted the family motto "all for norway".

blocks.caption: People stand in a crowd, two women hugging each other, against a line of flowers and flags on the ground, a statue behind them at the royal palace in Oslo.

blocks.text: Image source, Cornelius Poppe / NTB / AFP via Getty Images) / Norway OUT
Norwegians are grieving the death of the beloved King Harald V, as a period of national mourning begins and his son Haakon VIII assumes the throne.
After Harald's death was announced early on Friday, crowds amassed at the royal palace in Oslo, laying flowers and flags, some mourners visibly in tears.
The 53-year-old new king held an extraordinary council of state meeting with government ministers, saying he was taking on the royal family's motto "All for Norway".

Harald - who was on the throne for 35 years - died in hospital at 06:35 local time (04:35 GMT) aged 89, after being treated there for a rare blood condition. His coffin was later taken to the palace in a public procession.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Memorials outside the palace included a candle with the word "thanks" written on it

blocks.text: Image source, Odd ANDERSEN / AFP via Getty Images
Memorials outside the palace included a candle with the word "thanks" written on it
An estimated 10,000 people lined the streets in the capital to see the late king go past, Norway's public broadcaster reported.
The late monarch has been described as an inclusive, transparent and empathetic "people's king" who modernised the Norwegian monarchy.

European royals, including King Charles III - whose mother Queen Elizabeth II was Harald's second cousin - as well as political leaders and ordinary citizens, paid tribute to his service and the stability he brought to the country.
Norway's Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre, who laid flowers outside the palace and signed a book of condolences after greeting the new king, said the country was "united in grief and gratitude".

In a televised memorial address - one of multiple eulogies by ministers - he said the late king's "legacy lives on" and offered condolences to the royal family and Queen Sonja, who would have celebrated her 58th wedding anniversary with Harald on Saturday.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Støre was joined by ministers and a crowd of citizens grieving outside the palace

blocks.text: Image source, REUTERS/Dylan Martinez
Støre was joined by ministers and a crowd of citizens grieving outside the palace

Norway's superstar footballer Erling Haaland thanked Harald for "everything you meant to Norway" in a post on Instagram, adding that it had been an honour to meet him earlier in the summer at the palace following the Fifa World Cup.
In the country's capital, Norwegians shared their grief and affection for the late king.
"I personally will say he was everything for us, especially being an immigrant," Biteya Terfassa, an Oslo resident who was born in Ethiopia, told news agency Reuters outside the palace.
"He made us feel at home and he made us feel loved. So he was like a grandfather that I never had."
Norwegians have been laying tributes and remembering the late King Harald V following his death.
At noon, the Norwegian Armed Forces honoured Harald with a funeral salute of 21 shots from Akershus Fortress in central Oslo.
Later on Friday, a procession left the chapel at Rikshospitalet, where Harald died, taking his coffin in a hearse to the royal palace.

Norway has declared a period of national mourning until the day of his funeral, which has not yet been announced. Flags will be flown at half-mast, while his portrait will be displayed, candles lit and moments of silence held at professional events.
All non work-related social events will be cancelled or postponed. Oslo Mayor Anne Lindboe, who was due to get married on Friday, even postponed her wedding.
King Harald's coffin moving from Oslo hospital to Royal Palace
King Haakon, who is Harald's younger child, is now the monarch and his wife Mette-Marit queen.
He is due to take an oath before the Norwegian parliament on Tuesday and will later participate in a consecration service - a stripped-down version of a coronation, which Norway no longer has.

His daughter, the 22-year-old Ingrid Alexandra, who joined her father to meet ministers at the palace on Friday, is next in line to the throne as crown princess after the rules of succession changed in 1990 to allow firstborn women to inherit the crown.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Crown Princess Ingrid Alexandra, second from right, stood by her father's side

blocks.text: Image source, NTB/Lise Aserud via REUTERS
Crown Princess Ingrid Alexandra, second from right, stood by her father's side
Haakon assumes his new role at a difficult time, as the royal family has faced health challenges and scandals this year.

Now-Queen Mette-Marit came under scrutiny earlier this year when it was revealed that she had a three-year friendship with the late convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein, for which she has publicly apologised.

Later in the year, she received a lung transplant, after suffering from pulmonary fibrosis since 2018. Doctors will not declare her stable until next year, meaning her husband must balance his new official duties with her care.
Meanwhile, Mette-Marit's son from a previous relationship, Marius Borg Høiby, was convicted in June of rape and other offences and sentenced to four years in prison. He is appealing.
Høiby is not a member of the royal family, but was raised with them since he was four years old, when now-King Haakon married his mother.

blocks.caption: Family tree of King Haakon's family

blocks.text: Although Harald remained popular until his death, a poll for newspaper Aftenposten earlier this year found that support for the monarchy had dropped from 72% in 2024 to 54%.

However, Norwegian royal experts told the BBC that the new king, while facing questions about the turbulence surrounding his family, was respected, hard-working and, they believed, able to move forward despite the challenges.

articles.title: Police arrest seven more men in aftermath of deadly A66 crash
articles.summary:
Cleveland police say a total of 24 people arrested in investigation after crash that killed two officers

Seven more men have been arrested as Cleveland police attempt to disrupt organised…

blocks.text: Seven more men have been arrested as Cleveland police attempt to disrupt organised crime after the A66 crash that killed two officers.
The force said the total number of those arrested in the investigation had risen to 24, several of them charged with serious offences and a number of offenders recalled to prison.

The latest arrests include four men – aged 35, 25, 40 and 21 – who are in custody being questioned on suspicion of criminal damage with intent to endanger life, arson and possession with intent to supply class A drugs.

The alleged arson relates to a caravan that was set alight on Atlee Road in Middlesbrough at 5.30am on Wednesday, while the alleged criminal damage with intent to endanger life relates to a suspected ramming of a garden wall on Steele Crescent in Middlesbrough in the early hours of Sunday morning.
All four men were in a vehicle stopped by police on Kingsley Road in Grangetown at 10.30pm on Thursday.
Class A drugs and a Mercedes car were seized.

The three other men arrested were a 23-year-old man held on suspicion of threats to kill, a 42-year-old man detained on suspicion of threats to kill and possession of criminal property, and a 30-year-old man arrested on suspicion of possession of criminal property, the force added.
All three were released on conditional bail.
Officers also seized £15,000 in cash, PA Media reported.

articles.title: Russia ramps up rhetoric but wants to avoid war with Nato, Western officials say
articles.summary: But they say Moscow will likely continue its "hybrid activity" against Nato members, short of direct military action.

blocks.text: Russian President Vladimir Putin wants to avoid a direct military confrontation with Nato, despite increasingly hostile rhetoric aimed at the UK and other allies over their support for Ukraine, Western officials believe.
Some reports have suggested the visit by CIA chief John Radcliffe to Moscow this week was, in part, to warn Russia against a possible attack on a member of the Euro-Atlantic military alliance.

But the Western officials, who asked not to be named, said recent warnings from Moscow, including that UK forces could be targeted in future or that its weapons factories could be hit, were "nothing new".
They were, they suggested, consistent with Russia's military doctrine to apply pressure on the West.

The officials suggested that the hostile rhetoric was also a reflection of the growing pressure Putin is facing at home, with slow and costly gains in Ukraine along with the impact of Ukrainian long-range strikes deep inside Russia.

Putin and his officials have repeatedly dismissed warnings of Russian plans to attack Nato countries as hysteria. And US President Donald Trump appears to believe the Russian leader – saying this week that "he's not going to attack a Nato territory".

Not long before launching his full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, Putin had given public assurances that he had no intention of attacking Russia's neighbour - despite overwhelming US intelligence that such preparations were in full swing.

However, the senior Western officials said on Friday that Russia would likely continue its "hybrid activity", short of direct military action, using methods such as cyber-attacks, sabotage and even assassination attempts.

They said that was aimed at breaking Western resolve and support for Ukraine. One official highlighted the risks of that Russian strategy leading to a miscalculation -which could spark a military confrontation.
Russia is suspected of being behind a string of recent drone incidents in several Nato countries.

Earlier this month, a drone loaded with explosives reached a runway in Germany's Leipzig airport - a key logistics hub for transferring military equipment to Ukraine. There is no proof to link the incident directly to Russia, which has denied any role.
It came amid a string of drone sightings over European airports and military bases that began last year and which are also suspected of being the work of Russia, though it again denies this.
Following the Leipzig incident, the head of France's security services warned that "we must consider the possibility of direct, more violent hostile actions on our national soil".
Still, one Western official said Nato allies should remain calm but not complacent. The UK government has already made clear that recent Russian threats will not deter its support for Ukraine.
The Western officials said the Ukraine war had "escalated" this year, with both Moscow and Kyiv stepping up their own long-range strike campaigns.
Putin, they said, had not changed his maximalist objectives, despite some signs of increasing frustrations back home.

They said petrol shortages in Russia were having an impact on support for the war. They believed there was increasing political pressure on the Russian leader, but that this did not pose a critical challenge to his power.
Russia is still making slow gains in the eastern Donbas region. But it's also facing heavy casualties.
The officials said Russia was losing 6,000 more soldiers a month - either killed or wounded - than it can recruit.
That said, there is no indication yet that the Kremlin leader will resort to mass mobilisation.

articles.title: Large fire near Wembley Stadium disrupts tube and rail services
articles.summary:
About 125 firefighters tackle blaze at Neasden waste facility as nearby Amazon warehouse is evacuated

A large fire has broken out at a waste facility close to Wembley Stadium in north-west…

blocks.text: A large fire has broken out at a waste facility close to Wembley Stadium in north-west London, disrupting tube and train lines in the area.
Twenty fire engines and about 125 firefighters were sent to tackle the blaze at a mixed-waste facility on an industrial estate in Neasden, just under a mile from the venue.
Huge plumes of smoke could be seen in videos posted on social media, and more than 70 calls were made about the blaze.

There was no service on the entire Metropolitan line, which runs close to the blaze, and no service between Wembley Park and West Hampstead on the Jubilee line, with severe delays on the rest of the line, Transport for London said.
Rail services into London Marylebone were also disrupted.

blocks.caption: About 125 firefighters and 20 fire engines were sent to tackle the blaze. Photograph: Rasid Necati Aslim/Anadolu/Getty Images

blocks.text: A nearby Amazon warehouse, which is not related to the industrial unit involved, has been evacuated, according to PA Media.

The London fire brigade said: “Tube services on the Metropolitan and Jubilee lines will be impacted as crews respond. Rail services into London Marylebone are also disrupted as a result of this fire.”
The cause of the fire is not yet known.
It is the third major fire at a recycling centre in London this summer after two incidents at the Landmann Way Reuse and Recycling Centre in south-east London.
after newsletter promotion

Fires at recycling centres caused by wrongly discarded lithium batteries, such as those found in vapes, are occurring at the rate of more than 10 a week, according to figures from the Environmental Services Association.
Battery fires at waste facilities are estimated to cost £1bn a year and are causing growing frustration among fire chiefs.

articles.title: Trump administration pushing to hand parcel of Yosemite land to private developer – report
articles.summary:
Nevada-based Kingsbarn Realty Capital seeks to acquire land to construct private road to development outside park

The Trump…

blocks.text: The Trump administration is reportedly pushing to give a parcel of land inside Yosemite, the country’s first national park and one of its most popular, to a Nevada-based private developer.

Staff with the National Park Service have been exploring how the agency can give a quarter-mile parcel to a company operated by Kingsbarn Realty Capital, the news outlet Notus reported on Friday, citing agency documents and unnamed sources “directly familiar with discussions”.

The company already owns an 83-acre (34-hectare) plot of undeveloped land immediately outside the park. The previous owner of that land had hoped to create a resort and unsuccessfully lobbied the federal government for decades to allow him to construct a private road in the park, the outlet reported.

The current access road to the land, which Kingsbarn bought in 2024, is more than 10 miles (16km) from the nearest park entrance and would require travelers to take a longer, indirect route to reach popular park attractions. Jeff Pori, the company’s CEO, wants to construct a short road to connect the parcel to a central Yosemite route, according to Notus.

Administration officials have proposed that the park service give up the land in exchange for equally valuable land elsewhere in California, the outlet reported. The interior department’s top political leaders support the proposal, according to sources cited by Notus, and the situation has created tension inside the park service.

In a statement to the Guardian, Aubrie Spady, an interior department spokesperson, rejected the reporting, arguing there “has been no political pressure to reach a predetermined outcome”, and said “suggesting the Department is secretly working to hand over National Park Service land to a private developer [is] false.”

The report has sparked outrage among National Park Service supporters and environmental advocates. Jayson O’Neill, spokesperson for Save Our Parks, described it as part of a “push to sell off public lands and privatize America’s national parks” by the US interior secretary, Doug Burgum.

“If mismanaging parks and stealing entrance fees for Trump’s DC vanity projects wasn’t enough, now Americans find out Doug Burgum and his cronies spent a year secretly negotiating to hand a piece of Yosemite national park over to a well-connected developer, all while lying to us about protecting them,” O’Neill said.
“National parks belong to the American people, not monied developers who are part of Trump’s donor class.”
Both of California’s senators have expressed their opposition to efforts to develop the road, as has Jared Huffman, the Democratic California congressman representing the state’s north coast.

“Our parks belong to all of us. These places should be protected for every generation, not sold off to Trump’s ultra-wealthy friends to profit off of,” Huffman said. “I will fight this, both for Yosemite and for every treasured park that would be up for grabs if this domino falls.”

The interior department said no final decisions had been reached and that any land exchange or access proposal would be “subject to all applicable federal laws, regulations and Departmental policies, including required environmental review and public notification processes”.

articles.title: Air Canada will now allow you up to 3 mobility aids on flights in expanded policy
articles.summary: Air Canada announced an expanded mobility aid policy Friday that will allow customers to bring up to three mobility aids free of charge.

image.caption: A passenger gets information from a ground crew member at Pierre-Elliott Trudeau Airport in Montreal on Aug. 19, 2025. (Andrej Ivanov/AFP/Getty Images)

blocks.text: World
Air Canada announced an expanded mobility aid policy Friday that will allow customers to bring up to three mobility aids free of charge.
Expanded policy announced Friday

blocks.caption: A passenger gets information from a ground crew member at Pierre-Elliott Trudeau Airport in Montreal on Aug. 19, 2025. (Andrej Ivanov/AFP/Getty Images)

blocks.text: Canada's largest airline said the move is to allow greater flexibility to customers who use mobility aids or travel with adaptive sports equipment.

"Having this policy clearly defined means people with disabilities can travel, without having to explain or justify our needs," said Meghan Hines, chair of Air Canada’s accessibility advisory committee, in a statement Friday.

"As both a traveller with a disability and a Para athlete, it is meaningful to see Air Canada recognize that the equipment we travel with ... are extensions of our bodies, not an extra piece of luggage."
Air Canada said eligible items can include any combination of personal mobility aids, adaptive sports equipment, personal or patient lifts and similar transfer devices.
Some passengers with disabilities still struggling on Air Canada flights
If a device is too large to travel on the same aircraft as the customer, Air Canada said cargo will transport it within Canada, free of charge.

"This policy recognizes that accessibility needs do not look the same for everyone and that people with disabilities should be able to travel with the equipment they need without added uncertainty or having to advocate for an exception," Hines said.
Rachael Pinnock, chief commercial and impact officer with the Canadian Paralympic Committee, welcomed the move Friday.
"This new policy will make a significant difference in making travel easier and more affordable for athletes at all levels of sport, from recreation to high-performance," Pinnock said in a statement.
"This is a testament to Air Canada’s commitment to listening and learning from the experiences and perspectives of the Para sport community."
Last week, Canada's transport regulator ordered WestJet to scrap its 136-kilogram weight cap on mobility aids before July 2027.

articles.title: At least 90 Americans missing in Nepal flood among 2,000 unaccounted for
articles.summary:
Official death toll approaches 600, with many of the missing Americans having been on a pilgrimage to a sacred site

At least 90 Americans were still missing on Friday among almost 2,000…

blocks.text: At least 90 Americans were still missing on Friday among almost 2,000 people unaccounted for following the catastrophic flash flood along the Nepal-Tibet border on Wednesday.
With the official death toll creeping towards 600 on Friday and expected to continue rising, there were survivors, victims and missing people from many nationalities.

“We can confirm that three American citizens have been safely rescued in Nepal. We are not aware of any US citizen deaths at this time,” the state department said on Thursday, USA Today reported. At least 90 Americans who were in the affected area remained unaccounted for.
The Guardian has reached out to the state department for additional comment.
Many of the Americans who are missing were on a pilgrimage to Mount Kailash, a sacred site in Tibet revered by several faiths, including Hinduism and Buddhism.

There were 22 Americans returning from a pilgrimage hosted by the Isha Foundation, among 80 foundation members not yet located, founder and spiritual leader Sadhguru Vasudev said in a statement Thursday. The India-based spiritual organization has a US campus in Tennessee.

Leslie Crespi, a community liaison for the foundation’s US campus, said: “We had communication with the coordinator of the group at about 9.05am Nepalese time [Wednesday] saying that they had arrived there. And then by 9.14am is when this flash flood hit.”
Crespi described the trekkers as “like family”, adding that it was a “lifelong dream to go and be there” in Nepal for many of them.
Among the missing Americans is 45-year-old Venus Rajnikant Patel. His brother, Dennis, said Patel, who had recently moved from St Louis to Cincinnati, had been planning the pilgrimage for two years.

Patel’s friend Jolene Gosha said his hotel had been in the flood zone and “we’re just hoping, hoping, that by some chance he was able to climb his way out of it … I don’t want to give myself false hope because I know the reality is that he’s probably not with us.”
Meanwhile, the family of 72-year-old Jitendra Patel of Long Island in New York were still trying to reach him, his son Sunny Patel said.
Patel said his father called on Wednesday morning to say he had crossed into Tibet, and the family later realized he was in the flood zone.
“My heart sank,” Patel said, adding that he “didn’t think it was possible that my dad would be there at ‘ground zero’” of the flooding disaster.
The family is “maybe hopeful”, he said, but they have not heard from him and their WhatsApp messages remain unanswered. “It gets worse by every hour, obviously,” Patel added.
Also missing are Rekha and Rashi Shashidharan, a New York mother and 14-year-old daughter who were also on a pilgrimage to Mount Kailash.
They had spent several days in Kathmandu acclimating to the altitude before traveling towards Tibet with a tour group, Shekhar Agrawal, Rekha’s brother, told CNN.

Agrawal last spoke to them around 7.30am local time on Wednesday before they planned to cross into Tibet. “After that, there was radio silence, nothing, no contact whatsoever,” Agrawal said, adding that he believes they may have still been at their hotel when the flood hit.
Marco Rubio, the US secretary of state, said the US “stands ready to support the government of Nepal with needed humanitarian assistance”.

Meanwhile, the US embassy in Nepal said that the state department will “provide $500,000 (approximately 76 million Nepali rupees) in assistance through a global grant to Catholic Relief Services, which will help flood-affected communities with emergency shelter and relief supplies, as well as water, sanitation, and hygiene support”.
The Associated Press contributed reporting

articles.title: House prosecution bent on completing 'puzzle' of VP Sara confidential fund misuse
articles.summary: House impeachment adviser Robert Ace Barbers says the prosecution panel intends to finish the "puzzle"--so to speak--of respondent Vice President Sara Duterte's alleged misuse of confidential funds…

blocks.text: House impeachment adviser Robert Ace Barbers says the prosecution panel intends to finish the "puzzle"--so to speak--of respondent Vice President Sara Duterte's alleged misuse of confidential funds through the presentation of more witnesses.
This, even as Barbers claimed that what prosecutors had laid down so far was already sufficient to paint a picture of an official who deserved to be removed from office.
“Sa amin, sapat na so far, at meron pang idadagdag (For us, it is sufficient so far, and there is more to be added),” he said Friday, Aug. 28 during a virtual press briefing.

“Sa amin, sa prosecution, ay tuloy-tuloy lamang na buuin ’yung litrato o ’yung puzzle (For us in the prosecution, we will simply continue putting the picture, or the puzzle, together)," noted Barbers.

"Kasi bawat piyesa, bawat part ng puzzle na ’yan ay magbibigay ng totoong litrato o picture kung ano itong usapin na ’yan, o ano itong allegation na ito,” explained the former House quad-committee (quad-comm) overall chairman.
(Because each piece, each part of that puzzle, will provide the true picture of what this issue is about, or what this allegation is about.)
Respondent Duterte is being accused--among other things--of misuing P612.5 million worth of confidential funds released to the Office of the Vice President (OVP) and Department of Education (DepEd).
The procpsecution's presentation has covered the request, release, encashment, handling and liquidation of the funds, along with Commission on Audit (COA) findings on questioned expenditures.
Among the witnesses already presented by the prosecution were OVP officials Gina Acosta and Lemuel Ortonio, both of whom were declared hostile witnesses by the Senate impeachment court.

Acosta testified that she turned over four P125-million tranches, or P500 million, to then-OVP security officer Col. Raymund Dante Lachica upon Duterte’s instruction despite remaining the accountable officer for the funds.
Ortonio, meanwhile, testified about Duterte’s knowledge and authorization of the confidential activities and said he had no personal knowledge of their actual implementation.
The prosecution is expected to present additional witnesses as it continues with the confidential fund charge, including witnesses connected to the P112.5 million in DepEd confidential funds.
Barbers says each piece of evidence is intended to give senator-judges a clearer basis for evaluating the allegations when the time comes to decide.
“‘Pag dumating sa punto na kung saan ay magdedesisyon ang ating mga senator-judges, eh marami silang pwedeng paghuhugutan ng basehan para sa kanilang mga desisyon, na base sa ebidensya,” he said.
(When it reaches the point where our senator-judges have to make a decision, they will have many things they can draw from as a basis for their decisions, based on the evidence.)

articles.title: Impeachment prosecutor Mae Divinagracia and her comfort cross go viral
articles.summary: Atty. Mae Divinagracia, one of the private prosecutors in the impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte, conducted her direct examination of hostile witness Assistant Secretary Lemuel Ortonio…

blocks.text: Published August 29, 2026 1:42am
Make this your preferred source to get more updates from this publisher on Google.

Atty. Mae Divinagracia, one of the private prosecutors in the impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte, conducted her direct examination of hostile witness Assistant Secretary Lemuel Ortonio while holding what appeared to be a wooden cross.

The "comfort cross" has since gone viral following the many short-form videos posted about it, after its noticeable presence while the prosecutor sought answers regarding the disbursement of confidential funds from the Vice President's deputy chief of staff.
“It is for comfort, clarity of mind when I am holding it,” Divinagracia told reporters on the sidelines of the impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte.
Divinagracia said it calms her down.
Comfort crosses fit the palm of one's hand and are smooth, without sharp edges. They are used as a tangible source of comfort during prayer or difficulty.
“It is what I use every time I am doing trial,” Divinagracia said. –Llanesca T. Panti/NB, GMA News

articles.title: Venezuelan opposition up in arms over reports US wants big stake in oil and gas
articles.summary:
Critics call move to gain long-term access to country’s massive energy reserves ‘predatory’ and ‘unconstitutional’

Reports that the US is preparing to claim a big stake in Venezuela’s…

blocks.text: Reports that the US is preparing to claim a big stake in Venezuela’s massive energy reserves have sparked an outcry, with critics describing the move as “predatory” and a “rapacious” land grab.

Several media outlets this week reported that the Trump administration – which abducted Venezuela’s authoritarian president, Nicolás Maduro, in January and has steered the South American country ever since – hopes to secure long-term access to its oil and gasfields.
Venezuela has the world’s largest proven crude oil reserves with an estimated 303bn barrels, compared with Saudi Arabia’s 268bn and Iran’s 208bn.

On Thursday, the Wall Street Journal said Trump officials were in “advanced talks” with Venezuelan officials to take “a direct stake in more than a dozen oilfields” containing 90bn barrels, nearly a third of Venezuela’s energy reserves.

“This is real and being discussed at the highest levels of the US and Venezuelan governments,” a source told Reuters, which said the fields being negotiated were in the Orinoco Belt and Lake Maracaibo regions.
Axios claimed the deal would be “a legacy-defining moment for President Trump”, with one unnamed official telling the US outlet: “Calling this deal huge would be an understatement … It is massive.”
Citing sources familiar with the negotiations, Bloomberg said one deal under discussion was a 100-year-lease on several oilfields.
The reports caused unease and anger among members of Venezuela’s opposition, who are already up in arms about Trump’s failure to bring about genuine political change after capturing Maduro.

“It’s a land grab – a massive land grab,” said one well-known opposition figure who asked not to be named because of the sensitivities of criticising the US. “It’s revolting because this is not the United States one would have [expected]. This is not the United States of the Marshall plan. This is a rapacious, mafioso United States,” they added.

Since January’s special forces raid on Caracas, Venezuela has been led by an interim president, Delcy Rodríguez, who was Maduro’s vice-president and minister of petroleum. Other key members of Maduro’s regime have also retained positions of power, including the interior minister, Diosdado Cabello, who has been collaborating with Trump officials – despite having a $25m US bounty on his head for alleged drug trafficking. Meanwhile, the exiled opposition leader, María Corina Machado, whose movement is believed to have won the 2024 presidential elections, has been sidelined.

Ricardo Hausmann, an exiled former minister and opposition supporter, wrote on X: “An illegitimate interim government with an illegitimate hydrocarbons law has no legitimacy to strike this unconstitutional deal. It will be a fiasco for all involved.”

The economist Francisco Rodríguez urged Venezuela’s national assembly to reject what he called a “predatory deal”. “Handing over Venezuela’s oil wealth to the US contravenes the constitution and is not in the interest of the Venezuelan people – much more when it is done at gunpoint,” Rodríguez said.
Luz Mely Reyes, a prominent journalist and government critic, sarcastically called the “surrender” of Venezuela’s natural riches “the deal of the century”.

Gregory Brew, an energy historian and Eurasia Group analyst, anticipated “quite a lot of suspicion and rejection of any deal that would hand the United States government effective control over Venezuelan resources”.
after newsletter promotion
Brew said the reported deal reminded him of how BP, then the Anglo-Persian Oil Company, controlled the oil resources of Iraq and Iran at the start of the last century.

“Anglo-Persian was given a concession by the Shah of Iran in 1901 … in exchange for what was essentially a bribe to the Persian government, and it gave the company sweeping rights. The company was essentially in total control of any oil it found and would be able to retain virtually all the profits of any other oil it found and exploited and exported,” Brew said.

“From Trump’s point of view, the control over oil is something of an end in and of itself,” Brew added. “But if you do try to rationalise it, I think US dominance over Venezuelan oil reserves allows the US to regard Venezuelan reserves as its own reserves: a source of oil from which the United States can draw and that nobody else has access to. I think that’s how the administration is conceiving of this – excluding China, excluding Russia, but I think also excluding other potential customers for Venezuelan oil,” he added. “It sounds colonial, because it is.”

Venezuela’s post-Maduro conversion into what many call a US protectorate is the most dramatic play in Trump’s push to reassert Washington’s influence over Latin America as part of the so-called “Donroe Doctrine”.

That policy is a 21st-century adaptation of the 19th-century Monroe Doctrine by which President James Monroe sought to keep European powers out of the Americas. Trump’s version is about countering China’s growing footprint in the region and imposing US will through economic and military pressure.
Maduro’s downfall has brought some change to Venezuela, with hundreds of political prisoners freed under Rodríguez and talks about reforming the regime-controlled supreme court taking place.

But no date has been set for a fresh presidential election and Machado has been unable to return from exile. “Delcy’s been doing a fantastic job,” Trump told reporters last month, claiming Venezuela was “not really ready” for a vote.

articles.title: Satellite images reveal scale of flood devastation in Nepal villages
articles.summary: Before-and-after images show villages, bridges and a key Nepal-Tibet border crossing washed away by devastating floodwaters.

blocks.text: This destructive path continues westwards along with the swelled river, before heading southwards.

Satellite images also show the formation of a barrier lake at the base of the landslide's path, which Chinese authorities have warned poses a major risk of further flooding and has hampered rescue efforts.

Dr Argha Banerjee, a glaciologist at the Indian Institute of Science Education and Research, told BBC Verify that it was not possible determine from the images how stable the barrier was or how likely the lake was to drain suddenly.
But he said there was no significant increase in its surface area between Wednesday and Thursday, despite water continuing to flow into the lake.

Dr Banerjee said there was a visible drainage channel, which suggests some water was already escaping downstream, adding that the its volume was "not alarmingly large" and appeared to have stabilised.

The extent of the damage on the Tibetan side of the border remains unclear. It is a strictly controlled region which China annexed in the 1950s, where foreign media access is heavily restricted. BBC Verify has so far been unable find verifiable footage from the area.

The satellite imagery - which only provides an initial glimpse into the damage of the flood - has been published by Vantor as part of its Open Data Program to help aid authorities establish where best to focus their efforts to locate the missing, rescue survivors and recover the dead.
Additional reporting Shruti Menon, Merlyn Thomas and Alex Murray. Graphics by Mezut Ersoz.

articles.title: Junior hockey players in OHL, WHL can seek compensation for alleged abuse, court says
articles.summary: The Ontario Superior Court of Justice has approved an opt-in process for current and former players in the Ontario Hockey League and Western Hockey League who allege they were victims of abuse or…

image.caption: Canadian Hockey League players in the OHL and WHL are now able to seek compensation for alleged abuse. Claims will be accepted from current and past players, dating back to 1975, when the CHL was established. (The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: Sudbury

The Ontario Superior Court of Justice has approved an opt-in process for current and former players in the Ontario Hockey League and Western Hockey League who allege they were victims of abuse or hazing.
Ontario Superior Court recently OK'd opt-in process for current, former CHL players

blocks.caption: Canadian Hockey League players in the OHL and WHL are now able to seek compensation for alleged abuse. Claims will be accepted from current and past players, dating back to 1975, when the CHL was established. (The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: Junior hockey players in the Canadian Hockey League who claim they were victims of abuse or hazing may be eligible for compensation through the courts.

Ontario Superior Court recently approved a procedure for players who competed in the Ontario Hockey League (OHL) and Western Hockey League (WHL) to seek compensation for alleged abuse, bullying or hazing.
Claims will be accepted from current and past players, dating back to 1975, when the CHL was established.
Toronto-based law firm Koskie Minsky LLP is overseeing the claims, which can be submitted until April 6.
Gerry Antman, a lawyer and partner with the firm, said his practice focuses on institutional abuse and other class actions that involve personal injuries.
He noted this process is different from a traditional class action since the players must apply to be included.
“They would have to describe the nature and extent of the abuse they suffered, as well as the impacts that abuse had on them in the short-term as children, and now into adulthood."

items: 4 Hockey Canada players from 2018 junior team remain suspended

blocks.text: The opt-in process comes after the Ontario Superior Court of Justice didn't certify a class action proposed by former players against the CHL.

blocks.caption: Gerry Antman is a lawyer and partner with Toronto-based Koskie Minsky LLP, which is overseeing the hockey player abuse claims filed to the court. (Koskie Minsky LLP website)

blocks.text: Antman said his firm is routinely contacted by former junior hockey players who shared stories of abuse, including in recent seasons.
When asked about the details of what players allege have happened to them over the years, Antman said it would be too graphic to articulate over the airwaves.
“It’s now 2026, and some of these things continue to go on today, which is a bit shocking."
League, teams back court's work: OHL spokesperson
In an email to CBC, OHL spokesperson Josh Sweetland said the CHL and its teams support the court’s work to create the opt-in process.
He noted the league and its teams have been posting the notice of this process on their sites, as per the court’s requirements.

“The Canadian Hockey League takes the safety and well-being of players seriously,” he wrote. “Because this matter is before the courts, the CHL is not in a position to comment on specific allegations.”

items: 'Ringleader' in Manitoba high school hockey hazing complaint loses suspension appeal

blocks.text: In each lawsuit, Antman said, the CHL, the regional league and the team or teams the plaintiff competed on would be named as defendants, and would ultimately be responsible to pay out any applicable compensation.
“Our team is available to guide individuals through this process in a way that makes sure they can access justice in a way that’s supportive and trauma informed.”

articles.title: Thieves steal 600-diamond necklace from Vienna museum in broad daylight
articles.summary: Police are hunting two suspects they believe bought a ticket for the exhibition to get at the jewellery.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Vienna police released CCTV images of the suspects

blocks.text: Image source, LPD Wien
Vienna police released CCTV images of the suspects
ByBethany Bell
Vienna correspondent

An international manhunt is under way for two men who stole a necklace decorated with more than 600 diamonds from a museum in Vienna after buying a ticket for the exhibition in which it was being displayed.

Police said the two suspects smashed a glass display case at the Vienna Museum of Applied Arts (MAK) on Thursday afternoon and grabbed the platinum and diamond necklace, which is believed to be worth more than $4m (£3m; €3.5m).
The necklace, which was designed for the former Egyptian royal family, was part of an exhibition on the jewellers Van Cleef & Arpels, due to run at MAK until September.
The theft is the latest in a series of spectacular heists of artefacts at European museums.
Vienna police released photos of the two suspects, who were unmasked, captured on security cameras. They are appealing for the public to come forward with information.
The police said in a statement that one of the perpetrators was also believed to have been carrying what was thought to be a real firearm.
After seizing the necklace, they fled "towards the Vienna Stadtpark" just south of the museum, they said.

blocks.caption: Image caption, The more than 200-carat necklace was worn by Queen Nazli in 1939 for the marriage of her daughter to the future Shah of Iran

blocks.text: Image source, Austrian Interior Ministry
The more than 200-carat necklace was worn by Queen Nazli in 1939 for the marriage of her daughter to the future Shah of Iran
Lilli Hollein, MAK general director, said "the theft of a highly valuable piece of jewellery... has hit us hard".

She said in a statement that MAK had developed a security plan with Van Cleef & Arpels specifically for the exhibition, adding: "Security issues were taken very seriously and all security measures were carefully prepared."
Hollein said staff had reacted calmly and followed the established procedures when the "armed incident" occurred, and that no one had been injured.
She added that MAK had thoroughly reviewed its security measures ahead of the exhibition, "particularly in light of the incidents at major museums in recent years".
Also on Thursday was one of the most important troves of prehistoric jewellery and artefacts was stolen from a Spanish museum.

Four Renaissance paintings were stolen from a museum in Sicily earlier this month, while three paintings by Renoir, Cézanne and Matisse worth millions of euros were taken from a museum in Parma earlier in the year.
These heists came after the brazen daylight raid on the Louvre in Paris, in which a masked gang stole priceless jewels last October.

blocks.caption: Image caption, The exhibition, minus the stolen necklace, reopened later on Friday

blocks.text: Image source, Getty Images
The exhibition, minus the stolen necklace, reopened later on Friday
The string of thefts have raised questions about the security of European cultural institutions.
Europol said museum thefts were "becoming increasingly aggressive, with a shift towards violent and forceful methods", adding this "may indicate the involvement of new criminal networks".

The necklace stolen in Vienna on Friday was designed for the former Egyptian royal family and was worn by Queen Nazli in 1939 for the marriage of her daughter Fawzia to the future Shah of Iran, Mohammad Reza Pahlavi.
Van Cleef & Arpels describes it as a "triumph of white jewellery". The diamonds on the necklace weigh in excess of 200 carats.
When it was auctioned a decade ago, it had an estimated worth of $3.6m-$4.6m.
Police dog units have been deployed in Vienna and the province of Lower Austria, while forensic experts are analysing evidence and CCTV footage.
The exhibition has now been reopened.

articles.title: Dolly Parton's sister says singer was still thinking of others while battling cancer
articles.summary: Dolly Parton's long history of philanthropy is well-documented, but a touching tribute from her sister reveals how deeply the spirit of giving was entrenched in her.

image.caption: Dolly Parton, seen here at the Grammy Awards in 2019, donated $1 million US toward researching the coronavirus at Vanderbilt University Medical Center in Nashville. (Jordan Strauss/Invision/The Associated Press)

blocks.text: Entertainment
Dolly Parton's long history of philanthropy is well-documented, but a touching tribute from her sister reveals how deeply the spirit of giving was entrenched in her.
Stella Parton's emotional post shares Dolly's thoughts near end of life

blocks.caption: Dolly Parton, seen here at the Grammy Awards in 2019, donated $1 million US toward researching the coronavirus at Vanderbilt University Medical Center in Nashville. (Jordan Strauss/Invision/The Associated Press)

blocks.text: On Thursday, Stella Parton posted a statement to Instagram describing how she and Dolly used to wake up early and drink coffee together over the phone each Tuesday.

The statement says in one of their final conversations, Dolly told Stella "if there was no hope for her, she would still allow her medical team to try experimental drugs in the hope of helping others in the future."
CBC News asked Dolly Parton's publicist to confirm whether the star was receiving experimental treatment toward the end of her life, but has received no response.
However, Parton's contribution to another recent medical advancement is widely known.

In November 2020, it was revealed she made a $1-million US donation to Nashville's Vanderbilt University Medical Center for COVID-19 research — and part of it went toward the development of the Moderna mRNA coronavirus vaccine.

When it came time for Parton to receive her first dose, she did it on camera while singing alternative lyrics to her song Jolene. "Vaccine, vaccine, vaccine, vaccine, I'm begging you please don't hesitate."
The doctor seen administering her dose in that video is Dr. Naji Abumrad, who she first met at Vanderbilt University Medical Center in October 2013, after Parton was in a minor car accident.

The pair struck up a long and enduring friendship. According to an opinion piece this week in the New York Times by his son, Jad Abumrad, creator of the podcast Dolly Parton's America, his father was with Parton in her last moments.
Stella Parton said she believes the world saw the famous singer for who she really was.
"My sister was one of the most generous, thoughtful and kind people I've ever known," wrote Stella in her tribute. "She left the world a better place by being in it, so let's follow her example."
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Helen Surgenor is a producer for CBC News based in Toronto, currently working for the entertainment unit. She spent years waking up before dawn to make the daily news podcast World Report. She has reported in Alberta, Iqaluit and Barbados. You can reach her at helen.surgenor@cbc.ca.

articles.summary: A number of U.S. lawmakers called on Donald Trump to end the war with Iran as it reached its six-month mark on Friday, while the U.S. president has given off mixed signals regarding the state of the…

Trump expressed ambivalence this week over talks with Iran, after insisting it was imperative to get the country to the negotiating table to prevent them from producing a nuclear weapon. (Mark Schiefelbein/The Asso

blocks.text: World

A number of U.S. lawmakers called on Donald Trump to end the war with Iran as it reached its six-month mark on Friday, while the U.S. president has given off mixed signals regarding the state of the conflict.
Trump posts 'mission accomplished,' administration focuses on Iran's economic troubles

blocks.caption: U.S. President Donald Trump is shown Thursday at Ellington Airport in Houston, Texas. Trump expressed ambivalence this week over talks with Iran, after insisting it was imperative to get the country to the negotiating table to prevent them from producing a nuclear weapon. (Mark Schiefelbein/The A…

blocks.text: Trump has said that the combined effects of the military's offensive strikes and blockade of the Strait of Hormuz have helped the U.S. achieve its objectives. On social media on Wednesday, he shared a post declaring "MISSION ACCOMPLISHED 2026," alongside AI-generated images that included the face of Iranian supreme leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, who was killed on Feb. 28 as the U.S. and Israel launched airstrikes to begin the war.

Tehran and Washington have exchanged little more than bellicose statements in recent weeks, leaving the diplomacy to third parties, and Trump has been more preoccupied this week, at least publicly, with his anger over Canada calling a halt to trade talks on tariffs.

It is expected that the U.S. president will increasingly turn his attention to the Nov. 3 midterms, where he has been engaged in efforts to influence how votes are cast, while preparing for a unique, midterm Republican mini-convention in two weeks' time.

Rep. Adam Smith of Washington, the top Democrat on the House of Representatives' armed service committees, released a statement Friday raising a number of outstanding issues the war has caused, but leading with the toll to those serving in the military.

"Losses continue to accumulate, including 19 American service members killed and over 750 wounded, while thousands of innocent civilians have been killed across the region," said Smith. "Tens of billions of dollars of taxpayers’ money is being wasted while driving up the cost of gas, utilities, and groceries at home and throttling economies around the world."
'More costly and more unstable'

The U.S. and Israel have killed a number of Iran's top religious, military and political officials and Khamenei's successor, his son Mojtaba, hasn't been seen in public amid reports he was seriously injured early in the war.

As well, it has been estimated that the price of rice is up some 60 per cent since the war began and beef 150 per cent higher for Iranians, who have also dealt with long lines to fill up vehicles. The International Monetary Fund forecasts that Iran's gross domestic product will contract more than 5 per cent this year.

But costs have also been incurred on the U.S. side beyond the literal price tag for Operation Epic Fury, from the approval rating for Trump multiple polls to higher prices at gas pumps for many Americans due to the disruption in oil markets. The war has also strained relations between the White House and allies in Europe, the Middle East and Asia, as Trump has expressed anger that they haven't supported the U.S. in the war.

items: Trump orders joint military exercises with South Korea to be scaled back
Trump threatens to bomb Oman if it 'gets in the way' with Iran

blocks.text: Trump "has made the world more costly and more unstable," Brett Bruen, a former U.S. diplomat now at the D.C.-area public affairs agency Global Situation Room, told CBC News on Friday.

Iran found leverage after the initial shock and awe of the U.S. strikes through its own drone attacks and mining in the critical Strait of Hormuz. That dissuaded commercial vessels from countries not friendly to the regime from transiting the passage where substantial amounts of oil and liquefied natural gas typically were moved.

The U.S. eventually responded with its own naval blockade to prevent the movement of ships to Iranian ports. Trump has repeatedly said the strait is open, including this week, but ship-tracking services have estimated activity at roughly 5 per cent to 15 per cent of pre-war volumes.

blocks.caption: U.S. Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth is shown on Aug. 13 attending military exercise in Panama City, Panama. Hegseth in July estimated that the Iran war had cost the U.S. $37 billion. (Matias Delacroix/The Associated Press)

blocks.text: Democrats earlier this week called for more transparency on the cost of the war. Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth told a congressional committee in July that the war had cost the military $37.5 billion US, but the opposition and some think-tanks believe that total underestimates the cost, given the missile systems and munitions the U.S. has expended this year, diminishing stockpiles.
"Pete Hegseth should be fired, the war must end and taxpayer dollars should be spent to make life more affordable," House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries of New York posted on social media on Friday.

Few Republicans have expressed opposition to the war itself, though some have criticized military tactics. Rep. Thomas Massie of Kentucky, who generally opposes U.S. military interventions abroad, is an exception.

"The 1973 War Powers Act required Trump to withdraw forces within 90 days absent authorization from Congress," he posted on Friday. "[The administration] ridiculously claimed to stop the war & restart new hostilities @ 91 days. We are past 180 days. End the War."

Front Burner27:28Is Iran becoming a 'forever war'?
Some embassy staff in region reportedly set to return

Trump said this week he's "not in a hurry" to get Iran back to the negotiating table. It was a striking contrast to his messaging for much of the summer, where he said it was imperative to reach a deal with Iran to prevent it from obtaining a nuclear weapon.
There are no talks, but also no sense that a renewed military offensive is on the horizon.

The administration said it is focused on choking Iran economically, even as Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent's "Operation Economic Outcast," announced on Monday, was heavy on warnings and lighter on details.
The U.S. threatens Iran with ‘economic D-Day’ | About That

As well, Reuters reported this week that the Trump administration will soon start sending diplomatic personnel back to some missions in the Middle East that were evacuated or downsized due to the fighting. Posts in Lebanon, Israel, Saudi Arabia and Iraq are among those where staff will return, albeit at less than full capacity, two people familiar with the matter told Reuters.

Bruen told CBC News that the administration squandered an opportunity to affect change in Iran that would have been less costly, given the unusual level of domestic strife and protest seen there in January as demonstrators railed against perceived corruption of the regime and economic conditions.
Trump at the time promised Iranian protesters that "help is on the way," but by the next month the U.S. launched its military campaign with Israel.
Bruen, a former member of Barack Obama's administration, was pessimistic about what comes next after the six-month mark.
"It drags on indefinitely. I don't see an easy ending to this around the corner," he said. "I don't think the dynamic in the region changes very much."
With files from Reuters and the Associated Press
