articles.title: Russia ‘losing 6,000 more troops in Ukraine each month than it can recruit’
articles.summary:
Moscow recruits an estimated 1,000 people a day but western officials say it cannot keep up with casualty level

Russia is losing about 6,000 more troops in Ukraine each month than it can…

blocks.text: Russia is losing about 6,000 more troops in Ukraine each month than it can recruit, western officials have said.
While Russia is still acquiring new battlefield recruits at speed, with an estimated rate of 1,000 a day, in the last two months even this has not been sufficient to replace those killed or injured.
“We estimate that the gap between the number of people Russia is losing to casualties and the number they’re being able to recruit is around 6,000 a month at the moment,” one western official said.

“Putin’s response to this has been to escalate himself and to target civilian infrastructure and civilians in Ukraine, firing over 360 missiles since early July and exploiting Kyiv’s shortage of defence against ballistic missiles. It’s clear that Moscow intends to try and break Ukrainian morale by destroying its energy infrastructure this winter.”
Such tactics are in part because Putin has limited options for overcoming the huge losses on the battlefield with more recruitment.

Western officials believe further mobilisation would be a big risk both politically and economically, saying the last such event, in autumn 2022, saw about a million – often highly skilled – Russians leave the country, with less than half returning.
It is also unclear whether the Russian military could absorb the several hundred thousand new recruits which would result, given a lack of equipment and officers.
Ukraine has repeatedly attacked Russian targets connected to oil, creating fuel shortages, but has appealed repeatedly for more help from allies, both with offensive missiles and defence systems.

blocks.caption: Andy Burnham has told Volodymyr Zelenskyy that the UK will share information about Storm Shadow missile components with Kyiv. Photograph: Ukrainian presidency/Sipa/Shutterstock

blocks.text: Andy Burnham visited Kyiv on his first overseas trip as prime minister this week. He told Volodymyr Zelenskyy that the UK would give Ukraine previously classified information on the British-manufactured components for long-range cruise missiles.

Burnham has also urged the international community to do more to protect Ukraine against Russian attacks, particularly with more US-made Patriot interceptor missiles. He is expected to make this argument at next month’s UN general assembly in New York.
In response, Russia has made repeated threats of retaliation, including talk of attacks on UK military targets both inside and outside Ukraine.

The western officials said that while the threat from Russia remained very real, the situation had not changed, and the assessment was that “Putin absolutely wants to avoid a direct confrontation with Nato”.

One official said: “We are seeing a continuation of hostile rhetoric and various accusations against the UK. This is absolutely consistent with longstanding Russian military doctrine, which is to use rhetoric to both exploit fears in adversaries and to influence decision-making. So this is not a new phenomenon.”

Officials say Russia still has the capability to target the UK, with cyberattacks or physical attacks on civilian targets by proxies, for example on factories or warehouses. Last year, six men were jailed for their involvement in an attack ordered by Russia against a warehouse in east London housing aid to Ukraine.
But officials said their assessment was that Putin would limit any such action to avoid more direct conflict with Nato.

Putin’s overall aim in Ukraine, western officials believe, is to maintain a campaign of attrition, hoping that support from Ukraine’s allies will ebb away, particularly if governments are spooked by public alarm over Russian threats.
Such threats should be seen, one official said, as attempts to create a “fractured and more vulnerable Europe”.

Another said: “It’s important to keep in mind that this is not new. Russia has invoked the threat of the possible use of nuclear weapons numerous times in recent years to try to scare us into ending support for Ukraine.”

articles.title: New heart attack definition promises better care for women
articles.summary:
Leading cardiovascular health groups reclassify overlooked causes and introduce sex-specific diagnostic thresholds

Doctors have agreed the world’s first universal definition of a heart…
articles.byline: Andrew Gregory Health editor in Munich

blocks.text: Doctors have agreed the world’s first universal definition of a heart attack, paving the way for millions of women to finally receive better treatment after decades of being “deprioritised”.

In one of the biggest procedural shake-ups in a generation, the world’s four leading cardiovascular health groups have signed off on new guidance for healthcare professionals when seeing suspected heart attack patients.

Historically, some less common forms of heart attack, which evidence shows typically affect women far more than men, have been coded as less important, with treatment and care often worse as a result.
Until now, experts said, women had been getting less effective treatments, which did not always target the specific cause of their heart attack and could even make them more unwell.

Now the world’s top cardiologists have promised a “revolution” in care after agreeing the biggest overhaul of how heart attacks are defined and diagnosed in decades, in part to reduce the often deadly delays afflicting women.
The landmark agreement was announced in Munich on the opening day of the annual congress of the European Society of Cardiology (ESC), the world’s largest heart conference.
The new guidance will upgrade three types of attack that are up to 10 times more common in women and often caused by childbirth, exercise and emotional stress.
The most serious cases, previously known as “type 1” and now classed as “primary” heart attacks, had previously prioritised those caused by a clot blocking blood flow to the heart.

However, the types of attacks more common in women involve reduced blood flow for other reasons, such as a tear or tightening of arteries, and are more likely to be missed or not treated as urgently, with delays to care.
The new guidelines will also reduce the threshold for any type of heart attack to be diagnosed in women based upon the levels of a protein called troponin in their blood.
Until now, women had been expected to reach the same threshold as men for troponin – which is released when the heart is injured and damaged – to get a diagnosis.

Speaking to reporters in Munich, Prof Bryan Williams, the chief scientific and medical officer of the British Heart Foundation, Britain’s biggest heart charity, said: “This is a landmark moment, a radical shift in how we define and diagnose heart attacks worldwide which will transform people’s care.

“For decades, women have missed out on accurate diagnoses and treatment. This focus on finding less common causes of heart attacks, which predominantly affect women, should help to change that. It could be life-changing for huge numbers of women in the UK and worldwide.”
Crucially, the new streamlined heart attack categories will also help patients to fully understand the cause of their heart attack and what comes next, Williams said.
The three types of heart attacks that have been upgraded – and which mostly affect women – are coronary artery spasm, coronary embolism, and spontaneous coronary artery dissection (Scad).
The first involves the tightening of the artery, which can deprive the heart muscle of blood and oxygen and cause a heart attack, and can be caused by emotional stress, exercise or extreme cold.
The second is where a blood clot or fatty deposit travels to a coronary artery and causes a blockage.
And the third is caused by a tear in the coronary artery, which occurs in women at least 80% of the time and often happens during or soon after pregnancy.

Prof Nicholas Mills, a cardiologist at the University of Edinburgh who led the international taskforce of doctors that agreed the new guidelines, said it was “the first time that we’ve had a truly global approach to aligning how we diagnose what is probably the most important diagnosis there is”.
“It kills so many people, and we’ve never got everyone together around the world to agree how we’re going to describe it, classify it, explain it to our patients,” he said.

“Our job now is to implement this as widely as possible. It’s just as relevant for the UK as it is for any other country around the world. It is a revolution. It’s going to make care better for patients.”

Mills said there had been “unintended systematic bias against women”, including by using the key blood test for diagnosing heart attacks at an average level, which picks up all men but misses some women.
“This is used for all types of heart attack in every emergency department in the world, and we want to make sure that it’s used correctly,” he said.

The new guidelines, published in the European Heart Journal, were drawn up by the world’s four leading cardiovascular health groups: the ESC, the American College of Cardiology, the American Heart Association and the World Heart Federation.

articles.title: London Science Museum cuts links with BP after decades of partnership
articles.summary:
Campaigners say ‘seismic shift’ follows years of pressure to sever ties with oil and gas firm

The London Science Museum has ended its decades-long partnership with the oil and gas company BP…

blocks.text: The London Science Museum has ended its decades-long partnership with the oil and gas company BP in what has been described as a “seismic shift” for the museum.

The Science Museum Group academy, which was established in 2018 to provide training and resources, announced on Friday that it would be ending its partnership with BP. In a statement, the director and chief executive of the Science Museum Group, Sir Ian Blatchford, said the partnership had “drawn to a close at the end of the current contract term”.

Blatchford said BP’s “generous contributions helped us to inspire more than 11,000 education, museum and science professionals through research-informed science engagement training, supporting vital work to spark curiosity and bring science to life for more than 1 million young people across the country”.

BP’s relationship with the Science Museum, which goes back decades, has come under previous scrutiny, with the company accused by campaigners of having an “insidious influence” over the teaching of science, technology, engineering and maths (Stem) in the UK through its relationship with the museum.

blocks.caption: Scientist Rebellion activists demonstrate in the Science Museum’s energy hall against the museum’s sponsorship by Adani, BP and Equinor. Photograph: Andrea Domeniconi/Alamy

blocks.text: In 2024, the museum cut ties with the oil company Equinor over its failure to lower carbon emissions sufficiently to ensure it was aligned with the Paris climate agreement goal of limiting global heating to 1.5C.

Chris Garrard of the campaign group Culture Unstained said this “seismic shift” came after years of campaigning and growing pressure from educators and schools, some of which have pledged to boycott trips to the museum over its partnership with BP.

“BP’s commitment to climate action was never worth the paper it was written on but the Science Museum’s director passionately championed his partnership with the major polluter year after year. Now, with the world facing droughts and wildfires and BP recklessly ramping up its production of dirty fossil fuels, the museum has finally come to its senses and followed the rest of the culture sector in cutting ties to BP,” he said.

However, Garrard said this decision represented only a “partial victory”. The museum still takes money from Adani Green Energy Ltd, a subsidiary of the Adani Group, one of the world’s largest private coal mining and energy conglomerates.
The academy provides training and resources to teachers, museum practitioners and the Stem industry nationally and internationally.
BP has been contacted for comment.

articles.title: What next? Kurds say yes, Druze still say no to united Syria
articles.summary: The Druze minority in Sweida, Syria, is now the only group that hasn't accepted central government authority. How does the end of an independent Kurdish area impact Druze plans for a different,…

image.caption: Druze militias and Israeli threats have kept Syrian government forces out of the Druze-majority province of SweidaImage: Izettin Kasim/Anadolu/picture alliance

blocks.text: This week, Syria's Kurdish minority agreed to dissolve what had been their almost 14-year-long experiment in independent rule.

During the Syrian civil war, which began in 2011, the Kurds consolidated their authority over a large part of northeastern Syria, and wanted to maintain that after the civil war ended. But as Kurdish leader Mazloum Abdi said this week, "circumstances have changed."

Kurdish fighting forces, which go by the name of the Syrian Democratic Forces, or SDF, will now be integrated into the general Syrian military, and the oil-rich area they ruled will come under the authority of the central government.
All this means that Sweida province, home to much of Syria's Druze minority, is now the only area not to have accepted the authority of the central government.

blocks.caption: The Druze are ethnically Arab and one of Syria's many religious minorities, making up around 3% of the populationImage: Fahd Kiwan/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: End of idea of 'decentralized Syria'
There is no doubt that the change in the situation with Syria's Kurdish community will affect what is happening in Sweida, experts say.

When Omer Ozkizilcik, a nonresident senior fellow at US think tank, the Atlantic Council's Syria Project, met with Sheikh Hikmat al-Hijri in early 2025, the Druze leader said he was in daily phone contact with Abdi.

"He said that they were coordinating all their efforts and that they had a similar political vision for Syria — that is, decentralized with autonomous regions," said Ozkizilcik. "He basically repeated the Israeli approach, where they believe Syria should be divided, with an autonomous zone on the coast for the Alawite [minority], for the SDF in the northeast, and then in the south for the Druze. That shows that al-Hijiri's political vision was highly dependent on his alliance with the SDF."
That idea is no longer feasible. "Basically it puts an end to this vision of a fragmented, weak and decentralized Syria," the Ankara-based analyst argued.
That is also probably the reason why, earlier this week, al-Hijri again emphasized the Druze ties to Israel, Ozkizilcik suggested.
On Monday in Sweida, al-Hijiri declared the Druze an "inseparable part of the state of Israel."
"Even in terms of our beliefs, we share common ground," he said.

blocks.caption: Observers have pointed out while al-Hijiri (pictured) has said the Druze have common interests with Israel, it's not the same as linking religionsImage: Ali Haj Suleiman/Getty Images

blocks.text: ​​​​​​But it's clear that having Israel annex Sweida would be very difficult for a number of reasons, including geography and demographics. Sweida is also still dependent on the central Syrian government. Despite it being impossible for government forces to enter the area, Sweida still receives public services, salaries, pensions, power and water from Damascus.
What caused the rift?

The exclusion of government forces began after intercommunal violence in Sweida in July 2025. Fighting started between Druze and Bedouin locals. Government forces arrived, ostensibly to quell the violence, but they too were then accused of attacking Druze communities.
A report by the United Nations found over 1,700 people died as a result of the clashes.

The event resulted in deep Druze mistrust of the new Syrian government. Even locals who had been in favor of a united Syria began to question whether it might not be better to have a semi-autonomous Druze state.

"There has been a complete erosion of trust," Lubna al-Basit, a Sweida activist, told DW. "Before discussing solutions, the reality today is that the government must be held accountable for the massacres committed in Sweida."
Another Druze, now based in the US but who wished to remain anonymous for security reasons, believes the new Syrian government is more radical than it looks.

"They're trying to behave in way that appeases the West," he told DW. "But you know, we have this joke. They're indicating to go left when they're turning right. For the Druze, the priority would be security, dignity and a chance for prosperity. I don't think many people see that as attainable under the current Syrian government."

blocks.caption: The UN report also said that Druze, Bedouin and government-allied forces may all have committed war crimes in July 2025Image: Izettin Kasim/Anadolu/picture alliance

blocks.text: In September, a road map to repair relations was formulated with Jordanian and American negotiators. But Druze allied with al-Hijiri rejected the plan, and the central government hasn't done much to bring July 2025 perpetrators to justice. In June, the UN's special envoy to Syria said no progress had been made on the road map.

Since last year, Syria's central government "has dealt with the [Sweida] issue on the premise that a large-scale military confrontation would not resolve the crisis," researchers at the Syrian Center for Security and Defense Studies, or MISDAD, wrote in a paper this month.

Any such confrontation "would have deepened the rift with the local community and given external actors greater room to intervene or exploit the tension. Therefore, the Syrian government opted for a more cautious approach, based on calming the situation on one hand, and utilizing the state's security, administrative, and economic tools on the other."

Basically, the researchers at MISDAD continued, the Syrian government is waiting it out, hoping that increasing prosperity elsewhere in the country and the problems al-Hijiri's factions already have running the province's public services, will bring Sweida back to the fold.

blocks.caption: A memorial service in Sweida: The crisis of Druze trust in the Syrian central government is severe after last year's violenceImage: Shadi Al Dubaisi/JNA/ZUMA/picture alliance

blocks.text: A 'small authoritarian regime in Sweida'
What isn't likely to happen is any kind of revolution, Ozkizilcik explained.

"The issue here is that al-Hijiri has the guns, Israeli financial support and Israeli military advisers from the Israeli-Druze community," he continued. "There is basically a small authoritarian regime in Sweida that's controlled by al-Hijiri, so it would be very difficult for the Druze community to rise up against him."

Opponents of al-Hijiri have been forced out of the province, abducted or killed, there's been fighting between different Druze militias, and there have even been some small civilian protests. Reports say al-Hijiri loyalists have also stopped Druze civil servants from working with ministries in Damascus.
Ozkizilcik and other observers believe a resolution to the situation in Sweida won't come down to what al-Hijiri wants anyway.

Just as American military support — or rather, its withdrawal — for Kurdish forces was integral to the new resolution between the central government and Syrian Kurdish forces, what happens with the Druze community next is also likely to come down to external forces.

Some have argued that the situation in Sweida was a way for Israel to pressure Syria as the two governments tried to negotiate a new security agreement. Throughout 2025, senior Syrian and Israeli politicians were involved in talks, with mediation from the US, to potentially reactivate a 1974 disengagement agreement. However, these fell apart late last year.

Since the overthrow of the dictatorial Assad regime in Syria in late December 2024, the US has said it is in favor of a unified Syria. Israel appears to want the opposite, arguing that a divided Syria won't pose a threat.

"The real decision maker [on Sweida] will be Israel, not al-Hijiri," said Ozkizilcik. "Once — or if — there is a potential security deal between Syria and Israel, then I believe we will also see a political solution to Sweida and the Druze."
What needs to happen for the Druze to feel secure in Syria?

articles.title: Salmonella cases in UK likely to rise until source of outbreak is found
articles.summary:
Experts say imported eggs served in cafes and restaurants may be behind hundreds of infections and one death

Salmonella cases in the UK are expected to rise until the common source is…
articles.byline: Tobi Thomas Health and inequalities correspondent

blocks.text: Salmonella cases in the UK are expected to rise until the common source is identified, something that is notoriously difficult to establish, experts have warned.

There have been 474 confirmed cases and one death linked to the current outbreak, according to the UK Health Security Agency (UKHSA), with the latest investigations suggesting it is associated with eating imported eggs in cafes and restaurants.
About 1.6bn eggs are imported to the UK every year, according to the British Egg Industry Council, with the number having risen 60% since 2021.

The link to eggs consumed outside of the home is consistent with imported eggs commonly being used in catering, according to Paul Wigley, a professor of animal microbial ecosystems at the University of Bristol.

Wigley said: “Bought in bulk these eggs are cheaper than UK lion mark eggs and so can end up being used in schools and nursing homes along with cafes, restaurants and takeaways. The eggs may be mixed batches from different batches, but the clustering of cases suggests there may be a single source.”

He added: “As far as controls and the future, it’s difficult to judge, though identification of the source would help in being able to put specific controls on a producer or country in place. Avoiding runny eggs outside the home, unless lion mark eggs, is perhaps the only step an individual can make.”

Although previous salmonella outbreaks in the UK have been linked to eggs imported from European countries such as Poland, the current source of this outbreak has yet to be identified. For some experts, this makes the current surge in cases particularly worrying.
Prof Chris Elliott of the school of biological sciences at Queen’s University Belfast, said: “All we have been told is that the likelihood is that it’s been imported.

“There is a huge amount of difficulty in tracing the origins of something like this, particularly when it’s food service. Within the UK’s retail industry, they really know their supply chains extremely well. But with food service, less so.”

blocks.caption: British lion-stamped eggs are from UK hens vaccinated against salmonella. Photograph: Geoffrey Swaine/Shutterstock

blocks.text: He added that the number of cases would keep rising until the source was identified, which could take “not days, but weeks”.

Elliott added: “My expectation is those numbers will continue to rise until they can not only track the source, but right back to the country of production. It is fiendishly difficult to track the source of a food and ingredient, so I certainly wouldn’t be critical of the agencies. They’re under immense pressure, and the worst thing that can happen is that they feel pressurised to say that it came from Poland or it came from Romania when they’re not 100% sure about that.”

Prof Brad Spiller, the head of medical microbiology at Cardiff University, said the fact that this particular outbreak was linked to a common source was “probably the most concerning aspect” of the cases.
He said: “It is only once we have a better idea of which countries are involved, we can begin to track back the source.

“This is how they identified that both of the previous outbreaks seen in recent years that were happening simultaneously, and were both linked back to Poland as the source of that. I think until they identify the source, the source won’t naturally stop.”

Prof Mark Stevens, the chair of microbial pathogenesis at the University of Edinburgh, added that the outbreak was also unusual because cases were occurring at the same time, whereas salmonella cases across the UK were usually more spread out.
He said: “This is obviously a real challenge for the health protection agencies because they have to now identify that source and try to restrict its entry into the food system.

“It is of concern to have an outbreak of this size. There are thousands of salmonella cases each year, but rarely are they on this scale where hundreds of people are being infected by a common strain.”
Stevens added: “I think until we really understand the source of these infections, it’s possible that we’ll continue to see more of them.”

articles.title: Death toll rises in Nepal-China border disaster; lake poses new threat
articles.summary: KATHMANDU, Nepal — Rescuers pulled out survivors caked in dark brown mud and helicopters lifted stranded people to safety Friday, as Nepal and China raced to respond to catastrophic flash floods that…

blocks.caption: In this photo released by Xinhua News Agency, a drone photo shows a flood-hit area in Nuwakot, Nepal on Thursday, Aug. 27, 2026. (/Xinhua via AP)

blocks.text: KATHMANDU, Nepal — Rescuers pulled out survivors caked in dark brown mud and helicopters lifted stranded people to safety Friday, as Nepal and China raced to respond to catastrophic flash floods that killed more than 500 people and left more than 1,500 missing.

Rescue teams were put on high alert for more flooding from a new lake that has formed high up on the Himalayan mountains after the initial floods on Wednesday. Experts warn that the lake, formed after the glacier collapse that triggered the floods, was starting to overflow.

Nepal’s army was deployed to help rescue more than 100 people believed trapped inside a tunnel at a hydropower plant located in the country’s worst-hit district. Like elsewhere in the disaster zone, their work was complicated by thick layers of mud that covered the site.

The floods have killed 538 in Nepal, the country’s disaster management authority said Friday. Nepali police later put the number of deaths higher at 547. There was little information on survivors on the Chinese side, where the death toll rose to five Friday as state media showed evacuations of villages and leaders’ efforts to direct the relief response.

More than 3,700 people have been rescued in Nepal so far, but 977 people remain unaccounted for in the country. China’s state media previously said 558 people were missing on the Chinese side. Hundreds of the missing are foreigners in the area to work, trek or make a pilgrimage to a sacred peak.
Authorities warn of further flooding from a new lake

Nepali police issued a fresh alert Friday after receiving information that a dam on the Tibet side has burst. Security personnel and rescue and relief workers were told to stay on high alert and immediately move to a safe location if necessary.

It is unclear if the dam bursting is related to flooding concerns over a barrier lake that formed after the initial flash floods. Chinese broadcaster CCTV said the newly-formed lake, located more than 10 kilometers (6 miles) from Gyirong Port, the hard-hit border crossing with Nepal, sits at an elevation of 2,950 meters (9,680 feet.)

Nepali and Chinese authorities earlier warned of further flooding from the barrier lake, which was already overflowing. Rescue workers heading to the disaster zone were ordered to stop temporarily Friday morning due to concern the lake would release more torrents of water and debris, and people in potentially affected areas were urged move to safer ground.
Some 680 rescuers eventually reached the hardest-hit area at Gyirong by foot and via rafts after much effort. Some were dropped down from drones flown to the area, CCTV footage showed.
Nepali police spokesperson Abi Narayan Kafle told The Associated Press that the rescue operation was continuing but with high alert. “It hasn’t stopped,” he said.
Thousands of people have been evacuated, others await rescue

In Nepal’s Rasuwa district, Nepali Army rescuers were struggling to help more than 100 people believed trapped by thick mud in a tunnel that’s part of the Upper Trishuli-1 Hydropower Project. The army said it has rescued 350 people from the tunnel so far.
Video from the scene show rescuers helping a man, covered in dark brown mud, out of the tunnel by pulling and pushing.
Army spokesperson Brig. Gen. Raja Ram Basnet told the AP the focus was on survivors.
“It is complicated to find the entry and exit points of the tunnel because everything has been covered by mud,” Basnet said. “Our first priority is rescuing the stranded people.”
Nepal’s disaster management authority said 3,253 people had been airlifted by helicopter from the disaster area. Survivors, including injured people, were taken to Kathmandu and other locations.
Some felt the ground shake, then saw a ‘black storm’

Scientists who’ve studied satellite images said bedrock underneath a glacier high in the Himalayan region had collapsed, taking part of the glacier with it. The rockfall was so extreme that it reached a magnitude 5.2 seismic measurement. The rocks and melted water then swelled the rivers in the valleys below, causing a torrent of water that swept buildings, bridges and earth downstream in Tibet and Nepal.
Customs officer Karbir Gaire was among some of the survivors in Timure, the closest Nepalese village to the border with China, where some 1,500 people had lived.
Gaire reached his office around 8 a.m. Wednesday and was working on his computer when he first felt the ground shake.

“Right after the shake, I noticed a black storm coming towards us,” he recalled from Kathmandu, where he is back with family. “We all immediately started running out, and within a few seconds, we were climbing uphill on the opposite side of our office building. I think those 10 or so seconds saved some of us.”

Gaire doesn’t remember exactly how many people were in the office when the disaster struck, but 15 colleagues have gone missing. “It was like a Hollywood movie scene. I don’t call it a flood, it was a tsunami.”
Families around the world hope for news of loved ones
Nepal’s tourism board has said that among the missing are more than 500 foreigners.

About 90 Americans were unaccounted for. U.S. President Donald Trump said the flooding was terrible to see, and he told reporters in the Oval Office he offered to provide Nepal’s leaders “anything they want.”

Rajan Tamang, a restaurant owner in New York City, said he learned from family in Kathmandu that his mother and sister were among those who died, while many other relatives and friends remained missing.

“My family was just waking up, and they didn’t even get any information, and suddenly this flood came. Some of them are missing, some of them lost their life and only a few is alive,” he told the AP after a vigil in New York.
Some of the missing may have been on a pilgrimage to Mount Kailash in Tibet, a sacred site for Hindus, Buddhists and others.

Vishnuram Ramaswamy, who works at a private company in the southern Indian city of Puducherry, said that he last spoke to his mother and two sisters who were on that pilgrimage Wednesday morning. It was a highly anticipated trip, something his mother had always wanted to do, he said.

“My mother said they were on their way towards the border area and said they’ll reach their hotel and call us,” he said. While he’s in touch with government officials, and the travel agency, there’s been no news.

articles.title: Violence breaks out in Ceuta as migrant crisis continues
articles.summary: A group of migrants is accused of throwing stones at a military vehicle, while some locals set fire to their camps on the beach.

blocks.text: A month after tens of thousands of migrants entered the city of Ceuta, a Spanish exclave in North Africa, there have been outbreaks of violence as tensions mount between locals and foreign arrivals.
The Spanish government has been accused by opposition parties of struggling to manage the crisis effectively.
Ceuta's residents have complained of feeling unsafe on the streets, as well as expressing concerns about the burden being placed on public services.

At least 72,000 migrants crossed from Morocco into Ceuta on 30 and 31 July. Most swam around a border fence and at least 100 people died during the mass crossing, according to figures from Ceuta's mayor.
The vast majority of the migrants returned to Morocco within hours of their arrival, but several thousand remain in Ceuta, many of them children, and most are sleeping rough on beaches or streets.
Anti-migrant demonstrations earlier this month were largely peaceful, but in recent days they have become increasingly violent.

On Thursday, several dozen locals prevented Red Cross personnel from distributing food and water to the migrants. Afterwards, some set fire to migrant camps on Trampolín beach, the main site where they have been sleeping, and there were also clashes with the police.

Those incidents came hours after the arrest of 12 migrants who were accused of throwing stones at a military vehicle, breaking its windows and injuring the four men inside. That same morning there were reports of vigilante groups pursuing migrants through the streets.
Journalists and film crews have also reported being threatened.
"This is a city which has been under pressure, […] which has the right to normality," the mayor of the exclave, the conservative Juan Jesús Vivas, told Antena 3 television.
"The dignity of Spain is a stake right now in Ceuta," he said.
The socialist-led government of Pedro Sánchez has appealed for calm and accused Vivas's People's Party (PP) and the far-right Vox of stoking the tensions.
José María Figaredo, a member of Congress for Vox, is being investigated for a possible hate crime after saying, soon after the migrants' arrival, that they should be "hunted down, one by one".

Interior Minister Fernando Grande-Marlaska told a congressional committee: "We have heard during these weeks rhetoric and comments that contribute to the stigmatisation of immigrants and which feed social division at a moment when what we need is responsibility and statesmanship."
Javier Celaya, who represents Ceuta in Congress for the PP, accused the government of treating "the invaders as victims when the real victims are us, the people of Ceuta".
On Friday, all the parties in the Ceuta local assembly signed a declaration condemning violence.
Earlier this week, the government centralised management of the situation, overriding the local authority, after criticism that it had been slow to respond.

Defence Minister Margarita Robles also apologised to those in Ceuta who "may have felt, or who even still feel, abandoned or not sufficiently cared", as the government unveiled plans to overhaul the country's immigration laws.

Much of the recent ill-feeling in the city appears to be driven by government plans to move migrants into existing public buildings, such as sports centres, in order to be able to process their legal status in an orderly way and return those not eligible for asylum to Morocco.
Many local people, and Vivas, oppose this initiative, due to concerns that it will move the migrants closer to residential areas.
The government is also facing questions about who was behind the mass migrant crossing.
Politicians on the right and the far left have accused Morocco of involvement, pointing to its alleged use of the border with Spain in the past to exert political pressure.
Sánchez and his Socialist Party instead blame people traffickers, insisting that Rabat is a reliable partner which facilitated the immediate return of most of the arrivals.
Nonetheless, the crisis has placed the sovereignty of Ceuta, and its fellow autonomous city Melilla, under the spotlight.
Morocco has maintained a longstanding claim to the territories, which it has reiterated in recent weeks.
Spain's Foreign Minister José Manuel Albares said he "roundly rejected" such comments by Morocco.
"I don't speak about, nor have I spoken about, nor are we going to speak about Spain's territorial integrity with Morocco or with anyone else," he told the congressional committee.

articles.title: 'Lake America'? Trump's 'utterly ridiculous' renaming met with laughter in Kingston
articles.summary: The mayor of Kingston, Ont., says a snicker is the only response Donald Trump will be getting from his community following the U.S. president's renaming of Lake Ontario as Lake America. "The best…

image.caption: Kingston Mayor Bryan Paterson is shown outside city hall on May 9, 2023. (Dan Taekema/CBC)

blocks.text: Ottawa

The mayor of Kingston, Ont., says a snicker is the only response Donald Trump will be getting from his community following the U.S. president's renaming of Lake Ontario as Lake America. "The best thing we can possibly do is just ignore the silliness," Bryan Paterson says.
'The best thing we can possibly do is just ignore the silliness,' mayor says

blocks.caption: Kingston Mayor Bryan Paterson is shown outside city hall on May 9, 2023.                               (Dan Taekema/CBC)

blocks.text: The mayor of Kingston, Ont., says a snicker is the only response Donald Trump will be getting from his community following the U.S. president's move to have Lake Ontario henceforth be known as Lake America.
"The primary reaction is just laughter," said Bryan Paterson, who was still shaking his head hours after the announcement. "I mean, it's just so silly. It's so utterly ridiculous."

Paterson's voice was just one in a Canadian chorus denouncing the executive order Trump signed Thursday which the president said renames the body of water between Ontario and New York "effective immediately."
Among the dissenters on this side of the border was Prime Minister Mark Carney, who flatly denied the name was changing for Canadians.
In a post on social media, Carney wrote that the lake takes its title from "the Wendat word Ontari’io," meaning “'the lake is beautiful, the lake is big.'"

items: Trump signs order to rename Lake Ontario as 'Lake America'
Name of Lake Ontario not changing despite 'Trump's antics,' political leaders in Canada say

blocks.text: Carney pointed out the name is more than 400 years old, "predating both the Confederation of Canada and the Declaration of Independence of the United States of America."

The Wendat Nation also spoke out, with Grand Chief Pierre Picard writing in a statement that its members are "outraged, appalled, shocked," adding that he sees the change as an attempt to "eradicate" the nation's history.
Trump renames Lake Ontario as 'Lake America' in latest shot at Canada
Paterson said the lake runs "deep to the core" of what Kingston is and its name won't be "changed on the whim by someone sitting in the White House."
The city grew and flourished at the strategic intersection of three waterways: the St. Lawrence River, what eventually became the Rideau Canal, and Lake Ontario.
Kingstonians know the water. They swim in it, boat in it and live along its shoreline.
They've seen sunlight glitter and flash off its rolling surface on clear days and watched waves and ice slam the shoreline during winter storms.

blocks.caption: A man takes pictures of the waves on Lake Ontario during a wind warning at Portsmouth Olympic Harbour in Kingston, Ont., Jan. 5, 2022. (Lars Hagberg/The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: That's one reason Paterson said people in town are dismissing this episode as a "joke."
Kingston's Lake Ontario Park — one of the jewels of the city — is a popular place for families and friends to gather.
The mayor said he's already been asked if there are plans to rename it.
"I just laughed. I said, 'That's ridiculous. Of course, we would never do that.' It's always going to be Lake Ontario Park because, quite frankly, it's always going to be Lake Ontario."
Rochester, N.Y. city council denounces Lake America
Across the border, the largest U.S. city on Lake Ontario says it will continue referring to the Great Lake by its original name.
Rochester’s city council unanimously signed a proclamation on Friday to continue using Lake Ontario in all official local capacities.

“No government entity … has the right or the ability to erase centuries of Indigenous history simply by giving a new nickname to a Great Lake whose cultural legacy will outlive us all,” the council wrote in the proclamation.
Best to 'ignore the silliness,' says Kingston mayor
Paterson said everyone on council has been asked about Trump's latest move and how they intend to reply.
"The overwhelming sentiment is that it's not worth even responding," said Paterson. "It's not worth wasting our time. The best thing we can possibly do is just ignore the silliness."

blocks.caption: People take a photo at Lake Ontario Park in Kingston, Ont., on April 7, 2024. (Justin Tang/The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: A large Canadian flag has been hanging in front of city hall since the trade war with the U.S. first began.
The mayor said that, if anything, all of this "bluster and ... craziness" has only strengthened the community's resolve and sense of unity along with that of the rest of Canada.
Asked if he's ever looked across the border and coveted his neighbour's land or considered changing some names to lay claim to it, Paterson just laughed and said "definitely no."
He noted some officials in New York have reacted to the name change with "embarrassment and an apology."
"Being a border community ... we understand the value of friendship and relationship[s]," Paterson said. "We know that's going to be there long after Donald Trump is gone."
With files from Muriel Draaisma

blocks.text: Health·New

People from Ebola-affected countries will continue to be banned from entering Canada for another 30 days, prolonging the state of limbo for tens of thousands of people who have had their residency applications suspended since May.
Tens of thousands of residency applications remain on hold until late September
· The Canadian Press
· Posted: Aug 28, 2026 12:07 PM EDT | Last Updated: 24 minutes ago

blocks.caption: Workers unload doses of Ebola vaccines, made for a previous strain of the disease, from a plane at Ndjili International Airport in Kinshasa, Democratic Republic of Congo, last week. Canada will also keep a 21-day quarantine for anyone returning from the D.R.C., Uganda and South Sudan, a measure t…

blocks.text: The extension, confirmed Friday in a statement from the Public Health Agency of Canada, means decisions on immigration and visa applications from residents of the Democratic Republic of Congo, Uganda and South Sudan will remain on hold until Sept. 28. People from those countries who already hold valid visas will also be barred from entering Canada.
The government says the risk of Ebola in Canada is still low, but these measures are precautionary given the severity of the disease.
However, some public health experts say the decision is unjustified and goes against the guidance of the World Health Organization in favour of appearing to protect Canadians.
Ebola outbreak now deadliest in Congo’s history
Canada will also keep a 21-day quarantine for anyone returning from those three countries, a measure that aid agencies said impacts their ability to send humanitarian workers to the region.
Foreign nationals who have been in the D.R.C. within the past 21 days will also not be allowed to fly to Canada.
On Thursday, the Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention and the World Health Organization declared the outbreak over in Uganda. No cases have been reported in South Sudan.

The same cannot be said in neighbouring D.R.C., where 2,786 people have died out of 5,794 who have been infected. It has been deemed the fastest-growing Ebola outbreak and is on track to become the deadliest on record.

items: Parents and teachers in Congo urge delay of school resumption as Ebola outbreak rages on

blocks.text: Ebola spreads through bodily fluids like blood, vomit and semen, and people are only infectious when they are symptomatic. Public health experts say these factors make the risk of an imported case low and manageable for Canada, but a challenge in the D.R.C., where there are fundamental access issues to health care and clean water, alongside threats by rebel groups.

Immigration officials said 31,693 permanent residency applications and 10,465 temporary residency applications from overseas had been put on hold as of Aug. 12. The documents of people who have been granted residency but are not in Canada have also been suspended. Officials said that includes 1,534 permanent residents and 23,415 temporary residents who are overseas.

When Canada first announced its Ebola measures, there were a handful of cases in Uganda. That number later rose to 20, including two deaths. It's been 42 days since the last patient was discharged on July 16.
One of the added hurdles with tackling this outbreak is the rare species of Ebola responsible, the Bundibugyo virus, which has no specific vaccine or treatment.
Border measures were initially announced ahead of the FIFA World Cup, pitched as a precautionary safety measure aligned with the United States and Mexico.

articles.title: Another world with Dolly, Butch and others
articles.summary: HOTSPOT The world lost Dolly Parton this week, bringing Americans to tears. She was America’s sweetheart in so many ways that feeble text and video tributes cannot fully express. We could expect…

blocks.text: HOTSPOT
The world lost Dolly Parton this week, bringing Americans to tears. She was America’s sweetheart in so many ways that feeble text and video tributes cannot fully express.

We could expect Dolly’s songs to remain in the permanent playlist for the singing people of the Philippines, the world’s videoke and karaoke capital. The top three? Islands in the Stream (a duet with Kenny Rogers, another Filipino favorite), Jolene, and I Will Always Love You (Whitney Houston’s mighty version, no less).

Friends and colleagues also lost Butch Pongos this week. Butch was not a Dolly-like icon, singer or songwriter. He was an advocate and activist who gave his best to assist overseas Filipino workers in Japan, and went on to help and form an organization to advance the cause of Filipino wives and kids abandoned by their Japanese fathers. He was 64.

I don’t wish to preempt the tribute by Migrante International and the stories they would share with his family, neighbors and friends. They would certainly be surprised how their “kuya” lived his life, and what feats he accomplished.

My friends Juli, Ruth and myself worked rather briefly with Butch at the white house of Bayan at Sikatuna Village in the early 2000s. We knew him as a dedicated, disciplined, orderly and committed activist who also loved his family. We would later go our separate ways, and we would hear stories of Butch doing fantastic advocacy work in Japan.
When I visited the wake for Butch, I was surprised to see someone who looked almost exactly like him. It turned out it was Andy, one of his brothers and the one who came after him.
Andy reminded me a lot about Butch. The smile, the twinkle in the eye, and the laugh. We have a phrase in Tagalog that’s apt: pinagbiyak na bunga.
I don’t know how or why it started, but Andy told me stories about his Kuya when they were kids.
Like Butch nagging their mother, then the designated hermana mayor, to pick him as the Constantino in the village Santacruzan. Mother picked Andy, not Butch, to be the Constantino. Butch was furious.

Butch managed to go to UP for college. We saw his graduation photo online, dapper wearing his toga and steel glasses. Andy told me, he did not want to miss a single day in school. He only asked their mother for the ₱10 fare from Pulang Lupa to Diliman. Yes, P10! For lunch, Butch went to their father who worked at nearby Broadcast City, to use his meal stub.

Another time, Butch gave grocery money to their mother who apparently dropped it along the way. Their mother was inconsolable. Butch was so saddened by the sight of their grief-stricken mother, he went out for a few minutes to look for the money. When he returned, Butch gave his mother the exact amount lost, telling her he found the money just outside the house. Andy said Butch told them about it, and they were all absolutely touched to their very core by his concern for their mother.

I asked Andy to please tell these and other stories at the Migrante tribute, and I hope he does. I hope their other brothers also tell their stories. Their stories will somehow complete the picture of Butch who they knew as kuya as he transformed himself and others in the challenging but spiritually-rewarding activist life he chose.

Condolences too to the families of writer Marra P. Lanot, and human rights and health advocate Ruth Sampaga. I did not personally know Ms. Lanot, but like others knew of her mastery of the Filipino language and her participation in the anti-dictatorship resistance. Sampaga and myself worked together briefly with others in the Ecumenical Movement for Justice and Peace in the mid-2000s.

The passing of Dolly, Butch, Marra and Ruth gives us pause. They may be a lot different from one another. But in a world that elevates greed and self-interest as the supreme “virtues,” their common concern for others, and their giving their absolute best for causes far bigger than themselves have the subversive power to tell us another, better world is possible.
I end this with the words sung by Dolly and Kenny:
Islands in the stream
That is what we are
No one in between
How can we be wrong?
Sail away with me
To another world
And we rely on each other, ah-ah
From one lover to another, ah-ah

articles.title: He liked to listen to him (John)
articles.summary: REFLECTIONS TODAY Like the prophets of old, John the Baptist is zealous for the word of God. He does not allow a person’s status to becloud his judgment and so denounces Herod Antipas and Herodias…

blocks.text: REFLECTIONS TODAY

Like the prophets of old, John the Baptist is zealous for the word of God. He does not allow a person’s status to becloud his judgment and so denounces Herod Antipas and Herodias for their adulterous union.

Herod does not like John because, unlike his selfserving courtiers, John tells him off. But he admires John’s integrity and something in him aches for John’s virtue. He is, however, a slave to his own passion for Herodias and to his privileged existence.

In letting John be executed, Herod also lets his better nature be killed. John the Baptist proves himself to be like Jesus who does not regard a person’s status but teaches the way of God in accordance with the truth (Mk 12:14).
Are we like John who stands by his principle, to “respect no man” when our principles are at stake? Or are we ready to compromise in the face of strong opposition?
It is said that our conscience is God’s built-in warning sign in our person. We should be glad if it sounds an alarm if we plan to do evil.
We should, however, be alarmed if our conscience no longer bothers us because we have become inured to our sins and failings.
Gospel • Mark 6:17-29

Herod was the one who had John arrested and bound in prison on account of Herodias, the wife of his brother Philip, whom he had married. John had said to Herod, “It is not lawful for you to have your brother’s wife.”
Herodias harbored a grudge against him and wanted to kill him but was unable to do so. Herod feared John, knowing him to be a righteous and holy man, and kept him in custody.

When he heard him speak he was very much perplexed, yet he liked to listen to him. She had an opportunity one day when Herod, on his birthday, gave a banquet for his courtiers, his military officers, and the leading men of Galilee.
Herodias’s own daughter came in and performed a dance that delighted Herod and his guests.
The king said to the girl, “Ask of me whatever you wish and I will grant it to you.” He even swore many things to her, “I will grant you whatever you ask of me, even to half of my kingdom.”
She went out and said to her mother, “What shall I ask for?” She replied, “The head of John the Baptist.”
The girl hurried back to the king’s presence and made her request, “I want you to give me at once on a platter the head of John the Baptist.”
The king was deeply distressed, but because of his oaths and the guests he did not wish to break his word to her. So he promptly dispatched an executioner with orders to bring back his head.
He went off and beheaded him in the prison. He brought in the head on a platter and gave it to the girl.
The girl in turn gave it to her mother. When his disciples heard about it, they came and took his body and laid it in a tomb.
Source: “365 Days with the Lord 2026,” St. Paul’s, 7708 St. Paul Rd., SAV, Makati City (Phils.); Tel.: 632-895-9701; E-mail: [email protected]; Website: http://www.stpauls.ph.

articles.title: Poverty threshold on the streets
articles.summary: FILLERS On my way to the office one Monday morning, something caught my attention. Right by a stoplight along Roxas Boulevard, a row of five people sat on the grassy median strip (or island, as we…

blocks.text: FILLERS

On my way to the office one Monday morning, something caught my attention. Right by a stoplight along Roxas Boulevard, a row of five people sat on the grassy median strip (or island, as we call it in the Philippines). They all looked to be senior citizens or, at least, above middle age. Three of them carried an assortment of snacks and drinks. The other two held signs made of cardboard-like material.

When traffic stopped, the five strangers stood up and tried to get the attention of the drivers on the road. I noticed that people paid more attention to the two who were carrying cardboard signs. Those peddling snacks were largely ignored.
A thought came to me: There was nothing different between those begging for money and those selling snacks on the road. Both were hustling to get by, albeit with very different approaches.

Yet, because giving aid seems to be the kinder gesture, those who were begging got more attention. This is understandable, as not everyone on the road is thirsty or hungry enough to buy a snack while waiting for the traffic light to turn green. But there seems to be no lack of kindness to go around, enough for those begging on the streets to get ₱5 from an SUV here and ₱20 from a compact sedan there.

At the end of the day, who do you think earned more? But maybe this isn’t the right question to ask. Maybe it isn’t even a point worth considering. What is perhaps worth paying attention to is the fact that those five people had to be there on the road, struggling to get by.

This is especially worth thinking about in light of recent numbers from the Philippine Statistics Authority (PSA), showing that the country’s poverty incidence has gone down to a single digit—9.7 percent of Filipinos are living below the poverty line. Those who peddle products on the streets and those who have nowhere else to go but beg for survival are among that 9.7 percent, which translates to roughly 11.08 million Filipinos out of a total population of 112.7 million.

These figures were not drawn from thin air. The computations are based on what the PSA has set as the minimum income required for a family of five to meet its basic food and non-food needs. This so-called poverty threshold is currently set at ₱14,634, following a formula the PSA uses that looks at how much families actually spend on food and other essential goods in a month.

Of course, a lot has been said about whether this number truly captures what it means to be poor—or not poor, if you want to look at things from a more positive perspective. Poverty, after all, cannot simply be understood as a statistic. For the five people I saw on the road, it is a reality of life. The same can be said of the 11.08 million or so Filipinos who still fall below the poverty threshold.

This does not mean, however, that reaching this statistical milestone counts for nothing. On the contrary, it serves as a positive reminder—a pat on the back, perhaps—for having managed to lift a majority of Filipinos out of poverty.

But perhaps more than simply not being statistically poor, what Filipinos need is a comfortable enough life—not a life of comfort (or an easygoing, no-frills, problem-free life), but one with reasonable comfort.

In this day and age, a reasonably comfortable life is one where basic necessities are met but with enough financial wiggle room for emergencies, as well as for the occasional online shopping or “luho” purchase. A reasonably comfortable life is one that allows parents to send their children to school, which, although technically free, is not entirely without expense. A reasonably comfortable life means having a little more than what is enough.

At the end of the day, it is not entirely up to the government to make this happen. It is a combination of efforts. But these efforts will go nowhere if the opportunities to rise out of poverty are not there. These opportunities have to be created and made available to every Filipino—from drastically improving the quality of public education and access to it, to creating better jobs by welcoming more industries into the country. All these would amount to something in the long run, allowing more Filipinos to break through the poverty threshold.
This is, however, easier said than done. But if we are to look at the examples of other countries, some of which are our own neighbors, it is doable.
Then maybe succeeding generations would no longer need to peddle products on the streets or beg from passing drivers on the roads.

articles.title: Duty over growth: BSP’s courageous choice
articles.summary: With first-half gross domestic product (GDP) growth dragging at a paltry 2.6 percent, the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas’ (BSP) decision to hike its benchmark policy rate by 25 basis points to five…

blocks.text: With first-half gross domestic product (GDP) growth dragging at a paltry 2.6 percent, the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas’ (BSP) decision to hike its benchmark policy rate by 25 basis points to five percent—its third rate increase this year, bringing cumulative tightening since April to 75 basis points—runs directly counter to the chorus demanding cheap credit to stimulate the Philippines’ stalled economy.

Immediately after the announcement of the central bank’s decision, local financial markets reacted with predictable fury. The Philippine Stock Exchange index (PSEi) tumbled 2.16 percent to 6,004.58, while the peso slipped to a historic low of ₱61.888 against the United States (US) dollar.

Yet the BSP governor was entirely right to declare that the choice “wasn’t so hard.” In executing a preemptive strike against stubborn price pressures, the seven-member Monetary Board (MB) proved it understands the core boundary of its constitutional duty. The BSP’s primary mandate is price stability, not short-term growth engineering.

The instinct among politicians and equity investors to demand monetary easing during economic slumps ignores a fundamental truth that the central banks lack the mechanical apparatus to generate sustainable and long-term wealth out of artificially suppressed interest rates.

As the BSP governor candidly noted during Senate budget deliberations on Thursday, Aug. 28, monetary policy simply does not possess the tools to boost short-run output without stoking inflation. Attempting to force economic growth via cheap money while inflation expectations remain unanchored is a recipe for stagflation, a scenario far more destructive to businesses and household incomes than a temporary tightening cycle.

The central bank’s inflation projections underline why urgency was required. While price growth has cooled from its brutal peak of 7.2 percent in April to 6.2 percent in July, and the 2026 forecast was trimmed to 6.1 percent, the medium-term outlook has worsened. The BSP raised its 2027 inflation forecast from 4.5 percent to an elevated 5.4 percent, far above the official target band of two percent to four percent, with headline figures not expected to normalize until 2028.

These revised forecasts are not abstract academic exercises because they reflect the country’s real structural vulnerabilities. As an oil-importing economy lacking a high-tech export engine like artificial intelligence (AI) to absorb external shocks, the Philippines sits exposed to global commodity volatility.

Compounding these structural realities are severe supply risks: incoming El Niño conditions threaten agricultural output, while pending minimum wage adjustments threaten second-round inflationary spillovers. Waiting for these risks to materialize before acting would have required far more aggressive and painful tightening down the line.

Critics will point to the peso’s historic slide near the ₱62 level as evidence of market anxiety. But currency devaluation in this context is driven less by interest rate differentials and more by real-economy fears over projected 2027 price pressures. Trying to defend the peso by draining foreign exchange reserves would be a reckless squandering of national buffer stock. Interest rate hikes remain the cleanest mechanism available to absorb excess liquidity and temper the currency’s decline without burning through international reserves.

Responsibility for igniting second-half GDP growth now falls squarely where it belongs: fiscal policy. The executive branch and Congress, currently deliberating the proposed ₱7.2-trillion national budget, must deploy targeted spending, address agricultural bottlenecks, and execute infrastructure investments capable of supporting real economic output.

By prioritizing price stability over short-term popularity, the BSP has protected the purchasing power of ordinary Filipinos. Economic growth built on the shifting sands of high inflation is an illusion. The Monetary Board’s steadfast commitment to its core mandate ensures that when growth does return, it will rest on a solid foundation.

articles.title: A Pangasinan farmer’s fight against weather, and smugglers
articles.summary: Silence has been creeping into the farmlands of Pangasinan. It may be a long while before farmers hear Ilocano radio dramas blasting from their stereos at sunrise, playing until the mid-morning heat…

blocks.text: Silence has been creeping into the farmlands of Pangasinan. It may be a long while before farmers hear Ilocano radio dramas blasting from their stereos at sunrise, playing until the mid-morning heat turns oppressive. It has been nearly a month since the southwest monsoon began dumping rain across the country, leaving parts of the province submerged in floodwaters.

Rosita Mendoza, a 52-year-old tobacco grower in the town of Alcala, could only stare at the dim skies, the eaves dripping with rainwater, and her soaked land turning into a vast quagmire. Wooden planting pegs, chipped hoes, and plows sit stacked in her barn.

It isn't that Alcala farmers loathe the rain, but Mendoza and her peers were left praying for three straight dry days before they could begin sowing again. The Chinese cabbage she planted drowned, its remains hungry devoured by the mud.
For a woman who lived through an era when farm labor cost as little as ₱40 a day, losing seedlings to torrential rain is a familiar tragedy.

blocks.caption: Mendoza poses with a hauling truck, wishing she could one day take one home. It was the day President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. visited the province and vowed to strengthen the agriculture sector—something farmers “barely” feel improving.

blocks.text: Mendoza poses with a hauling truck, wishing she could one day take one home. It was the day President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. visited the province and vowed to strengthen the agriculture sector—something farmers “barely” feel improving.

“They say those who plant are gamblers. Just because you sow something doesn’t mean you’ll reap the fruit,” Mendoza said. She spoke with a quiet resignation, as if this setback wouldn’t soon force her back into the field to sow another sack of seeds, once again at the mercy of unpredictable weather.
Fresh off her midyear tobacco harvest, Mendoza proceeded to plant other crops, accepting the reality that tobacco alone cannot buoy her family through the rest of the year.
“If we plant only one commodity and if it gets destroyed, we won’t have anything to feed us,” she said.

blocks.caption: Mendoza checks on her eggplant field months after the tobacco harvest. While other commodities help sustain the farm between seasons, tobacco remains her biggest source of income.

blocks.text: Mendoza checks on her eggplant field months after the tobacco harvest. While other commodities help sustain the farm between seasons, tobacco remains her biggest source of income.

blocks.caption: Alcala farmers weigh their burley tobacco harvest before it is remitted to Universal Leaf Philippines, Inc. (ULPI).

blocks.text: Alcala farmers weigh their burley tobacco harvest before it is remitted to Universal Leaf Philippines, Inc. (ULPI).

blocks.caption: Tobacco growers flip strings of tobacco leaves to keep moisture at bay and prevent a decline in quality.

blocks.text: Tobacco growers flip strings of tobacco leaves to keep moisture at bay and prevent a decline in quality.

Tobacco season typically begins in September, but preparing the seedbeds has become a waiting game dictated by the rain—or the lack of it. “We can start again only when it stops raining for a few days,” Mendoza said.

When the earth finally breathes warm again, Mendoza will rise at four in the morning and leave her house an hour later to kick off her seedling nursery routine. “Around five in the morning, we’re already there in the fields because it becomes hot quickly,” she said.

Mendoza walks roughly a kilometer toward her half-hectare tobacco plot alongside other women, all wearing knee-length rubber boots, loose trousers, wide-brimmed hats, and handkerchiefs tied to block the sun.

To pass the time, they play a playlist of downloaded Ilocano dramas and rock music, the same tunes echoing through Ilocano-owned thrift stores in Metro Manila. Mendoza recalled that she and her late husband once tried to eke out a living in the capital region, but eventually took a bus back home to Pangasinan.

Upon her return, Mendoza turned to what came naturally: tobacco farming. She watched her family grow alongside the cycle of her crops. Her youngest daughter even earned a degree in agriculture and joined the workforce of their corporate buyers.

Mendoza considers herself fortunate. The burley tobacco she cultivates has a guaranteed buyer in Universal Leaf Philippines, Inc. (ULPI), a multinational tobacco firm. She laments, however, that native tobacco growers struggle to secure stable sales.
“Growers of native tobacco don’t have sure buyers. That’s why there are a lot of stocks—native farmers haven’t been able to sell them yet,” Mendoza said.

As a community leader, Mendoza offers a helping hand by renting farmland and allowing landless neighbors to till it. “There are a lot of people here who want to work, but they don’t have land. They don’t have the money to buy land,” she said.
Smuggling takes root

In a region where land is scarce for honest farmers, tobacco smugglers have found fertile ground to flourish and blend in with legal merchants. Early this year, Mendoza was offered illegal inventory to resell at her local retail store.

“Someone came to me with that kind of cigarette. I said, ‘I don’t want to sell it because it’s illegal. I’m the one who will get caught. It’s a big thing,’” Mendoza recalled. Yet, she noted that seeing bystanders smoking illicit cigarettes has become an almost everyday sight.
“I see them almost every day,” she said, adding that black-market products are “really cheap.”
Last year, the government lost more than ₱80 billion in tax revenues to illicit tobacco and vape products, turning the Philippines into a primary source of illegal vape leakage in Southeast Asia.

blocks.caption: Ashok Kaul, founder and director of the Institute for Policy Evaluation

blocks.text: Ashok Kaul, founder and director of the Institute for Policy Evaluation

Ashok Kaul, founder and director of the Institute for Policy Evaluation, argues that curbing black-market transactions should not come at the expense of lower excise taxes. “Do not just accept it and lower the tax rates. Fight it!” he urged.
According to the global tax expert, the government must tackle smuggling through stricter enforcement. Pinpointing the source of illicit cigarettes is crucial to crafting an effective response.
“If you know it’s all smuggled, you know where to invest—at the border. If you know it’s locally produced, the countermeasures are different,” Kaul said.

Kaul commended the Philippines’ broader tobacco policies, noting significant progress since the implementation of the landmark Sin Tax Law more than a decade ago. But he pointed out a glaring weak spot: enforcement.

“You’ve reached the limit… I would say, ‘Look, you’ve done so well, but you’ve neglected one dimension—measuring and fighting illicit trade,’” Kaul said, emphasizing that combating illicit trade must be the country's top priority.
While Kaul warned against lowering taxes to appease smugglers, he also declined to endorse a Department of Finance (DOF) tax bill that seeks to hike excise taxes on harmful products.
Beyond tobacco, the proposed reform would update taxes on sweetened beverages, plastics, and luxury automobiles.

Finance Undersecretary Karlo Fermin S. Adriano noted that these revenue-generating measures are intended to offset losses from income tax relief for middle-income Filipinos, projecting net revenue gains of over ₱190 billion over four years.
Kaul warned against treating behavioral taxes as a permanent piggy bank for other tax relief measures.
“It’s not wise to rely on revenue from sin taxes,” he said. “Sin taxes are designed for a different purpose—they aren’t meant primarily to generate revenue.”

blocks.caption: SMUGGLED cigarettes valued at P14 million were seized in Zamboanga City over the weekend. (Photo via Liza Jocson)

blocks.text: SMUGGLED cigarettes valued at P14 million were seized in Zamboanga City over the weekend. (Photo via Liza Jocson)

As raising tobacco taxes risks driving smokers further into the black market, the urgent call is for tighter border controls and stronger enforcement. Perhaps then, farmers like Mendoza can find relief, knowing they won't have to compete with smugglers just to scrape together an extra peso.

Of the millions of pesos in tobacco taxes that Alcala collected in 2025, Mendoza said farmers received only ₱2,000 each, alongside two bags of fertilizer and seedling bags. “That’s really not enough. Where will that go?” she asked.

Even the subsidies promised when global fuel prices spiked amid Middle East conflicts failed to reach the ground. Now that inflation has cooled, Mendoza has abandoned all expectations of receiving that support.

Still, she holds out hope that authorities will mandate a meaningful fraction of sin-tax collections to go straight into farmers' pockets. “I just hope that the excise tax will go to us even just a few percent,” she said.
Perhaps that extra support would give Mendoza and her community a fighting chance as illegal trade continues to threaten the legal market.

articles.title: The true currency of good governance
articles.summary: What is the most valuable asset of any government? Some would immediately answer natural resources, infrastructure, technology, military capability, economic strength, or political stability. Well,…

blocks.text: What is the most valuable asset of any government? Some would immediately answer natural resources, infrastructure, technology, military capability, economic strength, or political stability. Well, those are all important. But history teaches us something remarkably different. There are nations blessed with abundant natural resources that remain poor. There are also countries with limited land and almost no natural wealth, yet they have become among the most prosperous in the world.

The difference was never simply resources. The difference was trust—trust in institutions, trust in government, trust that laws are applied fairly, trust that taxes are used wisely, trust that public officials are accountable, and trust that public servants place the people's welfare above personal interest.
That is the most valuable asset of any government.

Once public trust begins to erode, every policy becomes questionable, every procurement becomes suspicious, every infrastructure project is viewed with doubt, every financial report is met with skepticism, and every accomplishment is overshadowed by suspicion. And rebuilding trust is infinitely more difficult than losing it.

That is why I firmly believe that public trust is the true currency of good governance. Without it, our laws lose their effectiveness, institutions lose their legitimacy, and leadership loses its moral authority.

This principle is not merely philosophical; it is embedded in our Constitution. The Constitution does not describe public office as a privilege, nor does it call it an entitlement. It declares that “Public office is a public trust.” I have always found those words remarkably profound because they remind us that government authority never belongs to those who occupy positions, whether in the past or in the present. Authority is merely entrusted to them—temporarily—by the Filipino people. And every trust carries accountability.

As Certified Public Accountants, we often work with numbers. We analyze financial statements, reconcile accounts, examine variances, evaluate controls, issue reports, and audit transactions. But the work of a CPA is not ultimately about numbers. It is about confidence—confidence that public funds are properly managed, confidence that financial reports faithfully represent reality, confidence that internal controls are functioning, confidence that decisions are supported by reliable information, and confidence that institutions deserve the trust placed upon them. In many ways, our profession does not merely account for money. Our profession accounts for trust. And that is a far greater responsibility.
So, how do we preserve public trust in an age of unprecedented change?

Governance today is no longer judged merely by compliance. Citizens are no longer satisfied asking, “Was the money spent?” Today, they ask: “Was it spent wisely?” “Did it improve people's lives?” “Was the process transparent?” “Who was held accountable?” “Could the outcome have been better?” Those questions have fundamentally changed what society expects from all of us.

For many years, the Commission on Audit has continuously evolved to respond to these changing expectations. Not because its constitutional mandate has changed—it has not—but because the environment in which accountability is exercised has changed dramatically. Government has become more digital. Risks have become more complex. Fraud has become more sophisticated. Citizens have become more informed.

Therefore, public auditing itself has also evolved: not merely to detect deficiencies, but to strengthen institutions; not merely to ensure compliance, but to improve governance; not merely to protect public funds, but ultimately, to protect public trust. That evolution is reflected in reforms that have strengthened performance auditing, citizen participation, digital governance, electronic audit evidence, fraud prevention, and the modernization of audit processes—all while remaining anchored on the Commission's constitutional mandate and international standards. These reforms demonstrate that accountability is most effective when it evolves alongside the changing needs of government and society.

As CPAs, let us look beyond accounting standards, beyond audit reports, beyond internal controls, and beyond compliance requirements. Instead, let us examine a more fundamental question: What kind of institutions must we build so that future generations of Filipinos will continue to trust them?

At the end of the day, our greatest contribution as accountants, auditors, financial managers, and public servants will not be measured by the number of reports we prepare, the number of audit findings we issue, or the number of regulations we comply with. Our legacy will ultimately be measured by something much simpler: whether the Filipino people have greater confidence in their public institutions because we chose to serve with competence, integrity, and accountability. That is the higher purpose of our profession, and that is what I hope we shall reflect upon in our work on a daily basis.

Whenever governance is discussed, we almost instinctively think about rules, policies, internal controls, compliance checklists, audit observations, and risk management. These are certainly part of governance, but they are not governance itself. Compliance is the minimum expected of us; governance is the standard we aspire to. Compliance tells us what we are required to do. Governance asks whether we are doing what is right, what is wise, and what best serves the public interest. That distinction is critically important—because an institution may comply with every procedural requirement yet still fail in its responsibility to the public.

(Atty. Pondoc is a Member of the Board of Trustees of the University of Mindanao; Chairperson of PICPA Davao Foundation, Inc.; PICPA Past National President; and former COA Commissioner and former Asst. Executive Secretary for Finance in the Office of the President.)
