articles.title: World's youngest reigning traditional monarch dies aged 34
articles.summary: King Oyo ascended to the throne of Uganda's Tooro kingdom when he was just three years old.

blocks.text: A traditional Ugandan ruler named as the world's youngest monarch has died aged 34, his prime minster announced.
Oyo Nyimba Kabamba Iguru Rukidi IV became king of Tooro in western Uganda at just three years old in 1995 after the death of his father.

The Toroo kingdom did not disclose the cause of King Oyo's death, but a Ugandan government minister was quoted in local media saying that he had been critically ill and was seeking treatment in the US.
Though Uganda is governed by an elected president, it has several traditional kingdoms which continue to have significant cultural influence despite not having political power.

Oyo, who Guinness World Records listed as the world's youngest reigning monarch, external, ruled over more than two million people. He was the 13th monarch of a kingdom that was founded in the early 19th Century.
Announcing his death, Tooro's Prime Minister Calvin Armstrong Rwomiire Akiiki called his passing on Thursday an "immeasurable loss" to the royal family and the people of Tooro.
"I call upon all the people of Tooro to remain united, calm and prayerful during this profoundly difficult time," Akiiki said on Friday. "May His Majesty the King rest in eternal peace."
The Tooro Kingdom follows a hereditary system in selecting its monarch.
Oyo was not officially married, but Akiiki said "the continuity of the Crown is assured".
"His Majesty leaves behind a Prince as his heir, whose identity will be formally revealed at the appropriate time, in accordance with the traditions and customs of Tooro Kingdom," he explained.
When he became king in 1995 a regency, including the queen mother, was established until Oyo turned 18 when there was an official coronation.

The young king was well respected by his people and according to a report in the Daily Monitor newspaper he promoted causes such as youth empowerment, education and climate conservation, as well as HIV/Aids awareness.

The country's largest and most influential traditional institution, the Buganda Kingdom, said it mourned with the people of Tooro following the death of their monarch, labelling him a valuable figure to Uganda.

articles.title: Lacson: LRA checking land titles linked to Taguig reclamation
articles.summary: Senator Panfilo Lacson said the Land Registration Authority (LRA) has been checking the origin and history of certain land titles related to the alleged illegally reclaimed areas on the Taguig side…

blocks.text: Published August 28, 2026 7:04pm
Make this your preferred source to get more updates from this publisher on Google.

Senator Panfilo Lacson said the Land Registration Authority (LRA) has been checking the origin and history of certain land titles related to the alleged illegally reclaimed areas on the Taguig side of Laguna Lake.

In a post on X, the senator said the LRA is looking at the materials provided by the Philippine Reclamation Authority (PRA) “to check if land titles have been issued over reclaimed portions of Laguna Lake.”

“I requested them to backtrack the history of the issued OCTs (original certificates of title) and other modes of titling, so we will find out how they were manipulated with the end in view of filing criminal charges against those responsible,” Lacson said in a statement.
Based on initial information, he said the OCTs were issued through judicial or ordinary land registration, while others were issued through homestead patents.
Other Stories
Lacson said these titles may be declared void should the PRA initiate forfeiture proceedings in accordance with the law.

He likewise said on Wednesday that several crates of documents from the Department of Public Works and Highways (DPWH) related to supposed anomalous projects in Taguig City were to be submitted to the Office of the Ombudsman.

In July, Lacson’s office also turned over to the Ombudsman documentary and testimonial evidence it gathered on alleged anomalies involving flood control projects in Taguig City for further evaluation and a possible motu proprio investigation.

Lacson linked the alleged anomalies to Senate Minority Leader Alan Peter Cayetano, who has since denied claims of ghost infrastructure projects in Taguig and called for similar investigations into projects in other Metro Manila cities.
Cayetano’s wife, Lani Cayetano, is the incumbent mayor of Taguig.

Alan Cayetano also previously invited Lacson to visit Taguig City and see for himself the projects in the city amid the investigation into the alleged anomalous flood control and other infrastructure projects in their bailiwick. —LDF, GMA News

articles.title: Nepal-Tibet flood deaths pass 500, thousands still missing
articles.summary: The Red Cross says more than 93,000 people are affected by the deadly floods and landslides on the China-Nepal border. Rescue efforts were temporarily paused after an overflowing lake threatened to…

image.caption: Over 1,000 people remain missing, including many foreign touristsImage: Navesh Chitrakar/REUTERS

blocks.text: Rescue workers have resumed a search for hundreds of people still missing two days after catastrophic flash flooding hit the border between Nepal and China.
Their efforts were briefly put on hold on Friday after a lake formed by debris began overflowing, threatening areas already devastated by the disaster.

"We have received a notice saying that the lake has broken its banks," Narendra Pariyar, the most senior bureaucrat of the hard-hit Rasuwa district, told DW. "We can see that the level of water in the river is rising."
Residents in Nepal's border district of Rasuwa were seen fleeing up hillsides as they braced for a surge in river levels, Reuters reported.
Authorities later said the threat had eased but that they were closely monitoring the situation.
Meanwhile, Nepal said the death toll had risen to 579, up from 390 a day earlier. China has updated its earlier count of three to five deaths in Tibet.
More than 2,000 are still believed to be missing, including over 500 foreigners from more than 30 countries.
Nepal: WHO and Red Cross warn disaster is 'not over'
The International Red Cross estimated that over 93,000 people have been directly affected by the catastrophe and are in urgent need of humanitarian assistance.

"We're of course very concerned about a secondary flood," said spokesman David Fisher at a press briefing in Geneva, adding that Red Cross relief trucks had been blocked by the lake which formed following the landslide.

Kamal Kishore, Head of the United ​Nations Office for Disaster Risk Reduction, warned of further "cascading hazards that might unfold" and said: "The disaster is ⁠not ​yet completely over. It is still ​unfolding in some ways."
The World Health Organization (WHO) warned of the risk of disease in the wake of the disaster.

"Following a disaster of this scale, displacement, overcrowding ⁠and disruption ​to water, sanitation and health services can increase the risk of infectious diseases, including diarrhoea and respiratory illnesses," said spokesman Tarik ​Jasarevic.

blocks.caption: Rescuers had to put their efforts on hold after an overflowing lake threatened to unleash more floodingImage: Niranjan Shrestha/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: What is the latest update from China?
Wednesday's disaster, triggered by a glacial collapse that sent rock and meltwater surging into rivers below, left a new danger in its wake: a barrier lake formed upstream by debris dams.

China's Ministry of Water Resources said the lake held roughly 2 million cubic meters of water as of Thursday and was expected to receive another 3 million cubic meters — equivalent to about 1,200 Olympic swimming pools — over the following three days, with peak flow expected around September 1.

Chinese national broadcaster CCTV said the lake's barrier sat more than 10 kilometers (6.2 miles) from Gyirong Port, the border crossing that was engulfed by the initial flood, and is at an elevation roughly 1,000 meters (3,280 feet) above it.
More than 1,000 believed missing after Nepal flash floods
To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The country had mobilized an eight-member engineering team to survey the lake by air and build 3D models of the site. Engineer Chen Hanxiao described the difficulty of the terrain: "After the glacier collapse created the lake, many isolated cliffs and steep cliffs appeared along it," he told CCTV.

He said the team's general strategy was to dig a drainage channel at a lower point of the dam, though the channel's exact width and depth would depend on calculations of water flow and how quickly the lake continued to fill.

Their survey found the lake to be about 150 meters long and 40-50 meters deep. Continuing rain in the area, which is forecast to last through the coming week, has further destabilized the surrounding soil and rock.
On Friday afternoon, Chinese state media reported that the first professional rescue teams had reached the "core rescue site" or the area wiped out by a mudslide.

blocks.caption: Hundreds of foreign tourists are among the missingImage: Navesh Chitrakar/REUTERS

blocks.text: What did Nepal say about search and rescue?
Nepal's Foreign Ministry said Friday it does not need foreign assistance for search-and-rescue operations, despite offers of help from several countries with nationals still missing.
Foreign Ministry spokesperson Lok Bahadur Chhetri said Nepal's security agencies were managing the response.
"The offer for help is natural. Our security agencies are doing the search and rescue operation. For now we don't require such help," he said.

Hundreds of foreign nationals remain unaccounted for, including from South Korea, which has already sent a response team and plans to dispatch a disaster relief unit. South Korea's Foreign Ministry confirmed that Nepal had indicated it was not yet ready to accept foreign rescue teams, adding, "South Korea will keep negotiating with Nepal over the matter."

Seoul has pledged $1 million (€860,000) in humanitarian aid through international organizations, after reporting nine of its nationals missing and 10 stranded after a hydropower plant they were working at was hit by the flood.

According to local media, India, China, the United States, Britain, Japan, South Korea, Sri Lanka and Bangladesh have all asked Nepal's government for permission to send their own search-and-rescue teams to assist.

blocks.caption: Nepal said it did not require foreign assistance for search and rescue at the momentImage: Sanjit Pariyar/NurPhoto/picture alliance

articles.title: Swift appeal likely as judge blocks Trump mail voting order – US politics live
articles.summary: Judge Indira Talwani placed a 14-day hold on government implementing Trump’s order to limit mail voting

blocks.text: Judge again blocks Trump mail ballot executive order in ruling likely to be appealed
Hello and welcome to the US politics live blog.
A federal judge has halted, at least temporarily, attempts to implement Donald Trump’s executive order limiting mail voting.
The president’s directive stalled for a second time about a week before the first mail ballots are due to be sent out for the rapidly approaching midterm elections.

In the US district court, judge Indira Talwani placed a 14-day hold on the government implementing the order in a case that could be headed back to the supreme court, which on Monday overturned an earlier ruling of hers that had blocked Trump’s order from taking effect.
Talwani wrote in her ruling:

double quotation markPlaintiff states have neither time nor funds to design new mail ballots, seek approval of the new designs, order production of mail ballots, update their own election management systems, train election officials to use the USPS portal and upload citizen data to the portal, all before the midterms.
The latest ruling came in advance of a 3 September hearing after Democrats and voting rights groups refiled their lawsuits to comply with the recent supreme court decision.

The high court’s conservative majority did not rule on the legality of Trump’s executive order. Still, it said the legal challenges against it that led Talwani to initially freeze it were filed too soon. Since then, the administration has issued a formal rule intended to govern whether the US Postal Service will deliver states’ mail ballots – effectively restarting the legal fight.

The president has long targeted mail voting, which he falsely blames for his 2020 election loss even though he himself uses it to cast his ballot. A report by the Brookings Institution published in 2025 found that mail voting fraud occurred in only about four cases out of every 10 million mail ballots cast.

The legal battle has major ramifications for the midterms. Nearly one-third of Americans vote by mail and election officials contend there is not enough time to revise their systems to comply with the new postal service directives.

blocks.text: US civil rights leaders and politicians to march on Washington for voting protections
Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez and senator Bernie Sanders are due to take part in the 63rd anniversary of the March on Washington later today.
The original march, in 1963, was to advocate for social justice and civil rights for Black Americans, culminating in Martin Luther King Jr’s I Have a ​Dream speech.

This year’s event is due to focus on voting rights in the wake of the United States supreme court’s decision to overturn section 2 of the Voting Rights Act, with attendees also expected to include Al Sharpton, Martin Luther King III, Arndrea Waters King and congressional black caucus chair Yvette Clarke.

“Defending ⁠the vote means defending the foundation of our democracy,” Martin Luther King III said in a statement to the Associated Press. “Sixty-three years after my father stood at the ​Lincoln Memorial, we are called to march again, not only in remembrance, ​but in ⁠action.”
In April, the supreme court struck down Louisiana’s congressional map and substantially rewrote section 2 of the Voting Rights Act, dismantling key protections against racial gerrymandering.

Campaign organisers told the AP that the decision had intensified a long-running ​fight over Black political representation. They describe the 28 August action as part of “the same call our elders answered” more than 60 years ago on their campaign website, and have planned a symbolic return to the Lincoln Memorial where King addressed voters during the peak of the civil rights movement.
“We return to the ground where a quarter million Americans once stood for jobs and freedom, and we carry their unfinished work into a new generation,” organisers said.
Pentagon’s blacklisting of Anthropic was unlawful, US judge rules

A US federal judge ruled Thursday that sanctions imposed in February by the Trump administration against AI giant Anthropic were illegal, finding that the government had punished the artificial intelligence company for publicly criticising the Pentagon.
“The empty invocation of national security is not a blank check to punish and retaliate against government critics,” Judge Rita Lin said in a 59-page decision.

She barred the federal agencies named in the lawsuit from enforcing President Donald Trump’s order to stop using the tools of Anthropic – creator of the Claude AI models – and overturned defense secretary Pete Hegseth’s designation of the company as a “supply chain risk”, a status previously reserved for foreign firms.
The ruling makes permanent the temporary suspension of sanctions ordered by the judge in March and takes effect immediately. The government may appeal.
“We welcome the court’s ruling that this supply chain risk designation was unlawful,” an Anthropic spokesperson said.

Hegseth’s unprecedented move, which followed Anthropic’s refusal to allow the military to ⁠use AI chatbot Claude for US surveillance or autonomous weapons, blocked Anthropic from certain military contracts. Anthropic executives ​have said it could cost the company billions ‌of dollars in lost business ‌and reputational harm.
Trump had lashed out at the company after its refusal, describing it in a February social media post as “a radical left, woke company” and “out-of-control”.
Trump official faces inquiry over claims he diverted wildfire resources to his own property

blocks.caption: Anna Betts

blocks.text: Anna Betts

Donald Trump’s administration is facing calls to launch an investigation into allegations that Michael Boren, a senior official who oversees the US Forest Service, pressed agency staff to deploy additional resources to fight a fire burning near his Idaho ranch.

Three Democratic senators accused Boren of “inappropriate interference” in a letter seen by the Guardian, demanding answers from Brooke Rollins, US agricultural secretary. Boren serves as undersecretary of agriculture for natural resources and environment.

Senators Ron Wyden, Amy Klobuchar and Martin Heinrich expressed “serious concern” over reports that Boren used his federal government position in July to remove firefighting personnel and resources from active fires elsewhere to tackle a fire near his private ranch in Idaho.

“We request a full investigation into the nature and extent of Boren’s involvement in response to the Cabin Creek Fire and a detailed accounting of the safeguards the agency has implemented or plans to implement to prevent political interference and conflicts of interest in wildfire response,” they wrote.

Their letter follows a report from the Washington Post earlier this month, in which several forest service officials, speaking on the condition of anonymity, said that Boren – who reportedly owns a 480-acre ranch in the Sawtooth national recreation area – contacted forest service officials multiple times in mid-July to question why more aircraft were not being used to fight the Cabin Creek fire in Idaho, which spread across several acres in Idaho’s Sawtooth national forest.

articles.title: Detroit despairs as ‘insanity’ of Trump’s Canada trade war punishes city
articles.summary:
Unpopular new policy comes as midterms loom and control of Congress could be decided by several Michigan races

Every day $1bn worth of…

blocks.text: Every day $1bn worth of goods crosses the river dividing Detroit, Michigan, and Windsor, Ontario, two largely blue-collar US and Canadian cities that have come to act as one in the creation of North America’s auto industry.

News this week of Donald Trump’s escalating trade spat with Canada has everyone worried. Political and economic leaders and observers labeled the move an act of “hubris” , blamed Trump’s “ego”, and called the escalation “insanity”.
“We don’t need Canada, they need us,” Trump declared.

But many are hoping that Trump’s plans to impose 50% tariffs on Canadian goods from 1 January, covering everything from automobiles to honey to hockey sticks, will prove another empty threat and cite the upcoming midterm elections as a pivotal reason the plan may be scrapped.

Control of the US Congress hangs in the balance and will almost certainly be decided by several close Michigan races. It also comes just two months after polling highlighted Michiganders’ fatigue with and opposition to the president’s unprecedented tariff program.

By a 63%-31% margin, residents here oppose tariffs on Canadian goods, according to a June Epic-MRA poll, including 35% of Republicans. Meanwhile, nearly 75% of Michiganders said the tariffs are fueling high prices.

Trump doubling down on an unpopular policy deep into election season is viewed by many observers as a gift to Democrats, and there is a real possibility that it contributes to a midterm loss for the Republicans. Meanwhile, there seems to be little upside for Trump.
“I don’t understand what Trump is thinking,” the Epic-MRA pollster Bernie Porn said.

Regardless, Michiganders have already suffered disproportionately as they pay on average over $3,200 annually for tariffs, or about 142% more than the rest of the country, because of the state’s shared border with Canada.
The Canadian economy would also take a major hit if the tariffs are imposed, said Patrick Anderson, a Michigan-based economist with the Anderson Economic Group.

blocks.caption: The Democratic US Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed greets supporters at Renaissance high school in Detroit, Michigan, on 7 August.  Photograph: Jeff Kowalsky/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: “Both will suffer – there are no two ways about it,” Anderson added.

This critical upper midwest swing state has picked the presidential winner in five consecutive elections, going from Barack Obama to Trump to Joe Biden and back to Trump. Democrats’ chances to retake the Senate rest heavily on the Democratic nominee Abdul El-Sayed beating Trump ally Mike Rogers in the 3 November general election race. Rogers has supported the tariffs, but so far has been silent on the latest escalation.

The tariffs and the unpopular Iran war’s contribution to inflation represent a “double hit” for Republicans, Porn said, and Trump is handing ammo to a particularly adept candidate in El-Sayed. He has energized people with his anti-establishment, populist political vision, and a no-holds-barred delivery.

“El-Sayed has proven to be very, very articulate on a number of issues,” Porn added. “I think that he is going to try and just throw bombs at Rogers [in an upcoming debate] because Rogers supports these tariffs and trade war. Trump’s low popularity is an anchor around Rogers’ neck.”
In a statement, El-Sayed hammered Trump and Rogers, saying that the president “cares more about his ego and saber-rattling than addressing the affordability crisis.

“Donald Trump is launching this trade war for his own vanity, and he’s asking Michigan families to pay the price,” El-Sayed said. “Trump has been failing Michigan through these chaotic tariffs and bad trade deals for far too long, and Mike Rogers won’t do anything but rubber-stamp them.”
El-Sayed said he would push for “real, fair trade deals that create good-paying jobs”. Rogers’ campaign did not respond to a request for comment.

The United Auto Workers (UAW), which has 350,000 members in Michigan and is often a political kingmaker here, has supported some of Trump’s targeted tariffs, but said in a statement it “rejects” the latest escalation.

“If we’re going to increase tariffs anywhere, it should be on countries where automakers continue to offshore jobs because they can pay workers $3 an hour, force them to work in unsafe conditions, and crack down on independent unions,” the UAW president, Shawn Fain, said. Canada has strong unions, and the UAW supports those.

“Tariffs work, but only if they are deployed intentionally to protect workers and grow our manufacturing communities, and it’s time to permanently end offshoring and the race to the bottom,” Fain added.

Mexico and Canada currently face 25% US tariffs on autos, though partial exemptions in the nations’ free trade agreement make the effective rate much lower, overall. Anderson estimated tariffs cost US auto companies about $12.5bn in 2025.

The Canadian government has announced it will impose retaliatory tariffs on $20bn of goods starting 1 January. The actions leading to the latest blow-up have been “rife with miscalculations, overreactions, and hubris”, Anderson said. He read through the list of goods on which tariffs would be imposed – feathers, sweaters, girls’ dresses, lobster.
“This is not a trade war. This is an annoyance list. Chest pounding,” Anderson said.

The North American auto industry over the last 60 years has integrated across the continent, and auto parts cross a border an average of six times before they land in a final product. That means there would be shared pain, Anderson said, and it would reverberate across the upper midwest, where bigger manufacturing cities are typically powered by industries that are often reliant on international trade.

But the Canadian economy is smaller, and Ontario’s economy is so concentrated that it would hit harder north of the border, Anderson added. Ultimately, the real threat is that “these two countries go pell-mell into it” and impose tariffs on oil, energy and commodities that hit harder than lobster.

The dialogue has devolved into the usual petty antagonism that is a hallmark of Trump’s beefs. Trump signed an executive order to rename Lake Ontario “Lake America” on Thursday, and Vice-President JD Vance referred to Canada as the 51st state.
“Let me say with great understatement that this is not helpful,” Anderson added.

blocks.caption: The American and Canadian flags fly at the midway point on the Gordie Howe International Bridge, that connects Windsor, Ontario, and Detroit, Michigan. Photograph: Canadian Press/Shutterstock

blocks.text: Indeed, the Windsor mayor, Drew Dilkens, took exception to that particular comment. In an interview, he expressed deep frustration over Trump’s moves, and labeled justifications Trump has used for issuing tariffs, including framing them as a response to illegal immigration on the northern border, “nonsense”.

The latest escalation “is an aggressive move, one that could not be ignored by our country”, added Dilkens, who leads the city of 230,000 people. “It’s just offensive that he launches these attacks at Canada, who is your largest trading partner, your closest ally, and your neighbor.”

The chaos has cooled investment in Windsor, and prices remain high on both sides of the border. He pointed out how much more US consumers are paying not just for automobiles, but for beef, which in part stems from tariffs on Canadian beef.
“What is really crazy is that he is willing to throw his own citizens under the bus to pursue his tariff agenda,” Dilkens said. “They have Donald Trump to thank.”

Highlighting the tension among the president and some in his base, the Michigan chamber of commerce, a trade organization that lobbies on behalf of the state’s largest corporations, normally vocally supports the president on economic issues. It has not made a public statement, and did not respond to a request for comment from the Guardian.
However, the typically pro-Trump Detroit chamber of commerce did not mince words.

“Escalating tensions and tariffs will only cause economic pain on both sides of the border, especially in Michigan and the binational Detroit-Windsor region,” the chamber said in a press statement, adding that global competitors like China benefited most.
“Our economies are intertwined, interconnected, and stronger together; the sooner normalcy is restored the better.”

articles.title: How Trump’s lumber tariffs made a bad situation worse in B.C.
articles.summary: Donald Trump is hardly the first U.S. president whose government has imposed steep duties on Canadian lumber. The tariffs are the latest chapter in a dispute that's been going on for more than four…

image.caption: Logs are seen piled up at West Fraser Timber in Quesnel, B.C., in April 2009. Over a dozen forestry facilities have closed in B.C. in recent years — but steep U.S. tariffs on Canadian lumber are an issue that have persisted for decades. (Jonathan Hayward/The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: More than 20 lumber mills closed across B.C. over the last three years. Billions in wood products affected by U.S. tariffs. Tens of thousands of jobs lost in Canada.
The state of B.C.'s forestry industry is, by most accounts, dire.
While there are many factors driving the decline, recent U.S. tariffs haven't helped.

But Donald Trump is hardly the first U.S. president whose government has imposed steep duties on Canadian lumber. The tariffs are the latest chapter in a dispute that's been going on for more than four decades.
Here's how we got here.

items: 'Absolutely worst situation': B.C. forestry sector fears it will be hardest-hit by U.S. tariffs

blocks.text: What is softwood lumber and why is it important?
Softwood lumber is manufactured from coniferous trees. In Canada, this is mostly spruce, pine and fir.

It's used in residential and non-residential construction, repair and remodelling and furniture manufacturing, according to Natural Resources Canada. The byproducts supply industries including pulp and paper, wood-based panels and bioenergy.
In 2024, softwood lumber made up 98 per cent of Canada's wood production, according to Statistics Canada.

blocks.caption: Nearly half of American wood product imports came form Canada in 2024, according to the U.S. Congress. Here, a truck carrying wood goes through a customs checkpoint in April 2017. (Ryan Remiorz/The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: That year, Canada exported just over half — 58 per cent — of its softwood lumber to the U.S.
Almost a third of that – 32 per cent – came from the B.C. Interior, which was the country's leading producer, according to Statistics Canada.
In 2024, nearly half of American wood product imports — worth about $11 billion US — came from Canada, according to the U.S. Congress.
Why is it a trade issue?
It boils down to differences in how much Canadian and American producers have to pay for access to wood, according to Export Development Canada (EDC).
In Canada, 94 per cent of forested lands are publicly owned, EDC says. Governments charge companies a fee, known as stumpage, for logging access to Crown land.
In the U.S., more than half of forested land (58 per cent) is privately-owned, according to the U.S Congress. Access prices are generally determined by the market, rather than government.

blocks.caption: In Canada, most forests are on public land, while in the U.S., they are on mostly privately-held land. (Bridgette Watson/CBC)

blocks.text: The U.S. has long argued that the low stumpage fees charged by Canadian governments amount to a subsidy that allows Canadian lumber to be sold in the U.S. at below-market value.

But Zoltan van Heyningen, the executive director of the U.S. Lumber Coalition, says these differences account for "one tiny, small aspect of Canadian subsidies," arguing the Canadian government has spent billions in taxpayer dollars in the last year supporting the industry.
In his view, the problem is one of chronic excess supply on the Canadian side, which ends up in the U.S. and drives down prices, harming American producers.
How long has the dispute been going on?

The American lumber industry first made this argument to the U.S. Commerce Department in 1982, out of concern over Canada's growing share of the U.S. market. The request was for tariffs on Canadian softwood lumber to level the playing field.

The first bilateral negotiations began in 1986. The two countries signed an agreement later that year, under which Canada agreed to impose a 15 per cent tax on its own exports of some softwood lumber to the U.S.

Over the next three decades, the dispute generally involved the U.S. imposing tariffs on Canadian softwood lumber, and Canada increasing stumpage fees or accepting export caps to minimize or avoid these duties.
Forestry sector hit with new tariffs, adding to industry woes, says analyst
Canada has regularly appealed U.S. duties, including at panels set up under the North American Free Trade Agreement (NAFTA) and its predecessor, as well as the World Trade Organization.
It has been generally successful in arguing the U.S. duties were unfairly high.
There were also periods when trade was governed by various softwood lumber agreements, the most recent of which expired in 2015.
How is it affected by the U.S.-Canada trade war?
In 2017, the U.S. Commerce Department again concluded Canada's softwood imports were unfairly subsidized, and imposed duties.

These duties, which were amended in the summer of 2025, are known as anti-dumping duties — tariffs placed on imported goods when they are sold below market value — and countervailing duties, intended to cancel out tax breaks or subsidies a foreign government gives its own producers.
Taken together, they added 35 per cent to the cost of most Canadian softwood lumber in the U.S., according to Global Affairs Canada.
Separating fact from fiction in the U.S.-Canada softwood lumber trade war

Later that year, in October 2025, the Trump administration imposed an additional 10 per cent tariff on softwood lumber following a Section 232 national security investigation into imports of timber, lumber and their derivative products.

This was in response to a report by the U.S. commerce secretary, which found wood product imports are "resulting in the persistent threats of closures of wood mills and disruptions of wood product supply chains, among other things," Trump said in a September 2025 proclamation announcing the tariffs.

blocks.caption: A 2025 report by U.S. Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick concluded Canadian wood imports were harming the U.S. economy. (Kevin Lamarque/Reuters)

blocks.text: The October 2025 duties brought the total tariff level on most softwood lumber imported from Canada to 45 per cent. They also added 25 per cent duties to imports of upholstered furniture and kitchen cabinets and vanities.
Most recently, the Trump administration imposed another round of tariffs under Section 338 of the Tariff Act of 1930, which took effect last week.

These 50 per cent tariffs are in response to what U.S. President Donald Trump called discriminatory Canadian treatment of U.S. motor vehicle, alcohol and dairy exports and apply to a wide range of products.

items: How 50% U.S. tariffs will impact the average British Columbian
Fact-checking the White House statement of facts about Canada

blocks.text: They don't apply to products, including those from softwood lumber, already subject to the Section 232 tariffs.

But they do hit a wide range of value-added wood products worth about $4 billion, including plywood, wood mouldings and particle board, according to Forest Products Association of Canada president and CEO Derek Nighbor.
The reaction
U.S. reaction is divided, with the lumber industry largely supportive, and those forced to pay higher prices for building materials — such as the National Association of Homebuilders — opposed.
"Building material tariffs heighten market uncertainty, strain supply chains and increase construction costs," the association said in a statement.
"As the president continues to advance his tariff agenda, NAHB is urging the administration to exempt building materials in light of the ongoing housing affordability crisis."

blocks.caption: The cost of building materials is likely to increase as a result of the tariffs, according to the U.S. National Association of Homebuilders. (Mike Crawley/CBC)

blocks.text: The U.S. Lumber Coalition's van Heyningen applauded the tariffs.

"Our industry is not able to produce to their full capacity, and they're not able to expand, when Canada takes up an artificially high market share because they're dumping their excess lumber capacity into the U.S. market," he said in an interview.
"So it's very much a jobs issue for us as well."

blocks.caption: Loads of western red cedar lumber is pictured at a sawmill in Vancouver. (Ben Nelms/CBC)

blocks.text: The Forest Products Association of Canada's Nighbor argued the shortfall in Canadian lumber has been made up with imports from the European Union, which faces a much lower U.S. tariff rate of 15 per cent.
"Americans cannot meet their domestic needs," he said. "And right now, even though the Canadian numbers are down, it's the Europeans who have primarily benefited from that."

articles.title: Treaty 6 was signed 150 years ago. First Nations worry a push for Alberta independence puts it at risk
articles.summary: First Nations from across Treaty 6 territory have been marking this month’s 150th anniversary of the signing of the 1876 agreement with the Crown. But for some, the discussion around the upcoming…

image.caption: A drum group at the Treaty 6 150th Anniversary Celebration powwow in Enoch Cree Nation. (Adrienne Lamb/CBC)

blocks.text: First Nations from across Treaty 6 territory have been marking this month’s 150th anniversary of the signing of the 1876 agreement with the Crown. But for some, the discussion around the upcoming referendum on Alberta independence is casting a shadow over the celebrations.

Included in Alberta’s fall referendum is a question asking people if the province should remain a part of Canada or begin the process of holding a binding referendum on separation. The outcome of that question is top of mind for many First Nations people who say it puts their treaty rights and other entitlements at risk.

“When it comes to this whole separatist regime … we’re going to be discussing amongst [First Nations] how we can get our people to vote, to rock the vote,” says Grand Chief Joey Pete of the Confederacy of Treaty 6 First Nations, a body representing the nations in Alberta.
“Our ancestors knew these things were going to happen, that’s why they signed a treaty.”
Pete says the treaty has nothing to do with Alberta, and that the province merely serves as a representative of the Crown when it comes to the signed agreement.
Pete says when his ancestors signed the treaty, they did not cede and surrender the land, but rather agreed to share it with settlers.

blocks.caption: Grand Chief Joey Pete with the Confederacy of Treaty 6 First Nations at the Enoch Cree Nation powwow grounds. (Nate Gross/CBC)

blocks.text: The treaty also guarantees other rights to First Nations, including health, education and the right to hunt and live off the land — rights they still hold today.

“Canada has the legal … fiduciary obligation to First Nations around acting in [their] best interests,” said Janice Makokis, an assistant professor in the faculty of law at the University of Windsor who is from Saddle Lake Cree Nation.
“Leaving Alberta would directly impact that … because our education funding, as well as funding … related to health, is directly tied to the federal government.”
Last year, the separatist group Stay Free Alberta launched a citizen initiative petition, which asked if Alberta should cease to be a part of Canada and become an independent state.
Alberta separation threatening 150 years of Treaty 6

The Alberta government opted to pose its own referendum question on the issue, rather than using the one Stay Free Alberta had been advocating for or another question on the matter that had been proposed by a group behind a pro-Confederation petition.

For months, First Nations have been battling the province in court, arguing the province failed to fulfil its duty to consult with them when it approved Stay Free Alberta’s petition application, and that the question itself threatens their treaty rights.
“We're ready and we will stand tall,” Pete said. “We'll continue to fight against the provincial government because what they do isn't … our laws.”

A judge quashed the approval of the petition. The province has appealed the judge’s decision, saying it didn’t trigger the duty to consult and that the judge failed to give weight to the democratic purpose of the petition process. Premier Danielle Smith previously called the judge’s decision “anti-democratic.”

items: Alberta government files appeal on court decision to throw out separatist referendum petition
Q&A: Why treaty rights and First Nations consultation stand in the way of an Alberta separation referendum

blocks.text: The Confederacy of Treaty 6 First Nations held a week of events leading up to the treaty’s Aug. 23 anniversary.
Pete says the fact Alberta’s UCP government didn’t send representatives reveals what he believes is a “hidden message,” and that “there’s no path to reconciliation.”
Alberta Indigenous Relations Minister Rajan Sawhney's office said in a statement that she was away but committed to maintaining strong relationships.
Treaty stretches across provincial borders

Treaty 6 was first signed at Fort Carlton in what is now Saskatchewan on Aug. 23, 1876. It covers a stretch of land across central Alberta and Saskatchewan, with Marcel Colomb First Nation and Mathias Colomb First Nation — both in Manitoba — later signing onto the treaty.
Dwayne Donald, a Tier 1 Canada Research Chair and professor of education at the University of Alberta, says the treaty played an integral role in terms of how Alberta became part of Canada.
“People need to understand that it was part of the British legal tradition to make treaties — actually a requirement — once Rupert’s Land was transferred to Canada,” he says.
When the Dominion of Canada finalized its acquisition of Rupert’s Land in 1870 from the Hudson’s Bay Company, the numbered treaties soon followed.
Donald says Treaty 6 itself should be seen as more than just an agreement between nations, but as a living covenant.
“My goal as an educator is to expand that treaty understanding so that people understand that it includes the sun, it includes the river, it includes the wind and the Earth.”
Separatist promises First Nations rights will be upheld
With a handful of separatist groups in Alberta, ideas have emerged on how relations between First Nations and an independent Alberta could look like.
The Alberta Prosperity Project has given few details, but says an independent Alberta would actually give more economic freedom to First Nations.

Lawyer Keith Wilson with the separatist third-party advertiser Let Alberta Decide, says “the treaties will carry on” if secession happens, and First Nations would have a seat at the table in deciding what an independent Alberta could look like.

blocks.caption: The Stay Free Alberta petitioners claimed more than a month ago to have the required 178,000 signatures that could trigger a referendum. (Julia Wong/CBC)

blocks.text: He says in an independent Alberta, First Nations would maintain their right to education, health and to live off the land.

“The only way that change could occur to their rights is if they ask for that,” Wilson says, adding that options would be available for individual First Nations to sign a modern treaty with an independent Alberta.

“I wouldn’t entertain that notion,” Chief Vernon Watchmaker of Kehewin Cree Nation says, adding that because his community has fostered a 150-year relationship with the Crown, it would not be advantageous for the nation to sever that tie.
“Right now, we’re not in support of creating division, we’re in support of creating unity.”
Makokis cautions that the treaties can’t be overridden.
“They are international treaties made between nations,” she says.
“There are spiritual sacred elements of the treaty that we entered … that would prohibit us from breaking the treaty.”
Wilson says First Nations could choose to stay with Canada, meaning stretches of reserve land would not transfer to an independent Alberta.
A forgotten history
Donald spends a lot of time walking in Edmonton’s North Saskatchewan River valley, teaching people the often forgotten history of the land north of the University of Alberta campus.
“Edmontonians know this river as the North Saskatchewan,” he says as he stands along the banks of the river.
“More properly, it’s known as kisiskāciwani-sīpiy, a river that flows at a swift walking pace.”
The Cree name hints at the history of the region, which was once home to Donald’s ancestors from the Papaschase First Nation.

blocks.caption: Dwayne Donald, professor at the University of Alberta's faculty of education, looking out at the North Saskatchewan River, which runs behind the campus. (Craig Ryan/CBC)

blocks.text: Originally the community settled south of the river. But federal officials later decided they needed to make room for a growing Edmonton, which in terms of population is now the largest city in Treaty 6 and also the home of Alberta’s provincial government.
Donald says it is not lost on him that Edmonton’s First Nations history is not mentioned in discussions around separatism.
“In the United States, they call it manifest destiny, which is this idea that this land was God-given to certain people to use in a certain way,” he says. “We are following that trajectory.
“What we see with this separation movement is … the desire to ignore sovereignty, … a desire to ignore that people have been living, well, for example, in this river valley for thousands of years.”

articles.title: Public warned that sinkhole in Bogo City could grow bigger
articles.summary: CEBU CITY–Residents in a barangay in Bogo City, northern Cebu were advised to take extreme caution after a sinkhole that was recently discovered in the area continued to expand. Following an…

blocks.text: The sinkhole in Bogo City, northern Cebu is cordoned off to prevent onlookers from staying near it.(Photo from Bogo PIO)
CEBU CITY–Residents in a barangay in Bogo City, northern Cebu were advised to take extreme caution after a sinkhole that was recently discovered in the area continued to expand.

Following an inspection, scientists from the Mines and Geosciences Bureau-Central Visayas (MGB-7) classified the sinkhole in Sitio Indilicio, Purok Libog 1, Barangay Guadalupe as a “high-risk ground collapse area.”
MGB-7 warned that the presence of the sinkhole could result in further ground collapse.
As additional safety precaution, the agency recommended a wider off-limits area around the site.
The city government was advised to establish and strictly enforce a no-entry buffer zone of at least 20 meters from the sinkhole’s rim.
A controlled-access zone extending at least 50 meters from the sinkhole was also proposed to ward off onlookers.
MGB-7 warned that allowing people to gather near the site could add surface load and vibration to already unstable ground.
The sinkhole was discovered last Aug. 20.
In its initial inspection, the MGB-7 identified the geological formation as a cover collapse sinkhole measuring roughly 15 meters by 25 meters.
The sinkhole expanded to about two meters between Aug. 22 and 23.

articles.title: PCSO steps up as key government partner with ₱97.84B in contributions since 2022
articles.summary: The Philippine Charity Sweepstakes Office (PCSO) contributed a total of ₱97.84 billion to the national government from 2022 to the first semester of 2026 through taxes, dividends, and mandatory…

blocks.text: The Philippine Charity Sweepstakes Office (PCSO) contributed a total of ₱97.84 billion to the national government from 2022 to the first semester of 2026 through taxes, dividends, and mandatory remittances that help fund healthcare and other public programs.
The agency recorded its highest annual contribution during the period in 2023, with total remittances reaching ₱22.99 billion.

PCSO subsequently contributed ₱22.26 billion in 2024 and ₱22.22 billion in 2025, demonstrating its sustained role as a major revenue-generating government corporation and a dependable partner in national development.
As of June 30, 2026, PCSO had contributed an additional ₱10.74 billion for the first semester of the year.
Of the ₱97.84-billion total, ₱73.05 billion was remitted to the Bureau of Internal Revenue (BIR) as taxes, while ₱10.30 billion was turned over to the Bureau of the Treasury as dividends.

PCSO also remitted ₱11.47 billion in support of Universal Health Care under Republic Act (RA) No. 11223. Another ₱3.03 billion was provided to various government institutions and beneficiaries pursuant to special laws and executive orders.

PCSO’s mandatory contributions support the programs of agencies and organizations such as the Commission on Higher Education (CHEd), Dangerous Drugs Board (DDB), Department of Energy (DOE), National Council on Disability Affairs, Philippine Sports Commission (PSC), Boy Scouts of the Philippines, Girl Scouts of the Philippines, Philippine Red Cross (PRC), Nutrition Foundation of the Philippines, Quezon Institute, and local government unit shares.

During the recent deliberations on PCSO’s proposed budget, House Committee on Appropriations Chairperson Nueva Ecija 1st district Rep. Mikaela Angela "Mika" Suansing commended the agency for its substantial contributions to government coffers.

“I would like to commend PCSO for all its contributions to the National Government. The funds the agency has contributed play a significant role in funding government programs and projects,” Suansing said.

House members Ramil Hernandez, Leody Tarriela, Joseph Tan, Maria Cristina Angeles, Presley de Jesus, Alexandria Gonzales, and Rebecca Maria Ynares likewise expressed their full support for PCSO’s proposed budget and thanked the agency for its contributions to nation-building.

“The nearly ₱98 billion that PCSO has contributed since 2022 shows how the public’s continued support for lotto generates meaningful resources for healthcare, education, sports development, disaster response, and other vital government programs,” PCSO General Manager Melquiades Robles said.
PCSO emphasized that the value generated by its games extends beyond prizes and jackpots.
A portion of its revenues is returned to the Filipino people through taxes, dividends, healthcare funding, charitable assistance, and other contributions mandated by law.

“As PCSO strengthens its operations and expands access to its legitimate games, we also increase our capacity to contribute to the government and help more Filipinos. Every legitimate bet helps generate funds that ultimately return to communities through public services and social programs. As we always say in PCSO, ‘Sa Bawat Taya, May Kawanggawa,’” Robles added.

articles.byline: Taz Ali (now); Mabel Banfield-Nwachi and Adam Fulton (earlier)

blocks.text: India’s foreign ministry spokesperson, Randhir Jaiswal, said 320 Indian nationals are still missing in the aftermath of the floods.
About 400 Indian ‌nationals have been located and are safe in the Chinese side of the border, Jaiswal said during a briefing.
Some more sobering images have just come in from the news wires, as rescue efforts continue to search for the more than 1,500 people missing after a brief pause due to a formed river overflowing.

blocks.caption: Coffins are prepared for dispatch at the helipad of the Army Operations Center in Nuwakot district, Nepal. Photograph: Narendra Shrestha/EPA

Residents look at the Trishuli River as they take shelter at an elevated place after a flood warning in the Pipaltar area of Nepal's Nuwakot district. Nepal issued a warning on August 28 to move to higher ground after a dam upstream in Tibet was reported to have burst, two days after a glacial co…

blocks.text: Australian foreign minister Penny Wong spoke to her Nepalese counterpart to convey Australia’s deepest condolences following the devastating floods.

In a post on X, Wong wrote that she had spoken to Shisir Khanal, and outlined Australia’s $5m humanitarian assistance package announced earlier today, which includes $2 million to the World Food Programme and $1 million to the Emergency Action Alliance.
Minister Wong also outlined the details of the deployment of Australian humanitarian response specialists to assist Nepal with response and recovery efforts.
She reaffirmed Australia’s readiness to provide further humanitarian and other assistance as needed, as the country works to confirm the welfare of those missing.
You can read her post on X here.
Death toll in Nepal-Tibet flood rises to 543
The overall death toll in Nepal has risen to 538 people, with more than 1,500 still missing, AFP report, citing the disaster authority.
Chinese state media earlier confirmed five dead following Wednesday’s disaster, taking the total killed to at least 543.
Earlier this morning, it was 469.
More than 100 tourists have been rescued from the floods in Nepal.
So far, 117 tourists have been rescued, including 85 Indians, 16 Chinese, 9 South Koreans, 2 Italians and 2 US nationals, Reuters reports, citing a tourism ministry source.
More than ⁠90,000 people are estimated to ⁠be affected ⁠by ​the Himalayan landslide, the Red Cross ⁠said on Friday, as aid ⁠officials voiced fears ​of ‌further flooding.
“We’re of ‌course very concerned ‌about the secondary flood,” said David Fisher, head of delegation for the ‌International Federation of Red Cross and Red ​Crescent Societies in Nepal.
He said that its trucks ⁠with relief supplies ​were ​blocked after a ​lake formed by ​the ‌landslide ​broke ​its banks.

blocks.caption: Hannah Ellis-Petersen

blocks.text: Hannah Ellis-Petersen
Bidur, on the banks of the Trishuli river, is one of the few areas affected by the floods that is still accessible by road.

But what was once a bustling town now lies in ruins. Most homes were completely washed away when a tide of mud, rocks and debris flooded down the river valley early on Wednesday morning. Those who survived described clinging on to buildings and trees as the water rushed over them.

The mangled concrete remains of a bank, a government office and an ATM booth were among the few structures left standing, still submerged deep in mud. Officials said there were still bodies buried inside the buildings but it was too dangerous to enter and dig them out.
Nearby, locals gathered desperately along the muddy road, calling out for lost relatives and trying to dig out remnants of their lives.

Yet rescue efforts in Bidur were quickly disrupted on Friday morning as the levels of the Trishuli river began to rise once again, after a lake upstream, close to the China border, burst its banks. Revsue workers were cleared from the area while residents who had tried to return to their site of their lost and ruined homes were told to evacuate again immediately.

Most of the areas battered by the flash floods still remained only accessible by army helicopter. In Bidur army camp, where much of the rescue efforts was being coordinated, rescue helicopters and army choppers flew in and out every five minutes, dropping off dozens of traumatised victims. Many said that in a matter of minutes, the floods had taken their loved ones, their homes and everything they owned.
This aerial footage shows the lake that formed as a result of the flooding, which started to overflow.

blocks.caption: Barrier lake forms at base of mountains near Nepal border

blocks.text: Rescue operations resumed after pause due to overflowing lake

Nepalese ⁠authorities have ⁠resumed ⁠rescue operations in ​the region ⁠hit by a ⁠devastating ​flood ‌this ‌week, an ‌army spokesperson said on Friday, after ‌a brief suspension due ​to water overflowing ⁠from ​a barrier ​lake.
An Australian woman has made contact with her family, more than two days after she was reported missing in flash flooding in Nepal.
Cara Severino, 25, is the first of 39 Australians reported missing in the tragedy to have been confirmed safe.
But she is still hiking away from the disaster zone, attempting to reach Kathmandu on foot with a group of Nepali hikers – a trek of more than 110km.

Her parents, Debbie and Frank Severino, confirmed in a statement that she had no phone reception, and her own phone had a flat battery, but that she had contacted them on Friday morning to say she was safe.
In a statement, they said:

double quotation markShe was hiking the Langtang trek and was stranded. With communications down we had no contact. This morning she was able to call us from Gosainkunda where she has been able to reach along with some other [Nepali] hikers. We understand that they are attempting to reach Kathmandu on foot. We eagerly await more information about her safe return. We praise God that she has been able to make this brief contact with us. Our thoughts and prayers are with all the families awaiting news.

articles.summary: Rappler's data visualizations map the cities and provinces where Filipino families earn the most, revealing a persistent Luzon-Mindanao divide, based on the PSA's latest Family Income and Expenditure…

Rappler's data visualizations map the cities and provinces where Filipino families earn the most, revealing a persistent Luzon-Mindanao divide, based on the PSA's latest Family Income and Expenditure Survey

items: The average annual family income in the Philippines was P411,350 in 2025, with significant disparities across regions and cities.
Makati had the highest average income at P796,990, while Zamboanga City had the lowest at P309,610, highlighting a Luzon-Mindanao economic divide.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.
MANILA, Philippines – An average Filipino family’s income can look vastly different depending on where in the country they live.

Nationwide, average annual family income stood at P411,350 in 2025, or about P34,300 a month, according to preliminary results of the Philippine Statistics Authority’s (PSA) latest Family Income and Expenditure Survey (FIES).

But families in some of the country’s wealthiest cities and provinces earned far more. Makati had the highest average annual income among highly urbanized cities (HUCs) at P796,990, while Ilocos Norte led the country’s provinces at P619,240.

Makati’s figure works out to around P66,400 a month, nearly twice the national average. The next four highest HUCs were also all in Metro Manila: San Juan at P735,960, Parañaque at P711,310, Mandaluyong at P676,130, and Quezon City at P648,150.

At the other end was Zamboanga City, where families earned an average P309,610 annually, or about P25,800 a month. Average family income in Makati was more than two-and-a-half times that in Zamboanga City.
The PSA comparison covers HUCs, rather than every city in the Philippines.
The FIES rankings point to a clear concentration of higher family incomes in Luzon, particularly around the country’s main economic centers.

At the regional level, National Capital Region (NCR) led with an average family income of P574,370, followed by Calabarzon at P526,070 and Central Luzon at P447,310. They were the only three regions above the national average of P411,350, further showing how much economic activity and higher-paying jobs cluster in and around Metro Manila. At the other end were the Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao (BARMM) at P246,050, the Zamboanga Peninsula at P286,340, and Soccskargen at P292,820.

The provincial rankings show a similar pattern. Ilocos Norte topped all provinces at P619,240, followed by Batanes, Cavite, Rizal, and Batangas. At the other end, the five lowest-income provinces were all in Mindanao, led by Maguindanao del Sur at just P177,750. Ilocos Norte’s average was nearly three-and-a-half times as high.

Ilocos Norte’s place at the top is striking because it sits outside the Luzon Economic Corridor. One clue may be where families in the province get their income. PSA data show they rely less on salaries and more on overseas remittances and business income than the national average. Wages accounted for just 39.8% of family income in Ilocos Norte in 2025, while cash receipts from abroad made up 20.2% and entrepreneurial activities another 19.1%. Nationally, wages accounted for 54.6% of family income and cash from abroad just 8.5%.

Ilocos Norte’s rise has also been unusually fast. Average family income there climbed from about P364,800 in 2021 to P447,860 in 2023, and P619,240 in 2025 – nearly 70% in four years versus about 34% nationwide. The increase also sped up after 2023, with income growth jumping from 22.8% in 2021-2023 to 38.3% in 2023-2025.

That timing overlaps with the presidency of Ferdinand Marcos Jr., whose family’s political dynasty has long counted Ilocos Norte as its bulwark. Still, the FIES by itself deoesn’t show what drove the province’s income surge or whether increased national government spending played any role.

blocks.caption: The Philippines is now upper-middle income. Really?

blocks.text: Speaking of growth, today’s richest places were not necessarily the ones where incomes grew fastest.

Average family income increased in every region from 2023 to 2025, with Cagayan Valley recording the fastest growth at 25%, from P310,550 to P388,220. Despite that increase, the region’s average family income remained below the national average.
Soccskargen posted the slowest regional growth at just 3.7%.
At the provincial level, Samar registered the biggest increase at 54.4%, with average family income jumping from P231,430 in 2023 to P357,340 in 2025.
Not everywhere saw gains. Sultan Kudarat posted the largest decline at 8.2%, from P293,830 to P269,610.

How families earn their income also differs across the country. Wages and salaries were the largest source of family income in every region except BARMM, where entrepreneurial activities accounted for 43.8% of total family income. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Who is Norway's new King Haakon VIII?
articles.summary: Haakon becomes the king at a turbulent time for Norway's monarchy.

blocks.text: King Haakon VIII has inherited the Norwegian throne after the death of his father, Harald V. Many in Norway believe he has big shoes to fill.
King Harald was immensely popular with ordinary Norwegians, as shown by his consistent high polling and the outpouring of emotion in the lead-up to his death.
Haakon is the fourth king to head Norway's modern monarchy, since it was restored in 1905 after the country gained independence from Sweden.
Among his first duties as monarch, he led an extraordinary cabinet meeting where he announced his royal title and adopted his father's motto "Everything for Norway".
Many commentators believe he is well-placed to follow in his predecessors' footsteps.

As crown prince, Haakon worked closely with his father as he carried out his royal duties and in recent years was handed more responsibility, increasingly acting as regent while Harald was ill or absent.
"I am so lucky that Crown Prince Haakon is the one who will carry this forward," King Harald wrote of his son in his biography The King Tells.
Historian Trond Norén Isaksen tells the BBC that Haakon will be a different type of king to his father, but no less respected.
"King Harald... [was] very charismatic, he [had] a great sense of humour, which everyone appreciates, and Haakon is a bit more reserved, a bit more like his mother.

"But in recent years he has also become a bit more relaxed and opened up a bit and showed a bit more of his sense of humour... he has been pulling enormous weight for many years given his parents have become older and his wife has been ill."
Haakon is a great-great-great-grandson of Britain's Queen Victoria.
His daughter Ingrid Alexandra, 22, now becomes the crown princess and heir to the Norwegian throne.
But their relationship was not without controversy and there was a fierce public debate in Norway from the moment Haakon first announced they were dating.

Some commentators even warned at the time that their relationship could spell the end of the Norwegian monarchy, with comparisons being made to the infamous union between American divorcee Wallis Simpson and British King Edward VIII which led to his abdication in 1936.
Mette-Marit was not the first commoner to marry into the Norwegian royal family - the late King Harald had already broken with tradition by marrying Queen Sonja three decades earlier.
She was, however, a single mother to a four-year-old child whose father had served time for a conviction of cocaine possession.

The royal couple's co-habitation in an Oslo flat had also drawn criticism from the conservative Lutheran Church of Norway - though polls from the time showed most ordinary Norwegians did not care about either.
What many Norwegians did question, though, was whether her former party lifestyle was one compatible with that of someone married to the future king.

In an emotional interview three days before their marriage, Mette-Marit publicly apologised for her "wild past" and condemned drug use after reports that drugs were taken at parties she attended in Oslo during the 1990s.
She did not say whether she had taken them herself.
It was seen as something of a turning point. She won the affection of ordinary Norwegians and for years has been seen as the embodiment of a modern monarchy capable of shaking up convention.
The couple have two children together, Ingrid and Prince Sverre Magnus.
In her new role as crown princess, she took up popular causes including support for people with HIV and promoting literacy.
Her diagnosis with pulmonary fibrosis in 2018 also led to widespread public sympathy.

Haakon has said Mette-Marit helped him come out of his shell and described her as an emotional counterweight to his analytical mind. "I am not very good socially," he wrote. "Mette is a natural talent. She can go into a room and get along with everyone."
But in recent times, Haakon's family has come under increasingly heavy public scrutiny and criticism.
Marius Borg Høiby's rape conviction hangs over the family. One of women was raped on Haakon's estate at Skaugum outside Oslo.
Høiby has always been treated as one of the family, although the royal house has repeatedly stressed he is not a royal.
Days before his trial began, documents were released revealing Mette-Marit's frequent contact with late sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.

She later apologised to King Harald and Queen Sonja for her three-year friendship with Epstein and admitted to "poor judgement", adding in a national TV interview that she wished she had never met him.
Several polls conducted earlier this year found nearly half of Norway's population felt the crown princess could not become queen, even though it was always bound to happen.
Two days after her son's trial came to an end, Mette-Marit received a lung transplant, eight years after her initial diagnosis.
Her doctors will not declare her stable until a year after the transplant, and the new king will face a difficult period of succession as he continues to support her.

Caroline Vagle, royal correspondent for Se og Hør magazine, says in regards to Epstein the most important thing the royal family can do is be "completely open about what actually happened, and not allow public speculation to take on a life of its own".
"But I also don't think we should overestimate the impact of one or two difficult cases," she says.
"What will ultimately matter is how the royal family handles them, and how Haakon and the next generation manage to build on the trust that Harald has earned over a lifetime."
Tove Taalesen, royal correspondent for Nettavisen, believes the scandals will be challenging but Haakon is "very much ready for the task".
"I'm sure that in the future he will be respected and loved, similar to King Haakon VII, King Olav V and also King Harald V."
Haakon's reign begins in the backdrop of these scandals, and how he navigates them might come to define his monarchy.

articles.title: Manlapaz stamps class, advances to Intercol Round of 16
articles.summary: University of Santo Tomas' Josh Manlapaz lived up to his billing as the top seed with a splendid performance after advancing to the next round of the collegiate men's singles at the 2026 Philippine…

blocks.text: University of Santo Tomas' Josh Manlapaz lived up to his billing as the top seed with a splendid performance after advancing to the next round of the collegiate men's singles at the 2026 Philippine Intercollegiate and Interscholastic Challenge on Friday,, Aug. 28, at the Home Court at Ayala Malls Manila Bay in Parañaque City.

The UAAP Season 87 Rookie of the Year bounced back from a hiccup in the tight second game to subdue San Beda University's Ace Gumabay, 11-6, 11-13, 11-2, 11-7, and clinch a spot in the Round of 16 later in the day.
"Honestly, nakaka-pressure kasi nga top seed ako. Inaasahan ring ako ng mga teammates ko na kaya kong manalo," said Manlapaz.

"Huwag lang patalo sa kaba at sana tapangan ko pa lalo," he added on what he needs to do to go all the way in the tournament, which is backed by Huaching Foundation, the Philippine Sports Commission, PLDT, Topcoms Marketing Inc., Mizuno Philippines, Cara Celine Dormtel, Gold Cross Security Agency, and Best Options Assistance Inc., along with Dino Jalandoni, Bombit Silva, and Eric Ongkauco.

Manlapaz, now one of the pillars of the reigning six-time UAAP champions, earlier dominated his group with a straight-set conquest of YING's Raul Mallen and a walkover win over De La Salle University-Dasmariñas' Carlos Batino VII.
The incoming Thomasian junior will face DLSU's Yves Reg, who defeated Philippine Women's University's Brent Melgarejo, 11-3, 11-1, 11-2, later this evening.
Elsewhere in the draw, up-and-coming stars also made their mark, with UST's Jebb Datahan and UP's Stephen Llemit securing spots in the last 16.
Both fresh off storied high school careers, Datahan and Llemit booked their tickets to the Round of 16 following clinical victories.

Datahan, a three-time UAAP High School Boys' MVP, swept Jose Rizal University's Dylan Pahimnayon, 11-4, 11-5, 11-7, while Llemit, a 2026 Palarong Pambansa multi-medalist, took down PWU's Alfredo Alejandre, 13-11, 11-9, 8-11, 11-1.
On the women's side, a former and the reigning UAAP MVP secured their spots in the main draw after sweeping their respective groups.
UAAP Season 86 top athlete DLSU's Angel Laude dominated DLSU-Dasmariñas' Georgina Turpin, 11-3, 11-3, 11-2, and UP's Maan Gomobao, 11-5, 11-3, 11-4.
Meanwhile, last year's MVP Chrishien Santillan of Far Eastern University waylaid Trisha Pachica of the Blue Paddlers, 11-2, 11-1, 11-5, and turned back PWU's Nicole Garcia, 11-6, 11-7, 9-11, 11-9.
In the high school division, familiar names also shone in the boys' singles.
UST stalwarts and top seeds Emmanuel Paculba Jr. and Joshua Banas secured outright places in the Round of 16 after sweeping their respective groups.
Paculba will face Liam Cabalu of Victory Christian International School, while Banas drew Ynigo Adriano of Centris for a place in the quarterfinals.
Selected matches can be viewed live on the CPlay app and the One Sports YouTube channel.

articles.title: Nepal-Tibet flood rescue efforts resume after being halted by overflowing lake
articles.summary: Risk of fresh flooding had forced rescue teams to withdraw as residents rushed up hills to escape possible river surge
articles.byline: Hannah Ellis-Petersen in Bidur, Sam Jones and agencies

blocks.text: Rescuers searching for survivors of deadly flash floods on the Nepal-Tibet border have resumed their efforts after suspending operations when a debris dam burst its bank on Friday, increasing the risk of fresh flooding.

Residents in Nepal’s Rasuwa district, on the border with Tibet, were seen rushing up hillsides ⁠on Friday to escape a possible surge in the river, ⁠according to witnesses. Fears of another flood came as authorities in Nepal and China said that at least 543 people had been killed in the disaster.

blocks.caption: Barrier lake forms at base of mountains near Nepal border

blocks.text: More than 500 foreign citizens were among 826 people missing in Nepal, police and tourism ⁠officials said, including 177 from India, 90 from the US, 34 from Australia, 33 from Britain and 25 from Canada. Chinese state media said at least 558 were missing on the Tibet side of the border, of whom at least 260 were foreign nationals.
The flood on Wednesday had destroyed power stations, roads and bridges along a route that links Kathmandu with Lhasa in Tibet and is ⁠popular with trekkers and pilgrims.

The Chinese state broadcaster CCTV reported that a lake formed by piles of debris from the mudslide had begun overflowing on Friday, sending water towards the area where rescue teams were headed, and forcing a brief pause in operations.

Rescue efforts in Bidur, the capital of the Nuwakot district in Bagmati province, Nepal, were disrupted on Friday morning as the the Trishuli River began to rise again after the lake near the China border burst its banks.
Rescue workers were moved from the area and people who had tried to return to what remained of their homes were told to evacuate again immediately.

Bidur, once a bustling town on the banks of the Trishuli, now lies in ruins. Most homes were washed away when a tide of mud, rocks and debris surged down the river valley early on Wednesday. Survivors described clinging to buildings and trees as the water rushed over them.

The mangled concrete remains of a bank, a government office and an ATM booth were among the few structures left standing, although they were submerged in mud. Officials said there were still bodies inside the buildings but it was too dangerous to recover them.
Nearby, local people gathered along the muddy road, calling out for lost relatives and trying to dig out what was left of their belongings.

Most areas battered by flash floods remained accessible only by army helicopter. At the Bidur army camp, where much of the rescue effort was being coordinated, rescue and military helicopters flew in and out every five minutes, bringing in dozens of traumatised victims. Many said that in a matter of minutes, the floods had taken their loved ones, their homes and everything they owned.
The international community is scrambling to get aid to flood-stricken parts of Nepal and Tibet.

blocks.caption: Sludge inundates homes after flash floods in Nuwakot district. Photograph: AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: Nepal has said it does not yet need foreign assistance as the search-and-rescue operation – complicated by the destruction of dozens of bridges and miles of roads across the mountainous region – continues.

“The offer for help is natural,” Lok Bahadur Chhetri, a spokesperson for Nepal’s foreign ministry, said on Friday. “Our security agencies ‌are doing the search and rescue operation. For now we don’t require such help.”

The Kathmandu Post reported that India, China, the US, Britain, Japan, South Korea, Sri Lanka and Bangladesh had asked the government to allow their search-and-rescue teams to assist in the operation.

Dinesh Bhattarai, a former Nepali ⁠ambassador to the UN in Geneva, said the government’s reluctance to ​accept foreign assistance may ​be linked to sensitivities over ​Rasuwa district and its border with China’s Tibet region.
after newsletter promotion
“They may have thought about ​the locational sensitivity ‌of the region and ​decided not to ​accept foreign teams,” Bhattarai told Reuters.
But Chhetri said Nepal’s own rescue teams were handling the operation and the decision to refuse foreign assistance had nothing to do with sensitivities involving China.

Scant information has emerged from Chinese authorities about the scale of the destruction in Tibet, the most tightly controlled part of China even under normal circumstances. Only brief, state-controlled media reports about the floods have been allowed to circulate in China and the authorities have confirmed only three deaths there. Chinese reports have focused on rescue efforts.
In Nepal earlier on Friday, army helicopter rescue teams were working to free about 100 people trapped in a tunnel at a flooded hydropower project.
“Our focus is in search and rescue of people … some people are trapped in the tunnel of Trishuli 3A hydropower project,” said the Nepal army spokesperson, Raja Ram Basnet.

“Two helicopters have been dispatched but it is challenging because it is tough to even locate the entry points of the tunnel. Relief efforts are also under way to provide the rescued people what they need.”
The prime minister’s office said the army was working in challenging conditions and had rescued 350 workers and local people who were trapped in the tunnel.

Rescue teams reported finding bodies hundreds of miles downstream from the disaster zone in the Chitwan district of Nepal, near the Tibetan border. Dozens of injured people were transported to Kathmandu for advanced medical care and more than 100 people were rescued by Nepali army personnel in helicopters.
CCTV said 499 Chinese nationals and 555 foreigners had been transported out of the disaster zone as of Friday.
With Agence France-Presse and Reuters

articles.title: A creative journey for a cause
articles.summary: Art can offer more than something to look at. For the artists participating in “Journeys,” it is also a way to help give underprivileged children an alternative outlet through free art workshops.…

blocks.text: Lifestyle | Arts and Culture
'Journeys' showcases works by established and emerging Filipino artists, with proceeds supporting free art workshops for underprivileged children
Art can offer more than something to look at. For the artists participating in “Journeys,” it is also a way to help give underprivileged children an alternative outlet through free art workshops.

Organized by Erehwon Art Foundation Inc. in cooperation with Art Lounge Manila (ALM), the fundraising exhibition brings together established and emerging Filipino visual artists, with proceeds from the sale of their works going toward free art workshops for children from disadvantaged communities. The initiative aims to provide them with a creative outlet while steering them away from violence.
The exhibition features works by National Artist nominee Luis “Junyee” Yee, modern sculptor Julie Lluch, and Filipino printmaker Pandy Aviado, alongside works by a younger generation of artists.

“Journeys” was organized with the belief that exposure to positive artistic experiences can play a role in shaping young people's outlook. Event initiator and Erehwon trustee June P. Dalisay, an art conservator, believes that such experiences can influence a more positive psychosocial outlook among the youth.

The exhibition also offers considerable variety in both subject and medium. The works range from serene and colorful to thought-provoking, unusual, and tongue-in-cheek. Materials include acrylic, oil, assemblage, pen and ink, collage, watercolor, and eco-conscious sculpture.
