articles.title: Why Germany's military is betting on gamers
articles.summary: For the past 10 years, the German armed forces — the Bundeswehr — have been represented at Gamescom, Cologne's video game trade fair. They've been criticized for trying to draw more young people into…

image.caption: The Bundeswehr will once again be represented at the Gamescom video game trade fair in Cologne in 2026Image: Kristina Reymann-Schneider/DW

blocks.text: Gamescom, which runs from August 26-30 in Cologne, is promoted as the world's largest video game trade show.

Last year, two-thirds of its non-industry visitors were male, with over 40% of them between the ages of 16 and 25. Those are precisely the young people the Bundeswehr, Germany's armed forces, is trying to reach as it urgently seeks to expand its ranks.

Germany's military aims to have 260,000 active-duty soldiers by 2035. The German government has supplied hundreds of billions of euros to modernize the country's armed forces. Defense has become a priority for Germany in the face of the current global security situation.
Career advice in camouflage
The Bundeswehr set up shop at Gamescom for the first time in 2016. It's been back every year since.

A brand-new, olive-green Caracal off-road vehicle is one of the main attractions. Alongside it are laptops belonging to the Bundeswehr's Center for Cyber Operations — tasked with cyber defense, among other responsibilities.
Under a watchful eye, visitors can try their hand at hacking.

blocks.caption: The Caracal off-road vehicle is a popular photo opportunity at the Bundeswehr boothImage: Kristina Reymann-Schneider/DW

blocks.text: At another station, visitors can put on VR headsets to get a glimpse into the working life of a soldier aboard a naval vessel. Pilots, aircraft mechanics and air traffic controllers present their professions in a 3D experience. Elsewhere, several fit mountain infantry soldiers stand beside a pull-up bar, where visitors are invited to test their strength.

New this year is a career lounge where interested visitors can have what the Bundeswehr is calling "career counseling sessions." The atmosphere is positive, with soldiers promoting their jobs without being pushy, taking time to answer questions from visitors — who have primarily come to Gamescom to have fun, meet friends and play the latest games.
Do gamers make good soldiers?

A representative study by Germany's Bitkom digital association found that one in five people found it likely that video and computer games teach skills that could be useful in wartime — training reaction speed and problem-solving, for instance. However, being a good gamer doesn't necessarily make for a good soldier.

blocks.caption: Lieutenant General Robert Sieger, president of the Federal Office for Bundeswehr Personnel ManagementImage: Kristina Reymann-Schneider/DW

blocks.text: "We need people who are comfortable with technology," Lt. Gen. Robert Sieger, president of the Federal Office for Bundeswehr Personnel Management, told DW. "What we don't want are people who think we're playing an ego shooter or some kind of shooting game. That doesn't do justice to the seriousness of the situation at all. War isn't a game. As a soldier and a general, it is important to me that people understand the seriousness of what we do."

For Sieger, educating people about the Bundeswehr and the range of careers it offers is a central reason for having a booth at Gamescom. "We're an integral part of our country's safety net. We have to simply be here and show what it means to stand up for the freedom of our country, be that as a soldier or a civilian."
Criticism of Bundeswehr presence
The Bundeswehr is represented alongside many other employers in the gaming trade show's Job Area, including Germany's federal police, retailer Edeka and software company DATEV.

Gamescom is, however, still a video game trade show — and not everyone is comfortable with the Bundeswehr getting close to the gaming world. The German Peace Society — United War Resisters has criticized the Bundeswehr presence at Gamescom, along with booths operated by Germany's foreign intelligence service and defense companies such as Airbus and Rheinmetall.

blocks.caption: 'Level Up for Your Career': Peace activists criticize the Bundeswehr's use of gaming jargonImage: Kristina Reymann-Schneider/DW

blocks.text: Peace campaigner Marius Pletsch says the Bundeswehr uses inappropriate slogans, designed to appeal specifically to gamers, and distorts the image of military service.

"We think it's wrong to lure young people to the booth by appealing to their sense of adventure. We don't think the Bundeswehr should be represented at a trade show that is primarily about video games and leisure to boost its personnel numbers," he told DW.
For two days, the peace organization will have a booth outside the trade show exhibition halls, providing information about conscientious objection to military service.
Bundeswehr: Not just any job
"Being a soldier isn't a normal job," the peace initiative said in a statement.
Lt. Gen. Sieger uses similar terms, but puts it somewhat differently: "Being a soldier isn't a job like any other. We put our lives on the line for the security of our people."

He reaches a different conclusion than the peace advocates, though. "It would be downright negligent for an organization responsible for our country's security not to be an inherent part of society," Sieger said. "As an inherent part of society and a modern employer, of course we have our rightful spot here in the Job Area, just as we have over recent years."
What do young Gamescom visitors make of the Bundeswehr's presence?

"Morally questionable, but a good employer," said Dennis, a 22-year-old computer science student, although he said the Bundeswehr wasn't for him. Dominik, 26, said he was pleased that the German military was represented at Gamescom. "You can actually have a pretty good conversation with them. They're all very nice," he said. He said he may even consider working for the Bundeswehr's cyber defense division.
This article was originally written in German.

articles.title: ‘So desperately loved’: ADF member among dozens of Australians missing in Nepal floods as families pray for safe return
articles.summary: Relatives ‘really worried, but hopeful’ as they wait anxiously for news in the aftermath of the flash flooding disaster
articles.byline: Henry Belot, Nino Bucci and Kat Wong

blocks.text: The families of an Australian defence force member and two Sydney boys who went missing with their parents in Nepal remain hopeful they will be found safe.

Dozens of Australians are missing after devastating flooding on the Nepal-Tibet border. Nepal police on Friday said more than 1,500 people remained missing and 469 have been confirmed dead after massive flash floods and landslides tore through the Bhotekoshi and Trishuli river basins.
One Australian woman contacted her family on Friday morning to tell them that she had survived the flood, the first of those reported missing to be confirmed safe.
Among the missing Australians is Karan Bhardwaj, a 40-year-old Brisbane-based member of the Royal Australian air force who was travelling in Nepal with Kailash Journeys.
“Karan is a dad to my beautiful seven-year-old nephew, as well as a brother, uncle and brother in law,” said his family member Jen, who did not want her surname published.
“He is so desperately loved by his family and right now we are desperately praying, hoping and believing that Karan is safe, alive and somehow making his way back to us.”
Shylaja Muralitharan, 42, her husband, Chandrasekaran Muralitharan, 47, and their two sons Ashwin, 14, and Aarush, 11, were taking part in a pilgrimage when the flood hit on Wednesday.
Shylaja’s younger sister, Vaishnavi, said that she had lost contact with the family shortly after breakfast on the morning of the flood.
The family of four planned to head towards an immigration checkpoint on the Tibet-Nepal border soon after, as part of the group of 15 Australians trekking with the Himalayan Glacier Adventures tour.
“Just like everyone else that’s part of that group, we’re really worried, but hopeful,” Vaishnavi said.
“Hopeful that they’re safe and just waiting to be rescued.
“It’s a very difficult time for our whole family … I just want to make people aware that they’re there, and we’re waiting, and we just want them to return.”

Vaishnavi, who asked that her surname not be published, confirmed the family were close with other members of the group who had also travelled from Sydney for the Hindu pilgrimage to Mount Kailash in Tibet.
The family had been training together for the long walk, she said.
“They had been planning for some time, and preparing, because it’s quite a trek.
“They were all working very hard together to make sure they could successfully complete it.
“We just didn’t expect anything like this.”
Vaishnavi said it was difficult to get clear information about what was being done to find those missing. She has spoken with Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade officials.
“We do want to know what efforts are being made … we’re not aware of what is actually happening there.”
Australian woman Sumi Adhikari was at an immigration office at the Gyirong Post crossing when the flood waters hit. She was travelling with an Isha Foundation pilgrimage to the region.
Her husband, Nava Pandey, has travelled to Nepal and is desperately seeking information about her whereabouts.

“She was in the same area when the flood happened,” said a flyer produced by Adhikari’s family, and published with their permission. “If anyone has seen her or has any information about her, please contact the family immediately.”

blocks.caption: Sumi Adhikari was travelling as part of an Isha Foundation pilgrimage. Illustration: supplied

blocks.text: Bharat Mangwani, 42, was travelling with the Isha Foundation as part of a pilgrimage to Lake Manasarovar when his family lost contact with him on Wednesday morning.
He was last seen at Gyirong before the group was set to depart for Kathmandu and then Delhi, his close friend Kushagra Tiwari said.
Mangwani’s family, including his nine-year-old son and three-year-old daughter, have travelled to India with a family friend, while his wife has gone on to Kathmandu to look for any information.
“All of us are praying for him and hopefully he comes back to us soon,” Tiwari said.
Suhasini Kandimalla, a mother of two from Springfield, near Brisbane, has also been reported missing.
Her sister, Supreethini Kandimalla, said that she was doing the hike with another Springfield local.
after newsletter promotion

blocks.caption: Suhasini Kandimalla from Queensland who has been reported missing in Nepal. Photograph: Supplied

blocks.text: While she was a New Zealand citizen, Suhasini had been approved for Australian citizenship, her sister said. She had planned to attend a citizenship ceremony for it to be granted soon after she returned.
“I don’t know if it was a religious calling for her to do it,” Supreethini told the Guardian.
“But she certainly loved the treks in New Zealand too, and would go on lots of long hikes.”

A Brisbane man, Narayan Panthi, is also missing in the region. According to Nepal police, he was travelling with Kathmandu Holiday but he has also been conducting charity work in the capital with an education fund, the NeNas Foundation.

blocks.caption: Narayan Panthi from Brisbane is missing in Nepal. Photograph: Supplied

blocks.text: Panthi’s cousin, Amrit Bhusal, said his family was devastated but “holding on to hope and praying for positive news”.
“We are still hoping,” Bhusal said. “We are still searching. We are still praying for Narayan to come home safely.”
Bhusal said Panthi was “helping disadvantaged children in Nepal reach their full potential through education”.
New South Wales couple Venkatraman Balakrishnan, 52, and his wife, Chitra Venkatraman, 46, were also among the 15 Australians travelling to Mount Kailash.
So too were Sreedharan and Lakshmi Iyer, and their adult sons Rishab, 23, and Rudhra, 20.
The brothers played cricket for West Pennant Hills Cherrybrook Cricket Club in Sydney’s north-west.

“WPHCCC is aware of the reports that two of our players, Rishab and Rudhra Iyer, along with their family members and other Australians, are unaccounted for in the ongoing floods in Nepal,” the club said in a statement.
“We continue to live in hope, and our thoughts are currently with them, their loved ones and all affected by this tragedy in Nepal.”
The University of Newcastle’s vice-chancellor, Alex Zelinsky, said Rishab and Rudhra were both medical students the at the university.

“We are thinking of them, their families, their fellow students and teaching staff, as well as the many people who have been impacted by this devastating event and we hope that both students can be located soon,” Zelinsky said in a statement.
Separate groups of Australians – 11 travelling with Trekkers Society and six with Kailash Journeys – are also unaccounted for. Both tour companies have been contacted for comment.
Several other Australians were travelling with other tour groups. It is understood the majority of missing Australians are from New South Wales, but there are also some from Victoria and Queensland.
The founder and chief executive of Himalayan Glacier Adventures, Sagar Pandey, said he had lost all contact with his tour group of 47 people, which included the 15 Australians.
Pandey told the Guardian on Thursday he had flown by helicopter over the Rasuwa area, where the tour was staying, since the flood and had little hope they survived.
“To be honest … you would think there was no human civilisation there at all.
“The flash flood swept away everything, everything. You couldn’t see any human creations.
“Still, I have a hope.”
The Isha Foundation confirmed that 11 Australians were among a group of 80 missing pilgrims who had been in an immigration building when the flood hit.
The foreign minister, Penny Wong, spoke to her Nepali counterpart, Shisir Khanal, on Friday evening to convey Australia’s deepest condolences following the devastating floods.
She outlined Australia’s humanitarian assistance package in which Australia was “rapidly mobilising consular and humanitarian support in response” to the flooding.
Wong said the government would send an initial team of three humanitarian response specialists “within the next 48 hours’” to help Australian staff already on the ground.
“The extraordinary scale of this disaster and the remoteness of the affected region mean immense challenges lie ahead for the response and recovery.”

blocks.text: The Bulacan provincial government trained local officials on faster, clearer, and more transparent service delivery during a capacity‑building workshop on Wednesday, Aug. 26, at the Hiyas ng Bulacan Convention Center.

blocks.caption: Provincial Cooperative and Enterprise Development Office head Atty. Jayric L. Amil with business permits and licensing officers, local economic development and investment promotion officers, and anti‑red tape focal persons during the “Building Better Public Service” workshop in Malolos. Also in p…

blocks.text: Provincial Cooperative and Enterprise Development Office head Atty. Jayric L. Amil with business permits and licensing officers, local economic development and investment promotion officers, and anti‑red tape focal persons during the “Building Better Public Service” workshop in Malolos. Also in photo are officer Mary Grace Evangelista, Anti‑Red Tape Authority Regional Chief Mary Grace B. Manabat, Supervising Administrative Officer Jonina D.C. Madrid, and other officials. (Photo from Provincial Public Affairs Office – PPAO)
Led by the Provincial Cooperative and Enterprise Development Office (PCEDO) with the Anti‑Red Tape Authority (ARTA), the program focused on Republic Act 11032 or the Ease of Doing Business Act.
Topics included citizen’s charters, client satisfaction measurement, and complaints handling.
Governor Daniel R. Fernando, in his message, reminded public servants that leadership is measured by action.

“Efficiency at work creates trust and confidence among our people. That trust attracts businesses and investments. And when there are more businesses and investments, there are more opportunities -- that’s what grows our local economy,” he said.
The training is part of Bulacan’s Ease of Doing Business Champion Program, which rewards LGUs that excel in citizen‑centered governance and smooth investment processing.

articles.title: Satellite images show bedrock and glacier collapsed on Nepal-China border, then rivers flooded
articles.summary: As rescue teams searched for missing people following catastrophic flooding along the Nepal-China border, Earth scientists reviewed satellite imagery for clues to the cause and assessed the…

blocks.text: As rescue teams searched for missing people following catastrophic flooding along the Nepal-China border, Earth scientists reviewed satellite imagery for clues to the cause and assessed the devastation.

blocks.caption: This satellite image provided by Vantor shows Syapru Besi, Nepal on Oct. 18, 2023. (Satellite image ©2026 Vantor via AP)

blocks.text: This satellite image provided by Vantor shows Syapru Besi, Nepal on Oct. 18, 2023. (Satellite image ©2026 Vantor via AP)
The flooding Wednesday killed hundreds of people in Nepal and Tibet, and hundreds more are missing, including foreigners and pilgrims.

Geomorphologists Kristen Cook and Dan Shugar said initial images from Nepal were obscured by clouds and dust from the debris, so they could only see that part of a glacier had broken off from Langtang Lirung peak, near the border with Tibet. In clearer images from Thursday, they said they could see that the bedrock underneath the glacier had collapsed, taking the massive chunk of ice down with it and sending boulders and ice into the valley.

"It shows the whole area without anything hidden, and we could see that, yes, it looked like there was not only this glacier that had failed, but a much larger chunk of the bedrock of the mountainside itself that had given way," said Shugar, associate professor at the University of Calgary. "You have this big bedrock failure that took part of the glacier with it."
Shugar said it's heart-wrenching to look downstream from there on the images, to where people were living, and see how the debris has buried villages.

After slamming to the valley floor, the debris maintained its momentum through the steep, narrow valley as ice melted, said Cook, at the Université Grenoble Alpes in France. Water and mud several stories high swept through communities.

The Trishuli River surged during the flooding. Before and after satellite images of the Kolpurtar, Betrawati and Syapru Besi areas of Nepal show that the river is now much wider, and brown and black, because it overtopped its banks in some areas and filled with debris in others. The change in the color of the water shows how much sediment the flow was carrying, turning from greenish to very brown because it's full of mud, Cook said.
Towns and villages that were devastated along the river banks are submerged in debris and mud. They appear as areas of brown. Some houses are still poking through in an image of the Betrawati area.

The flooding toppled and swept away buildings in Syapru Besi, a popular tourist spot where a famous trek to Langtang begins. In before and after images, a side river is now wider too, because the flow was so powerful it pushed upstream.

The flooding "left a wasteland in its wake" that will take many years to recover from, said Alton Byers, a mountain geographer at the University of Colorado at Boulder. Byers lived in Nepal and now returns there yearly to study glacial hazards and work with communities to prepare. This is the largest glacier flood he has seen, by far.

Byers, faculty research scientist at the university's Institute of Arctic and Alpine Research, said he thinks Wednesday's flooding is related to climate change. The Earth's warming is melting glaciers and permafrost, causing instability and the breakage of massive amounts of snow and ice at high altitudes. That can be a catalyst for a series of cascading events, he said.

"All the indicators, to me, point to the impacts of warming trends," he said. "In this case, the permafrost that for millennia has helped to hold together high-altitude rock and ice and soil and glaciers is now weakening and becoming unstable."

Cook and Shugar said that at this point, they can't say for sure there's a direct link to climate change. Slopes fail and landslides happen, Cook said, though permafrost is melting and that is destabilizing mountainsides.

"While we cannot at this point directly link this collapse to climate change, it is not unexpected to see more events of this type with a warming climate," Cook said. "Not this big, hopefully not this big."

articles.title: 'Not far enough' - US parents and teens on Meta's new limits for young users
articles.summary: As part of an $18bn settlement in a child-safety lawsuit, Meta announced new restrictions on its apps. We asked families what they thought.

blocks.text: For Elizabeth Cardner, a mother of two girls in Houston, Texas, Meta's new limits on how teenagers can use its platforms are a welcome sign that more people are aware of social media's potential dangers.
But, she tells the BBC, they probably won't help much in the long-term.
"It will save a few arguments at home, but it doesn't go far enough," she says.

This week, Meta announced new restrictions on its platforms - which include Instagram, Facebook and Whatsapp - as part of an $18bn (£13.25bn) settlement with US states in a lawsuit on social media's effects on children.

The company said it would set a daily two-hour time limit, hide the number of likes that a post receives, remove autoplay on videos, mute push notifications during school hours, and ban extreme make-up filters.
It also announced changes to its age-verification process and parental controls as well as agreeing to appoint an independent auditor to check the measures are implemented and maintained.

Many parents across the US see the restrictions as helpful, but are still sceptical. Those who spoke to the BBC described feeling stuck - where they feel they can't cut their children off from social media but also can't protect them from the harms they believe it causes - and they are waiting to see how much of a difference these new rules will make.

Cardner's 14-year-old, Paige, believes the restrictions will lead to "more real-life scenarios" and less "fake content", which she says dominates social media. She and her sister both approve of hiding the numbers of likes and restricting filters.
But Paige sees those gains as short-lived, "since AI is evolving".

"People will find new ways to have fake filters, and correct certain parts of their videos or pictures," she says. "So I think it'll help until people use other resources to try and find new ways to do that."
Cardner says banning her daughters entirely from social media would only result in them being left out by their peers.
"Damned if you do, damned if you don't," she says. "I don't think there's any winning on it."

Another mother of two teens, Andria Rose, told the BBC that she feels defenceless and "no matter how much I protect my kids, Facebook, Instagram - they're coming in and literally, like, taking them out of their rooms".
Even though she calls Meta's changes "fantastic", Rose, who lives near Boston, Massachusetts, doesn't believe they are fully addressing the problem.
"They're trying to limit the drug, but they're not controlling the drug," she says. "They're still dealing."
Rose notes her personal use of social media costs her sleep at night.
"I'm hooked," she says. "So what do you think is going to happen to a kid?"
The settlement was announced on Wednesday in the middle of a highly-anticipated trial, where Meta owner Mark Zuckerberg was expected to testify. The settlement did not include any admission of fault.

The lawsuit was originally filed in 2023 by 29 US states, alleging Meta deliberately designed its platforms to be addictive and lied about risks. They also accused it of violating a federal law on collecting children's personal information.
The settlement - announced this week - included 48 states, plus the District of Columbia and three US territories.

Several studies have found social media to be harmful to mental health, especially for children. Last year, a BBC investigation found children were being exposed to content about bullying, suicide and weapons on social media platforms.

For Rose, Meta's settlement payment "is like throwing a couple of dollar bills at a problem", given how much money the company makes and how much she believes the industry profited from children during the pandemic.
Joanie Story, a mother of four boys in Long Island, takes issue with another part of Meta's announcement - its conditions involving other platforms.
The company will withhold $5bn of the settlement, and only release it if YouTube, TikTok and others also enter into similar agreements.
It also said it would further tighten its time limit to one hour if other platforms implement similar restrictions. Story sees that as "petty".
"That's like saying: 'You know, we have the ability to fix what is broken, but we're only gonna fix it halfway,'" she says.

Still, Story is greeting the new rules as "good controls". She says she saw what a lack of controls could do when two of her sons were accidentally exposed to explicit content on a non-Meta platform. One boy has been in therapy for four years, she says.

articles.title: This Indian pilgrim was about to enter Tibet for her dream tour - then her WhatsApp messages stopped
articles.summary: Her family is among hundreds anxiously waiting for news after the deadly flash floods.

blocks.text: This Indian pilgrim was about to enter Tibet for her dream tour - then her WhatsApp messages stopped

blocks.caption: Image caption, Subhrasree Chakraborty in Kathmandu a day before she set out for the pilgrimage

blocks.text: Image source, Sudipto Bhattacharya
Subhrasree Chakraborty in Kathmandu a day before she set out for the pilgrimage
Early on Wednesday, Sudipto Bhattacharya received what would be the last messages from his wife.
She'd sent a picture of a departure stamp in her passport at 07:57 (02:27 GMT) - immigration at the Nepal border was done.
Six minutes later, at 08:03, she wrote: we are waiting to enter China. Then the messages stopped.

Subhrasree Chakraborty and the group she was travelling with had been waiting to cross into Tibet for the next stage of their pilgrimage to Mount Kailash, the sacred Himalayan home of Hindu god Shiva that Subhrasree had dreamed of visiting for years.

The 43-year-old is now among at least 290 Indians reported missing after deadly flash floods struck along Nepal's border with Tibet. Many of those unaccounted for were on the pilgrimage, which resumed last year after being disrupted by the pandemic and then by tensions between India and China. Thousands of Indians have been making their way to Mount Kailash for years.

Subhrasree was travelling without her family, as part of a group of about 30 people. A medical technologist working in critical care at a city hospital, she was used to emergencies. She knew CPR and intensive-care procedures and, according to her husband, was physically fit.
But none of that has brought her husband Sudipto Bhattacharya any closer to knowing what happened after that final message.
"After 08:03am, what happened? We don't know anything," he says.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Chakraborty sent her husband a photograph showing her Nepal immigration clearance before she crossed towards Chinese immigration (blurred from source)

blocks.text: Image source, Sudipto Bhattacharya
Chakraborty sent her husband a photograph showing her Nepal immigration clearance before she crossed towards Chinese immigration (blurred from source)
Subhrasree had been looking forward to the journey for years.
The photographs she sent home from Kathmandu, taken just days before she went missing, capture something of that excitement.

In one, she stands in a blue tunic in the ornate courtyard of a temple, smiling gently at the camera. In others, she is dressed in red, posing by the ancient brick-and-carved-wood architecture of Kathmandu valley's historic Durbar Square.
She told her husband the countryside was beautiful.
"She was very excited," says Bhattacharya, a government officer. "This was her dream tour."
The journey had begun on Friday 21 August.
She took the Mithila Express from Kolkata and reached Raxaul on 22 August. From there she crossed into Birgunj and travelled by bus to Kathmandu, arriving that night.
She stayed in Kathmandu for three nights, sightseeing.

Then, on the morning of 25 August, the group left Kathmandu by bus for Syabrubesi, a small mountain settlement roughly 122km north of Kathmandu and a gateway to the trekking hub of Langtang region. The journey took almost 12 hours - and was not entirely a smooth one.
A landslide blocked their route for about four hours before the army cleared the road. But when Subhrasree spoke to her husband, she told him the skies were clear.
There was little to suggest what was coming.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Chakraborty told her husband she the pilgrimage was her 'dream trip'

blocks.text: Image source, Sudipto Bhattacharya
Chakraborty told her husband she the pilgrimage was her 'dream trip'
"She kept saying the weather was good," he says. "She said it was rather warm, it was raining sometimes."
The next morning, 26 August, Subhrasree left her hotel shortly after 07:00.

Bhattacharya spoke to her on the phone, and the two continued messaging afterwards. Around an hour later, she told him the Nepal immigration formalities were complete and that the group was waiting to cross into Tibet.
After clearing Nepal immigration, pilgrims cross the border on foot to the Chinese immigration facility in Gyirong.
Bhattacharya believes his wife may have been inside, or close to, the Chinese immigration building when the disaster struck.
"I knew there would be connectivity issues on the Tibet side," he says. "So I waited for the next message."
At about 15:00, he saw reports of the floods in the media. He started calling pilgrims in her group. Nobody answered.
He tried the tour operator and then the two managers accompanying the group. Again, there was no answer.
The family has heard nothing from Subhrasree since.
"Have they been rescued? Was this group among those rescued in China?" Bhattacharya asks. "We want to know more."

He believes his wife and the others may already have crossed into Chinese territory before the floods struck. But he has received no confirmation of who made it across - or what happened to them afterwards.
"Please get me a list from the Chinese government," he says. "Missing, dead and rescued. We need an update."
Then comes the admission that captures the agony of those waiting at home: "What do I tell you? Sleepless nights, working on the phone."

blocks.caption: Image caption, The death toll has risen to 475, more than 48 hours after flash floods devastated the Himalayan border region

blocks.text: Image source, AFP via Getty Images
The death toll has risen to 475, more than 48 hours after flash floods devastated the Himalayan border region
For the family of 54-year-old Rina Banerjee, there is more uncertainty.
They do not even know which side of the border she was on when they lost contact.
Rina, an unmarried private tutor from Kolkata, was travelling alone with a tour operator as part of the same pilgrimage group.
Until then, her journey had appeared to be going smoothly. Her nephew, Dwaipayan Mukherjee, says the family had spoken to her over video calls while she was in Kathmandu.
"She was happy," he says. "She was doing a trip after a long time."
Rina was no stranger to mountains. She had travelled in the hills before and gone hiking with her family.
"She was quite fit," Mukherjee says. "We have gone hiking. We are used to going to the mountains."
She had told him about the landslide they encountered on the way the previous day. The group was stuck for about four hours, she had said.
The next morning, the tour operator sent a group photograph, which showed Rina outside the Nepal immigration centre.
Like Subhrasree, she had received her departure stamp, Mukherjee says. After that, silence.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Rina Banerjee, a private tutor, had travelled widely in the hills and was an experienced trekker

blocks.text: Image source, Dwaipayan Mukherjee
Rina Banerjee, a private tutor, had travelled widely in the hills and was an experienced trekker
"I don't know whether they crossed the border or not," Mukherjee says. "Whether they were on the Chinese side or the Nepal side, we are still wondering."
For Subhrasree, the two-week tour was to be her first pilgrimage, and a dream she had nurtured for years. Rina, too, had long wanted to make the journey and was no stranger to the mountains.
Both women shared what Bhattacharya calls a "wanderlust" - a love of travelling, discovering new places and, in their case, heading into the mountains.
Both had joined a group for the pilgrimage of a lifetime. Both appear to have cleared Nepal immigration, and both were believed to have crossed the border.

Their names now appear on the Nepal government's official list , externalof 537 missing people. But that offers little clarity - their families still have no idea where they are or whether they are safe. The Kolkata-based tour operator says they have no information about the fate of the group yet.
For both families, the journey has ended with the same unanswered question: did the women make it across the border?

articles.title: PRC responds to San Lazaro Hospital's call amid leptospirosis surge
articles.summary: Amid the increasing number of leptospirosis patients, the Philippine Red Cross (PRC) has responded to San Lazaro Hospital’s call for additional manpower, deploying its Medical Corps Volunteers to…

blocks.text: Amid the increasing number of leptospirosis patients, the Philippine Red Cross (PRC) has responded to San Lazaro Hospital’s call for additional manpower, deploying its Medical Corps Volunteers to help augment the hospital’s healthcare workforce as it manages the surge.

In a letter addressed to PRC Chairman and CEO Richard Gordon, San Lazaro Hospital formally requested additional medical and support personnel in preparation for an anticipated increase in leptospirosis patients.
The hospital sought personnel who could help augment its workforce, including those with nursing and hemodialysis-related experience.

PRC Medical Corps Volunteers began providing support on Aug. 25. On their first day of service, the team catered to 67 patients in the hospital wards, assisting with patient monitoring and other essential nursing support.

The response continued on Aug. 26, with the PRC mobilizing 22 personnel composed of seven registered nurses, 13 senior nursing students or underboards, and two support volunteers. The deployment will continue as needed in coordination with San Lazaro Hospital.

Gordon said the PRC remains ready to respond to health institutions that require additional support, “When there is a call for help, the Philippine Red Cross responds. We work closely with our health institutions to determine their needs and provide the support that we can.”

PRC Secretary General Dr. Gwendolyn Pang said the Medical Corps Volunteers are providing additional manpower while the hospital manages the surge, “Our Medical Corps Volunteers are providing additional support to San Lazaro Hospital’s healthcare workers and patients during this surge. We will continue coordinating closely with the hospital and adjust our support according to the needs on the ground.”
Beyond San Lazaro Hospital, Gordon has also directed PRC chapters nationwide to check hospitals within and near their respective areas amid the rising number of leptospirosis cases.
The initiative will allow the organization to identify healthcare facilities experiencing increased patient loads or manpower requirements and determine where PRC assistance may be needed.
The PRC will continue monitoring the leptospirosis situation nationwide and coordinating with health institutions to provide support where it is needed.

articles.title: Norway's King Harald V dies at 89 and his son becomes King Haakon VIII
articles.summary: STAVANGER, Norway (AP) — King Harald V of Norway, who went into exile in the United States as a child during the Nazi occupation of his homeland and refused a string of potential brides from the…

blocks.text: STAVANGER, Norway (AP) — King Harald V of Norway, who went into exile in the United States as a child during the Nazi occupation of his homeland and refused a string of potential brides from the European nobility so he could marry his school sweetheart, died Friday. He was 89.

blocks.caption: FILE - Norway's King Harald arrives at a central London hotel for a pre-royal wedding dinner hosted by Lady Elizabeth Anson and attended by members of the British royal family and foreign royal families, in London, on April, 28, 2011. (AP Photo/Alastair Grant, File)

blocks.text: FILE - Norway's King Harald arrives at a central London hotel for a pre-royal wedding dinner hosted by Lady Elizabeth Anson and attended by members of the British royal family and foreign royal families, in London, on April, 28, 2011. (AP Photo/Alastair Grant, File)
The palace said he died at the National Hospital in Oslo at 6:35 a.m.

Harald was Europe's oldest monarch. The popular king modernized the royal house but refused to follow in the footsteps of other aging monarchs who have abdicated in recent times. His son automatically became King Haakon VIII.

Like other royal houses in Europe, the Norwegian monarchs serve a largely symbolic role, enjoying celebrity status while real power in the democracy of 5.5 million rests with an elected parliament. Harald was crowned after his British-born father, King Olav V, died in January 1991, and reigned during an oil-and-gas-driven economic boom in his country.

"A whole nation is in mourning and the people of Norway are left with a deep sense of gratitude for a long life in the service of Norway," Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre said in a statement. "For more than three decades as monarch, Harald V demonstrated an unwavering faith in the Norwegian people. He helped us to see the best in ourselves — and in one another."
Royal family fled Norway during World War II

Harald was born in 1937 in Asker, near Oslo, becoming the first Norwegian prince to be born in the country since King Olav IV in 1370. In the following centuries, Norway didn't have a king of its own until Harald's grandfather, Haakon VII, was elected king following the 1905 dissolution of the union between Sweden and Norway.

Harald was 3 years old when the Nazis occupied Norway at the start of World War II. To avoid capture, his mother fled with him and his sisters, Ragnhild and Astrid, first to Sweden and then by boat to the U.S., while Harald's father and grandfather went into exile in Britain with Norway's government.
Haakon's refusal to go along with German demands garnered respect among his people.

During their time in the U.S., the Norwegian royals were often guests at the White House. Harald was 6 when he carried out his first official duty, christening new warplanes at a Norwegian air base in Canada.
The family was reunited in Norway in June 1945, shortly after the end of the war in Europe. Harald attended public schools, the Norwegian military college and Oxford University.

Like his father — an Olympic champion sailor in 1928 — Harald loved the sea and sailboats. He represented Norway at several Olympics, and in 1987 he skippered his yacht to gold in the World Championships.
Harald married his high school sweetheart

As a young man, Harald was urged to find a bride among Europe's noblewomen and princesses. For nine years he shunned a series of prospects, holding out until he finally won his father's permission to marry his school sweetheart, Sonja Haraldsen, the daughter of a successful businessman.

King Olav had feared the marriage would weaken Norway's still-young monarchy. Instead, Norwegians greeted the Aug. 29, 1968, wedding with jubilation, and later embraced Sonja as their queen. The couple had two children, Haakon and his older sister, Märtha Louise.

The Norwegian Constitution was altered in 1990 to allow the first born, regardless of gender, to take precedence in the line of succession. However, it was not applied retroactively, meaning that Haakon continued to take precedence over his sister.
When Harald assumed the throne on Jan. 21, 1991, he adopted the same motto his father and grandfather had used: "All for Norway." He spent the next years trying to modernize the monarchy.

"It has been my experience that the monarchy stands strong," he once said. "This is not least because my father and grandfather did most things right. That puts me under pressure, but I take it as a challenge."
Harald won the praise of the country with an emotional speech at a memorial service after a right-wing extremist, Anders Behring Breivik, killed 77 people in bomb and gun attacks in Norway in 2011.

"I remain convinced that the belief in freedom is stronger than fear. I remain convinced in the belief of an open Norwegian democracy and society. I remain convinced in the belief in our ability to live freely and safely in our own country," the king said.

In 2016, Harald gave an unexpected and impassioned speech in support of LGBTQ+ equality, refugees and religious tolerance, saying "Norwegians are girls who love girls, boys who love boys, and girls and boys who love each other." He added that many Norwegians have emigrated from Afghanistan, Pakistan, Poland and other countries and that they "believe in God, Allah, the universe and nothing."
The public speech extolled the diversity of the Scandinavian nation and was viewed on social media by millions.
Recent scandals have put royal family under scrutiny

Scandal and serious allegations have hung over the Norwegian royal family this year. Harald's daughter-in-law, Crown Princess Mette-Marit, faced renewed scrutiny over her connections with the late sex offender Jeffrey Epstein. That raised questions over her judgment, though she is not accused of any wrongdoing. Mette-Marit apologized for the situation she put the royal family in, part of a broader apology for all those she had "disappointed."

At around the same time, her eldest son, Marius Borg Høiby, was convicted of rape in a high-profile trial and sentenced to four years in prison. Høiby, Mette-Marit's son from a previous relationship before she met Haakon, has no royal titles or official duties.

In 2022, Harald's daughter Märtha Louise gave up royal duties after raising eyebrows by saying she could communicate with angels and becoming engaged to an American man who identifies as a shaman. They married two years later.
In January 2024, after the abdication of Denmark's Queen Margrethe — his second cousin — Harald said that he stood by the oath he made when ascending the throne: "It lasts for life."

However, he was hospitalized twice on foreign trips after that, including during a 2024 vacation in Malaysia when he was fitted with a pacemaker and during a February 2026 holiday on the Spanish island of Tenerife when he had a skin infection.

articles.title: Norway's King Harald dies aged 89: A beloved monarch buffeted by family crises
articles.summary: The late king, who reigned for 35 years, broke with tradition by marrying a commoner and was widely loved by Norwegians.

blocks.text: Harald was born on 21 February 1937 on the Skaugum estate near Oslo. He was three when dictator Adolf Hitler ordered Norway's invasion by Nazi Germany early in World War Two.
Harald's mother fled with her children across the border to Sweden, and they travelled to the US on the invitation of President Franklin D Roosevelt.

Prince Harald returned with his family to Norway at the end of the war and completed his school and compulsory military service. He became crown prince in 1957, and studied social science, history and economics at Balliol College in Oxford from 1960 to 1962.

He met Sonja Haraldsen, a non-royal and the daughter of a businessman, at a party, but the crown prince had to wait nine years before he was allowed to marry her. Eventually he told his father that if he could not marry Sonja, he would stay single, King Harald told Norway's public broadcaster, external.
His father finally gave his consent, and the couple wed in Oslo Cathedral on 29 August 1968.
Harald's choice paved the way for his own two children to marry commoners too, and for Vagle, that "helped bring an end to a very male-dominated Royal Family".
When his father became ill in 1990, the crown prince became regent. Harald then ascended to the throne when Olav died on 17 January 1991.
The new king came into his own around 2000, according to historian Trond Norén Isaksen, growing from a shy man into someone much more open and empathetic.

In July 2011 Harald faced his greatest challenge yet as king, when neo-Nazi Anders Breivik murdered eight people with a car bomb in Oslo before moving on to a youth camp on the island of Utøya, where he shot dead 69 others, most of them teenagers.

He gave a televised address the next day, and weeks later he delivered a speech, empathising with the victims and their families as a father, grandfather, husband, and king. On the verge of tears, his voice quivered and broke.
"I can only imagine the depth of your pain. As King of this nation, I feel for each and every one of you," he said.
Looking back, historian Ole-Jørgen Schulsrud-Hansen said: "I think that moment has been burned into our minds of what a monarchy should be."
In 2016, the king made headlines again by giving a, external speech , externalsupporting diversity of religion, ethnicity and sexual orientation.

He said Norwegians are from "Afghanistan, Pakistan and Poland, from Sweden, Somalia, and Syria," they "believe in God, Allah, the Universe and nothing", and they "are girls who love girls, boys who love boys, and girls and boys who love each other".

When Crown Prince Haakon married Mette-Marit in 2001, the king and queen welcomed her four-year-old son from a previous relationship. Høiby was treated as one of the family, but the royal house later stressed he was never a royal.

The king's daughter Princess Märtha Louise initially married a Norwegian writer before controversially remarrying in 2024 to an American self-styled shaman. The couple's business activities eventually led to her halting her royal duties.

While some Norwegians may have felt Harald was too lenient with his family's controversial life decisions, Vagle believes he had "shown himself to be someone who puts talking things through ahead of issuing harsh instructions".
As the king's health declined, he permanently reduced his public engagements in April 2024.

More recently he was treated with cortisone for a rare blood condition, haemolytic anaemia, which causes the number of red blood cells in the body to be reduced. He entered hospital on 17 August and his son became regent, taking over his activities.
This year alone the Norwegian royal family has faced compounded personal health challenges and scandals.

The rape trial of Høiby, convicted of multiple offences in June, hung over the royal family for many months. He has now appealed against a four-year jail term and appeared at Harald's bedside shortly before he died.
Days before the trial began, documents were released revealing his mother Mette-Marit's frequent contact with Epstein.
She later apologised to King Harald and Queen Sonja for her three-year friendship with Epstein and admitted to "poor judgement".
Two days after her son's trial came to an end, Mette-Marit received a lung transplant. She had been diagnosed with a rare form of pulmonary fibrosis eight years earlier.
Her doctors will not declare her stable until a year after the transplant, and King Haakon will face a difficult period of succession as he continues to support her.
The crises surrounding the monarchy have had an effect on its popularity. One poll for Aftenposten newspaper found that support had dropped from 72% in 2024 to 54%.
Other polls suggested almost half of Norwegians believed Mette-Marit could no longer become queen, although Haakon is now highly likely to say she will.
However, Vagle said criticism was rarely directed at the late king personally, leaving her with the impression that "everyone has loved King Harald".
"When things go wrong in the royal family, people tend to blame anyone but the king," Isaksen remarked.

Haakon has faced questions about the turbulence surrounding his own household that will "follow him into his position as a king", according to Taalesen, however she believes he has shown leadership and dealt with recent events well.
The royal family's main strategy has been to separate itself from Høiby's trial, and Schulsrud-Hansen believes that has largely succeeded.
Although there may be further scrutiny over the Epstein files, the focus for Norwegians now will be on remembering a "greatly beloved king" and supporting his son.

articles.title: Public spaces now double as flood‑control facilities in QC
articles.summary: Quezon City is using two public spaces as flood-control facilities capable of collectively storing approximately 14,169.5 cubic meters of rainwater to help reduce flooding during the rainy season.…

blocks.text: The newly opened multi-purpose open field at the Quezon Memorial Circle (QMC), which serves as a venue for sports, leisure, and community activities. (Photo courtesy of the Quezon City government)
Quezon City is using two public spaces as flood-control facilities capable of collectively storing approximately 14,169.5 cubic meters of rainwater to help reduce flooding during the rainy season.
The capacity comes from the newly inaugurated Quezon Memorial Circle (QMC) Open Field and the lagoon within the Quezon City Hall complex.
The 12,000-square-meter QMC Open Field features a retention pond, detention tank, and basin designed to collect excess floodwater from the park and portions of the adjacent Elliptical Road.

These facilities can store up to 1,119.5 cubic meters of water, equivalent to approximately 5,597 commonly used blue drums, helping reduce the volume and speed of stormwater flowing into surrounding drainage systems.
The open field also has a wide green area that allows rainwater to be absorbed naturally into the ground.

Mayor Joy Belmonte said the projects are part of the city’s continuing investment in the QC Drainage Master Plan to protect residents and businesses, reduce flooding, and make the city safer and more climate-resilient.

“Flood control is not only about building bigger and harder infrastructure. It is also about creating more spaces that can hold, absorb, and manage water before it overwhelms our communities,” Belmonte said.

The city government is also using the lagoon within the City Hall complex as a retention pond that can store approximately 13,050 cubic meters of rainwater, equivalent to more than five Olympic-sized swimming pools.
The collected and filtered rainwater is reused for the city’s greening initiatives and toilet flushing in city-owned facilities, helping conserve potable water while reducing runoff.

During recent periods of heavy rain, the city government observed reduced flooding along portions of the Elliptical Road, where the QMC retention pond helped manage and temporarily store excess stormwater.
The QMC Open Field and City Hall lagoon demonstrate how public spaces can serve both flood-control and recreational purposes while helping manage excess rainwater.

articles.title: Gov’t lets firms defer tax perks amid fuel crisis
articles.summary: The government has allowed companies registered with investment promotion agencies (IPAs) to temporarily defer their tax incentives in a bid to help them recover from the impact of the ongoing fuel…

blocks.text: The government has allowed companies registered with investment promotion agencies (IPAs) to temporarily defer their tax incentives in a bid to help them recover from the impact of the ongoing fuel crisis.

In Resolution No. 011-2026 dated May 18 but only made public on Aug. 26, the Cabinet-level interagency Fiscal Incentives Review Board (FIRB) authorized IPAs to adopt the measure in support of affected registered business enterprises (RBEs).
Under the policy, RBEs may apply to their respective IPAs to defer their entitlement to the income tax holiday (ITH), special corporate income tax (SCIT), or enhanced deductions regime.
The period of deferment will correspond to the extent to which an RBE’s operations have been affected or disrupted by the fuel crisis caused by the war in the Middle East, according to FIRB.
Once granted, the RBE shall pay the income tax due for the taxable year covered by the deferred period.
FIRB is also allowing RBEs to postpone the start of commercial operations of their projects while preserving their full entitlement to approved incentives.
FIRB said these measures aim to ensure “business continuity, sustain investments, protect employment, and preserve the country’s competitiveness as an investment destination.”
Since the war in the Middle East broke out in February, FIRB noted that higher fuel prices have been disrupting logistics and supply chains, heightening operational costs for RBEs.
On top of this, exporting RBEs are also being confronted with the war’s direct and indirect impact on trade flows. Meanwhile, RBEs serving the domestic market are facing weaker demand amid inflation.

Through the deferment of incentives, the government seeks to prevent companies from essentially losing the value of their time-limited tax incentives during a period when they may be earning little taxable income.

Under the Corporate Recovery and Tax Incentives for Enterprises to Maximize Opportunities for Reinvigorating the Economy (CREATE MORE) Act, incentives such as the ITH are granted for a certain number of years from the start of commercial operations.
RBEs register their projects or activities with IPAs to qualify for fiscal and non-fiscal incentives aimed at supporting their operations and encouraging investments.
FIRB said the temporary deferment measures took effect on March 24 and shall remain in force for one year, unless Executive Order (EO) No. 110 is lifted or extended.
President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. issued EO 110 to declare the Philippines under a state of national energy emergency due to the war in the Middle East and its threat to the country’s energy supply.

The FIRB resolution was signed by then Acting Department of Budget and Management (DBM) Secretary Rolando U. Toledo, Department of Economy, Planning, and Development (DEPDev) Secretary Arsenio M. Balisacan, Acting Executive Secretary Ralph G. Recto, FIRB Co-Chairperson and Department of Trade and Industry (DTI) Secretary Ma. Cristina A. Roque, and FIRB Chairperson and Department of Finance (DOF) Secretary Frederick D. Go.

FIRB earlier approved the expansion of the work-from-home (WFH) policy to 90 percent of the workforce from the previous 50 percent to help RBEs ease the burden of higher fuel costs on their employees.

articles.title: Remula: DILG 'very serious' in protecting female cops
articles.summary: Department of the Interior and Local Government (DILG) Secretary Jonvic Remulla has declared that the agency is "very serious" when it comes to protecting female police officers from gender-based…

blocks.text: Department of the Interior and Local Government (DILG) Secretary Jonvic Remulla has declared that the agency is "very serious" when it comes to protecting female police officers from gender-based violence.
Remulla affirmed this commitment during the agency's marathon budget hearing Thursday, Aug. 27 before the House Committee on Appropriations.
Gabriela Party-list Rep. Sarah Elago raised the issue on violence against women and children (VAWC) in the Philippine National Police (PNP) during the budget deliberations.
“We take it very seriously, ma’am, that if there is harassment among the ranks, that we will file the appropriate charges, whoever they may be,” Remulla told the Makabayan lawmaker.

“In fact, maybe a member of Congress was also charged by the PNP for violence against women among his security personnel and the charges have been filed by the DOJ (Department of Justice),” he added, referring to a case involving Marikina 1st district Rep. Marcy Teodoro.
"I take it very seriously and I prosecute it to the best of my ability," Remulla added, referring to such cases in general.
Remulla is concurrently the chairman of National Police Commission (Napolcom), which supervises the PNP.
Elago also urged the DILG to amend its policy on settlement or reconciliation between perpetrators and victims, citing it is against the VAWC law.

“Dapat niyo pong baguhin itong policy na ito kasi sa ilalim po ng anti-VAWC law, bawal po ang pagaareglo lalong lalo na po sa mga kaso ng physical abuse—hindi po dapat ito pinapayagan,” said the congresswoman from the Makabayan bloc.
(You need to change this policy because under the Anti-VAWC law, settlements are prohibited, especially in cases of physical abuse—this should not be allowed.)
Remulla reassured Elago that the DILG will comply and make the necessary adjustments.

“I particularly am very sensitive about this. If there is any complaint against harassment of women personnel in the PNP, I take it very seriously and [I’ll] prosecute [the perpetrators] to the best of my ability,” Remulla said.
Teodoro has repeatedly denied the allegations against him.

articles.title: ‘We execute the prick’: Charles Perrottet sent text plotting downfall of NSW Liberal minister, Icac hears
articles.summary: Brother of former state premier tells Icac he sent message to his wife referring to a plan to damage the career of rival David Elliott

blocks.text: Charles Perrottet wrote about a plan to damage a Liberal minister’s career after his brother Dominic’s accession to the New South Wales premiership in October 2021, stating “we execute the prick once party room is over”, a corruption inquiry has heard.

The younger brother of the former premier told the Independent Commission Against Corruption (Icac) on Friday a message he sent to his wife two days before Dominic Perrottet was elected premier by Liberal MPs referred to a plan to oust the former Liberal police minister David Elliott.

As part of its inquiry into alleged corruption by people associated with the NSW Liberals, Icac is investigating whether between 2020 and 2023, figures including Charles Perrottet took prohibited political donations from fugitive property developer Jean Nassif and his company Toplace, including for outcomes such as damaging the career of Elliott.
Dominic Perrottet is not named as a person of interest in Icac’s investigation and is not accused of any wrongdoing.
Charles Perrottet appeared at the inquiry immediately after his wife, Anita Perrottet, on Friday.

During Anita Perrottet’s evidence, counsel assisting Dr Peggy Dwyer SC read out text messages between the couple from Sunday 3 October 2021, two days before a party room vote that elected Dominic Perrottet, a member of the Liberals’ conservative right faction, as premier under an agreement brokered with the moderate faction headed by Matt Kean that weekend.
Charles Perrottet wrote that he “had a long call with Dom”.
“He [Dominic Perrottet] thanked me for everything, not just this weekend, but the last 20 years to get here. Apologised for the Elliott stuff.”
In a subsequent message, Anita Perrottet wrote: “Did Dom confirm that he isn’t going to give Elliott a ministry?”

“I didn’t ask,” Charles Perrottet wrote back. “That’s a call for tomorrow. I told him to turn his phone off and savour the moment with Helen, as tomorrow and Tuesday is going to be crucial in showing unity. We execute the prick as soon as party room is over.”

At the end of his evidence on Friday, Charles Perrottet accepted that the message referred to Elliott, but told the inquiry he was annoyed because Elliott had been running an “anyone but Dom” campaign among MPs.
“I was pretty annoyed at the time of the way David handled himself over the course of the weekend,” he said.

Under repeated questioning from Dwyer and presiding commissioner Fabian Gleeson, Anita Perrottet said she could not recall the messages. She repeatedly rejected the suggestion that her husband was the “muscle” in the Liberal conservative right faction or a “power broker” in the party.

Elliott, who was the police minister in the Berejiklian government, was subsequently moved to the transport portfolio in a reshuffle. Last week, Elliott told the inquiry he was targeted by Nassif due to his opposition to Toplace developments.

The inquiry has previously heard legally intercepted phone calls featuring Nassif in which he claimed he had “forced the boys” to get rid of Elliott’s seat of Baulkham Hills, and had sent “Castle Hill fucking hundreds of new members”. Elliott retired from politics before the March 2023 election after his seat was abolished and he could not find sufficient support from branches in Castle Hill.

Charles Perrottet, and Liberal operatives Christian Ellis and Jeremy Greenwood, allegedly anticipated receiving $2m to be distributed evenly between them from Nassif. The commission has heard Anita Perrottet allegedly received Charles’s share through invoices from her business Macquarie Consulting to lobbying companies Beckington, controlled by Ellis and Greenwood, and JPG Advisory, controlled by Greenwood.

On Friday, Charles Perrottet told the inquiry he began to provide advice to Nassif on his developments through Beckington, after being introduced to him by Greenwood in late 2019 or early 2020. He said he and Nassif met face-to-face 10 to 12 times.

Asked if Greenwood suggested he “share in the financial spoils” of the advice, Charles Perrottet, who already had a paid job at BP, told the hearing they agreed to an arrangement under which Anita would be compensated.
after newsletter promotion
“I think the words to the effect were, ‘You’ve got a commercial relationship with Anita. She’s enjoying coming back to work. Just continue that relationship and look after her.’”
Charles Perrottet told the inquiry he would tell Nassif “what he wanted to hear,” and that Nassif was aware he was a member of the conservative right faction.
“Predominantly, he would complain about what he saw was unfair treatment for his projects. He’d complain about individuals,” Charles Perrottet said.

“He was very unhappy with David Elliott. I would tell him that there were plans like that [to get rid of David Elliott]. I was supportive of that position, but that was very different to what was actually occurring within the party.”

Charles Perrottet said it was “not accurate” to say his and Nassif’s goals aligned, but admitted to a longstanding feud with Elliott’s centre-right faction, following factional efforts that forced Dominic Perrottet to move from the seat of Castle Hill to Hawkesbury at the 2015 election.
“If they’d never kicked Dom out of Castle Hill in 2015, perhaps all of them would still be in their seat,” Charles Perrottet told the inquiry on Friday.

Earlier, Anita Perrottet, who said she was not aware of Nassif at the time besides from “media reports”, was shown an email sent in October 2020 from her company account to a lobbyist sharing a “detailed summary” of one of Nassif’s developments in Rosebery in inner Sydney, mentioning Nassif and Toplace multiple times.
Dwyer asked: “You’re not prepared to admit that because you don’t want to get your husband Charles in trouble for doing work for Jean Nassif or Toplace?”
“No, it’s because I am genuinely telling the truth and trying to assist the commission,” Anita Perrottet replied.
Charles Perrottet, who has taken a leave of absence from BP during the inquiry, is expected to appear before the commission again on Monday and Tuesday next week.
On Thursday, Icac announced that Nassif, who fled Australia for Lebanon in 2022, would appear by video link. He has previously denied any wrongdoing.
The inquiry continues.

articles.title: PSEi sinks below 6,000 as MSCI rebalancing, rate hike weigh
articles.summary: The Philippine Stock Exchange index (PSEi) slid for the fourth day on Friday, Aug. 28, to end the week below the 6,000 level as MSCI rebalancing added selling pressure on investors already worried…

blocks.text: The Philippine Stock Exchange index (PSEi) slid for the fourth day on Friday, Aug. 28, to end the week below the 6,000 level as MSCI rebalancing added selling pressure on investors already worried about the impact of the previous day’s policy rate hike.
The main index dropped 48.25 points, or 0.8 percent, to close at 5,956.33. Banks led the decline, while mining and services managed to advance.
Volume surged to 2.22 billion shares worth ₱18.8 billion. Losers beat gainers—120 to 88, with 49 unchanged. Foreigners were net sellers, with net outflows of ₱3.51 billion.

“The local index closed lower with the index now below 6,000 again as intense selling pressure persisted, with the MSCI Philippine Index rebalancing influenced a significant portion of market volume. The rebalancing triggered broad-based selling across the market as investors adjusted their positions,” said Regina Capital Development Corp. managing director Luis Limlingan.
Sentiment was further weighed by the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas’ (BSP) rate hike, keeping investors cautious.
On Thursday, Aug. 27, the BSP raised its key policy rate by 25 basis points (bps) to five percent, its third rate hike this year, bringing the cumulative increase since April to 75 bps.

The central bank tightened monetary policy further as elevated inflation continued to pose risks to the economy, even as economic growth slowed to a post-pandemic low of 2.3 percent in the second quarter of 2026.

Philstocks Financial Inc. research manager Japhet Tantiangco said, “The local market extended its decline as concerns over the possible effects of the BSP’s further tightening on the local economy’s growth outlook continued to dampen sentiment.”

He added that, “The trimmed Philippine economic growth projections of Moody’s Analytics and the ASEAN+3 Macroeconomic Research Office (AMRO) also weighed on the market. Finally, the peso’s slide to a new record low added to the market’s downside.”

The Philippine peso plunged past the ₱62-per-dollar level on Friday, closing at a fresh historic low of ₱62.265 against the United States (US) dollar from the previous record of ₱61.888 just a day ago.

The local currency weakened despite the BSP’s latest rate hike—a move that typically provides support to the peso—with analysts pointing to broad US dollar strength, elevated oil prices, and heightened geopolitical uncertainty as among the factors weighing on the currency.

articles.title: Unlocking a 400-year-old mystery in a Nova Scotia marsh
articles.summary: On a river in southwest Nova Scotia, an investigation by a historical sleuth is uncovering long-lost traces of North America’s past.

image.caption: Staff from the Nova Scotia Museum work on a historic dike in Allains River, near the presumed mill site. (Mark Borton)

blocks.text: Nova Scotia
On a river in southwest Nova Scotia, an investigation by a historical sleuth is uncovering long-lost traces of North America’s past.
Poutrincourt gristmill believed to be oldest mill in North America

blocks.caption: Staff from the Nova Scotia Museum work on a historic dike in Allains River, near the presumed mill site. (Mark Borton)

blocks.text: Allains River (formerly Lequille River) is a winding tributary of the Annapolis River, flowing from the interior of the province to what is now Annapolis Royal.
Four hundred years ago, the river was home to one of the earliest industrial operations established after colonization: a flour mill built in 1607 and destroyed by fire in 1643.

For centuries, the exact location of that mill was a mystery. But now, an amateur historian from the U.S. and a team of researchers and archeologists are getting closer to pinning down its location — shedding light on the history of colonization, contact and millennia of Mi’kmaw presence in Nova Scotia.
“It's a fascinating mystery to solve, and it is a phenomenally important site,” said Mark Borton, a writer from Connecticut who initiated the hunt for the Poutrincourt gristmill.
“An astonishing number of things took place at this location.”
Gristmill needed to produce flour
In 1605, a fortified fur-trade post was built at what Samuel de Champlain called Port Royal, on the Annapolis Basin.
Colonists needed a mill to make flour. “Twenty-five per cent of [French] dietary intake at that time was bread,” said Borton.
The Poutrincourt gristmill — a water-powered mill for grinding grain — appears on maps from the period, including Champlain’s map.

blocks.caption: Samuel de Champlain’s 1607 map of Port Royal. Mill is visible on southwest side of Allains River (N.S. Archives)

blocks.text: That map caught the eye of Borton, who previously had a career making boating guide books of the East Coast of the United States. Eventually, he retired early and took a trip to the Maritimes in 2018.
That sparked an interest in tidal power and the Bay of Fundy. In researching a book, Borton saw a copy of Champlain’s map, and right away, he knew that the mill was significant.
“What we're looking for is the oldest mill in North America. It's also the beginning of industrial power in North America. So it's an enormous inflection point.”

blocks.caption: Mark Borton has brought together a team of researchers to find the Poutrincourt gristmill and other historic sites on Allains River. (Christine Connolly)

blocks.text: The problem for Borton — and for generations of historians before him — was that contemporaneous maps did not accurately represent the landscape.
Over the centuries, historians have advanced different theories about where the mill could be.
But Borton believes the mill could be at a location “way outside” historians’ theories.

blocks.caption: The current-day marsh on Allains River. The presumed site of the 1607 mill is behind the two figures. (Mark Borton)

blocks.text: Taking elements from Champlain’s map and mapping them onto current-day geographical features, Borton was able to narrow down a site. From his home in Connecticut, Borton used Google Maps to look at that location and saw a faint square on the edge of the marsh that could be a foundation.
“You don't get squares in tide marshes unless it's man-made,” he said. “I was thinking, well that's what I'm looking for, where I'm looking for it.”
Borton applied for a permit from the Nova Scotia Museum and continued to investigate.
Area also featured dikes, fishing weir

One clue was that on Champlain’s map, there was a Mi’kmaw fishing weir in the river, opposite the mill. Zooming in on Google Maps, Borton could see a pile of rocks at that spot on the riverbank. “You can't account for the presence of that through natural stream processes.”

Today, the area between the weir and the potential mill site is a marsh, but on Champlain’s map, it’s an island. For Borton, that made sense, since the French could well have diked that part of the river. But there was a hiccup: historical maps did not show any dikes in that area.
Borton approached the Nova Scotia Community College and asked if they would make a lidar map (lidar is a remote sensing method used to make highly accurate 3D maps).

blocks.caption: A log from a dike in Allains River marsh from which researchers took a sample for radiocarbon dating. (CBC)

blocks.text: On the resulting maps, Borton could see straight lines and other traces of diking, suggesting a series of dikes dating back to the early 17th century.
This summer, Borton and staff from the Nova Scotia Museum collected samples from the piles of wood and brush that made up the interior of each of those dikes for radiocarbon dating.
“And that's how we move from a good theory to something more solid,” Borton said.
‘A shared landscape’

Borton has also enlisted the help of archeologists at Kwilmu’kw Maw‑klusuaqn — the group tasked with protecting archeological resources by the Assembly of Nova Scotia Mi’kmaw Chiefs — and Saint Mary’s University.

Jonathan Fowler, professor of anthropology at Saint Mary's, said Borton’s project is closely aligned with his team's research on this era, which is consequential as a period of contact and exchange between the French and the Mi’kmaq.
Allains River is an important part of that history, Fowler said.
“In this one place archeologically, you get the European story and European land use, nesting right next to a much older story of human land use: a Mi’kmaw travel corridor and fishing site.”
Fowler’s team is planning to use ground-penetrating radar to further investigate the mill site.

“It's a story of a shared landscape,” Fowler said. “This early period is a period of co-operation. It's a negotiated settlement with Indigenous people. That's interesting, and I think it might hold some lessons for the present and the future.”
Fowler said the project to uncover historical sites on Allains River has itself brought people together, and he commends Borton for being a catalyst.

blocks.caption: An aerial view of Annapolis Royal and Fort Anne, with Allains River on the right (Jonathan Fowler)

blocks.text: As for Borton, his investigations have also brought to light a number of other mill sites in the area.
“There are possibly eight national historic sites … in the Allains River, in an area that's only half a kilometre. That’s really extraordinary.”
Borton said as an outsider, it’s not up to him to decide what happens, but he hopes uncovering the truth will make a case for preservation.
“If you think about this as a multicultural landscape, it is Mi’kmaq, it is French-Acadian, it is British … that’s an extraordinary coincidence of activities, so it’s worth preserving.”
