articles.title: Who really owns the Caspian Sea?
articles.summary: Five countries border the Caspian Sea, but none owns a fixed share. A 2018 convention established rules for navigation, security and fishing while leaving some seabed borders unresolved.

image.caption: Since the collapse of the Soviet Union, the Caspian Sea's legal status has been the subject of lengthy negotiations among its five bordering statesImage: Morteza Nikoubazl/NurPhoto/picture alliance

blocks.text: For decades, debate in Iran over the Caspian Sea has often centered on a deceptively simple question: What percentage belongs to the country?
Iran, Russia, Azerbaijan, Kazakhstan and Turkmenistan all border the body of water. But the Caspian is treated neither as a conventional sea nor simply as an international lake.
Instead, the five countries have developed a special legal regime governing navigation, territorial waters, fishing, security and seabed resources.
The most important step came in 2018, when the five presidents signed the Convention on the Legal Status of the Caspian Sea in Aktau, Kazakhstan.

It established territorial waters of up to 15 nautical miles and an additional 10-nautical-mile exclusive fishing zone for each country. But it did not divide the entire Caspian into five fixed national shares.
Why doesn't Iran own half the Caspian Sea
Before the Soviet Union collapsed in 1991, Iran and the Soviet Union were the only two countries bordering the Caspian.
The 1921 Russo-Persian Treaty of Friendship restored Iranian navigation rights restricted under Imperial Russia. A 1940 treaty further regulated trade and navigation.
None of the agreements, however, awarded Iran 50% of the Caspian.
Ahmad Vakhshiteh, director of the Moscow-based Center for Strategic Research on Developing Relations with the Middle East, says that this distinction is central to understanding the dispute.
"None of these treaties specified a percentage for either Iran or the Soviet Union," he told DW. "They emphasized common use rather than dividing the sea into ownership shares."
No tanks: What V-Day parade says about Russia's military
To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video
After the Soviet collapse, Azerbaijan, Kazakhstan and Turkmenistan emerged as independent states, turning a bilateral legal arrangement into a five-country negotiation.
Some Iranian politicians argued for a 50% share since it had previously shared the sea with the Soviet Union alone; others called for 20%. So far, neither claim has gained international recognition.
What the 2018 Caspian Sea agreement settled
"The Caspian is neither completely a sea nor completely a lake," Vakhshiteh said.
"The 2018 convention created a special legal regime that distinguishes between the water, seabed, security and resources," he added.
The convention does not divide the surface into national sectors. Each country has territorial waters and fishing zones, while other areas remain available for common navigation.
The seabed can be divided through agreements between neighboring states. These agreements matter because offshore oil and gas rights depend largely on such boundaries.
Russia, Kazakhstan and Azerbaijan have already reached several bilateral delimitation agreements. Iran's southern boundaries remain among the more politically sensitive issues.
How security became central to Caspian Sea politics

The 2018 convention prohibits the presence of armed forces belonging to non-bordering states in the Caspian. Coastal countries are also not supposed to allow their territory to be used for military action against a neighboring Caspian state.

But Iran recently accused Ukraine of attacking an Iranian commercial vessel in the Caspian, killing a sailor. Kyiv said it had targeted vessels involved in transporting military cargo linked to Iran and Russia.
Vakhshiteh argues that such incidents demonstrate why Tehran considers keeping outside military powers away from the Caspian a strategic priority.

"Iran may still negotiate over seabed boundaries, but on one important principle a common legal rule already exists: the Caspian should not become a military base for powers from outside the region," he said.
Currently, Iran is the only one of the five signatories that has not completed parliamentary ratification of the convention.
Oil and gas in the Caspian Sea
Behind the legal and military debates is another major issue: energy in the form of oil and gas.
Azerbaijan and Kazakhstan have developed substantial offshore oil resources, while Turkmenistan possesses major natural gas reserves.
Umud Shokri, an energy strategist and senior visiting fellow at George Mason University, says that Iran has meaningful hydrocarbon potential, too.
Its most important Caspian discovery, Sardar-e Jangal, was found in 2012 but development has been slow and it has not entered commercial production.
Iranian estimates suggest the area may contain around 2 billion barrels of oil, with roughly 500 million potentially recoverable, plus natural gas.
"Iran has confirmed hydrocarbon discoveries and promising prospects, but its commercially recoverable Caspian resource base remains uncertain and largely undeveloped," Shokri told DW.

blocks.caption: Azerbaijan  and Kazakhstan have charged ahead and are both actively expanding offshore oil and gas developments in the Caspian Sea Image: Anatoly Ustinenko/TASS/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: The southern Caspian is significantly deeper than many of the areas developed by Iran's neighbors. Sardar-e Jangal lies in water around 700 meters deep, requiring advanced drilling equipment, subsea technology and substantial investment.
Sanctions have made access to international companies, financing and specialized offshore technology much harder. The country also has simpler options.
"Iran has huge oil and gas fields in the Persian Gulf and onshore that are generally easier and cheaper to develop," Shokri said.
For Tehran, investing billions in difficult deepwater Caspian projects has often been less attractive than expanding production around the Persian Gulf like its South Pars gas field.
So, who owns the Caspian?
In the end, no single country owns or controls the Caspian Sea. And no treaty gives Iran, Russia or any other state a fixed share of the body of water.
The five neighboring states have territorial waters and exclusive fishing zones, while other parts remain open to common use.

Seabed boundaries, which determine many offshore oil and gas rights, are negotiated separately between neighboring countries. For Iran, that means some of its offshore resource rights are still subject to negotiation.
But ownership percentage is no longer the central question.
Today, the bigger issues are a combination of how the Caspian's resources are managed, where maritime boundaries are drawn and its ability to keep out external military forces.
Edited by: Tim Rooks

articles.title: Messi retirement hint highlights football era nearing an end
articles.summary: Soon after propelling Argentina to a second consecutive World Cup final, Lionel Messi has cast some doubt on his future. While retirement doesn't seem imminent, it still beckons for him and Cristiano…

image.caption: Lionel Messi was a key figure for Argentina at the recent World Cup, though he rarely ranImage: Thomas Coex/AFP

blocks.text: "I'm really not sure if I'll carry on doing it for much longer."
Those words earlier this month from Lionel Messi, a man who famously says very little, sparked a global conversation about whether his storied career was about to end.

The Argentine posted a tribute to his father, who recently died, on Instagram. "You were by my side from the beginning; there was so little left until the end. Why couldn't you hold on just a little longer so we could finish it together?" he wrote.

Messi turned 39 during a World Cup in which he belied his advanced years to drag Argentina to the final despite rarely breaking into a sprint. During the 2026 tournament, Messi scored eight goals in eight games to further cement his reputation as the best footballer of all time.

"He is the greatest footballer I've ever witnessed. You can still see that even though he's 39 years old," wrote Philipp Lahm, the former Germany captain, in a column for Kicker, a German football magazine.
Lahm, who faced Messi several times, including Germany's triumph over Argentina in the 2014 World Cup final, said the forward was "the best player I've ever played against by far."
Argentina is Messi's home, but Spain is where he found football fame
While Messi grew up in Argentina, he came of age in Spain with Barcelona, who he joined at the age of 13. In 17 seasons, Messi won 10 La Liga titles and four Champions Leagues with Barca.

He has added further silverware with Paris Saint-Germain and then Inter Miami, where he has a contract until December 2028. He has won the Ballon d'Or, the award for the world's best footballer, a record eight times.

Messi's impact on European football is hard to underestimate. While Barcelona had enjoyed periods of success before, the time Messi was there was an era without compare. The club, which produced other star graduates from its La Masia academy such as Xavi and Andres Iniesta, bestrode the continent. Even his rivals could do little but admire.

"I've never seen a footballer play as consistently as Messi. You have to bear in mind that he's never played for clubs that I like, which proves that I'm serious, the best I've ever seen," said then-Germany and Real Madrid midfielder Toni Kroos after Messi lifted the 2022 World Cup with Argentina and ensured he'd won basically everything worth winning.
Late-stage Messi remains a threat

As he has edged beyond the age when most players retire, Messi has adjusted, with his energy-saving approach to the 2026 World Cup the zenith of that. His move to Inter Miami in 2023, when he was in his mid-30s, was the precursor to that change.
"I've changed my style of play because of the moment, the situation and my age," he told the 433 app in 2024.
"I am adapting a little bit to everything. I started reinventing myself and adapting to the league, which for me was new."
His off-pitch impact in the US has also been significant and somehow stretched his fame, profile and marketability still further.

"A lot of people are walking around cities and towns in the UK and Europe wearing that flamingo pink of Inter Miami with zero affiliation to Miami, having never been there," sports brand strategist James Kirkham told the BBC.

A promotional tour of India in 2025 was supposed to do the same there, but his non-appearance at a match caused fans to invade a pitch during an event. In the long-term, though, that did little to dent his appeal across the globe.
Messi, Ronaldo the last big hitters of their age?

It is all proof of a shift in football fan culture that has progressed rapidly since Messi started his career more than 20 years ago. Increasingly now, fans follow players rather than teams, with Messi and the challenger to his crown, Cristiano Ronaldo, at the forefront.

"The athlete is more than just a competitor or the labor on the field, but I feel like it wasn't until really the emergence of social media and technologies that the boundaries of what the athlete is really transcended," Nataliya Bredikhina, a sports branding expert from the University of Delaware in the US, told DW with regard to Messi's place in this growing phenomenon.

blocks.caption: At 41, the 2026 World Cup is likely, but not certain, to be Cristiano Ronaldo's lastImage: Ulrik Pedersen/NurPhoto/picture alliance

blocks.text: Many observers had expected the baton of that global fan attention to have been passed on by now. But despite the emergence of younger superstars such as Kylian Mbappe and Erling Haaland, Messi and Ronaldo still stand supreme off the pitch.

On it, the pair both still deliver, though the physical decline is clearer by the week. While Messi is playing Major League Soccer in the US, Ronaldo is chasing his own 1,000-goal milestone in Saudi Arabia. Messi could potentially reach such heights too. And with his style adapted to disguise his fading fitness, a career that stretches into the 40s, as Ronaldo's has, seems possible. But the man himself says he will know when the time is right.
"I know that the moment I feel that I am no longer able to perform, that I no longer enjoy or help my team-mates, I will quit," he said in a 2024 interview on the Big Time podcast.
Despite the loss of his father, and the difficulties in envisaging a future without him, that moment still seems a way off. When it comes, it will, like his talent and legacy, be seismic.
Edited by: Chuck Penfold

articles.title: In drought-stricken France, tankers supply drinking water
articles.summary: France is seeing water shortages in regions that usually have plenty of supply. This summer's extreme heat is exposing how unprepared much of the country, and Europe, is for increasing water scarcity.

image.caption: Tanker trucks visit Sainte-Marie-aux-Mines twice a week, delivering waterImage: Jean-Christophe Verhaegen/AFP

blocks.text: Since early August, huge silver tanker trucks have been paying a visit to the town of Sainte-Marie-aux-Mines in Alsace, eastern France, twice a week. They aren't delivering heating oil or milk, but drinking water from the nearby town of Liepvre.

Sainte-Marie, with its population of 5,000, is located in a green valley in the Vosges Mountains and usually relies on about 20 mountain springs for its water. But the flow rate has fallen after weeks of intense heat and drought.

Liepvre, just a few kilometers away, is connected to a larger water supply network that extends toward the Alsatian plain. Here, there is still enough water despite the drought but because there is no permanent connection between the two systems, tanker trucks are effectively functioning as a water pipeline on wheels.
According to the French government, more than 40,000 people have been affected by water cutoffs or supply disruptions this month, and 550,000 are at higher risk of losing stable access.

blocks.caption: Drought conditions have been severe across France this summer, including in the Loire regionImage: Stephane Mahe/REUTERS

blocks.text: The drought has affected large parts of France and water restrictions have been put in place in many regions, but tanker trucks are only being used in certain areas. This depends on what sources or groundwater reserves a municipality relies on for water and whether it can easily switch to other resources.
More than a dozen municipalities in the Jura Mountains, further to the south in the department of Doubs, are also currently being supplied by tanker trucks.
Drought increasingly frequent in France

This situation is not new for France. In the summer of 2022, which was also exceptionally dry, tanker trucks were used to supply hundreds of municipalities with water. Others depended on bottled water.
Coucouron, a village in the Massif Central region of southern France with just under 800 residents, was severely affected.

blocks.caption: The village of Coucouron experienced drastic water shortages in 2022Image: Andreas Noll/DW

blocks.text: Though it's located at a height of more than 1,000 meters (3,280 feet) in a region rich in water and where three major French rivers — the Loire, the Allier and the Ardeche, have their sources — an important spring ran dry after months of drought. Tanker trucks had to bring water to the villagers for months.

But drought wasn't the only reason for these problems. Experts discovered that there were several major leaks in the water supply network. Once they had been repaired, the village's water consumption dropped by about 40 cubic meters per day. A 6-kilometer-long (3.7-mile) pipeline linking to an additional water source is expected to bring more stability.

Coucouron is not an isolated case. On average, only about 79% of the water fed into supply networks in rural France reaches consumers. Nationwide, the average is around 84%. But repairs are slow, and currently only about 0.6% of pipes are replaced every year.
Extreme heat batters economy

Extreme heat and drought are also taking their toll on the economy. Monique Barbut, France's minister for the environmental transition, has estimated that the direct and indirect costs of this year's heat waves now could reach between €10 and 15 billion (up to $17.4 billion).

After the dry summer of 2022, President Emmanuel Macron declared water a national priority. A "Water Plan" unveiled in spring 2023 included more than 50 measures, including the target of a 10% reduction in water consumption by 2030 and plans to modernize the water supply network and fix leaks. Since then, some €1.4 billion has been spent on the national plan.
Supply chains at risk as Rhine dries up
To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video
In 2023, authorities identified some 170 municipalities whose water systems lost more than half of the water supplied to them. Within three years, over 100 had managed to reduce their losses.

Saving water is not only a matter of tapping into additional water sources or repairing dilapidated pipes. The scarcer water becomes, the more competition there is for this precious resource. Households need drinking water, farmers need water for irrigation and factories also need it for production. Increasingly, the question is how to determine which uses should be restricted and prioritized in an emergency.
One-third of EU population lives with water scarcity

France isn't alone in being unable to cope with long periods of drought. According to the European Environment Agency, seasonal water scarcity and water stress affect roughly 30% of the European Union's land area and almost one-third of its population.
In 2025, the European Commission presented the first European Water Resilience Strategy, which outlines plans to increase water efficiency by at least 10% by 2030 and modernize infrastructure.
German municipalities impose water restrictions
On the other side of the Rhine River in Germany, there is currently evidence in the Black Forest region that spring and groundwater levels are declining.

So far, the Badenova service company seems to have enough groundwater supplies. But several municipalities in the Dreisam Valley have asked the company to make preparations for transporting water by tanker truck, if need be.
Technology can't solve all problems

How Europe deals with increasing water scarcity depends heavily on its geography. Thanks to a network connecting lakes, canals, locks and pumps, the Netherlands can usually supply households with water from the Rhine and Meuse rivers. But this summer there has also been an official water shortage in that country, so additional freshwater is being stored and distributed strategically.

Southern Europe has long been planning for water shortages. Large reservoirs and long-distance pipelines have become standard in Spain, which also relies on seawater desalination processes in particularly arid regions.
This article was originally written in German.

articles.title: Minors living alone on Ceuta's streets at risk of abuse
articles.summary: Several thousand unaccompanied minors have gathered in Ceuta, a Spanish enclave on the northern coast of Africa. Illness and abuse are rife, and the authorities admit they are overwhelmed.

image.caption: Thousands of children have been left to their own devices in CeutaImage: Jan-Philipp Scholz/DW

blocks.text: It's 8 a.m. at the Tarajal industrial park in the autonomous city of Ceuta. But there are no workers and truck drivers to be seen near the warehouses today. Instead, there are makeshift tents, some of them made out of cardboard, with mainly children and teenagers sleeping under dirty blankets.

According to certain estimates, there could be between 3,000 and 5,000 unaccompanied minors in Ceuta. Some are living on the streets because they cannot find a spot in one of the already overcrowded reception facilities in the enclave.

Amina (not her real name), a 14-year-old Moroccan girl, and her brother were among the 80,000 people who crossed the border into Spain from Morocco in late July. Though most of these have since left Ceuta, some 9,000 remain, according to the local authorities — and many are minors. "
What's worst is that we don't have toilets," said Amina. "We have to go somewhere in the bushes, but I don't dare go alone."

Close by is a Moroccan woman called Malika (also not her real name) who has spread out several blankets for herself and her four children. She told DW she was not making enough as a cleaning lady in Morocco, adding that she earned the equivalent of €7 ($8) per day.
"That's just not enough to provide for everyone," she said. "School will start again soon, and I don't have any money for books, nor even decent clothes for the children."
That's why she decided to take part in the mass crossing of the Spanish border last month when she read about it on social media. But now she doesn't know what to do.

blocks.caption: Malika said she does not know what to do now that she is in CeutaImage: Jan-Philipp Scholz/DW

blocks.text: "One child got sick. He had a high fever, but I couldn't get help anywhere," she said. In the end, she made compresses with water and vinegar to see if that would help.

But now she is particularly worried about her 12-and 14-year-old daughters, because the number of sexual assaults has risen sharply in the past week. Police are currently investigating at least 15 suspected cases of rape. The local authorities suspect the actual number of cases to be much higher.
Conditions particularly difficult for girls
Susana Ascaso, an emergency doctor at Ceuta University Hospital, said she had treated several young girls in recent days.

"Just yesterday, another 12-year-old came to the emergency room," she said. "She said that other migrants had harassed her and touched her inappropriately. She arrived here completely terrified and in tears. She was with a woman who had found her on the street. That woman saved the girl."

Ascaso said conditions were particularly difficult for "girls under 18" who were "particularly at risk." She added that there was a major imbalance in the numbers of male and female migrants. "That doesn't help, of course."
Did Morocco instigate the Ceuta migrant incident?
To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Several high-ranking politicians in Ceuta have called for more support from the central government in the Spanish capital, Madrid. Nabila Benzina, the regional minister for health and social affairs, told DW that the current crisis was the "worst moment in Ceuta's history" and said more police officers were needed in the enclave. "Especially to protect young women, but also for the general protection of the population."

Ceuta's president, Juan Jesus Vivas, spoke of a "high-risk situation," in which it was increasingly difficult to maintain public services. "As far as minors are concerned, we are currently 5,000% over capacity," he said. "That means nobody can look after them adequately."
'I'd like to be an architect one day'

The Spanish government has announced plans to transfer unaccompanied minors to the mainland but there is no concrete timeline. Several regions, in which the far-right Vox party is part of the government, have said they refuse to take in any migrants.

Vivas told DW that the minors should be "reunited with their families. Otherwise, the Moroccan social services should assume responsibility for them." He said this was the only solution, adding that Madrid should put the "appropriate legal proceedings" in motion.
Ceuta migrant surge puts pressure on Spain, Morocco
Many of the minors in Ceuta said they do not want to go back to Morocco or elsewhere in Africa despite the conditions in Ceuta.
Ibrahim, a 7-year-old child from Sudan, said he would not give up until he could provide "a better life for his parents back home." Amina, 14, also said she would not go back to Morocco.
"The schools here are really bad. I want a different future for myself. I'd like to become an architect someday," she said.
This article was originally written in German.

articles.title: Will Germany's drought push up food prices?
articles.summary: Germany's main farmers' association has warned of a below-average harvest after drought and crops damaged by extreme heat. DW looks into what lower yields could mean for food prices and grocery bills.

image.caption: This summer's drought has dried out entire fields in parts of GermanyImage: Patrick Pleul/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: 1. How severe is Germany's 2026 harvest decline?
The German Farmers' Association (DBV) on Tuesday warned of a "below-average" harvest due to ongoing drought that has left large areas of farmland severely parched.

In a statement, DBV President Joachim Rukwied warned that the country's grain harvest would be 7% lower than last year, blaming an "overly dry spring and a heat wave in the second half of June," which had "significantly damaged many crops."
Overall grain production was expected to be 41.9 million tons this year, the DBV said, a shortfall of some 3.3 million tons compared with 2025.
Rapeseed saw the largest fall, with 3.3 million tons harvested, nearly 17% lower than last year. Barley remained at last year's level despite a lower yield, as more land was used to grow the crop.
The potato crop was also expected to be below average and some regions would see a "significantly worse" harvest for sugar beet, DBV said.
Rukwied noted how location played a bigger role in determining crop yields this year than usual, and pointed to poor crop yields and even crop failures, particularly in southern and western Germany.
German farmers face harvest losses, price uncertainty
To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video
Separately, Germany's Federal Statistical Office warned that the country's apple harvest was forecast to drop 18% compared with last year.

Germany is experiencing a severe drought during a summer of frequent record-breaking temperatures, which has exacerbated the effects of below-average rainfall since March, according to the German Weather Service.
2. How will the drought affect food prices and availability?

Agriculture Minister Alois Rainer told public broadcaster ZDF on Tuesday that ministers "don't expect prices to rise immediately," leaving open the possibility of a time lag before consumers pay more for groceries.

However, Philipp Spinne, managing director of the German Raiffeisen Association (DRV), which represents 1,600 agricultural cooperatives, told DW its members had already suffered "pure losses in the field" of €600 million ($696 million).
"At the moment, many areas of farming and the chain are not covering their costs," Spinne warned, describing how higher fertilizer, energy and logistics costs were adding to the pressure on farmers.

blocks.caption: In Germany, some fields have suffered total or near-total crop failure due to drought and excessive heatImage: Frank Hoermann/SvenSimon/picture alliance

blocks.text: Germany does have a 2 million-ton grain surplus from last year's harvest, according to government data, which could prevent a hike in bread prices.
Yet, the sharp drop in rapeseed and sugar beet production may strain domestic oil and sugar supplies, requiring imports to make up the shortfall.
Local media reported last week that the drought had also caused a drastic fall in animal feed stocks in several states, particularly in southern Germany.
The German Farmers' Association warned of a reduction in livestock numbers, due to “major challenges” in feed supply. This could push up prices for meat, milk and eggs.

In the hardest-hit areas of the country, potatoes and other vegetables could become more expensive as supply tightens. For most shoppers, however, the main impact is more likely to be gradual price increases rather than shortages.
3. How does this drought fit into wider food security concerns?
Farming, both at home and globally, has faced repeated pressures since the COVID-19 pandemic.
German food prices have risen by over 36% since 2020, according to government data published last month.
The price hikes were especially strong for poultry meat, many dairy products and eggs, edible fats and oils, and sugar, the government calculated.
Russia's war in Ukraine disrupted Black Sea exports of Ukrainian grain in 2022 and drove energy prices higher, impacting the cost of fertilizer, transport and food processing.
More recently, the closure of the Strait of Hormuz due to the Iran war prevented oil, gas and fertilizer ingredients from leaving the Gulf.
The conflict has pushed up prices of diesel fuel, fertilizers and pesticides, with some farmers cutting back on soil nutrients.

Compounding crises over the past six years have left large parts of the German agriculture sector financially stretched, the industry has warned. Many farmers have said they face much higher costs and rising debts, and have limited room to absorb further losses.

blocks.caption: In previous years, farmers have used tractors to blockade roads to pressure the government for helpImage: Daniel Bockwoldt/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: 4. What support are German farmers seeking?
The German Farmers' Association said some farmers may need interim financing to secure their futures. Rukwied called on Berlin to launch an "immediate package" to help support the agriculture sector.
Recommendations include boosting the European Union's fertilizer aid package from €60 million to €180 million, paid out quickly and without red tape.
DBV also called on ministers to cut the tax on agricultural diesel, at least until the end of November.
For several months from late 2023, German farmers blocked highways with tractors over plans to scrap fuel subsidies for the agricultural sector, which were later partially reversed.
Agriculture Minister Rainer promised targeted help to farmers, but only when reliable official figures are available at the end of August.
Edited by: Tim Rooks

articles.title: Dressed for power: Giorgia Meloni and the language of fashion
articles.summary: From Giorgia Meloni's shift from dark suits to pastels to Angela Merkel's signature jackets, politicians have long used clothing to shape how voters see them. In this day and age, power dressing has…

image.caption: Meloni has become known for her pastel colors and casual clothingImage: Stefano Carofei/ipa-agency/picture alliance

blocks.text: Often dressing in pastel colors, with wide-legged pants falling over her high heels, Italy's first female prime minister can't escape fashion scrutiny — and not only because Giorgia Meloni is the leader of the world's fashion capital.
"Fashion is a language — it tells us what its wearer wants to say without any actual words," Michela Bonafoni, who teaches fashion at Unicollege in Florence, told DW.

"Perhaps what you wear is very close to your personality. But if you want to give a different impression of yourself, you can also do this through clothing — this is what Meloni does constantly," explained Bonafoni.

blocks.caption: Meloni began her tenure as prime minister wearing dark suits ,as seen in this photo from December 2022Image: IRAQI PRIME MINISTER'S PRESS OFFICE /AFP

blocks.text: Meloni's clothing style can be read as part of a broader political transition: from outsider to establishment figure. When she first took office in 2022, her appearance was closely tied to the political identity she had built as a leader of the right-wing Brothers of Italy party with post-fascist roots. Her look: dark suits with chunky boots, serious and even combative.

Enter the concept of "power dressing," which emerged in the 1970s and became influential in the 1980s, as second-wave feminism coincided with more women entering professional and managerial roles. The suit became a way for women to signal authority in traditionally male workplaces.

Italian designer Giorgio Armani played a key role — his softer, more fluid tailoring offered a new version of the power suit — borrowing from menswear while creating a more feminine language of authority.

During her first official public appearances, Meloni was often seen in dark Armani suits, a nod to traditional power dressing, and a look that said, according to Bonafoni: "I'm here in this kind of government and that's all there is to it."
From masculine suits to pastels

Since then, Meloni's look has softened — she's often seen in wide-legged silhouettes and suits in cream, beige, pink and other muted or pastel shades. The style change also coincides with how she has become a more established figure in European politics, moving closer to the European Union and becoming a prominent supporter of Ukraine.

Yet, Meloni has maintained a conservative approach to domestic politics, which hasn't gone down well with much of the public — including many in the country's fashion industry. No luxury brand, including Armani, has publicly stepped forward to style her or support her use of their clothing.

This hasn't stopped Meloni from using fashion to appeal to a broader public. "When Meloni understood that many Italians didn't like some of the actions of her government, she started to wear the pastel colors, which incite understanding and say 'I'm Giorgia, a woman who is kind,'" said Bonafoni. The author also pointed out that Meloni sports "Made in Italy" designers as part of her brand of nationalism — attaching its power to her own.

blocks.caption: Today, Meloni (seen here meeting German Chancellor Friedrich Merz in June) often wears wide trousers and softer colorsImage: Chris Emil Janßen/picture alliance

blocks.text: At the Salone del Mobile, Italy's premier design event in Milan this past April, Meloni chose an informal look: jeans and a casual beige blazer.

"Her look said: I'm casual because I'm just like you — but I'm also exactly where I want to be right now in this moment and in this government," said Bonafoni. Such a style exudes confidence and is closer to the more relaxed style of female politicians in the US, Bonafoni added.

blocks.caption: Merkel wore a distinctive 'uniform' during the years she served as Germany's chancellorImage: Kay Nietfeld/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: A political 'uniform'
But political power doesn't always require a changing wardrobe. For some female leaders, consistency itself can become a form of power dressing.

Former German Chancellor Angela Merkel developed one of the most recognizable wardrobes in modern politics. Her formula was remarkably consistent: trousers and a three-button jacket, with the jackets appearing in an extraordinary range of colors. The simplicity itself became a kind of uniform, putting Merkel herself, as a politician, rather than her fashion, at the center.
"Her 'second skin' of clothing was very close to her character, her attitudes and political decisions she made," said Bonafoni.

Former British Prime Minister Margaret Thatcher also had her fashion uniforms so to speak, down pat. Her appearance was carefully constructed — tailored suits, pearls, handbags — an instantly recognizable version of feminine political authority in her era.

These days, Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum offers another prime example of a politician who uses clothing to send a message. She frequently wears garments made by women artisans from Mexico to show her support and solidarity with Mexico's Indigenous communities.

blocks.caption: Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum is known for wearing clothing made by women in Indigenous communitiesImage: Carlos Santiago/Eyepix Group/IMAGO

blocks.text: From hipster dad to tactical wear

While the few women politicians we have on the world stage fall under increased fashion scrutiny, men too have long understood the political power of appearance — perhaps now more than ever. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy often chooses to wear tactical clothing that's far from the standard suit and tie look of most world leaders.

As Ukrainian journalist Illia Ponomarenko told Politico last year, it's part of his anti-elitist message, one that directly confronts the world leaders he meets. "His clothes are basically asking: What are you about? Are you about the business of saving lives, or are you about fancy protocols?" said Ponomarenko. "Even when he meets with kings, he dresses in a way that represents the average Ukrainian involved in this war effort. So it's a message to say, 'I've come to the corners of power as a representative of my humble people.'"

blocks.caption: President Volodymyr Zelenskyy (right) and UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham (left) opt for more casual looksImage: Press Service Of The President Of Ukraine/SvenSimon/picture alliance

blocks.text: Similarly, the UK's Labour Party Prime Minister Andy Burnham, whose look has been referred to as "hipster dad," chooses smart-casual styles; T-shirts, polo shirts and trainers. It's a political messaging move that says he's on the same level as the public.
As for Giorgia Meloni, Bonafoni expects the world will soon see another style change as she is challenged by far-right politician and former army general Roberto Vannacci.

"Meloni has said she doesn't want Vannacci in her government, but her party will need him in a coalition if it wants to remain in power," said Bonafoni. "I'm sure if and when Vannacci challenges her, she will change her style again because she'll have to present herself as someone who's even more powerful."
Edited by: Tenzin Sekhon

articles.title: How to grow food for more people in a hotter world
articles.summary: Inside futuristic labs, plants are scanned, stressed and analyzed. The aim is to use the results to produce plant strains that can better serve a growing population in a warming world.

image.caption: As the world gets hotter, scientists are exploring ways to make crops more resilientImage: Manuel Vering/DW

blocks.text: Rows of tomato saplings stand in a room packed with cameras. Just a few weeks old, they're under constant surveillance as scientists monitor them for tiny changes in color, temperature and photosynthesis.

These plants are growing in a chamber designed to mimic the heat and humidity of India's climate. By analyzing their reactions to different stressors, researchers at Wageningen University in the Netherlands are aiming to uncover genetic traits that have the potential to make crops resilient to human-caused climate change.

"We can regulate the temperature. We can give them a heat stress phase, we can freeze shortly, so we can simulate night frost, which could be very disruptive for young plants," explained Rick van de Zedde, program manager at the Netherlands Plant Eco-phenotyping Centre (NPEC). "We can introduce salinity by adding salt."
In fact, the scientists can simulate almost any condition on the planet. "I would call it a gym for plants," said van de Zedde.
Why understanding plants is so important

This research is becoming ever more essential. Agriculture has traditionally relied on predictable seasons and conditions, with farmers planning around established weather patterns — planting in the spring and harvesting in the autumn, for example.
But as societies burn fossil fuels that heat the planet, rising global temperatures are disrupting that rhythm.

blocks.caption: Farmers are grappling with more unpredictable weather conditions as a result of a warming worldImage: Jens Büttner/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Increasing heat waves, longer and more intensive droughts and severe flooding caused by global heating is increasingly putting crops at risk.

Following soaring temperatures this summer, farmers in some regions of Germany are warning of harvest failure. Grain production losses have already been registered in countries including France, Hungary and the United Kingdom.

With the global population predicted to hit 10 billion by 2050, the pressure is on to produce enough food. That race is intensified by rising meat consumption, which implies growing more grain for animal feed.
Simultaneously, demand for crops to use as biofuels, which are made from organic material including plants or animal waste, is also on the rise.
For researchers, the question is no longer just how to grow more food, but how to do so under increasingly challenging conditions.
A high-tech way ahead

Dubbed the 'Silicon Valley' of agriculture, the Netherlands has long been a leader in farming innovation. Despite its relatively small size, the country is the world's second-largest exporter of agricultural products by value — after the US.

blocks.caption: Researchers say crossbreeding plant varieties could help them grow with traits more resilient to a hotter climateImage: Manuel Vering/DW

blocks.text: Inside the Wageningen University greenhouses, scientists recreate environmental conditions such as drought, tropical humidity or frosty nights, and use a range of technology to monitor the plants.

Over a period of weeks, automated scales record the weights of tree species every three minutes to reveal how much water they need. Sophisticated scanners track the movement of leaves as part of a process known as phenotyping — which measures plants and their features.
Though botanists have been tracking flora for thousands of years to select the best plants, the processes were historically manual and therefore slow and painstaking.

"All the lab measurements were restricting the size of the experiments," van de Zedde told DW. "If you look around here in NPEC, you see that we are talking about thousands of plants in one experiment."
Taking experiments into the field
Despite the sophistication of the lab, it cannot completely mirror real-world conditions. Factors like hailstorms, high winds or differing soil temperatures remain difficult to recreate.

Near the university, experimental barley fields provide an important reality check. It is there that researchers deploy mobile imaging and use GPS positioning systems to collect data on hundreds of crop varieties in the field.
By comparing greenhouse and field results, they are better able to identify the plant traits that will help produce food that is going to be resilient to a changing climate.
"It's all about fitness. We simply score: how do these plants respond to the stress? Which ones can cope with it, which ones suffer from it," said van de Zedde.

blocks.caption: Scientists are able to test thousands of plants in closely monitored greenhousesImage: Manuel Vering/DW

blocks.text: Researchers can use the data to see the DNA profiles linked to tolerance to certain stressors. They can then crossbreed varieties — one with a high yield and one that is robust, for example, to produce resilient offspring.
What's next for the research?
The goal is to fast forward evolution. The Dutch government and plant-breeding companies funding the research will decide which variants to continue to breed.
But Alan Pauls, a Ph.D candidate in the university's Laboratory of Genetics, said the process has been met with criticism from some quarters.

"When you talk to the older generation, I definitely do feel like they don't trust it," he said. "The moment you talk about taking food or plants into a lab, immediately [what] you think about is GMO."
Why does genetic engineering have such a bad image?
To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Genetically modified organisms, or GMOs, have had their genes changed artificially to make them take on a particular characteristic. One way it's done is to insert a gene from a different species, like bacteria, into a plant.

In the European Union, genetic modification is strictly legally regulated and requires rigorous safety checks. At Wageningen, just 5% of experiments involve genetically modified plants. Most focus on selecting existing traits through phenotyping, speeding up natural processes rather than creating new characteristics.
Pauls believes the argument that too much interference makes food artificial is outdated.

"Are we thinking that it's artificial because a machine is involved? Are we thinking that it's artificial because it's happening so fast, or it's happening in a lab?" he said. "I can still harvest rice with a sickle, but is it going to feed a billion people in time? No."
Edited by: Tamsin Walker
This article was adapted from a video in DW's Planet A series.

articles.title: Belgium wildfire: Rains help High Fens containment efforts
articles.summary: Firefighters continue to battle one of the worst wildfires in Belgian history near the German border. Rains and cooler temperatures are helping them bring it to heel after it ravaged an area half the…

image.caption: Firefighters said the blaze was no longer spreading amid improving weather conditions on Tuesday, but it continued to burnImage: Yves Herman/REUTERS

blocks.text: Belgian firefighters were pushing to encircle and contain the country's largest wildfire in a century.
Rain and cooler temperatures provided some natural relief against the blaze on Tuesday but also teamed up with winds to hamper air support and waterbombing operations.
The fire expanded to cover an area of around 3,000 hectares — about half the size of Manhattan in New York — by Monday.
The High Fens, or Hautes Fagnes, nature reserve is a vast expanse of boggy peatlands, pine forests and hiking trails, with parts of it difficult to access with large machinery, except from above.

blocks.caption: Light rain fell on Tuesday morning, with heavier precipitation forecast later — this both helped to douse the fire naturally but also hampered efforts to use planes and helicopters to drop water en masse from aboveImage: Sascha Thelen/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: What's the latest on the firefighting efforts?
"We are trying to definitively encircle the fire today," regional government spokesman Niolas Yernaux told the AFP news agency on Tuesday.
Firefighters worked through the night to try to make a crucial link-up between the eastern and northern fronts, despite difficult access conditions in the hilly and wooded area.

blocks.caption: The hilly and densely forested nature reserve is dotted with rough farm tracks and hiking trails, not an abundance of paved roads suited to heavy machineryImage: Oliver Berg/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: "We're talking about one or two kilometers, and we're on the verge of achieving it," Yernaux said.
He said that the fire was "under control and contained" in areas where firefighters could operate.

blocks.caption: Belgium's interior minister warned the fire was so vast that efforts to douse it and prevent it from rekindling would need to be thorough and could take weeks, even once it is extinguishedImage: Yves Herman/REUTERS

blocks.text: However, Yernaux said the hard-to-reach front stretching towards the German border and the town of Monschau remained a concern; much of this area is only really accessible from above. The wind and rain could delay such aerial operations, potentially until Tuesday evening, he warned.
How far from the border is the fire, what's the situation in Monschau?

Residents of Monschau have already been told to leave their homes because of the smoke hazard, with the fire roughly 2.3 kilometers (roughly 1.5 miles) from the border. Yernaux said that "strong winds" were blowing towards the east and the German frontier.

blocks.caption: Firefighters and civilian emergency response crews are on hand in Monschau, some of them also assisting colleagues in Belgium Image: Oliver Berg/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: "At the moment it's manageable," Monschau fire service spokesman Tobias Schnell told the dpa news agency. Should the winds pick up further, he said that could fan the flames in the town's direction.

He said that water tanks and other equipment had already been placed in its potential path in case it is needed. He said around 170 people were working on a three-shift rotation around the clock, and that authorities were working on the assumption the operation would last several more days at least.

blocks.caption: Flames could be seen from the border overnight at the peak of the blazeImage: Thomas Banneyer/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Smoke has spread dozens of kilometers to the east, with major cities like Cologne and Wuppertal both warning residents of the risk of poor air quality and smoke.
"At present the smell of the fire can be perceived throughout the city," Wuppertal's fire department warned, recommending that people close doors and windows. "A health risk cannot be ruled out."
Locals start to return, but still urged to limit movements
Villagers in places like Sourbrodt, which was evacuated at the peak of the fire over the weekend, started returning to their homes as the threat subsided on Monday evening.
Nevertheless, the local Waimes municipality asked residents to exercise continued caution.

"Residents are asked to limit travel within this area to what is strictly necessary and to act with particular vigilance and responsibility," it said. "Despite the return of evacuated residents, operations carried out by the various emergency, security and response services remain a priority and must be able to proceed under the best possible conditions."

blocks.caption: Affected areas of the nature reserve itself are also strictly off limits for summer hikers at presentImage: Yves Herman/REUTERS

blocks.text: Two villages in the Bütgenbach municipality, meanwhile, remain cleared, with conditions not yet safe there.
Wallonia's Agriculture Ministry also said on Tuesday that it would review compensation for farmers who volunteered to help with the firefighting efforts.

blocks.caption: Farmers in the area turned their machinery into water transporters or helped to try to clear foliage from the path of the fire to halt or slow its spreadImage: Nicolas Lambert/Belga/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: This is was "under review — regarding both the substance and the procedure, as well as the legal feasiblity of doing so," Agriculture Minister Anne-Catherine Dalcq's office said on Tuesday.
This followed an appeal from the presdient of the Royal Federation of Belgian Firefighters, who demanded reciprocal aid after the farmers' help battling the blaze.
"Who will cover the cost of the equipment damaged during this operation? Without them, the situation would be far worse," Marc Gilbert had said in an interview with the Belga news agency.
European aircraft join battle as Belgium's wildfire spreads
To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video
The vast fire gathered pace just after another a few kilometers east across the German border in the Hürtgenwald forest was contained late last week.
Edited by: Saim Dušan Inayatullah

articles.title: How Germany's Hyrox became a global fitness craze
articles.summary: Created in Germany and now a global success, Hyrox combines running and functional training into a unique format. How a German concept became an international sports phenomenon.

image.caption: These competitors in Toulouse look like fitness pros, but everyone can take part in Hyrox events, regardless of gender or fitness levelImage: Nathan Barange/Icon Sport/Sipa USA/picture alliance

blocks.text: There is probably no other sport in the world that has experienced a boom like Hyrox in recent years. What started as an idea in 2017 has, within just a few years, evolved into one of the fastest-growing fitness movements in the world.

The format was developed by event organizer Christian Toetzke, communications expert Michael Trautmann, and Moritz Fürste, a former member of the German national field hockey team that won gold at the 2008 and 2012 Summer Olympics.

Their basic idea was very simple: to create a competition that combines the atmosphere of a running event with the intensity of functional strength training that many people know from time in the gym. Hyrox consists of eight functional stations interspersed by eight 1-kilometer (0.62 miles) runs.

blocks.caption: Moritz Fürste went from national field hockey player to Hyrox founderImage: Peter Hartenfelser/Hartenfelser/IMAGO

blocks.text: "People love to either challenge themselves or compete against others, take part in a contest and battle their own inner demons," Fürste told DW.
People were already doing this. Hyrox standardizes it as a competition format.
Hyrox gives people a new purpose
To develop their concept, the founders analyzed the global sports landscape and found a gap in the established sports market.
"Most sports — such as tennis, football or ball sports in general — are very clearly defined," explained Fürste.

"They've all been around for hundreds of years, but the one area of the sports world that was never really defined was the world of the gym. We wanted to give these people a goal to train for, aside from being healthy or looking good in the mirror."

Hyrox is not the only attempt at creating competition around gym work. CrossFit is perhaps its most famous rival. It started back in 2007, changes daily and features Olympic weightlifting and gymnastics.

Hyrox is the same each time, offering more functional fitness development. The closest in style to Hyrox is DEKA Fit, although the latter's global reach is affected by its focus on local US affiliate gyms.
For Fürste, the definition of success is what happens at the end of races.
"No one finishes a race with any energy left; everyone is completely exhausted. But everyone thinks about being faster next time," Fürste said.
Why young men are obsessed with lifting weights
To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video
Clearly, Hyrox isn't the only way to train, but Fürste believes it is a good way to train for competition.

The standardized format means that events are comparable worldwide, regardless of whether you compete in Hamburg, London, New York, or Sydney. As a result, there has been a surge in interest in recent years.
Hyrox growing 100% in all markets

In a 2025 interview with Sports Illustrated, Fürste spoke of two pivotal moments for Hyrox; first, when 650 participants turned out for their first-ever event and second, when they sold out an event in London in 2022, after the COVID pandemic. It was clear then that they were on to something.
In the 2022–23 season, around 90,000 athletes took part in Hyrox competitions. By 2025, that number had already risen to more than 650,000.

blocks.caption: Hyrox is also successful in ChinaImage: China News Service/VCG/IMAGO

blocks.text: "No matter where we've gone so far, we've seen tremendous growth in the first two to three years," Fürste said.
"There wasn't a single market that didn't grow by 100% from one event to the next. This shows that the product works. It's a great experience for those who take part."
Next stop: 2032 Olympics
With more than a million athletes set to compete in Hyrox events worldwide this season, it looks like there's no sign of the boom ending anytime soon.
"This shows that we're neither a trend nor a niche," Fürste said. "It shows that we've made our mark in the sports world."

Hyrox is now present in more than 85 cities in around 30 countries across the world. Studies confirm the series' extraordinary growth, with more than 278,000 finishers recorded by the end of the 2023-24 season alone.
"I invested a lot and met with people who have been working in the industry for years," said Fürste, who believes Hyrox is like the modern sports version of a music festival.
"I had to risk everything to get where I am now and to be part of this team."

While he never doubted Hyrox's success, he also never imagined it would become so big. And now the next goal looms on the horizon. Fürste told Sports Illustrated that he aims to make Hyrox part of the Olympic program in Brisbane in 2032, taking the popular fitness event to the world's biggest sporting stage.
This article was originally published in German.

articles.title: Ukraine, Russia trade strikes; Wildberries site hit again
articles.summary: Ukriane reported 10 dead in a missile strike in the northeastern Kharkiv oblast near the border. Russia, meanwhile, reported more than 600 drones approaching the Moscow area and warned the UK on…

image.caption: Ukrainian officials reported 10 dead and 18 wounded in Pechenihy in the Kharkiv regionImage: Ukrainian Emergency Service/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: Ukraine and Russia traded more attacks overnight, with the Kharkiv regional governor reporting 10 dead civilians not far from the Russian border and the Moscow mayor saying Ukraine launched some 620 drones toward the region.

This follows one of the largest Ukrainian attacks on Russia during the war over the weekend, and the UN warning that amplified Russian strikes on towns and cities in July meant that civilian deaths in the conflict rose to levels not seen since May 2022 and the earliest months of combat.
The drone attacks on the Moscow area again caused minor damage at a facility belonging to Russian online retail giant Wildberries, a frequent target for Ukrainian forces of late.

blocks.caption: Rescuers responded to the Tuesday morning missile strike near Ukraine's northeastern border to RussiaImage: Ukrainian Emergency Service/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: What happened in the Kharkiv missile strike?
The governor of the Kharkiv oblast, Oleh Syniehubov, on Tuesday said that the 10 people were killed and 18 more wounded in a Russian missile strike on the village of Pechenihy.
"The strike damaged 10 private houses, a cafe, a post office, a shop and at least seven cars," Syniehubov wrote on Telegram, noting that the casualty figures were preliminary.
He said emergency services were responding and dealing with the attack.
Parts of the Kharkiv region in northeastern Ukraine are occupied by Russian forces. Both Kharkiv and the Belgorod region across the border in Russia have been targeted frequently throughout the war.
Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said the attack targeted a busy intersection.
How Ukraine fights in the Black Sea without a navy
To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video
What happened as hundreds of drones approached Moscow?

Moscow's Mayor Sergei Sobyanin said on Tuesday that some 620 drones had flown towards the capital region overnight. He said that most were intercepted on approach, and another 180 were shot down over the Moscow area.

blocks.caption: Moscow's regional governor posted an image of what he said was a fire at a construction site after a drone attack near Russia's capitalImage: Moscow Region Governor Andrei Vorobyov's official telegram channel/AP Photo/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Russian state news agency TASS called it the heaviest such attack in two years. Russia's Defense Ministry said that, in total, it repelled 791 Ukrainian drones overnight across Russian territoy and the annexed Crimean Peninsula. The figures cannot be verified but indicate the intensity of Ukrainian strikes into Russian territory in recent days.
Moscow's regional governor, Andrei Vorobyov, issued more details on the damage caused by the drones shot down over the capital, giving a slightly lower figure of "over 150."
He said that three people were injured in three separate districts, including a young girl with a shrapnel wound to the hand.
Vorobyov also reported damage to several mainly residential buildings, including one house that "burned down completely in the village of Kuznetsy."
He said that a drone also struck a "Wildberries warehouse near Atlant-Park" in the city of Kolomna, which also logged damage at a retail site near a shopping center.
Russian court confirms anti-war party election ban
What did Russia say about reports of UK drones being used in strikes on its territory?

Russia's Embassy in London also turned its attention to drone attacks this week, responding critically on Monday evening to reports in newspaper The Times saying that drones supplied by the UK had been used in attacks on Russian territory.
The embassy asserted that such reports "confirm that London is deliberately opting for an escalation of the Ukraine crisis, while hypocritically professing a desire for peace."

It accused the UK of "acting as an accomplice and co-perpetrator of the bloody crimes and terrorist attacks committed by Ukrainian neo-Nazis," and said that "London's actions will inevitably carry consequences for which it will have to answer."
What did Germany's environment minister say during his visit to Kyiv?
Also on Tuesday, German Environment Minister Carsten Schneider traveled to Kyiv.
The Social Democrat (SPD) politician planned to spend several days in the country this week if circumstances allow.

"The goal of the trip is to work with our Ukrainian partners to identify, at an early stage, opportunities for a climate-friendly, resilient renewal of infrastructure and further reconstruction, including with the participation of the German business community," the Envirnoment Ministry said on Tuesday as Schneider was arriving.
The minister was accompanied by business representatives, not least from companies specializing in climate-friendly technologies.

Schneider also planned to be briefed on the situation for Ukraine's nuclear power plants, including the damage to protective dome covering the Chernobyl or Chornobyl reactor that melted down in the 1980s during the Soviet era.
"Its repair is highly complex," the ministry said.

Ukraine's main functioning nuclear power plant at Zaporizhzhia, meanwhile, has been under Russian military occupation and operational control since the first weeks of the war in 2022. Its reactors are in cold shutdown status but the plant still requires external power, cooling and maitenance. Close to the front lines, the plant and the surrounding area has fairly frequently come under fire.
Edited by: Louis Oelofse

articles.title: Do not inhale! How wildfire smoke 'affects the whole body'
articles.summary: Wildfires destroy lives and livelihoods. But survivors and firefighters also suffer long-term harm to their health. A growing body of research suggests particulate matter (PM2.5) in wildfire smoke is…

image.caption: Research indicates that wildfire smoke is uniquely toxic for human healthImage: Pedro Rocha/REUTERS

blocks.text: Researchers are beginning to understand the long-term impact of wildfire smoke exposure on human health. And it's not good. "Your whole body is affected," said Yang Liu, Professor of Environmental Health at Emory University in Atlanta. "Wildfire smoke causes oxidative stress to your system and exacerbates or accelerates the development of diseases."
In a study published in January 2026, Yang Liu and other researchers found that repeated exposure to even moderate amounts of smoke increases the risk of stroke among older adults.
A month later, another study found that long-term exposure to wildfire smoke had contributed to an average of 24,100 deaths a year in the United States between 2006 and 2020.
Wildfire smoke contains a mixture of hazardous air pollutants. But one of the most aggressive components appears to be tiny specks of particulate matter, known as PM2.5.
PM2.5 is made up of soot, dust, and other substances that act like sponges, binding toxic metals and organic compounds to them.
If inhaled, PM2.5 particles can get into the lungs and bloodstream, from where they cause inflammation and damage to various other organs in the body.
Long-term exposure to PM2.5 has been linked to lung diseases like asthma, as well as heart disease, diabetes, dementia, and cancer.
Wildfire smoke is particularly dangerous for pregnant women. It can increase the risk of premature births and low birth weight.
What makes PM2.5 in wildfire smoke so toxic
Wildfire PM2.5 is particularly toxic due to complex mixtures of burning materials found at any site, which can differ between rural fires and those that spread to urban areas.

"It really does depend on the location of the fire. It might even vary from block to block — the smoke may consist of different components," said Mary Johnson, a principal research scientist in the Department of Environmental Health at the Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health.

blocks.caption: Researchers have detected heavy metals and other potentially carcinogenic compounds, such as PFAS, or "forever chemicals" in wildfire smoke Image: Tomas Cuesta/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: Johnson led an international team that studied toxic substances in wildfire smoke in a group of healthy firefighters and civilians who had recently been exposed to wildfire smoke. They wanted to understand how these toxins disrupt immune cell function and increase the body's susceptibility to infections and chronic diseases.

The researchers found mercury and cadmium — both heavy metals found naturally in plants and soils, as well as in man-made materials. They also found carcinogenic compounds and so-called forever chemicals, known as PFAS.
PFAS are synthetic chemicals used in many everyday products and building materials. They have been linked to various cancers and metabolic conditions.
Their findings led them to suggest future research should focus on developing treatments for vulnerable groups like children and elderly people and those with chronic health conditions.
Wildfire smoke becomes more toxic over time and distance
Wildfire smoke becomes more dangerous as it ages, undergoing chemical reactions that increase its ability to damage cells.

Researchers in Greece found that smoke can get up to four times more toxic in the days following a fire. It can also travel long distances quickly and spread to areas thousands of miles away from the original source of the fire.

"If there is no rain to wash out these particles, they can stay in the atmosphere for ten days or sometimes more. They can go around the whole hemisphere and come back to the departure point within this time," said Nikolaos Mihalopoulos, director of the Institute for Environmental Research and Sustainable Development at the National Observatory of Athens.
During the Canadian wildfires of 2023, for example, 6,000 fires burned 15 million hectares of land, causing "long-range PM2.5 pollution" to spread across North America and even reach Europe and Asia.

In a paper published in September 2025, researchers estimated that about 5,400 acute deaths in North America and about 64,300 chronic deaths in North America and Europe could be linked to PM2.5 exposure from the 2023 Canadian wildfires.

However, it is worth noting that other sources of air pollution — traffic exhaust fumes, industrial emissions, and burning fuel for cooking — still cause more health problems overall because people are exposed to them daily.
Wildfires on the rise: Rethinking prevention across Europe
To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

"When we look at what really drives mortality in the population as a whole, it's still all these other sources [of air pollution] that are really responsible for so many deaths," said Cathryn Tonne, an environmental epidemiologist at the Barcelona Institute for Global Health.
How to protect yourself against wildfire smoke
Wildfire smoke is uniquely toxic, especially for people living near areas prone to fires.

"The more you can do to minimize exposure, the better," said Johnson, who recommends staying indoors during and immediately after fires, using filters on heating and air conditioning systems, keeping N95-grade masks available, and ensuring vulnerable people have emergency supplies of medication and inhalers readily accessible.

Ahead of fire seasons, people should clear their properties of flammable materials and set up neighborhood monitoring groups that look out for early fire signs and help stop small fires from becoming catastrophic ones.
Edited by: Zulfikar Abbany

articles.title: Germany: Bundeswehr troop numbers reach 13-year high
articles.summary: Germany's Defense Ministry is reporting a comparatively rare success story in its bid to bolster troop numbers. At the end of July, the total stood at around 186,700, roughly 3,700 more than a year…

image.caption: Germany, like several European countries, has been rushing to expand military spending and to recruit new soldiers [FILE: July 20, 2026]Image: Mike Schmidt/photowerkstatt/picture alliance

blocks.text: Germany's Bundeswehr military employed roughly 186,700 soldiers as of July 31 this year, the Defense Ministry said on Monday.

The increase is a relatively rare positive headline as Germany and its military try to ramp up recruitment, procurement and defense spending — to meet new NATO targets, appease the Donald Trump administration, and respond to perceived threats from Russia and beyond — encountering a string of setbacks and bottlenecks along the way.
By the mid-2030s, Germany aims to recruit some 70,000 more full-time troops than it currently has on retainer, to reach a full-time force of around 260,000 plus around 200,000 reservists.
Some, including Defense Minister Boris Pistorius, have voiced concerns that this might be difficult to achieve without reintroducing some form of military service.

blocks.caption: Defense Minister Boris Pistorius aims to set in motion an increase in troop strength in the region of one-third of the total German force over the coming decadeImage: Uwe Koch/HMB Media/picture alliance

blocks.text: What's the latest data on Bundeswehr troop numbers?

items: The Defense Ministry said the total of around 186,700 put the military inside its recruitment target window for this year with months to spare
It was aiming to reach between 186,000 and 190,000 personnel in 2026, and anticipates further increases this year
It also said it was the highest total in 'around 13 years,' soon after the 2011 abolition of the country's former period of mandatory national service for many young men
The total was an increase of roughly 3,700 troops, or around 2% of the total force, since the previous July
Applications were also up 26% year-on-year, at 47,300 in total
New hires from those applications rose 12%, to 15,400
Roughly 61,500 are career soldiers on permanent contracts
The bulk of the full-time force, around 113,000 troops, are on long-term temporary contracts
Short-term contract soldiers and volunteer forces' numbers also rose by about 6%, to around 12,100 in total

blocks.caption: Many members of the class of 2026 took their oaths on July 20 in a ceremony in Berlin, which is held on the anniversary of the failed 1944 plot to assassinate Adolf Hitler, in a bid to remind new recruits of the German army's modern valuesImage: Mike Schmidt/photowerkstatt/picture alliance

blocks.text: How are the new service surveys for young people faring?
The Defense Ministry also published information on the new service availability questionnaires that are trying to boost recruitment among people of school-leaving age.
A survey trying to gauge a person's availability, interest and suitability is sent to young men and women alike. Men are obliged to respond, women and people of other sexes or genders are not.
At present, responding in no way commits you to any form of service, no matter how great an interest you express or aptitude you demonstrate.
The figures do clearly point to the obligation to respond having a major impact on participation.
New military service rules: Young Germans face tough choice
To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video
Of around 194,000 men surveyed, 96% responded. But of 184,000 women and people of other genders questioned, only 4% voluntarily replied.
The ministry said that if you excluded people who responded with a 0 when asked to rank their interest in joining the military from 0 to 10, then the average figure given was a 5.
It said the questionnaires had led to 2,630 people coming in for assessments, and 865 people signing up for active service, starting either this year or in 2027.

"This proportional increase in staff is an 'add-on' — that is, a supplement to the extensive recruitment efforts that have contributed to the very encouraging number of applications and hires mentioned above," the Defense Ministry wrote.

blocks.caption: Fewer than 1,000 of Germany's military personnel are currently on deployment, but all manner of tasks await closer to home — such as fighting and containing a major wildfire in the Hürtgenwald forest in western Germany late last weekImage: Federico Gambarini/dpa/picture alliance
