articles.title: Norway wealth fund sounds alarm on AI stock market bubble
articles.summary: The head of Norway's sovereign wealth fund has warned that soaring AI-driven stock valuations could trigger a sharp correction. How exposed is the world's largest sovereign wealth fund to a market…

image.caption: Some global investors are warning of a bubble in artificial intelligence (AI) stocks as valuations surgeImage: Lev Radin/ZUMA/picture alliance

blocks.text: As if the vast scale of artificial intelligence (AI) investments wasn't scary enough, the head of the world's largest sovereign wealth fund is also sounding the alarm.

Nicolai Tangen, CEO of Norway's Government Pension Fund Global (GPFG), warned last week that, in an extreme market collapse, a massive loss to its $2.4 trillion (€2.07 trillion) portfolio is "not completely improbable."

The fund, created to invest the Nordic country's vast oil and gas revenues, delivered a record profit of 1,753 billion Norwegian kroner ($186 billion/€161 billion) in the first six months of the year.

blocks.caption: Nicolai Tangen, the head of Norway's sovereign wealth fund, has presided over record growthImage: Ole Berg-Rusten/NTB/IMAGO

blocks.text: Yet, Tangen warned that the AI-chip trade — whose lofty valuations helped drive those gains — now poses a serious risk. A sharp correction, he warned, could potentially erase much of the massive wealth built up over the past 30 years.
During what Tangen called an "abnormal" period of low taxes, low inflation and low interest rates, the investments now finance roughly a quarter of the Norwegian government's budget.
Why fund managers remain invested despite AI concerns

While Tangen might sound overly alarmist, Bill Megginson, a leading researcher on sovereign wealth funds, believes many established fund managers share his cautious stance on stock valuations, but are "staying the course, queasily."

"Few managers are inclined to take profits when such a fundamental technology buildout, fueled by literally unprecedented levels of capital spending, shows little evidence of brittleness," Megginson, a finance professor at the University of Oklahoma, told DW.
Major technology companies are expected to invest more than $1 trillion in AI-related infrastructure like chips, data centers and power infrastructure in the race to match or beat human intelligence.
AI is watching you: tracking, traps and surveillance
To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video
China, meanwhile, is developing capable AI models at a fraction of the cost of their rivals in the United States.
The Bank for International Settlements warned in June that AI "exuberance" risks ending in a bust if returns fall short of expectations.
Why Norway's wealth fund cannot easily hedge risk

Unlike Saudi Arabia or Singapore's sovereign wealth funds, which make large investments in private equity, infrastructure and real estate, Norway largely follows a benchmark-based investment strategy by buying index funds that track major global markets.
Technology accounts for roughly a third of the fund's stock investments.
"The oil fund follows a very passive, broadly diversified global index strategy," Karin Thorburn, research chair in finance at the Norwegian School of Economics, told DW.
Although this approach "eliminates a lot of the uncertainty of picking individual stocks," Thorburn said Norway's GPFG fund managers have "almost no room to deviate from the index or actively hedge."
A strict government mandate means the Norwegian fund cannot take significant protective positions, including holding large amounts of cash.
Most institutional investors, on the other hand, hedge by buying options or futures, which rise in value when regular investments like stocks drop, offsetting some of the declines.
Thorburn, who served on a 2022 Norwegian government panel probing the growing geopolitical risks to the fund, said portfolio managers trust in the collective knowledge of the financial markets.
"If you were to start betting against the markets, you could be right 50% of the time, but also wrong 50% of the time," she said. "So wisely, the government has decided that we don't do that."
How vulnerable is Norway's fund to an AI-driven sell-off?
Javier Capape, a Madrid-based sovereign wealth fund specialist, thinks Norway is "unusually exposed" through its investment strategy of roughly 70% equities and 30% bonds.

"I would not describe Norway as literally 'unhedged,'" Capape said, noting that Norges Bank Investment Management, a unit at the central bank that manages the country's sovereign wealth fund, also uses currency, interest-rate and equity derivatives to protect against a crash.
Norway's strategy also contrasts sharply with that of Berkshire Hathaway, until last year run by one of the world's most successful investors, Warren Buffett.
Berkshire is currently sitting on around $365 billion in cash and short-term Treasuries.
Norway's fund does, however, benefit from continuous inflows of oil and gas revenues from its North Sea fields. In 2026, this is projected to be the equivalent of €63 billion.
Private equity and real estate face risks, too
While its Asian and Middle Eastern peers are more diversified, they face similar risks in their alternative investments.

Some private equity funds have temporarily suspended or limited investor withdrawals due to a severe liquidity squeeze. Commercial real estate has underperformed since the COVID-19 pandemic, especially the office sector.
Capape noted how globally, these alternative investments now account for 24% of sovereign wealth fund portfolios.

blocks.caption: Nvidia has partnered with six Wall Street firms to boost spending on AI infrastructure by more than $500 billionImage: Ina Fassbender/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: According to the Sovereign Wealth Funds Report 2026, these funds now manage more than $15 trillion in assets worldwide, up from roughly $3-4 trillion during the 2008/09 financial crisis.
They are now "the single most important global source of investment capital for both private equity funds and direct investment in public companies," Megginson said.
How much could an AI-driven market correction cost Norway?
After a sharp pullback in June and July, many AI-related stocks have rebounded, with Nvidia, Amazon and Microsoft rising in the double digits in recent weeks.
Some analysts now expect AI stocks to reach new all-time highs by the end of the year. Though what follows is anyone's guess.
"Norges Bank Investment Management itself has stress-tested an AI correction, estimating that such a scenario could reduce the value of the entire fund by around 18%," Capape said.
This would represent around €432 billion being wiped off the fund's value, the equivalent of nearly seven years of Norway's energy revenues.
Edited by: Tim Rooks

articles.title: Can the cool north handle a surge in climate tourism?
articles.summary: With heat records continually being broken and southern summers getting hotter, travelers are heading north. Fragile ecosystems are paying the price.

image.caption: Georg Sichelschmidt (pictured) says tour operators like himself can help make tourism sustainableImage: Petr Pavlicek/JVB Travel

blocks.text: A ridge with sweeping views across Jotunheimen, a mountain region in southern Norway, seemed like the perfect hiking route for tour operator Georg Sichelschmidt to bring visitors. Then locals informed him it was home to nesting eagles.
The trail remained open. But Sichelschmidt didn't want to disturb the apex predators at home in the massive peaks, dotted with turquoise lakes and glaciers.
"We decided not to use this trail anymore. We had to find another solution," said Sichelschmidt, who runs nature-based tourism company JVB travel.

Norway's right-to-roam rules, known as allemannsretten, give people broad access to nature regardless of land ownership, but also require them to respect it. For Sichelschmidt, who moved from Germany to Norway 16 years ago for its nature, the decision was an easy choice.

blocks.caption: Sichelschmidt (leading the group) no longer takes hikers along a trail that passes nesting eagles Image: Petr Pavlicek/JVB Travel

blocks.text: But with climate change reshaping summer travel, protecting nature will require far more than individual decisions. According to a 2026 OECD tourism trends report, longer and more intense heat waves across Southern Europe are helping drive interest in cooler destinations. That shift is raising concerns about whether nature in countries like Norway can withstand growing visitor numbers.
Is heat changing the way we travel?

The travel industry has coined the term "coolcation" to promote the shift in summer travel habits. It's too early to know how widespread the trend is, said Daniel Scott, a professor specializing in climate and tourism at Canada's University of Waterloo.

Booking companies, hotels and airlines don't publish data showing how many travelers switch destinations because of heat alone, he said. Still, he added, "we know that people are thinking about it. Some say they are acting on it."

Sichelschmidt said he's seeing the trend firsthand. Partner tour operators offering trips to Mediterranean and the Nordic regions report growing interest in "active" northern vacations, such as hiking and biking, during summer.

"It is difficult to go hiking in France, Spain or Italy in July and August when it is 40 degrees [Celsius, 104 Fahrenheit] plus. The Nordics are a good option to escape from that," he said, adding that Mediterranean travel is shifting to spring and autumn.
More visitors, more pressure on nature
Northern Norway already offers a glimpse of what rising visitor numbers can mean for fragile environments.

Lofoten, with its dramatic cliffs, deep fjords and wild beaches, is home to around 25,000 people. In 2025, it recorded more than 807,000 commercial guest nights, according to Statistics Norway. Increased interest in cooler vacations could add to existing pressure on nature there.

blocks.caption: Puffins are a feature of wildlife in Norway, but their numbers are in decline Image: Rebecca Naden/REUTERS

blocks.text: The archipelago is home to hundreds of bird species, including a colony of puffins that could be disturbed by growing visitor numbers. Nesting birds are vulnerable in late summer. But other wildlife can be impacted too, including reindeer during calving season in May and early June, said Elina Hutton, a tourism researcher at UiT The Arctic University of Norway.

Lofoten's coastal heathland, bogs and alpine vegetation are also highly vulnerable to foot traffic. When hikers walk on wet ground, they can damage roots and strip away the thin soil covering mountain bedrock.

Using satellite data, Hutton tracks how growing visitor numbers are affecting trails on Lofoten. Along the route to Kvalvika Beach, an isolated bay only reachable on foot, the worst trails have widened to about 20 meters (65 feet), destroying surrounding vegetation. Northern ecosystems recover slowly from damage.

blocks.caption: Picturesque Lofoten is attracting lots of tourists because of social media posts. The coolcation trend could put more pressure on nature thereImage: IMAGO/VWPics

blocks.text: "That kind of damage is pretty much permanent here," said Hutton, who urges visitors to stick to established trails rather than seeking out "hidden gems" to post on social media.
Managing tourism, not just promoting it
Sichelschmidt believes tour operators can help reduce environmental harm by steering visitors onto well-managed trails, while avoiding the most sensitive areas.
"When we're talking about a large number of people, we need to direct them to where they can go so that the trails can be maintained without destroying nature," he added.

But decisions like Sichelschmidt's to avoid the eagle's nest cannot be left entirely to tour operators. Destinations will have to decide where visitors should go, which areas need greater protection, and how much pressure nature can sustain.

Norway is already experimenting with ways to manage tourism. Under a new law, communities facing particularly high tourism pressure will be allowed to charge a 3% accommodation tax starting in 2027. Hutton said the tax would not reduce visitor numbers but could help in other ways.
"At least it gives us a bit more tools, a bit more money to build better trails, to build better toilets and have better infrastructure to receive this number of tourists," she said.

Some countries are offering ecotourism initiatives that involve visitors in nature conservation work. In the Faroe Islands, for example, the "Closed for Maintenance" initiative invites volunteers to repair trails and maintain natural areas before they reopen to visitors.

blocks.caption: Extreme heat, fire and drought in traditional vacation hot spots in Spain and France are causing holidaymakers to rethink their destinations of choiceImage: Maximilien Lamy/AFP

blocks.text: Still, destinations, municipalities and tourism businesses need to consider how many visitors they can accommodate and spread tourism evenly throughout the year, Hutton told DW. "It's not good for anybody if we just get more tourists."
Even 'cool' destinations are warming

But as humans continue to burn the fossil fuels heating the planet, the search for reliably cool destinations is becoming harder. Daniel Scott shared preliminary findings from an unpublished study with DW examining how heat risk is changing across Euromonitor's top 100 global city destinations.
The research suggests tourists will increasingly be exposed to higher temperatures and more frequent heat-related risks.

According to the analysis, only nine cities, including Dublin, Auckland and San Francisco, averaged fewer than 10 days per year with temperatures of 32 Celsius (90 Fahrenheit) or higher between 2015 and 2025.
By the 2050s, that number is projected to fall by more than half, highlighting how even traditionally cooler destinations are expected to become significantly warmer.

Hutton finds it concerning to see destinations welcome tourism business opportunities created by Europe's extreme heat. "The same climate change impacts us too in one way or another, and no destination is going to be a winner when the situation evolves like this," she said.
As more vacationers seek cooler weather, Sichelschmidt has decided not to use the term "coolcation" in his company's marketing.

"We don't want to use this situation for promotion," he said. "It's a real situation, but it's sad that we have to talk about it — or that we realize that we are destroying our planet and things change so fast."
Edited by: Jennifer Collins

articles.title: Germany's AfD is labeled far right, populist or extremist
articles.summary: Right wing, far right, fascist: Many terms are being thrown around in the debate about the AfD. What do they mean, and how appropriate are they when discussing the AfD? DW has a glossary.

image.caption: According to some polls, the Alternative for Germany (AfD) is currently the country's most popular partyImage: Christoph Hardt/Panama Pictures/picture alliance

items: Far-right extremist

blocks.text: The Alternative for Germany (AfD) is often classified as a "far-right extremist party." However, the term has no clear-cut definition. In the broadest sense, it means that a party stands far to the right of the political center.
Far-right parties are often associated with strong nationalism, racism, an authoritarian view of the state and a rejection of a liberal, pluralistic society.

Political scientist Armin Pfahl-Traughber of Germany's Federal University of Applied Administrative Sciences is one of the most renowned German researchers on extremism. He does not think that a far-right party is necessarily anti-democratic.

Speaking with DW, he explained why he considers the term "far-right extremist" more appropriate when discussing the AfD. "When it comes to the rejection of the fundamental values of a modern democracy — such as democracy, the separation of powers, human rights and pluralism — coupled with an overemphasis on ethnic identity, I use the label 'far-right extremist.'"

In his view, the AfD has undergone a transformation since its founding in 2013. "What began as a right-wing democratic party with a right-wing extremist minority has, over the years, developed into a right-wing extremist party with a right-wing democratic minority," he said.
How much of a neo-Nazi party is the German AfD?
To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

items: Right-wing populist

blocks.text: The word "populism" is derived from the Latin populus, which means "the people." Aside from that the term has no clear definition. It is frequently used to describe politicians or political parties who seek to curry favor with the masses.

According to Pfahl-Traughber, right-wing populism has several defining characteristics: It views the people as a single entity (and thus rejects pluralism), and it posits an opposition between "them" and "us," which usually means "the people" versus "the elites."

Furthermore, right-wing populists often seek to align themselves directly with the "common people" and claim to know what the people are thinking and demanding. The term is also frequently used to describe the AfD because its political style embodies these defining characteristics.

items: Right-wing conservative

blocks.text: The term "right-wing conservative" is usually applied to politicians or parties that emphasize the importance of conservative values such as homeland and the traditional family, as well as nationalism, a strong state and "law and order."
Unlike right-wing extremists, they do not necessarily view the people as a racial or ethnic unity. They generally accept the fundamental principles of democracy and the existing constitutional order.

However, there have also been historical instances of anti-democratic movements emerging from right-wing conservatism: for example, the supporters of the Conservative Revolution in Germany, whose leading figures included Oswald Spengler, Ernst Jünger and Carl Schmitt. They rejected parliamentarism, modernity and social diversity, and called for a state ruled by an authoritarian leader.

To this day, there are great admirers of these ideologues within the AfD and its circles. Björn Höcke, one of the most influential AfD politicians, for example, repeatedly refers to such thinkers in his book, "Nie zweimal in denselben Fluss" (Never in the same river twice).

items: Völkisch

blocks.text: "Völkisch" is an adjectival form of the German noun, das Volk, or the people. However, since the late 19th century, das Volk has been used to refer to an ethnically pure community and has been strongly antisemitic from the outset.

The völkisch movement was a precursor to the murderous National Socialism under Adolf Hitler. His party, the NSDAP, named its official party newspaper the "Völkischer Beobachter" (The Völkisch Observer).
Today, politicians and experts accuse the AfD of holding völkisch views because its officials repeatedly distinguish between Germans with and without a history of migration.
Pfahl-Traughber believes that today it is a "vaguely defined concept that is used excessively."

items: Fascist

blocks.text: The word describes an extreme political posture that invokes a nationalist, anti-democratic worldview. The term is derived from the Italian word fascio, or "bundle."

Originally, it was the self-designation of the movement surrounding the Italian dictator Benito Mussolini in the early 20th century. Key characteristics of fascism under Mussolini included ultranationalism, the endorsement of the principle of a leader, the rejection of democracy and the glorification of violence and war. German National Socialism under Adolf Hitler drew on the Italian fascist movement and was later classified by historians as an extreme form of fascism.
The applicability of the term to far-right extremist movements today is a matter of debate among scholars.
"In most cases, the groups in question cannot be equated with Hitler or Mussolini's movements," argued Pfahl-Traughber. Many of his fellow academics share this assessment.

In Germany, AfD politician Björn Höcke may be described as a "fascist." A court ruled that this statement is protected by freedom of speech. Furthermore, the Administrative Court in Meiningen ruled that the statement was based on a "verifiable factual basis." In 2024, Höcke — the AfD leader in the state of Thuringia — was fined twice for using a slogan associated with the terrorist Sturmabteilung (SA) from the Nazi era.
Threat from the far right: Never quite German enough?

items: 'Suspected case of right-wing extremism'

blocks.text: This label is used by Germany's domestic intelligence agency, the Federal Office for the Protection of the Constitution, and the AfD has been classified in Germany as a suspected case of right-wing extremism.

Pfahl-Traughber explained this classification: "This means that there are actual grounds for suspecting an intention to undermine the free democratic basic order and that these grounds require further investigation."

For a party to be classified as a suspected case, it is not sufficient for it to merely hold anti-constitutional views. The decisive factor is whether a party is planning to take actions that go against the fundamental values of society.

According to findings by the Office for the Protection of the Constitution, the AfD's efforts to assign a legally inferior status to Germans with a migration background constitute such actions because it violates the German constitution. This ruling was upheld in 2024 by the Higher Administrative Court of Münster.

items: 'Confirmed right-wing extremist'

blocks.text: According to Pfahl-Traughber, this classification by the Office for the Protection of the Constitution is "the result of an assessment concluding that the political actor is indeed considered extremist."

In Germany, the classification has consequences, meaning "a party may henceforth be monitored using intelligence agency methods." This means it may be monitored via telephone or observed by informants.

Furthermore, members of a party classified as "confirmed right-wing extremist" may be denied employment as teachers, police officers or soldiers because their loyalty to the constitution cannot be guaranteed. The Office for the Protection of the Constitution's classification of the AfD as "confirmed right-wing extremist" is currently being reviewed by the Cologne Administrative Court.
Notably, at the state level, five of the sixteen AfD state branches have already been classified as "confirmed right-wing extremist."
This article was originally written in German. It has been updated with additional information.

articles.title: Fatty food raises risk of colorectal cancer
articles.summary: Did you know fatty foods can increase production of an acid in your gut that promotes tumor growth? That's on top of all the other health risks linked to fatty foods, like fries and burgers.

image.caption: It's a quick and easy dinner option, but fast food can increase your cancer riskImage: CFOTO/picture alliance

blocks.text: The list of health risks associated with foods high in fat and low in fiber is long:

items: low-density lipoprotein cholesterol (LDL) or "bad" cholesterol
clogged arteries
weight gain
heart disease
liver stress
blood sugar spikes
bad digestion

blocks.text: And the list goes on.

Now a team of German researchers has shown how so-called Western diets that are often full of fatty foods can lead to the development of one of the most common — and deadliest — cancers in adults under the age of 50.

The researchers from the Technical University of Munich, RWTH Aachen and the German Institute of Human Nutrition Potsdam-Rehbrücke (DIfE) found that these unhealthy diets sustain certain gut bacteria that produce a secondary bile acid — which in turn promotes tumor growth.
Their results were published in the August 2026 issue of the journal Gut.

"What's special about our study is that it shows the causality," Annika Osswald, the first author of the study and a Ph.D student at the German Institute of Human Nutrition, told DW. "Until now, we only knew there was some sort of connection between [a certain] secondary bile acid and colorectal cancer."
How diet fuels silent inflammation — and how to reverse It
To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video
How bile acid is linked to colorectal cancer

The fat in the food you eat triggers the production of primary bile acids in your liver. These acids are important ― your body needs them to break down and absorb fats. Most of the primary bile acids are reabsorbed and returned to the liver.

But a small fraction reaches the colon, where certain bacteria convert them into secondary bile acids, including one called deoxycholic acid (DCA). The more fatty foods you eat, the higher the concentration of DCA in your colon. And that's where the problems start.
Osswald and her colleagues tested this in mice in a lab. "At the core of our work to prove causality were the mouse models," Osswald explained.

The research team implanted DCA-producing bacteria into mice whose intestinal microbiome they controlled completely. Then the scientists induced colorectal cancer in these mice, and also in mice without the bacteria. The mice that had DCA-producing bacteria in their gut saw more tumor growth than the mice that didn't have it.

Cell division in the mice with DCA was increased as well. Increased cell division makes it more likely for cancer to develop, because it multiplies the chances of DNA replication errors. These DNA mutations during cell division can stack up and lead to cancer.

To see whether the process they had observed in mice also takes place in humans, the researchers analyzed stool samples from more than a thousand people, both with and without colorectal cancer. Genes of DCA-producing bacteria were found more frequently in people with colorectal cancer.
"Our results show how much a Western high-fat diet and the associated changes in the gut microbiome can affect human gut health," said microbiologist Sören Ocvirk, another author of the study.

Osswald emphasized that the team's work is foundational, and that more research needs to be done. Still, having proven the causality between more DCA-producing gut bacteria and increased tumor growth points to possible treatments of colorectal cancer as well.
Why it's vital to better understand colorectal cancer

Colorectal cancer is the only cancer for which the mortality rate in people under 50 has increased in the past few decades. That's according to findings published in the Journal of the American Medical Association in January 2026.

The number of deaths from brain cancer, breast cancer, leukemia and lung cancer all went down in the US from 1990 to 2023. But the number of deaths from colorectal cancer increased by 1.1% annually, starting in 2005. While the US is only one region in the world, it is often considered a sufficient indicator of such trends, especially when it comes to the Western diet.
When detected early, cancer starting in the colon or the rectum is treatable.

But symptoms frequently don't present in the early stages of the disease. And when they do, they may be misinterpreted as indications of less harmful conditions like hemorrhoids or irritable bowel syndrome.
Symptoms for colorectal cancer include:

items: blood in or on your stool
intermittent or constant diarrhea or constipation
persistent abdominal pain
gas or cramps
feeling bloated

blocks.text: Another obstacle to early detection is that some people may feel embarrassed discussing colorectal health symptoms with their doctor.
So, try not to be embarrassed, talk to your doctor.
Is your gut your second brain?
How can study results help with treating colorectal cancer?
One option to be considered in the future could be microbiome transplants.
"You could transplant the microbiome of people who have fewer DCA-producing bacteria in their gut into patients with colorectal cancer," Osswald said. "That could potentially slow down tumor growth."
But the best option is to prevent colorectal cancer in the first place. While some people may have a genetic disposition to developing colorectal cancer, a lot is down to lifestyle factors.
Eating healthily, reducing the amount of meat and fatty foods in your diet and not smoking are some good ways to decrease your colorectal cancer risk.
Edited by: Zulfikar Abbany

articles.title: Germany news: Belgium blaze kept out of Germany for now
articles.summary: Some residents in the Eifel town of Monschau were evacuated as a massive fire in Belgium threatened to cross the border. Meanwhile, shipping shortfalls amid low river water levels could hit the…

image.caption: The fire came within 300 meters of the German borderImage: Yves Herman/REUTERS

blocks.text: August 17, 2026
WATCH: Belgium's largest wildfire on record remains out of control
Warner Poland
Belgium's largest wildfire in a century hasn't been brought under control despite cooler weather and rain.
Firefighters say limited rainfall has increased smoke, reducing visibility and making it harder to detect flames burning deep in peat soil.
Because of the blaze's size and difficult terrain, aerial firefighting remains crucial.
Belgium has activated the EU Civil Protection Mechanism and is receiving support from several European countries.
The fire is also threatening the German border and the medieval town of Monschau, where precautionary evacuations have been ordered due to smoke risks.

Fuel prices creep back toward 2026 highs, with Iran still tense and river deliveries failing

blocks.caption: Diesel is still fairly far off its 2026 highs, but gasoline prices are close to their March and April peaks [FILE: August 14, 2026]Image: Rene Traut/Rene Traut Fotografie/picture alliance

blocks.text: Prices for diesel and petroleum at German filling stations, particularly gasoline, are nearing the highest levels of the year, even though oil prices are well adrift of their highest levels amid the war in the Gulf.

Sunday's daily average for E10 gasoline, the cheapest variant, was €2.161 per liter around the country. That equates to $9.47 per US gallon. That was a rise of almost 7 cents compared to the previous Sunday.
Diesel, meanwhile, climbed by just over 8 cents last week, reaching a national average of €2.243 per liter, or $9.83 per US gallon.
Since Friday, these quite elevated levels have been more or less stable.
The main motoring club the ADAC still attributes the prices in large part to strains on oil prices, even though costs are far adrift of the highs seen between March and May.
Another factor is that the German government's special two-month tax rebate expired at the beginning of July without extension, and prices have crept back up ever since.

And finally, the low river levels are causing disruptions, particularly at a regional level, to some fuel transportation systems. The Rhine, in particular, is a commonly used delivery method for fuel that is currently either entirely unavailable or forcing barges to run well below their freight capacity.
Gasoline prices are currently much nearer their 2026 highs than diesel, which is still quite a lot cheaper than at the high points of March and April.
EVs back in the fast lane as oil prices surges

Belgium's King Philippe visits border blaze

blocks.caption: King Philippe and several leading Belgian politicians were on hand talking to emergency services on MondayImage: Nicolas Lambert/BELGA/picture alliance

blocks.text: Belgium's King Philippe cut short his summer vacation to survey efforts to combat the wildfire in the High Fens (Hautes Fagnes) nature reserve near the German border on Monday.
Philippe called it a "difficult moment for all of Belgium," and voiced hope that "this tragedy will quickly be behind us."

The king was briefed by local emergency services and also by a contingent of local, regional and national politicians already at the scene, including the head of Wallonia's government Adrien Dolimon, Interior Minister Bernard Quintin and Deputy Prime Minister Jan Jambon.
Philippe was set to visit some of the worst-hit communities like Sourbrodt and Waimes, after first arriving at the local disaster management response center in Vottem earlier in the day.

blocks.caption: The fire is only a short distance away from the Hürtgenwald wildfire that hit on the German side of the border late last week, but its scale is considerably largerImage: Nicolas Lambert/BELGA/picture alliance

Germany: Bundeswehr troop numbers reach 13-year high

blocks.caption: Germany, like several European countries, has been rushing to expand military spending and to recruit new soldiers [FILE: July 20, 2026]Image: Mike Schmidt/photowerkstatt/picture alliance

blocks.text: Germany's Bundeswehr military employed roughly 186,700 soldiers as of July 31 this year, the Defense Ministry said on Monday.

The increase is a relatively rare positive headline as Germany and its military try to ramp up recruitment, procurement and defense spending — to meet new NATO targets, appease the Donald Trump administration, and respond to perceived threats from Russia and beyond — encountering a string of setbacks and bottlenecks along the way.
By the mid-2030s, Germany aims to recruit some 70,000 more full-time troops than it currently has on retainer, to reach a full-time force of around 260,000 plus around 200,000 reservists.
Read our full report on Geramny's latest troop figures here.
https://p.dw.com/p/5IyGE
Madison Air spends €5.1 billion on German cooling company ebm-papst
US company Madison Air Solutions is spending $5.4 billion or roughly €5.1 billion to buy out German family-owned ventilation company ebm-papst.

The companies' bosses argued the move was a way to "make one plus one equal three," as ebm-papst chief executive Klaus Geissdörfer put it. He said Madison Air knew how to help the German company realize its plans to expand.

"We will also benefit from better access to the US market," Geissdörfer said, noting that, in turn, his company could provide Madison Air Solutions with better access to new markets in Europe and Asia. "Ebm-papst is well positioned here. That's why we complement each other very well."

The US market for cooling and ventilation solutions is booming in no small part thanks to the race to make data centers. The vast processors in these facilities create large amounts of heat and require constant cooling.
And in Germany, a particularly hot summer has brought questions on more widespread use of air conditioning back to the fore.
Madison Air's chief executive Jilly Wyant said that as a longstanding customer of ebm-papst, "we have a deep appreciation for its integrated airflow technology and custom engineering expertise."
She said the new duo was "confident we can accelerate growth, enhance performance and create significant long-term value for shareholders.
The deal still requires regulatory approval before it can go ahead.
The physics trick that could halve energy use of AC
https://p.dw.com/p/5IxUG
Mixed forests needed to lessen wildfire risk — Forestry Council

blocks.caption: Fires like the recent one in Hürtgen Forest are becoming ever more frequent in GermanyImage: Sascha Thelen/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: The head of the German Forestry Council has said Germany should urgently convert its conifer forests into mixed forests in the face of the growing wildfire threat as climate change advances.
Christian Haase told the public broadcaster Deutschlandfunk that the increased fire danger "means for us as forest owners: forest conversion, forest conversion, forest conversion."
"We must move away from pure conifer stands towards mixed forests," he said.
However, he conceded that the shift would take some time.
"This will certainly take another decade," he said.
Studies suggest that monocultural forests are more frequently affected and more severely affected by fires.
Pine forests in particular are considered highly flammable as their trees are rich in resins and oils.
Germany has seen several recent wildfires, including one in Hürtgen Forest that was the worst in the recorded history of the western state of North Rhine-Westphalia.
https://p.dw.com/p/5IviK
People in Germany taking more domestic trips

In 2025, people in Germany cut the number of trips they took abroad, while the number of trips taken within the country with at least one overnight stay rose, figures from the Federal Statistical Office (Destatis) showed on Monday.
The number of trips within Germany climbed by 3.9% in comparison with 2024 to 169 million, Destatis said.
Foreign travel went down by around 8.3% in comparison with the year before, to 105 million.
The most popular destination was Italy, followed by Austria, Spain, France and the Netherlands.
For all trips, the most popular means of transport was the car (60.2%), with rail (19.2%) and plane (15.2%) lagging well behind.
How to travel by train in Germany
https://p.dw.com/p/5IvWl
Growing number of young people not in work or training
The number of 20 to 24-year-olds in Germany who were neither employed nor doing training or studies rose to 10% in 2025 as part of a continuing trend, new figures have shown.
In 2022, the figure was 8.8%, the Federal Statistical Office said, using international comparative data from the European statistics authority Eurostat.
However, the figure from Germany is relatively low among all 27 EU nations and below the average of 12.9% for the bloc.
The Netherlands had the lowest percentage of people in the 20-24 age group who were unemployed or not doing some professional training, at 5.6%.
The figure was highest in Romania (22.8%), Bulgaria (17.3%) and France (16.2%).
Young people in rural areas of Germany were less likely than those in big cities to fall into the category (7.9% and 10.6% respectively).

Low water levels in rivers could impact construction: industry associations

blocks.caption: Cargo ships on the Rhine have been greatly reducing their loadsImage: Thomas Frey/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: The building sector could face supply shortfalls as ships on German rivers carry less cargo because of falling water levels, construction industry associations say.
"Transport by water is becoming increasingly difficult," Thomas Reimann, the president of an association representing construction contractors in the German state of Hesse, told the DPA news agency.
He said that sand and gravel, which are often shipped in large quantities to concrete plants, are becoming harder to come by and more expensive.
The German Construction Industry Federation (HDB) also said suppliers had already warned that continued low water levels could lead to shortages in some building supplies.
Bitumen, aggregate, natural stone, fuels and mineral construction waste are among the other materials affected by the reduced shipping capacity.

HDB chief executive Tim-Oliver Müller said it was unlikely that construction would be brought to a widespread halt but that the risk of shortages, higher logistics costs and delays was growing as low water levels persist.

Precautionary evacuations in Monschau as Belgium fire rages

blocks.caption: Monschau is known for its pretty, half-timbered housesImage: Horst Ossinger/picture alliance

blocks.text: Several homes in the Eifel town of Monschau were evacuated overnight as a wildfire burning in Belgium's High Fens nature reserve threatened to cross the border.
Around 30 residents from 17 homes were evacuated, with emergency accommodation set up at a nearby school.
However, by Monday morning the fire was said to have stopped its advance toward Germany amid weather conditions that are more favorable to firefighting efforts.
The fire had previously moved to within about 300 meters (984 feet) of the German border.
A spokesman for the local fire brigade said meadows between the fire and homes had been soaked with water for hours to help stop the spread of the flames.

Some streets in the border town of Monschau were evacuated late on Sunday as the flames threatened to enter German territory, but they have fortunately been successfully held back for now.

articles.title: How Germany supports recovery of Berlin Pride attack victims
articles.summary: After a terrorist attack, public attention tends to focus primarily on the perpetrator. But what about the victims? What support can they expect? And what lies ahead for them?

image.caption: Commemorations for the victims of the Berlin Pride attack started arriving mere hours after the attackImage: IMAGO/Wolfgang Maria Weber

blocks.text: On the evening of July 25, according to German authorities, Abdul Ballout, drove a white van into a crowd in Berlin's Tiergarten park near the Brandenburg Gate, where thousands were celebrating Berlin Pride. He then got out of the vehicle and began attacking people at random with a large knife. He killed a 65-year-old woman from Poland and injured her daughter, along with 30 other people, some of them seriously.

Many details have emerged about Ballout, his links to extremists, his criminal record and his family. A day after the incident, he was shot dead by police officers while trying to flee during an arrest attempt.

The identities of the victims, and how they are coping after the attack on the event celebrating LGBTQ+ rights, are not publicly known. Still, many are likely to live with its consequences for months, if not years, to come. The only details disclosed by Berlin's governing mayor concern the age and nationality of the woman who was killed. Otherwise, Germany's strict data protection laws protect victims' privacy.

Victims can approach the media themselves at any time if they choose to make their stories public, Roland Weber, the German federal government's commissioner for victims of terrorism and extremist violence, told DW.
Calls for political consequences after Berlin Pride attack
To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video
Support for the victims

In Germany, people affected by such attacks are often reluctant to come forward publicly or identify themselves as victims, said Julia Kühne. She should know: Kühne is the spokesperson for the Association for Victims of Terrorism (VoT Germany), which is part of an international federation of terrorism victims.
"The perpetrator needs to disappear from the media, now that he has been caught and killed. Those affected should naturally be brought much more to the forefront," said Kühne.
How are those who were injured in the attack doing today? Weber has visited some of them in hospital.
"What I saw there was distressing. But thanks to modern medicine, and because the doctors are optimistic, there is reason for hope that everyone will recover as fully as possible," he said.

"In some cases, however, that remains uncertain. Only time will tell. Some of the injured have already been discharged from hospital and are now receiving outpatient treatment. Others will begin various forms of therapy and rehabilitation."
How are the victims being supported?

The Federal Commissioner for Victims and Weisser Ring, a victim support organization, arrange trauma treatment, provide immediate financial assistance, and advise victims on long-term care and victims' pensions.
Weisser Ring is a volunteer-run organization that works closely with the police to provide advice and support to victims of crime in Germany.

"In cases of terrorist attacks, there is also a special provision: victims can apply for hardship payments," said Weber. "These are funds made available by the Bundestag. Hardly anyone knows about them, and making people aware of them is part of our job. We provide guidance and help ensure that applications are submitted as quickly as possible."
Germany reviews Berlin Pride attack security failures

Weber is also responsible for supporting the relatives of the Polish woman who was killed and her daughter, who was injured in the attack. Nationality is not a factor in this regard. He assists victims with follow-up costs and compensation whenever an act of terrorism or extremist violence has been committed on German soil.
Number of traumatized victims still unclear

The victims of the attack are not only those who sustained physical injuries. According to VoT Germany's Kühne, even people who witnessed the attack from several hundred meters away may be considered victims.

"There are people who do not develop problems until years later," she told DW. "They may suddenly begin to suffer from sleep disturbances, experience nightmares, develop panic attacks or struggle with social phobia. In some cases, these symptoms do not emerge until years afterward because those affected were initially either still in shock or had returned to their everyday lives and were therefore able, at least to some extent, to suppress what they had experienced."

Kühne also noted that survivors of previous terrorist attacks may be retraumatized by media coverage of the current attack in Berlin and find themselves in need of support once again. She knows this from personal experience: she herself survived the 2016 attack on Berlin's Christmas market, which ultimately claimed 13 lives and left more than 70 injured.
In the shadow of RAF terror: The children left behind
Victim support: Problems in practice

Weisser Ring, which supports victims of crime across Germany, believes adequate compensation schemes and pension entitlements for victims of terrorism are now in place. However, not everything runs smoothly in practice, said Rolf Schmachtenberg, the organization's state chairman in Berlin.

"In cases where people have suffered permanent harm, the assessment procedures are often quite lengthy," he said. "We also continue to encounter administrative bottlenecks, with some authorities still relying on paper files and fax communications. They then have to wait for information from other agencies, which can significantly delay the application process. In my view, the main problem is one of implementation."

Over the past decade, Germany has experienced 13 terrorist attacks motivated by Islamist or political extremist ideologies, leaving 39 people dead and 475 injured. The support provided by the federal government's commissioner for victims has no time limit. Weber continues to assist people affected by attacks dating back to the 1980s.

blocks.caption: Commemoration continues of the nine people killed in 2020 in a racially motivated terrorist attack in the city of HanauImage: Kadir Ilboga/Anadolu/picture alliance

blocks.text: Victims seek answers

For many victims, coming to terms with the horror and suffering also means finding answers to the question of why the perpetrator acted and why they, in particular, were targeted, said Weber. In some court proceedings, perpetrators have remained silent. In the case of the Berlin Pride attack, however, the perpetrator was killed, meaning there will never be complete clarity about his motives.
In Germany, investigations are discontinued once a suspect has died. No court will ever determine whether Abdul Ballout selected his victims for one particular reason or another.
"As a result, some questions will remain unanswered," said Weber. "The search for answers is something most victims have in common, but it cannot always lead to certainty."
This article was originally written in German.

articles.title: In Germany, record heat meets climate action fatigue
articles.summary: Climate action does not seem to be a priority for the German government — despite record temperatures, heat-related deaths and drought. Why aren't more people taking to the streets in protest?

image.caption: Record low water levels on the Rhine and elsewhere in Germany have highlighted changing climate conditionsImage: Thomas Frey/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: When Lars Werner of the "Last Generation" climate activist group glued himself to the road four years ago to protest for greater climate action, Germany had not yet seen 12,500 heat-related deaths (the 2026 toll, so far), or record temperatures across Western Europe, and fully loaded ships were still navigating the Rhine without difficulty.
"Of course, I could say 'I told you so,' because it was foreseeable and comes as no surprise whatsoever," Werner told DW.
"The fact is, even back then, I was constantly explaining in my presentations that the Rhine would eventually run dry during hot summers and that this would have an incredible impact on the economy."
Rhine River drops to record low levels, grounding ships
To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

This summer, entire villages have been evacuated due to forest fires, farmers are expected to lose about 3 million metric tons of grain and rapeseed to drought, and hospital patients and the elderly in nursing homes are facing an acute threat to their lives in buildings with no air conditioning.
But so far, the federal government has remained astonishingly quiet. Despite the crisis, it has still not convened a "heat summit."

"It is utterly irrational for the federal government to resort to tinkering with regulations — such as lifting the Sunday ban on truck traffic — in the hope of somehow scraping by without implementing a comprehensive climate protection policy for the long or even short term," said Werner.
Fridays for Future finds it difficult to motivate people

The government no longer has to worry about "Last Generation" protesters calling out its inaction by setting up road blockades. The climate activists halted their protests two years ago, worn down by hostility, fines and prison sentences. Now, the task of fiercely criticizing political decision-makers on climate policy falls primarily to the Fridays for Future Germany (FFF) movement.

"The federal government is doing virtually nothing when it comes to effective climate policy. Instead, various 'pseudo-solutions' are being promoted — such as dredging the Rhine to make it deeper or lifting the Sunday driving ban for trucks," FFF spokesperson Linda Kastrup told DW. She deplores what she sees as short-term fixes for the symptoms of the climate crisis, and notes that effectively nothing sustainable is being done.

blocks.caption: In November 2022, activist Lars Werner glued himself to the street in Munich to protest CO2 emissionsImage: Benjamin Rückert

blocks.text: Only a few hundred protesters turned out for a demonstration outside the chancellery in Berlin a week ago. It was a far cry from the protests in 2019, prior to the COVID-19 pandemic, when hundreds of thousands of people took to the streets to demand climate action.

A recent study by the Bertelsmann Foundation found that 80% of people in Germany are worried about climate change, and more than 50% want to see more government spending on climate protection. But that doesn't mean they're take to the streets.
Kastrup isn't surprised.

"When Chancellor Friedrich Merz completely dismisses and ignores climate policy — when we see tens of thousands of heat-related deaths in Germany alone yet not a single word is said about it — it inevitably leaves people with the impression in their private lives that climate protection doesn't matter. Naturally, that makes it very difficult to motivate people to take to the streets," she said.
In addition, there has been a rise in hateful speech directed at climate activists on social media.
"Two days ago, I posted a reel and within a very short time, there were 2,000 hateful comments on it," said Kastrup.
Focus has shifted to Ukraine, Gaza

Sebastian Haunss, a political science researcher at the University of Bremen, said it's surprising that the scorching summer of 2026 has not led to climate protests. He finds it remarkable that on the one hand, more and more people in Germany are installing solar power systems, but on the other, they take vacations on environmentally damaging cruise ships.

"A strong counter-position has emerged," he said. "Specifically, political actors like the AfD [the far-right populist Alternative for Germany Party — Editor's note] are pursuing an agenda that opposes climate protection regulations. Such actors — whether at the international or national level — did not exist just a few years ago."

Also, Haunss pointed out that large organizations like Fridays for Future have been replaced by a vast number of local groups, who operate largely out of the public eye. However, he believes a pivotal event could bring people back onto the streets in large numbers at any moment.

"Then there is the competition for attention; the COVID pandemic and the war in Ukraine pushed the climate issue out of the spotlight, and current economic concerns also play a major role," said Haunss, adding that many of those who took to the streets against climate change a few years ago are now focusing on different topics.
"In some cases, their issues have shifted, and other topics — such as the war in Gaza and solidarity with Palestine — have moved to the forefront."
A divided government

German Environment Minister Carsten Schneider of the center-left Social Democratic Party (SPD) now wants to amend the constitution, the Basic Law, to make heat protection a joint responsibility of the federal government, the states, and the municipalities.
However, the larger coalition partner, the center-right bloc of the Christian Democratic Union and Christian Social Union (CDU/CSU), is skeptical of the plan and has cited "legal concerns."

"Within the coalition, I do indeed see us — the SPD — as the bulwark for energy transition to renewables," Nina Scheer, energy policy spokesperson for the SPD parliamentary group, told DW. "All my colleagues in our parliamentary group would like to achieve more in terms of climate protection. But we also have to accept setbacks regarding climate measures in order to maintain unity within the coalition."
For instance, Scheer said, she voted in favor of making air travel cheaper and expanding regional airports, although she personally finds it wrong.
Climate activists try bold new strategies to make an impact

Scheer has long advocated for a faster expansion of renewable energy, and does not see eye to eye with Economy Minister Katherina Reiche (CDU), who favors gas over wind and solar power for energy supply.

"Reiche goes around pushing the narrative that while we do want climate protection and remain committed to the goals, renewables are simply too expensive. And to that, one has to say: 'No, that is simply not true,'" said Scheer.

Under the 2015 Paris Agreement and the national Climate Action Act, Germany has committed to achieving climate neutrality by 2045. However, recent statements by some politicians have raised doubts as to whether the federal government is pursuing this goal with great determination.
"We cannot halt climate change from Germany alone," Chancellor Friedrich Merz said recently, a statement that Scheer considered disastrous.
"Fundamentally, it is a rejection of greater climate action, even though we ought to be stepping up our efforts," she said.
This article was originally written in German.

articles.title: Afghan allies still waiting for the safety Germany promised
articles.summary: After the Taliban retook power on August 15, 2021, Berlin promised to bring Afghan staff to Germany. But people are still waiting to leave in Pakistan and Afghanistan.

image.caption: Thousands of Afghan local staff and their families have been evacuated to Germany since 2021Image: Moritz Frankenberg/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: It's hard to know which promise from German politicians the "local staff" — Afghans who assisted German efforts in the country — relied on most. Perhaps that from then-Foreign Minister Heiko Maas, who on August 26, 2021, 11 days after the Taliban took power, said: "Our work continues until all those for whom we carry responsibility in Afghanistan are safe."

By June 2026, more than 37,000 Afghan nationals had arrived in Germany since the Taliban retook power. These are people who worked alongside Germany's Bundeswehr armed forces or German aid programs, plus their relatives. It also includes people who are especially at risk, such as activists and journalists who advocated for human rights and against the Taliban.

For Ahmad Samid, who worked for the Bundeswehr as an audio engineer, Germany kept its promise. For Javad Niazi, who worked for the Ministry for Economic Cooperation and Development (BMZ), it did not. He remains stuck in the city of Peshawar in Pakistan. Both are using false names because they still fear the Taliban and possible repercussions for themselves and their families.
Hundreds of Afghans still waiting

Samid works as a receptionist at a hotel in a large German city and told DW in very good German: "I am very grateful to Germany. But if someone says, 'I will help you,' then it must remain that way. One must keep a promise."
In August 2026, five years after the Taliban quickly seized back power in Afghanistan, it seems that Germany no longer wants to know about the big promises it made.

In the case of Javad Niazi, Germany has, one must say, broken its promise. He is in the same position as 600 other Afghans who are desperately holding out in Peshawar and in Kabul, continuing to hope that they can leave for Germany.

He and his family say they feel trapped in a small cage, he told DW. Their savings have been used up, he has no residence permit for Pakistan and he cannot leave his temporary accommodation for fear of Pakistani security forces, who arrest and deport Afghan nationals daily.

"My 14-year-old son goes shopping when it gets dark here. We cannot go to any bazaar, park or hospital; my children cannot go to school. It is an enormous strain on us. We never would have thought that a country like Germany would take back its decision, it's unbelievable," he said.
Afghan refugees at risk as deportations surge in Pakistan
To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video
New government does not want to take in any more local staff

Taking back its decision, as Javad Niazi put it, is what the new German government, comprising the conservative bloc of Christian Democratic Union and Christian Social Union and the center-left Social Democrats under Chancellor Friedrich Merz did in May 2025 with its coalition agreement to scrap the resettlement programs.

Half a year later, those who had been left behind appealed to the chancellor directly for help in a two-page letter: "We wanted and needed to escape Taliban rule to survive. We cannot go back to Afghanistan. It would end brutally and violently for many of us," they wrote.

But the German government has remained firm and, in the meantime, is cooperating with the Taliban "on a technical level" via the Afghan diplomatic mission in Germany to send Afghan nationals who have committed crimes in Germany back to Afghanistan — and recently also the first person from Afghanistan with no criminal record.

German Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt offered the waiting Afghans money in exchange for forgoing their departure to Germany. A one-time payment of up to €2,500 ($,2887) before departure, up to €10,000 for a return to Afghanistan or a third country, plus medical care, board and lodging for several months. So far, 300 people have accepted this offer and in doing so given up on a future in Germany.
Afghan migrants stuck in Pakistan reject German cash offer
Fate of local staff also depends on German courts

Since then, the issue of the future of the 600 waiting Afghans has been primarily dealt with via the court system. In July 2026, Germany's Federal Constitutional Court ruled: The German government's blanket decision revoking the admission program for at-risk Afghan citizens is in breach of the constitutional prohibition of arbitrariness. Each person's specific case and individual interests must be considered.

In response to questions from DW, the German Interior Ministry has maintained it is in the right. "The Federal Constitutional Court largely aligns with the Federal Government's argument that declarations around admissions can be revoked if political interests change. However, the Federal Constitutional Court also instructs the Interior Ministry to consider affected people's individual circumstances when making such decisions."
According to the Interior Ministry, the Federal Constitutional Court allows broad leeway for political decision-making when deciding on the admission of foreign nationals.
German aid organization continues support

Javad Niazi and his family continue to worry for their future. He would probably have given up long ago if not for the support of Kabul-Luftbrücke (Kabul Air Bridge). In response to the chaos at Kabul airport in August 2021, the German nongovernmental organization arranged a charter plane to fly 18 people out of Afghanistan. Since then, it has rescued 4,424 people from the Taliban, mostly overland to Pakistan.

Eva Beyer, who had worked as a filmmaker in Afghanistan, recalled the organization's 2021 beginning. "We chartered this plane, flew to Kabul and could haul out a few people," she told DW. "And then we realized, actually the work is just beginning. From early 2022 — I was then in Pakistan — there I organized the land transport on the Pakistani side, took in the people at the border and looked after them in Islamabad. What was originally planned to be four weeks has now become five years."

Recently, Kabul-Luftbrücke has mainly focused on providing legal advice and support to Afghans — with success. They've won more than 200 lawsuits, and as a result, 1,018 people have been able to travel to Germany since September 1, 2025.

"About 75% of the people who are now still waiting are women and children. That means for all these women and children, who are not attending school, who can no longer build an independent life or pursue a career, the way to a secure future has been blocked," said Beyer.

She advocates for people who have already passed all security checks to quickly receive a visa. "There are also people who already had a visa in their passport and those whose visa had already been issued, but at the last minute they could not take the flight because it was canceled," she said.
This article was originally written in German.

Correction, August 15, 2026: An earlier version of this article incorrectly stated that Alexander Dobrindt is Germany's foreign minister. He is the German interior minister. DW apologizes for the mistake.
'The world has forgotten Afghanistan'

articles.title: Germany: Evacuated villagers return after Eifel wildfire eases
articles.summary: Most residents evacuated from the village of Gey have returned home after firefighters brought a major wildfire in Germany's Eifel region largely under control. DW has more.
articles.byline: Richard Connor, Roshni Majumdar, Emmy Sasipornkarn, Timothy Jones

image.caption: Firefighters walk through the village of Gey, evacuated amid the wildfire in the Hürtgen ForestImage: Georg Hilgemann/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: August 16, 2026
Thanks for reading!
Much of the weekend in Germany was focused on the efforts tocontain the wildfire in Hürtgenwald in the Eifel region.
Germany's largest recorded forest fire in North Rhine-Westphalia was under control on Sunday after a dayslong emergency operation.
Most emergency crews have withdrawn, but helicopters and thermal imaging flights were still monitoring hotspots for any signs of reignition.
Around 2,000 residents evacuated from the Hürtgenwald district of Gey also returned home.
Meanwhile, firefighters just across the border in Belgium continued battling a major wildfire that has destroyed about 3,000 hectares in the High Fens nature reserve.
Separately, about 400 firefighters were tackling a fast-moving wildfire in Saarland, a small state in southwest Germany.
https://p.dw.com/p/5IuxG
Hundreds of firefighters respond to fire in Saarland

blocks.caption: Police helicopters are being used as firefighting helicopters in HirzweilerImage: Steven Mohr/SNS/picture alliance

blocks.text: Four hundred firefighters were battling a fast-moving wildfire in Saarland state.
Officials said the blaze had burned nearly 15 acres (6 hectares) of forest near Hirzweiler in the municipality of Illingen.
Emergency crews said rough terrain and limited access to water were making firefighting efforts difficult.
A helicopter was supporting teams on the ground.
The smoke plume was visible for miles, and authorities urged residents to stay away from the area, keep access roads clear for emergency vehicles and avoid the closed forest zone.
https://p.dw.com/p/5Iuod
Published August 16, 2026last updated August 16, 2026
Residents of evacuated village return home as Eifel fire subsides

blocks.caption: The village of Gey, seen here on Friday, is now safe to return toImage: Federico Gambarini/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: A wildfire in the western Eifel region that forced the evacuation of the village of Gey on Friday has been brought enough under control that residents can return, local authorities have said..
"Firefighting operations are continuing but the situation continues to ease up," the Düren district administration said on Sunday.
It said around two-thirds of Gey residents, who number around 1,800, had returned by Sunday morning after being given the all-clear on Saturday evening.
The blaze, which has burnt out some 300 hectares (741 acres) has been described as the most serious wildfire in the recorded history of the western state of North Rhine-Westphalia.
It has, however, now been dwarfed a nearby fire in Belgium's High Fens region, which is raging across 3,000 hectares and has approached to within 3 kilometers (2 miles) of the German border.
The fires in western and other parts of Europe come amid a prolonged period without meaningful rain that has left undergrowth and many trees parched and highly inflammable.
Climate scientists say that such conditions are occurring ever more frequently as the Earth warms owing to the human use of fossil fuels.
https://p.dw.com/p/5IuTp
WATCH: Germany reviews Berlin Pride attack security failures
What can surveillance, electronic ankle monitors and deradicalization programs realistically achieve? And what are the limits of Germany's justice and security system?
Germany reviews Berlin Pride attack security failures

Russian authorities open criminal case against German reporter

Russian authorities have opened a criminal investigation against a journalist from the German daily Frankfurter Allgemeine Zeitung (FAZ) on suspicion of inciting hate and hostility, Russia's state-run TASS news agency has reported.
The case centers on a question asked by the journalist to Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy earlier this month.
The reporter asked Zelenskyy at a press conference in Belgrade what Europeans could do to help Ukraine kill more Russian soldiers as it fights Moscow's full-scale invasion.
According to TASS, the journalist could face up to six years in a penal colony if convicted in Russia.
Russian courts also hand down sentences in absentia.
The paper has previously said it regrets that the question had been phrased ambiguously, saying that killing as many Russian soldiers as possible was not the FAZ's editorial position.
It, however, also criticized as "unacceptable" what it described as "defamation and threats" against its correspondent.
"We will respond to threats against our employees using legal means," it said.
The FAZ press office told the DPA news agency that it was not aware of the proceedings in Russia.
The journalist concerned covers southeastern Europe for the newspaper from Vienna.
https://p.dw.com/p/5IuWb
Yiddish festival in Weimar draws thousands of visitors

blocks.caption: Ahead of the festival, Weimar saw numerous events associated with Yiddish cultureImage: Shendl Copitman/Religion News Service/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: The 26th edition of a festival celebrating Yiddish and related cultures in the eastern city of Weimar ended on Saturday evening after some 12,000 people attended.
This year, the focus was on women in Yiddish culture.
Organizers said more than 300 people from around the world participated in workshops on the Yiddish language, music and dance, as well as youth projects.

blocks.caption: Participants could take part in dance coursesImage: Shendl Copitman/Religion News Service/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: "From the beginning, (the idea was) to present Yiddish culture as something which is alive, and not something that was entirely destroyed by the Shoah (Holocaust)," said Alan Bern, the founder and artistic director at Yiddish Summer Weimar, the body behind the festival.
The Yiddish language first emerged in the Middle Ages in the German-speaking regions of Europe and later spread to other parts of Europe in various waves of Jewish migration.
It is a Germanic language and partially mutually intelligible with German. In its written form it typically uses a modified form of the Hebrew alphabet.
Who speaks Yiddish?

In the 1930s, Yiddish was spoken as a vernacular by around 11 million Central and Eastern European Jews. The number of speakers was drastically diminished by the murder of some 6 million Jews in the Holocaust under Nazi Germany.
Yiddish also declined as Jewish communities began adopting other languages like English, Hebrew, Russian and French.
Now, the language is spoken by between 500,000 and 1 million people.
It is mostly spoken as a mother tongue by certain tight-knit ultra-Orthodox communities in North America, Israel and to a lesser extent parts of western Europe.
However, enthusiasts from other communities also learn it as a second language out of cultural or academic interest or in an effort to preserve it.

Yiddish Summer Weimar presented 97 events in all this year in Weimar, Erfurt, Eisenach and other towns and municipalities in the eastern state of Thuringia, as well as in Istanbul, Agios Lavrentios in Greece and the German town of Zittau.
https://p.dw.com/p/5IuE0
German investment in US falls to three-year low
German companies have cut investment in the United States to its lowest level in three years, as uncertainty over the Trump administration's trade policies weighs on new spending.

Direct investment fell by almost two-thirds year on year to €4.3 billion ($5 billion) in the first half of 2026, according to calculations by the German Economic Institute, or IW, based on Bundesbank data.
Compared with the first half of 2024, investment was down by nearly 80%.
In the five years before the COVID-19 pandemic, German companies invested an average of €15.8 billion in the US during the first half of each year — almost four times the 2026 level.
The IW said the decline continued a trend visible since Donald Trump began his second term in January 2025.
Trump has repeatedly used or threatened import tariffs against US trading partners in an effort to secure concessions.
The European Union last year struck a deal aimed at avoiding heavier US duties that included a pledge of $600 billion in investment.
The IW said uncertainty around such policies was making German companies more reluctant to commit fresh capital in the US.
Europe pushes back after Trump threat over US troops
https://p.dw.com/p/5IuBt
Twelve police injured at abortion protest in Göttingen
Proests over abortion have escalated in the northern German city of Göttingen, leaving 12 police officers injured after officers intervened to keep rival groups apart.

Police said around 20 people had initially gathered in the city's market square for a registered anti-abortion demonstration under the slogan "Public rosary against abortion," with some participants travelling from France.
A spontaneous counter-protest formed nearby, with demonstrators disrupting the anti-abortion gathering through heckling and loud music, police said.
Officers formed a police line to separate the two groups.
After the registered demonstration ended, some counter-protesters allegedly tried to break through the police cordon.
Police said protesters used pressure and violence against officers as they tried to push through the line.
Officers responded by forcing the crowd back and using physical force and pepper spray. Police said force was used on around 200 occasions during the operation.
Why are abortions still illegal in Germany?
https://p.dw.com/p/5IuBo
Germany increasingly revokes protection for Syrian refugees
Germany has sharply increased the number of Syrians losing refugee or other protection status as authorities reassess cases following the fall of dictator Bashar Assad.
In the first half of 2026, 23.2% of 8,320 reviews ended with protection being revoked or withdrawn, according to a government response to a parliamentary question from the socialist Left Party.
The proportion has risen significantly from previous years.
In 2025, only 3.7% of reviewed Syrian cases resulted in protection being withdrawn, compared with 3.1% in 2024.
Most cases involved the loss of formal refugee status or subsidiary protection — a separate status accorded to refugees but with fewer protections.
Syrians who lose protection may still qualify for another residence permit, for example through employment, or potentially for German citizenship.
Even without another legal status, deportation to Syria remains difficult because returns require cooperation from Syrian authorities.
What is Germany's debate around Syrian refugee returns?
Germany resumed deportations to Syria following Assad's fall in December 2024. They were the first deportations since 2011, when Syria's civil war broke out.
Earlier this year, Chancellor Friedrich Merz suggested that some 80% of Syrians living in Germany could return to Syria over the next three years.

The comments sparked considerable political backlash, with experts arguing the timeframe was unrealistic and others pointing to the large number of Syrians working in Germany's already understaffed medical system.
Around 973,000 Syrians were living in Germany at the end of 2023, with some 700,000 having refugee status or subsidiary protection.
Over 200,000 Syrians have acquired German citizenship — making them the largest group of new naturalizations in recent years — and around 70,000 have permanent residence.
