articles.title: EU waste packaging rules: Why small businesses are worried
articles.summary: The EU has introduced new rules targeting packaging waste and "forever chemicals." Although the changes will be phased in slowly, some small sellers have already paused shipments due to the…

image.caption: The EU wants to cut the use of PFAS 'forever chemicals' in food packagingImage: Arnulf Hettrich/IMAGO

blocks.text: What changes from Wednesday?
In a drive to cut waste and improve public health, new European Union rules take effect on Wednesday, banning high levels of PFAS "forever chemicals" in packaging.
Under the EU's Packaging and Packaging Waste Regulation (PPWR), any new packaging products entering the market will now have to meet tighter standards if designed to come into contact with food.
PFAS have been linked to increased risks of certain cancers and other health conditions.
Although the amount of material people are exposed to from food packaging is usually low, scientists are worried about the long-term effects.
After all, PFAS are highly persistent chemicals and accumulate in the body and the environment.
PFAS are used to make paper and cardboard packaging both grease- and water-resistant and are found in everything from pizza boxes to TV dinners.
Packaging with lower PFAS reduces the risk of these persistent chemicals migrating into food or the natural world when thrown away.
The new rules are in addition to curbs on bisphenol A (BPA) in food-contact materials, which took effect across the EU last month.

blocks.caption: Recycling rates in the EU are rising, but lower than the increase in packaging wasteImage: Robert Michael/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Under PPWR, businesses will not be required to recall or destroy packaging or goods that were already on the market before Wednesday.
While consumers won't notice any difference, businesses have fiercely criticized the changes, which also require packaging to meet new sustainability standards.
Are the new packaging rules too complicated?
Many small businesses and online traders believe the additional cost and red tape are too cumbersome.
They complain that they now have to register their packaging in multiple EU states, often with fees.
"Instead of facilitating cross-border trade, the new rules threaten to make it significantly more difficult," warned Händlerbund, the German online retailers' association.
Händlerbund warned its members: "There is no minimum quantity and no exception for small businesses."
EU lawmaker Elisabeth Dieringer of the far-right Freedom Party of Austria has warned that PPWR would mean five-figure costs for medium-sized firms.
"While corporations have their own departments for this [red tape], the Mittelstand [medium-sized firms] has little choice but to 'eat or die,'" she wrote on X on Tuesday.
Several businesses, from sole traders to medium-sized firms, said they had paused deliveries to and within the EU due to the new rules.
"Under these rules, I would need to appoint an authorized representative in every single EU country I send to," wrote the owner of a small online store, Monstaas Workshop, in an Instagram post.
"The cost is around €300 ($346) per country, per year ... these costs are simply not affordable."
From pollution to progress: Tackling PFAS across continents
To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video
Swedish embedded electronic devices maker iLabs Electronics said it would halt web shop orders from EU countries.
"The cost and administrative burden [of PPWR] is now out of proportion to our direct sales volume," iLabs wrote on its website.
A petition on change.org had been signed by more than 45,000 people by Wednesday morning, calling on Brussels to "stop destroying EU micro-businesses."
How bad is the EU's packaging waste problem?
According to the European Commission, the bloc's executive arm, EU countries have witnessed a 20% increase in packaging waste over the last decade.
Without PPWR, Brussels says, discarded packaging was set to rise by another 19% by 2030, driven by the boom in online shopping and convenience food.
EU data shows that 178 kilograms (392 pounds) of packaging waste was generated per person across the bloc in 2023. Of this, 35.3 kg was plastic packaging, only 42% of which was recycled.
At 215 kg per capita (in 2023), Germany's waste from packaging is much higher than the EU average.

blocks.caption: Scientists are worried about long-term exposure to 'forever chemicals' in food packagingImage: Tobias Steinmaurer/photosteinmaurer.com/IMAGO

blocks.text: Each EU resident generates the equivalent of roughly half a kilo of packaging waste every day, data from Eurostat, the EU's statistics agency, shows.
According to Brussels, the volume of waste has grown faster than recycling rates over the past decade.
Packaging also ⁠accounts ⁠for about 40% of plastic consumption in Europe, an EU official told reporters at a briefing on Tuesday.
What are the EU's long-term waste targets?
Although PFAS is the main focus of this initial phase of PPWR, the EU has set binding targets to cut packaging waste by 5% by 2030 and 15% by 2040.
From 2028, packaging manufacturers will be required to carry standardized labels that clearly show the materials used and how it should be recycled or disposed of.
Some stores, particularly restaurants and cafes, will be required to offer customers reusable packaging as an option, often at no extra charge.
Deposit-and-return schemes for plastic bottles and soda cans, such as those operational in Germany and the Netherlands, will be rolled out across the EU by 2029.
Then from 2030, all packaging placed on the EU market, including single-use plastic bottles, must be designed to be recyclable.
Packaging will also be required to be kept to a minimum to protect the product and fulfill its function.
This measure is meant to reduce the overuse of packaging for marketing purposes.
Meanwhile, single-use plastic packaging for fresh produce will be banned from 2030.
EU states will be able to set their own penalties for non-compliance, with German authorities allowed to impose fines of up to €200,000 ($230,000) for more serious breaches.
Edited by: Kristie Pladson

articles.title: AI helping create popular mobile sports games
articles.summary: After the World Cup and before the domestic season, many fans still crave more football. Amateur coders are helping to fill this gap.

image.caption: Football mobile games made by amateurs are changing the industryImage: Wolfgang Maria Weber/IMAGO

blocks.text: After the World Cup and before the domestic football season begins, the world's most popular sport tends to enjoy a relatively quiet period. For some though, the need for football remains.

This summer that demand has been met by the creation of a raft of mobile sports games in which players can dive into nostalgia and storytelling. This craze has seemingly been inspired by the viral 82-0 basketball game in which players can draft an all-time NBA starting five by spinning a random wheel for teams and decades.

Inspired by this, Deniz Sancar, a hobbyist coder who works in advertising, created 38-0-0. Sancar told Mobilegamer.biz that despite having no previous coding experience, he built the game overnight with Claude Code, an advanced AI assistant that is designed to help with coding. The game was No. 1 in the UK App Store games charts in June.
Destiny Eleven: From TikTok to France and the world

Another example is Destiny Eleven. Maxence Pigne, a PSG fan and a project manager, was inspired by a game he saw on TikTok that allowed players to play out the career of a professional footballer. After the 2026 World Cup, Pigne released his version, also created with the help of AI assistant Claude, which took the original idea further by offering more variety and choices in the career.

The man who specializes in computer science told French weekly Le Point that the decision to publish the free game earlier than planned paid off because by the end of July, the game had over 1 million players with 14 million careers having been created. Leverkusen striker Martin Terrier is reportedly a fan of the game, which has seen many variations in different languages emerge in the weeks since its arrival.
Mobile games are big business

It's clear mobile games have come a long way since Nokia released "Snake" back in 1997. They are now big business. According to digital market intelligence platform Sensor Tower, approximately 50 billion mobile games were downloaded in 2025, generating $82 billion (€71 billion) in in-app purchases. According to Game, the German games industry association, revenue in Germany in 2025 was approximately $3.12 billion, with 28.1 million players.

"This clearly indicates that mobile gaming in Germany is no longer a niche topic, but rather a serious genre with significant purchasing power," Kyle Kuscu, chairman of the German Mobile Gaming Association, told DW.
"This is also relevant for the esports sector: Germany has a broad player base, and mobile gaming is the largest platform in the country in terms of user numbers."
This summer, the emergence of sports-drafting games has clearly benefited from a World Cup summer but also because of game design.
"The World Cup or tournament effect only amplifies this, but it doesn't fully explain the hype on its own," Kuscu said.

"Such games satisfy a fundamental human need shared by many users: control, optimization and imagination in a very compact format — in other words, the feeling of having it all in your own hands, of building the perfect team or career, without a long learning curve or complex controls."
What counts is the 'idea and final execution'

AI has been involved in video game creation for years, but with smarter and faster AI in 2026 comes an even more financially efficient approach for game developers. This is particularly important in the tough economic conditions in which free-to-play mobile games operate.
"The trend toward smaller, faster-to-develop games with AI support is likely to continue and may even grow. But I don't believe that every viral success story will be repeated," Kuscu said.

blocks.caption: AI is playing an ever-increasing role in the creation of mobile gamesImage: egunes_/Depositphotos/IMAGO

blocks.text: "Based on our own experience and confirmed by external sources, we know that AI has long been used extensively and intensively in game development, especially for coding, prototyping, research and repetitive tasks. At the same time, many people remain skeptical about quality, dependencies and creative limitations. Even if we advocate for the use of AI-assisted programming, what ultimately counts is the idea and the final execution of a game, and that won't change."
Short shelf life a key problem in a competitive market

The challenges for such games to maintain their success remains a major challenge though, especially given the overall gaming market remains a far from profitable industry. More teams can release more games, but that makes competition stiffer than ever.

"The biggest hurdle is no longer just production, but the business model behind it: Mobile games are extremely dependent on user attention, repeat usage, and, above all, in-app purchases," Kuscu said.

"A viral launch does not yet equate to a viable, let alone successful, business. They must get a handle on session duration, community building, update frequency and monetization very quickly. This is precisely where the crux of the matter lies, because otherwise the hype will fizzle out before the game can become a sustainable title."

Whether it's the immersive storytelling nature of these games or the ease with which a virtual world can be reached, it's clear that these games have found a gap in the market. History suggests they might not be popular for long, but even if this summer is their moment in the sun, their emergence appears a significant reminder of the challenges the mobile game industry will face with the increased involvement of AI.
Edited by: Chuck Penfold

articles.title: Solar eclipse: What to look forward to
articles.summary: The last solar eclipse visible from the European mainland was in 1999. Here's what to expect, and how to prepare for this rare occasion.

image.caption: Millions of people across the US, Canada and Mexico witnessed a total solar eclipse in April 2024Image: Henry Romero/REUTERS

blocks.text: On Wednesday, about 980 million people across parts of the Northern Hemisphere will have the chance to observe this upcoming solar eclipse.

They will be joined by hosts of researchers who will be taking advantage of the fleeting minutes when the sun's corona is visible from Earth to test specialized instruments and capture rare images. With them, they hope to gain a deeper appreciation of the material above the sun's surface.
What's going to happen?

During a solar eclipse, the moon orbits between Earth and the sun during the daytime, casting a shadow which temporarily darkens the sky and appears to blot out the sun. At the height of an eclipse, the moon's disk appears to align with the sun, revealing the sun's corona — its outermost atmosphere that flares outward like a crown (hence the name).
As the moon approaches and the sky darkens, you might also notice the temperature dropping, shadows appearing crescent-shaped, the wind beginning to shift and animals behaving unusually.
Eclipse fever sweeps Spain ahead of rare spectacle
To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video
Solar panels will be able to produce less energy in this time. In Germany, this is expected to lead to a brief surge in electricity prices.

Right before the eclipse reaches its maximum point, known as totality, watch out for Baily's beads. These are the final rays of sun reaching Earth through valleys on the moon's surface. They appear as white specks encircling the moon like a string of pearls.
As night closes in during totality, keep an eye out for the stars that appear. Some might even be able to catch a glimpse of auroras or passing meteors.
Where will the eclipse occur?
If you live in Greenland, Iceland, northern Russia, northern Spain or northeastern Portugal, you're in luck! Viewers in these locations will be able to observe a total solar eclipse.
In most of Western Europe, as well as parts of northern Africa and northern America, astronomy enthusiasts will still be able to watch a partial solar eclipse.
And this is just the first of two eclipses in August. The second will take place on August 27-28, when Earth moves between the sun and the moon to create a lunar eclipse.
The next solar eclipse will happen February 2, 2027, over much of Africa, South America, as well as parts of Antarctica.

While eclipses themselves are fairly frequent occurrences, it's not that often that a total solar eclipse is visible on inhabited parts of the globe. The last solar eclipse visible for most of mainland Europe, for example, was in 1999.
What time is the eclipse happening?

The spectacle will begin at 15:34 GMT, with the moon slowly dimming the sun's light as it creeps into position. About two hours later, at 17:46 GMT, the eclipse will reach totality for about two minutes.

But where on the globe you are watching from will make a difference. While Icelanders will be able to observe the eclipse's totality at 17:48 GMT, viewers in Spain will have to wait until 18:27 for their chance.
Where can I watch the eclipse?

Since the eclipse is happening relatively late in the day, viewers are recommended to watch from high places to catch a good view of the sun as it dips toward the horizon. Most west-facing hills, towers and (safe) rooftops with an unobstructed view should do the trick.
If you're the kind who prefers crisper images, NASA is also offering a livestream.
Can I wear normal sunglasses to watch the eclipse?
In short, no. Looking directly into the sun can cause permanent damage to the retina at the back of your eye. Ordinary sunglasses, even polarized ones, are far too weak to provide enough protection.

Instead, you'll need certified ISO 12312-2 glasses, available at most pharmacies and opticians. Most are sold out already, but there are plenty of directions online for building a pinhole camera to safely watch the eclipse with small children.
You can also use a kitchen colander, or any other tool with small holes, to project tiny crescent-shaped shadows onto a safe surface.

Whether or not you are wearing eclipse glasses, never look at the sun through a camera, telescope or binoculars without a specialized filter, as the concentrated light can cause serious damage to your eyes.
Edited by: Martin Kuebler

articles.title: Making sense of Trump's executive order on US vaccinations
articles.summary: President Donald Trump and his Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. have long tried to reduce the number of vaccinations available to the US public and even farm animals. The latest move in context.

image.caption: The Trump Administration wants to separate the combined measles, mumps, rubella (MMR) vaccine into single shotsImage: Rebecca Blackwell/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: US President Donald Trump signed another executive order on Monday, August 10, 2026: "Delivering gold standard childhood vaccine recommendations for Americans."
The order reduces the current recommendation of 18 vaccines for children down to 11, which puts it almost in line with the World Health Organization (WHO) recommendations.
As DW reported in May 2025, there are vaccines against 30 infectious diseases. The World Health Organization recommends that every child get vaccinated against 12 of those:

items: Tuberculosis
Hepatitis B
Polio
Diphtheria
Tetanus
Pertussis (whooping cough)
Haemophilus influenza type B
Pneumococcal disease
Rotavirus
Measles
Rubella
Human papillomavirus

blocks.text: This is the WHO making recommendations for all nations — both rich and poor.
Many poor countries face challenges around access to vaccines at prices they can afford and distributing them safely to people living in remote areas.
Protecting vaccines in Ghana's rising heat
To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video
Rich countries, on the other hand, can afford and therefore usually offer more vaccinations than the WHO's base level of 12. But not all of them do.
Germany, for example, recommends 14 vaccinations for children in their first two years after birth.

Germany no longer recommends the BCG vaccine against tuberculosis (TB), which is on the WHO list. It does recommend vaccination against Respiratory Syncytial Virus (RSV), which is not on the WHO list.

This just goes to show that there are variations around the world. It's not just the US. These variations often depend on which diseases are considered by local health experts to be an ongoing threat to any given community.

Taking the example of TB in Germany: In 1998, the country's Standing Committee on Vaccination (STIKO) decided the risk of TB infections was low, and herd immunity was deemed high enough at 50-80%. Therefore the STIKO stopped recommending the vaccine.
What does Trump's new childhood vaccine recommendation say?
Trump wants to create three distinct categories for vaccination.

The first category includes immunizations recommended for all children: measles, mumps, rubella, diphtheria, tetanus, pertussis, polio, Haemophilus influenzae type b (meningitis), pneumococcal disease, human papillomavirus and varicella (chickenpox).
That removes vaccination against hepatitis B, rotavirus, influenza and RSV from this baseline category that were on the recommended list until now.

These illnesses however can still affect newborns. As we reported in 2022, cases of RSV have risen in the US and Europe. Babies who don't receive the vaccine would remain unprotected against the illness.
By contrast, Germany recommends vaccination for RSV, rotavirus and hepatitis B in a child's first six months.
Trump's executive order also recommends that the combined MMR vaccine for measles, mumps and rubella — which is a global standard — be split into individual jabs, spaced over time.

This appears to be a reflection on long-held rhetoric from the Trump administration suggesting that the combined MMR vaccine causes autism. The US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) says there is no published evidence to suggest there is any benefit in single jabs.

In fact, its advice on the MMR vaccine states that "the CDC and the American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP) agree that MMR vaccine is not responsible for recent increases in the number of children with autism."
But Trump and Robert F. Kennedy Jr. have long suggested vaccines are dangerous in general.

Kennedy also thinks that the common painkiller Tylenol causes autism when taken during pregnancy. It is the only painkiller allowed during pregnancy in the US. And as we reported in September 2025, no high-quality scientific evidence substantiated their claim.
Is the US experiencing a vaccine crisis?

Trump's second category would include immunizations for high-risk groups or populations: respiratory syncytial virus monoclonal antibodies, hepatitis A, hepatitis B, meningococcal B, meningococcal ACWY, and dengue.

The third would include vaccines to be given "based on shared clinical decision-making" — so, doctor and patient or parent of a patient would have to agree. These include: hepatitis A, hepatitis B, rotavirus, meningococcal disease, influenza and COVID-19.
The effect of political — rather than scientific — rhetoric on vaccines
While there's no direct recommendation to ban any vaccine, the second Trump administration has repeatedly attempted to destabilize public consensus over vaccination.

That can cause confusion in the community and rising rates of infection. For example, in July 2026, DW reported how "amnesia" about measles and how dangerous it is had led to a rise in measles infections in the US. People had missed opportunities to get vaccinated because infection rates had been low, but then they rose again.
This is not just the case in North America. Germany has also seen measles infections rise, with experts citing anti-vaccination rhetoric that emerged during the COVID-19 pandemic.
Allowing bird flu to spread

Kennedy however takes his hands-off rhetoric to farming communities, too. In March 2025, DW reported how the health secretary suggested bird flu should be allowed to spread through bird populations, even in places where it had already infected cattle.

Kennedy said it would enable researchers to develop "super" chickens. But instead, more than 150 million birds got infected. Bird flu virus was detected in raw milk. And there were bird-to-human infections as well.

On Monday, when Trump's executive order was released, the AAP's Andrew Racine said it was "not based on 'gold-standard science.' There is no new evidence to justify significant changes to childhood immunization guidance."
Edited by: Carla Bleiker
This article was updated on August 13, 2026, to correct an error in the original version. We had equated varicella virus with smallpox when it is in fact chickenpox.

articles.title: How one German city plans to challenge climate extremes
articles.summary: Western Europe has recorded its hottest-ever June and July, and extreme weather from drought to storms is here to stay. How can we adapt to a fundamentally altered climate? Cities like Kiel are…

image.caption: The worst storm surge in 150 years wreaked havoc along the Baltic Sea coast in 2023Image: Daniel Bockwoldt/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: In October 2023, the worst storm surge in more than 150 years hit the Baltic Sea coast. It destroyed dikes, collapsed coastal cliffs and devastated marinas in the northern German state of Schleswig-Holstein and parts of southern Denmark.

The catastrophic surge wiped away 2.68 meters (8.79 feet) of coastal bluff in Kiel, a port city and Schleswig-Holstein's capital. That was more than four times the yearly average lost over the previous two decades.
Human-caused climate change is supercharging extreme weather such as storms. And in coastal cities like Kiel, the consequences are already impossible to ignore.

"The impacts of climate change are hardly abstract in Kiel," said Martina Baum, who heads the city's climate adaptation division. "Since at least the 2023 storm surge, we have all been reminded of the profound effects it can have on us, on our daily lives, and on the environment around us."

Those effects are forcing Kiel — among the first cities to declare a climate emergency back in 2019 — to rethink its design, and how it works. It has since become a front-runner in adapting to the realities of a changing climate, establishing Baum's division in 2025 to help make the city more resilient to weather extremes and adopting an adaptation plan in February 2026 to step up those measures.
Is climate adaptation giving up on fighting climate change?

For city officials like Baum, adaptation is not a substitute for cutting the fossil fuel emissions heating the planet. Climate protection remains the first line of defense, because limiting warming will reduce future damage.

"For a long time, there was hesitation to engage officially with the issue of climate change adaptation. I also felt uneasy about it at first, because it felt as though it would somehow take the pressure off climate protection efforts," Baum told DW.

But the move to adaptation in Kiel reflects what's happening in other cities around the world from Santa Cruz in the US to Quezon City in the Philippines, as governments increasingly prepare for the impacts of heat, heavier rainfall and stronger storm surges that are already here.

blocks.caption: With days getting hotter, Quezon City in the Philippines has also intensified its adaptation plansImage: Aaron Favila/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: That doesn't mean climate protection and adaptation always align. Installing power-hungry air-conditioning in housing, daycare or senior centers, for instance, protects vulnerable people in heat waves. But it increases energy consumption, "which would run counter to climate protection goals," Baum said.

"Even if we use renewable energy, demand is not yet covered by renewable sources 100% of the time, so any additional energy we consume will ultimately result in the emission of climate-damaging greenhouse gases," she added.
Redesigning cities for unavoidable impacts

While AC will sometimes be necessary, Kiel is working on solutions that cool the city naturally. It's adding vegetation to building facades, redesigning a park to channel cooler air into the city center, and making it easier for residents to access permits, information and grants for adaptation projects.

The city is also testing which tree species can survive future conditions. A decade ago, Kiel planted five specimens each of 20 different species to find out which can best withstand heat, drought and salt spray from the nearby Baltic Sea.
Kolkata's tree ambulance rushes to save urban trees
To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video
Trees provide shade, cool streets by roughly 1.5 degrees Celsius (2.7 Fahrenheit) and improve air quality, but not every species will thrive as the climate changes.
"There is no one-size-fits-all climate tree; different sites require different tree species," said Nicole Holz, who works in the department responsible for the city's green spaces.
The research requires patience.
"It's going to take some 20, 30 years until you get some real results," said Petra Holtappel, head of the same department.
Living differently: No more daytime soccer?
Adapting to climate change will also require changes to daily life, said Baum. Children, for example, may no longer be able to play soccer tournaments at 3 p.m. because it's too hot.

blocks.caption: It may become the new normal to play only during certain times of the dayImage: Fabio Teixeira/Anadolu Agency/IMAGO

blocks.text: Although Kiel is getting warmer, it is expected to fare better than much hotter cities in Southern or Central Europe when it comes to heat. Still, the city is vulnerable to more storm surges and heavy rain and needs more retention areas to manage all that excess water. The city is dredging a pond in the park earmarked for redesign to store stormwater during heavy rainfall, but is also exploring other ideas.

"One idea is what's known as multi-use design, meaning that in future, a soccer pitch could be built slightly lower than the surrounding area. During periods of heavy rain, water could then be directed there and allowed to gradually infiltrate into the ground or evaporate," Baum said.

The downside is the pitch might be unusable for up to 60 days a year, she added. But residents would need accept that, said Baum, who emphasized the need for greater public debate about adaptation measures.
How to reach people who don't think about the climate?

Helping residents understand those trade-offs and what's at stake is part of Annafried Stürmer's work. Stürmer organizes educational events, leads public excursions with scientists and attends neighborhood fairs to meet people who might not otherwise engage with climate issues.
At Kiel Week in June, the world's biggest annual sailing event, Stürmer displayed a map showing city flood risk from extreme rainfall.

blocks.caption: The 2023 storm surge caused caused millions of euro in damage in the port city of KielImage: Daniel Bockwoldt/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: "People often find that interesting, because it doesn't immediately seem like it's connected to climate change. Instead, the initial reaction is , 'Wow, if we get one of those intense heavy rainfall events, my house could be in serious trouble,' or 'My backyard could end up flooded,'" Stürmer said.
Stürmer has often found it easier to talk about climate adaptation than about climate change, because the former is more tangible.

"It's easier to talk about the need for a better-developed sewer system to handle heavy rainfall, or about planting different types of trees and vegetation, than it is to talk about reducing CO2 emissions," Stürmer told DW.
Recent record heat waves have made the adaptation conservation more urgent too.
"People noticed that it hadn't been as hot before," she said, adding residents increasingly recognize the need to protect children, the elderly, pregnant women and outdoor workers.
Climate adaptation not 'optional'

Even with growing public awareness of the need for adaptation, funding remains a problem in cash-strapped Kiel. Still seen as optional, climate action can quickly come under pressure when budgets tighten.

"I disagree with the idea that climate adaptation and climate action are optional responsibilities. I keep asking myself: what are the alternatives?" Baum said. "After all, it has been demonstrated time and again that investing in climate adaptation and climate mitigation will simply pay off."
Edited by: Jennifer Collins

articles.title: How the Rhine drought threatens Germany's economic recovery
articles.summary: Germany's inland waterways still move around 5% of the nation's goods. With the Rhine at a critically low level, DW explores how the drought is hitting the economy where it hurts most.

image.caption: A drought has severely reduced water levels in the Rhine, Germany's longest riverImage: Michael Probst/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: Water levels on the Rhine River — a small but critical artery for goods vital to Germany’s industry — remain critically low as a result of weeks of drought.

At one of the river's shallowest stretches, Kaub — between Mainz and Koblenz — the water level stood at around 16 centimeters (6.3 inches) at Monday lunchtime, according to the Federal Waterways and Shipping Administration (WSV).
Although the real navigable channel is roughly a meter deeper, 40 centimeters is regarded as the lowest for standard commercial vessels at Kaub.
Ship operators use the reading at Kaub to decide how much cargo their barges can safely carry and whether a passage is feasible at all.
According to local media, in recent weeks, carriers have significantly cut their cargoes along the Rhine — in many cases to as little as one-fifth of normal capacity.
The problem isn't just limited to the Middle Rhine, the 130-kilometer (80-mile) stretch between Mainz and Bonn that is the narrowest and shallowest section of the river.
Areas around Cologne, Düsseldorf, Duisburg-Ruhrort and Emmerich are also at historic lows.
Jens Schwanen, the head of the BDB association of inland shipping, told the Rheinische Post newspaper on Monday that the Rhine may become impassable at Kaub before the end of the week.
This would effectively split the river in two for commercial traffic.
What effect will the drought have on the German economy?
The drought could not come at a worse time for Germany’s economy, which is already grappling with weak growth, high energy costs and fading industrial competitiveness.
Germany still relies on its long rivers and waterways to transport some 5% of goods around the country, most of them bulk materials, including iron ore, coal, sand and petroleum products.
Out of 3.28 billion tons of goods transported in 2024, 173 million tons were carried by inland water, including the Rhine, according to BDB.

Eurostat, the European Union's statistics agency, calculated in 2023 that the Rhine corridor — from the Port of Rotterdam in the Netherlands to the German-Swiss border — accounts for around 40% of freight by ton-kilometers.
After two previous droughts, the Kiel Institute for the World Economy calculated in 2023 that for every 30 days of low water on the Rhine, Germany's industrial production declines by about 1%.
In an economy that has barely grown for the past two years, even a temporary 1% hit to industrial output is highly damaging.
The German Economic Institute (IW) now predicts a 0.4% drop in gross domestic product, effectively wiping out this year's economic growth, which was expected at 0.5%.
"A prolonged disruption of navigability on the Rhine could completely stifle the tiny seed of growth we have," warned IW economist Thilo Schäfer in an interview with Bild newspaper last week.
Other experts have warned of losses of €1 to €2 billion ($1.2 to $2.3 billion) in the third quarter alone, with the steel, chemicals and energy sectors hit especially hard.
What happens if the River Rhine is effectively split in two?
The BDB's Schwanen warned that "due to the lack of rainfall, a single-digit reading is forecast for the first time this week at the Kaub gauge."
"In principle, this means the Rhine is no longer navigable along its entire length and is therefore effectively divided in two," he told the Rheinische Post.

This would result in two separate areas. On the one hand, shipping traffic would continue between the North Sea ports of Amsterdam, Rotterdam, and Antwerp and the Cologne region via the Rhine and the Western German canal system.

Further south, shipping would operate on the tributaries of the Neckar, Moselle, and Main, as well as the Main-Danube Canal, which is regarded as a key global link on the route to and from Southeast Europe.
Between the two sections, shipping companies would then try to move cargo onto trucks and freight rail services.
However, Germany's roads cannot absorb the typical 50 to 150 truckloads that a single large barge can handle without severe congestion and substantially higher costs.
Baden-Württemberg said Monday it would join four other German states in easing restrictions on truck movements on Sundays to help ease congestion.
Following urgent talks last Thursday, Transport Minister Steffen Bilger announced several other measures to shore up Germany's supply chain.
These include cutting red tape for heavy loads shifted to the road network, stopping unnecessary roadworks and better coordination with DB Cargo, the rail freight arm of Deutsche Bahn.

blocks.caption: Many vessels are carrying a fifth of their normal cargo volumesImage: Rüdiger Wölk/IMAGO

blocks.text: Are regular droughts a new reality for Europe's waterways?
Extremely low water on the Rhine and other major European rivers used to be rare events.
Yet, many scientists believe climate change is now making them more frequent, longer and more severe.

According to the EU’s Copernicus Climate Change Service, western Europe has just experienced its warmest June and July on record, with exceptionally low rainfall driving much lower than average water levels on the Rhine, Danube and Seine.
The current crisis marks the third major low‑water episode in eight years, after major droughts in 2018 and 2022.
The Rhine has traditionally been supported during dry summer months by meltwater from Alpine snow and glaciers. As those glaciers retreat and snow cover declines, this natural buffer is weakening.
Germany’s Federal Institute of Hydrology (BfG) projected in 2023 that severe low-water events like 2018 could strike every five to 10 years by mid-century.
Can shipping adapt as Germany's busiest river runs dry?
To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video
Edited by: Kristie Pladson

articles.title: UEFA, other football federations unite against Infantino
articles.summary: A few weeks ago, Gianni Infantino looked set for another unopposed term as FIFA president. Now, with an election looming, the beleagured football executive is counting the numbers and could be…

image.caption: Gianni Infantino is under threat but still has support within FIFAImage: Luisa Gonzalez/REUTERS

blocks.text: Gianni Infantino's already perilous position as FIFA president took another blow on Monday, as three continental football federations banded together in an apparent attempt to try to force him out.

An "Open Letter to the Football Family" signed by the heads of UEFA (Europe), CONCACAF (North and Central America and the Caribbean) and AFC (Asia) appeared to take aim at Infantino — without actually mentioning him by name.

"This is about something more fundamental: the integrity of the game, and the integrity of those elected to lead it. Leadership in football is not a possession. It is not about holding — or demanding — power to be held," the statement read.

"It is a duty of service to the football family that entrusts it. When trust is broken through deception, when an individual places himself above the collective that entrusted him with authority, that duty has been abandoned."
FIFA accused of blackmail in exchange for Infantino support
To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The letter criticizes Infantino's now scrapped plan to form a subsidiary arm of FIFA (International Federation of Association Football) in order to sell off part of its commercial operations to investors.
It says that even in withdrawing the plan, FIFA "did not acknowledge that the proposal itself was inherently wrong."

It also labels the plan a "fundamental breach of trust" and lambasted Infantino's seemingly unilateral actions in bypassing the executive FIFA Council for his initial proposal and then holding a summit in Morocco with only selected senior figures within the organization.

"It is not the conduct of a custodian of the game, but of one who believes the game is answerable to him. There is silence where there should be accountability, distance where there should be openness," the letter reads.

The statement comes after media reports that UEFA paid off an alleged mistress of Infantino during his time at the European confederation. FIFA in response criticized "unsubstantiated assertions and demonstrably false claims" and said that "it is increasingly evident that there is a concerted and ongoing effort by some to undermine FIFA and its President."
FIFA have not yet replied to a DW request for comment on the open letter.
What does this change for Infantino?

Were the national federations of the three confederations to fall in line, there would be easily enough votes to oust Infantino at the presidential election in March 2027. FIFA has 211 voting members and thus a presidential candidate in a two-horse race would require 106 votes. UEFA (55 members) AFC (46) and CONCACAF (35) would easily have enough if each confederation's members voted as a bloc.

However, this seems unlikely. While UEFA, who have driven much of the opposition, seem relatively united, the picture in the two other confederations is more mixed. Mexico, one of CONCACAF's most powerful nations and a World Cup 2026 cohost, have backed Infantino while Qatar, who hosted the 2022 World Cup, is one of several Asian nations to have broken ranks.

The South American federation CONMEBOL (10) does not yet have a clear position on Infantino, but one of its most powerful nations, Argentina, have lent Infantino their support. The Oceania federation (11) has also yet to make its position clear.
Perhaps the best news for Infantino was the backing of the African confederation, CAF (54), last week.

A statement from the organization's executive committee said that CAF "unanimously reconfirmed its support for FIFA President Gianni Infantino and thanked him for his support for African Football over the years."
Is there a candidate to challenge Infantino?
This is the big question. As it stands, no candidate has stepped forward. Infantino won the last presidential election unopposed and looked likely to do so again next March, until a few weeks ago.

Though the clear positioning of several confederations against Infantino suggests that running unopposed again is now unlikely, a candidate that can unite those federations in opposition to the Swiss administrator is the next step.
"There's such an imperative to get a candidate who could unite the whole world of football, not just Europe in this case," UEFA vice president, Laura McAllister, recently told DW.

"It's not as easy as people might think. The right candidate has to also have the right level of support," McAllister said. "But if we're talking about the right candidate, then I think that person, that man or woman, needs to be somebody who recognizes that we are simply custodians of the sport and that we look after it and hopefully leave it in better health."
What might happen next?

There will no doubt be plenty of backroom talks about finding a candidate and announcing them at the right time. But given that Infantino retains a reasonable amount of support, football's powerbrokers will likely want to ensure whoever they might put up can win. UEFA executives will likely discuss this at the Super Cup (between the winners of last season's Champions League and Europa League) later this week, while other federations will look to do similar.

Looming in early September is the first FIFA tournament since the controversial sell-off plan was announced. The U-20 Women's World Cup is being held in Poland, a UEFA member, and it is not yet clear whether European teams will participate in the tournament with Infantino still in charge.
Edited by: Chuck Penfold

articles.title: Type 2 diabetes in young women increasingly common
articles.summary: British researchers say rates of type 2 diabetes are growing most among women under 40. The disease is often underdiagnosed in women or diagnosed too late to reverse the condition's progression.

image.caption: Type 2 diabetes is on the rise in young people under 40 years. One reason is that we don't move enough in our day-to-day lives.Image: Giorgio Magini/Westend61/IMAGO

blocks.text: There used to be a clear-cut way to distinguish diabetes type 1 and type 2. Medical jargon aside: Type 1 diabetes was a genetic autoimmune disease that presented in young people, and type 2 was a disease that presented in older patients in their fifties or sixties due to an unhealthy lifestyle.
But that distinction of young and old doesn't work anymore.
More and more, younger people are being diagnosed with type 2 diabetes. In England, for example, the biggest increase in new diagnoses of type 2 diabetes is among young women.

This was revealed when a team of researchers from Imperial College London evaluated data from an English National Diabetes Audit between 2011 and 2024. They found that while the prevalence of type 2 diabetes was decreasing in adults between 60 and 79 years of age, it was rising in under-40-year-olds.
The results, published in The Lancet Regional Health Europe journal, showed the sharpest increase was among white, Asian and Black women in their 20s, and white women in their 30s.

"Much of the discussion around rising type 2 diabetes in younger people has focused on ethnic minority groups," said Shivani Misra, the lead author of the study and a clinical associate professor for diabetes at Imperial College London.

"While these ethnic groups are disproportionately affected with early-onset type 2 diabetes, we now see that incidence is […] increasing in white populations too, showing that this public health challenge is broadening across the generation."
Lifestyle behind rise in type 2 diabetes among young people
In Germany, the situation is similar to the UK, said Baptist Gallwitz, an endocrinologist and spokesperson for the German Diabetes Society (DDG).
"Type 2 diabetes is on the rise in many countries," Gallwitz told DW. "It's basically a pandemic. In Germany, we're also seeing an increase in children and teenagers diagnosed with the disease."
From 2014 to 2023, there was an increase in type 2 diabetes cases of 5.8% a year among youth aged 11 to 17 years, according to a 2026 health report on diabetes released by the DDG.
Nigeria faces a silent diabetes epidemic
To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video
While genetic disposition can play a role in the development of type 2 diabetes, the biggest factor is lifestyle.

"We live in a world where we don't move enough and where our nutrition contains too much sugar and too many calories," Gallwitz said. "That leads to more obesity among young people, and that in turn greatly increases the risk of type 2 diabetes."
In people with type 2 diabetes, reduced insulin secretion or a weaker effect of insulin on its receptors lead to a higher glucose content in the blood.
Type 1 diabetes is characterized by a full loss of insulin-producing cells, leading to severe insulin deficiency.
Fighting the rise of diabetes type 2 in young people
The increase is particularly concerning because in young patients, the progression of the disease can be more serious than in older patients.

"Any diagnosis of type 2 diabetes is serious, but it can be more aggressive in younger people, increasing the risk of devastating complications and cutting lives short," said Helen Kirrane from Diabetes UK, a charity that campaigns on the issue.
That's why it's important to intervene early. Gallwitz said the DDG welcomed the introduction of a tax on sugary sodas in Germany, but added that it wasn't enough.
The DDG is calling for a tiered value-added tax (VAT) system, with fresh fruit and vegetables being sold with no tax and the VAT increasing the more the products contain saturated fats and sugars.
The organization also wants healthier food in kindergarten and school cafeterias and one hour of mandatory movement per day to be incorporated into class schedules.

Asking for more exercise during the school day is one thing. But conditions in the general environment also need to be improved to stop the increase of type 2 diabetes in young women, said Alexandra Kautzky-Willer, head of the division for endocrinology and metabolism at the Medical University of Vienna.
"More movement is important, so we need to ensure conditions in which it's safe for women to move," Kautzky-Willer, who is also a professor of gender medicine, told DW.
For example, a woman who fears being catcalled, ridiculed for her weight or even attacked in the dark is less likely to go running after work or join a gym.
How a young Ghanaian is determined to beat diabetes
Diabetes type 2 underdiagnosed in women

The number of women with type 2 diabetes might be even higher than what current data show. In 2025, Kautzky-Willer and a colleague wrote a report for the Deutsches Ärzteblatt, a German medical journal, saying that the disease is underdiagnosed in women.

"Men are usually diagnosed with [type 2 diabetes] at a younger age," they wrote in the the article. "At the point of diagnosis, more women are obese, they have hypertension more often and have gained more weight" than men when they are diagnosed.
Those factors contributed to an increased risk of stroke and heart attacks as well. So, why is it that diabetes type 2 is often only diagnosed in women when they are already this sick?
"For one, the value often tested in initial diabetes diagnosis is fasting blood sugar," Kautzky-Willer said.
Your fasting blood sugar is your blood sugar level when you haven't eaten for eight hours. It's just a single snapshot in time, however, and misses blood sugar spikes after a meal.
Fasting blood sugar "is generally lower in women than it is in men," Kautzky-Willer said. "It would make more sense to do a glucose tolerance test, but that is more work."
More complex tests for diabetes could save lives
A glucose tolerance test involves taking blood several times in the span of two hours, during which patients need to stay at the doctor's office.
Kautzky-Willer says it would be good if HbA1c levels were tested as well. Tests for HbA1c levels show a person's average blood sugar level over a two or three-month period.
HbA1c refers to glycated haemoglobin, which is when glucose in your body sticks to red blood cells. This prevents the body from using the sugar properly.

A high HbA1c means you have too much sugar in your blood and are more likely to develop diabetes complications. But testing HbA1c levels requires specialized lab equipment and is more expensive than testing the fasting blood sugar.

The glucose tolerance and the HbA1c tests are not covered by health insurance in Germany and Austria, only the fasting blood sugar one is covered, and that may be influencing the options for people in those countries.

Experts who spoke to DW agreed that to bring type 2 diabetes numbers down among young people, it's important to know when their blood values get close to the line for the disease, a condition known as being "pre-diabetic."

People who find out they have a problem at this early stage still have a chance to turn the ship around. With lifestyle and nutrition changes, diabetes progression can be stopped in some cases, saving them from a host of health problems later on, which may require regular medication and lead to a reduced life expectancy.
Edited by: Zulfikar Abbany

articles.title: Study: Obesity 'bigger cancer risk' than previously thought
articles.summary: A new study has found that being significantly overweight could be responsible for more cases of cancer than previously known. Abdominal fat, in particular, increases the risk of cancer — especially…

image.caption: Obesity could be causing as many as one in ten cancer cases, according to a new studyImage: Jan Woitas/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Being overweight or obese significantly increases the risk of developing colon cancer, breast cancer or liver cancer, and is a major risk factor for 10 other types of cancer, a new study has found.

Until recently, researchers believed that 2% to 8% of all cancer cases were attributable to excess body weight. But a new study by a team led by Hermann Brenner, an epidemiologist with the German Cancer Research Center (DKFZ), suggests that this was a serious underestimate.
According to the study, up to 11.5% of cancers may be attributable to being overweight.

The DKFZ researchers "have not only updated existing risk estimates, but have also questioned whether the link between excess weight and cancer may have been underestimated until now," Michael Leitzmann, an epidemiologist at the University of Regensburg, told DW.

Leitzmann, who was not involved in the study, researches diet, body weight, physical activity and the development of chronic diseases at the university's Institute of Epidemiology and Prevention, and has advised German Cancer Aid.
The abdominal-fat 'trigger'

The DKFZ team changed its research methods for the new study. Previous research used body mass index (BMI), which is calculated based on height and weight, as an indicator of excess weight. But BMI does not distinguish between fat and muscle mass, and does not provide information on how fat is distributed throughout the body.

This is important, because not all fat is the same. Fat cells that accumulate around the abdomen are more than just a passive store for excess calories, unlike those in other parts of the body. "They trigger what is known as a chronic inflammatory metabolic state," Leitzmann said.

Excess abdominal fat functions like a gland that releases various signaling molecules, known as adipokines. These travel through the bloodstream to different parts of the body, where they influence other metabolic processes — including cell growth and division, as well as the inhibition of programmed cell death. "These are all mechanisms that can contribute to the development and subsequent growth of tumors," Leitzmann said.

The DKFZ researchers therefore focused not only on BMI but also on waist circumference and the waist-to-hip ratio. Data from 458,543 women and men from the UK Biobank, which holds one of the world's biggest health datasets, were included in the study. The participants were followed for and average of 12 years, during which 50,000 new cases of cancer were identified.
Understanding previous underestimates
The researchers wanted to rule out a potential methodological bias in previous studies: the fact that cancer can lead to weight loss even before diagnosis — that is, while it is still developing.

That suggests that previous studies failed to identify a link between obesity and cancer because the participants had already lost weight because they had developed cancer by the time they entered the study.

For this reason, the team excluded the first few years following the participants' enrollment from the analysis. Only cancer cases that occurred seven years after the start of the observation period were considered — and that made the statistical link between being overweight and cancer clearer.
How AI is expanding breast cancer screening in Mexico
To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video
Women at risk

The study suggests that the proportion of overweight women who develop cancer is higher than that of men, but Leitzmann urges caution when interpreting these findings. Further studies with a similar design are needed to see whether the results can be replicated.

Leitzmann offered a theory on why being overweight might have a more severe impact on women. Being overweight is blamed, among other things, for breast, uterine and ovarian cancers. "These types of cancer, which affect women, are hormone-dependent," Leitzmann said. For example, the hormone estrogen can stimulate the growth of breast cancer, and excess abdominal fat can contribute to elevated estrogen levels.

Most people are now aware that obesity increases the risk of cardiovascular disease or Type 2 diabetes, Leitzmann said. Conversely, this also means that people who lose weight also reduce their risk of heart attacks, strokes and diabetes.

Though the DKFZ study emphasizes the increased risk associated with obesity, Leitzmann said the findings were also a reason for optimism: "To me, this clearly indicates that, by preventing obesity, we will be able to make a greater contribution to cancer prevention than previously assumed."
This article was originally written in German.

articles.title: FIFA warns against 'concerted effort' to undermine Gianni Infantino
articles.summary: Pressure is mounting on the FIFA president Gianni Infantino after plans to sell a stake in the World Cup collapsed and fresh allegations emerged relating to his time at UEFA.

image.caption: Gianni Infantino has been FIFA president since 2016 [FILE: July 14, 2026]Image: Eric Gay/AP Photo/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: FIFA warned against what it calls a "concerted and ongoing effort" to "undermine" the organization and its president, Gianni Infantino.

The statement, issued late on Saturday, comes amid a growing dispute over Infantino's leadership after the failed plan to create a subsidiary to run the men's World Cup and other events, with up to a 20% stake offered to external investors.

The proposal drew criticism from European governing body UEFA, which threatened to boycott future World Cups, as well as several national associations and senior FIFA officials, and prompted calls for Infantino to resign.
Amid the growing criticism Infantino persuaded FIFA's Board of Management to express its full support for him at a crisis meeting in Rabat, Morocco, on Wednesday.
FIFA accused of blackmail in exchange for Infantino support
To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video
Report raises new questions over Infantino

The pressure on Infantino intensified on Friday when British newspaper the Daily Telegraph reported a six-figure sum was paid to a female employee alleged to have been in a relationship with him during his time as UEFA general secretary.
UEFA confirmed a departure payment and said it also funded her MBA course, stating both were in line with regulations at the time.
A FIFA spokesman told the Telegraph on Friday: "FIFA president Gianni Infantino strongly denies these allegations, and they are categorically untrue."

Responding to the latest scrutiny, FIFA said on Saturday, without directly mentioning the Telegraph report, "recent reporting has included unsubstantiated assertions and demonstrably false claims concerning FIFA and its President."
Investment plan dispute deepens leadership crisis
The fallout over the shelved private investment plan has overshadowed Infantino's bid for a fourth term as FIFA president.
After this week's crisis meeting, UEFA said it no longer has confidence in him, and Norwegian FA President Lise Klaveness called for his resignation.

Despite the controversy, Infantino retains strong backing among FIFA members, with the Confederation of African Football (CAF) unanimously supporting his leadership and South American governing body CONMEBOL opposing any attempt to remove him without a vote of all member associations.

FIFA said that those who lacked the support of its member associations should not seek to achieve "allegation, insinuation or misinformation what they cannot achieve through FIFA's established democratic processes."
Edited by: Emmy Sasipornkarn

articles.title: Eco wins: Hungary goes solar, marmots go viral and Rome gets an upgrade
articles.summary: From Hungary's accidental solar revolution to marmot crowdfunding and a long-overdue upgrade for Rome's big snake, good news comes in strange packages this week.

image.caption: Yellow-bellied marmots are now officially internet famousImage: All Canada Photos/IMAGO

blocks.text: Hungary's former leader Viktor Orban called European Union climate policy a "utopian fantasy" and effectively banned wind turbines. And yet the country has quietly become Europe's solar leader, with 25% of its electricity now being being generated from the renewable energy source, ahead of sunnier countries like Spain, and Greece.

The boom was driven not by climate concern but by self-sufficiency politics and cheap subsidies. Now a 450-megawatt park, just east of Budapest, is due online by September 2026. It's set to power around 106,000 households.
Marmot researchers find a new way to fund their science

When US federal funding dried up, researchers from UCLA and the Rocky Mountain Biological Laboratory got creative. They launched OnlyMarms: a free platform posting videos of yellow-bellied marmots eating, digging and scampering in the wild, where fans can donate to support the science.

The team has tracked individually marked marmots in Colorado since 1962, building six decades of data on family lives, social behavior and responses to environmental change — and say studying marmot hibernation could even hold clues about human aging.
Rome's 'big snake' gets a cooler future

Corviale, a kilometer-long brutalist housing complex outside Rome nicknamed "the big snake," was completed in the 1980s and has since fallen into decay. With summers in some parts of Italy's now averaging around 30 degrees Celsius (86 Fahrenheit), life inside has become tough for its more than 4,000 residents.
But upgrades are coming: a new library doubling as a cooling shelter, more trees and energy efficiency improvements, all aimed at helping Corviale stay cool as temperatures keep rising.
Senegalese designer turns discarded textiles into sustainable fashion

Berlin-based designer Mame Khady Badji transforms discarded clothing into bold garments inspired by her Senegalese heritage, combining traditional Ndiakhass techniques with contemporary streetwear. Her creations have drawn musicians, performers and creatives — and recently appeared at Berlin Fashion Week 2026.

After moving to Germany in 2017, Badji built her label with support from Berlin's textile community. Now she's pursuing an ambitious goal: proving that recycled fashion can be both culturally rooted and commercially viable.
Can sustainable fashion be profitable?

articles.title: Testosterone and fertility: the trade-off men aren't told about
articles.summary: Testosterone is trending in gyms, on social online and in politics. US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth even wants troops screened for low testosterone. But taking supplements can shut down the body's…

image.caption: More men than ever are taking testosterone-boosting medicationImage: BREUEL-BILD/IMAGO

blocks.text: Making sperm is, in large part, what testosterone is for. Which is why it is ironic when a man who doesn't need it starts taking it anyway: His brain registers an unusually high level of the hormone in his blood, concludes his body has made too much, and sends the order to stop. The testes go silent and sperm production declines.

Testosterone is having a moment. It is all over social media, gym culture and wellness forums, sold by online labs, gym contacts and telehealth services. The information surrounding it ranges from oversimplified to outright dangerous. Men are taking more of it than ever, in pursuit of feeling more like men. In doing so, they may be telling their bodies to stop producing it themselves.
Here is what the science says — what testosterone does, who genuinely needs treatment, and what it can cost the men who take it without needing it.
How does taking testosterone stop sperm production?

Your body regulates testosterone the way a thermostat regulates heat. When the brain detects abnormally high levels of the hormone in the bloodstream, it sends a signal to the testes to stop producing it naturally. The testes effectively go offline, and because sperm production depends on what happens inside them, that shuts down too.

Some men who self-medicate with testosterone push their levels to more than four times the clinical lower threshold. The consequences include blood clotting disorders, cardiovascular stress, mood instability and, in some cases, irreversible fertility damage. What's sold as a shortcut to strength and libido can, unsupervised, cost a man his fertility.
What are normal testosterone levels by age?
Testosterone peaks during puberty, typically between 13 and 15. After that, it declines slowly for the rest of a man's life. A lower level at 40 than at 15 isn't a disorder — its aging.
What counts as low testosterone?
The threshold that doctors use is 300 nanograms per deciliter of blood.
But this threshold comes with a condition: It must be confirmed by at least two blood tests taken at different times of the day, because levels fluctuate.
Below that number, a doctor may begin to consider treatment. Above 300, there is no clinical basis for intervention.
How can you increase testosterone naturally?

Before any medical treatment is considered, four key lifestyle factors should be examined: sleep, alcohol consumption, smoking and drug use, and chronic stress. Each of these has a measurable impact on testosterone levels. Addressing them may be all that's needed and carries none of the risks of hormonal therapy.
What is testosterone replacement therapy (TRT) and who actually needs it?
Testosterone replacement therapy, or TRT, treats a diagnosed hormonal deficiency. It's a legitimate medical procedure — involving injections, pills, creams — that works for men who need it.

But plenty of men taking it don't have that deficiency. Men with normal testosterone levels are increasingly seeking TRT out anyway, not as a treatment but as a performance enhancer. They're getting it from unregulated online labs, gym contacts and telehealth services that write prescriptions without adequate medical assessment.
Can testosterone therapy cause permanent infertility?
In some cases, yes.

Men who stop taking testosterone are likely to recover their own production within months. But not all of them. Depending on the dose and how long a man has been using, research puts the share who never recover at somewhere between one in ten and one in five.
Low testosterone: What it does to men's health
To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video
Does testosterone therapy actually work – or is it a placebo?
Many men who self-administer testosterone report feeling stronger, sharper and more energetic. Some of that may reflect genuine physiological change.

A significant portion is likely the placebo effect — a well-documented human tendency to feel better when we believe we are being treated. That does not make the feeling less real. It does mean that unsupervised hormonal intervention is a high-risk gamble for a benefit that may exist entirely in one's mind.
The bottom line
Doctors' advice is unambiguous: Get tested, know the number, and treat everything else — the websites, the influencers, the gym contacts — as anecdote, not medicine.
A lot of men aren't waiting. Chasing peak masculinity online, they're reaching for the one substance that could tell their own bodies to stop making it.
Edited by: Kaukab Shairani

articles.title: Drought threatens power supplies in Danube countries
articles.summary: Droughts, heat and falling water levels in the Danube are hitting central and southeastern Europe hard. Hungary and Romania are experiencing an energy crisis — whereas countries like Bulgaria are…

image.caption: Cargo ships anchor near Petrovaradin, Serbia, on the Danube amid extremely low levels of water following an extended period of drought Image: Darko Vojinovic/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: Riverbeds reduced to tiny streams, asphalt melting like butter, dried-up fields — these are currently the images of drought in Central and Southeastern Europe. The record-breaking lack of rainfall in recent months and this summer's heatwaves have caused severe damage to the region's economy and infrastructure.

In the agriculture sector, it has been clear for some time that harvests in Southeastern Europe, especially maize and sunflower crops, will be significantly below average. The heatwaves are also repeatedly disrupting road, rail and, above all, shipping transport. But, most importantly, the drought has triggered an unprecedented crisis in electricity generation in several Central and Southeastern European countries, forcing companies to halt production due to the historically low water level of the Danube.

Hungary and Romania are currently most affected by the energy crisis. Other countries bordering the Danube — Austria, Slovakia, Serbia and Bulgaria — are also suffering from low water levels, although not as severely as Hungary and Romania.
DW outlines the situation in each country and explains why, despite facing similar weather conditions, some are more severely affected than others.
Hungary: Most severe energy crisis in decades

No country in the region is currently as severely affected by drought and heat as Hungary. For months, there has been little or no rainfall in large parts of the country. On Wednesday, temperatures reached 43 degrees Celsius (109.4 degrees Fahrenheit) in the capital Budapest, and exceeded 40 degrees in many places across the country.

Due to the record-low water levels of the Danube, the Paks nuclear power plant south of Budapest had to largely shut down operations, as there is no longer sufficent cooling water available and the temperature of the Danube water is too high. The plant is currently operating at around 12% of its capacity. If Danube water levels continue to drop, the plant will have to be shut down completely.

Due to the energy crisis, the Hungarian government has been urging large energy consumers to conserve electricity. As a result, several car manufacturers, including Audi Gyor, oil and gas company MOL and other large companies have scaled back production. Hungary's energy crisis — the worst in decades — is so severe because of the country's unfavorable energy mix. Paks generates around 50% of the electricity produced in Hungary and about one-third of the electricity consumed. Although Hungary has significant solar energy capacity, it lacks storage facilities, has too few modern gas-fired power plants and very little wind or hydropower capacity.

blocks.caption: In Prahovo (eastern Serbia), the Danube's low water level has revealed the remains of a German WW II warshipImage: Darko Vojinovic/AP Photo/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Even if the Danube water levels rise significantly again, the Paks nuclear power plant cannot simply be brought back online quickly — the process takes a considerable amount of time. Therefore, Hungary's energy crisis will continue for at least several more weeks, during which the country will have to import electricity at high prices. In response to the crisis, the new government under Peter Magyar has announced a comprehensive review of Hungary's energy development strategy.
Romania: Blasting rocks to redirect water

Romania is experiencing a similar, though somewhat less severe, energy crisis. The Cernavoda nuclear power plant, also located on the Danube in the southeast of the country, produces roughly one-fifth of Romania's electricity. Due to the river's exceptionally low water level, one of the plant's two 700-megawatt reactors was taken offline last week.

Southwest of the Cernavoda plant, Romanian authorities blasted a rock formation this week to divert more water into the Danube's eastern branch, where the nuclear plant is located. In addition, dozens of tons of rock were dumped into the river to channel more water into that branch.

blocks.caption: Romania's navy carried out a controlled blast of submerged rocks to allow more water to flow into the eastern branch of the DanubeImage: Vadim Ghirda/AP Photo/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Romania has a relatively balanced energy mix consisting of hydropower, nuclear energy, natural gas, coal and wind power. However, because hydropower accounts for around one-fifth of the country's electricity generation — primarily through the Iron Gate hydroelectric plant on the Danube — Romania is particularly vulnerable to droughts such as the current one.

Due to the energy crisis, several major companies, including Dacia and Ford Romania, have scaled back production. The government has announced that it would, if necessary, issue a decree ordering large factories to suspend production.

Romania is also among the Southeastern European countries most affected by aridification — the long-term climatic process through which regions become increasingly dry — and desertification, as soils gradually become barren and take on desert-like characteristics.
Serbia: An unfavorable energy mix

Serbia, too, is suffering badly from drought and the Danube's low water level. Its energy mix is similarly ill-suited to prolonged dry periods. Around 65% of its electricity is generated by coal-fired power plants, while about 25% comes from hydropower.

The two Iron Gate hydropower plants are currently generating only a fraction of their average electricity output. The coal-fired power plants Kostolac A and B east of Belgrade, which rely on Danube water for cooling, have also had to cut back production.

blocks.caption: In Hungary, dropping water levels of the Danube threaten the complete shutdown of the Paks nuclear power plant Image: David Balogh/Xinhua/IMAGO

blocks.text: Serbia relies heavily on the Danube as a transport route for coal and petrochemical products. However, due to the low water level, cargo vessels can currently only carry a fraction of their normal loads. Nonetheless, the energy crisis has so far not been so severe that large industrial plants have had to scale back production.
Slovakia, Austria less affected

In Slovakia, some 60% of electricity is generated by nuclear power plants, with another 20% by hydropower. Unlike Hungary and Romania, Slovakia's two nuclear power plants, Bohunice and Mochovce, are located on smaller rivers and use cooling towers rather than once-through cooling systems. Once-through cooling requires large quantities of river water that are drawn from the river and then channeled back to it at a higher temperature. In contrast, cooling towers recirculate water in a closed system, releasing heat mainly through evaporation. As a result, Slovakia's nuclear plants require much less river water and are therefore less affected by the current drought.

In comparison, Slovakia's Gabcikovo hydropower on the Danube has been significantly affected by the low water level. At present, only one of its eight turbines is in operation. Electricity generation in Gabcikovo, however, is only about 12% lower compared to the same time last year. So far, Slovakia has not experienced any major industrial production stoppages.

Austria, which generates around 60% of its electricity from hydropower, has also been less severely affected than Hungary. One reason is that part of Austria's hydropower capacity comes from storage and pumped-storage plants rather than run-of-river facilities.

Run-of-river plants depend directly on the volume of water flowing through rivers, whereas storage and pumped-storage plants can generate electricity using water stored in reservoirs when needed, making them less vulnerable during prolonged heatwaves and droughts.
In addition, Austria generates some 30% of its electricity from other renewable energy sources.
Bulgaria: Large battery storage capacity
Unlike in neighboring Romania, drought and heat are not yet causing an energy crisis in Bulgaria.

The country generates up to 40% of its energy through the Kozloduy nuclear power plant, which is also located on the Danube. Its cooling system, however, is better designed to operate under low-water conditions than those of Hungary's Paks plant and Cernavoda in Romania. As a result, it is currently operating at almost full capacity.
At the same time, Bulgaria depends only marginally on hydropower and has, in recent years, considerably expanded its solar and wind energy capacity.

The biggest difference to all the other countries lies in Bulgaria's large-scale battery storage facilities. The country currently has storage systems with a capacity of 3.4 gigawatts and a storage capacity of 8.6 gigawatt-hours. This storage capacity corresponds to 16% of the country's total installed power generation capacity — a figure unmatched by any other country in the world.

These storage facilities enable Bulgaria to balance supply shortages and peak demand, without relying on expensive imports. At the same time, the country is developing into a regional market leader in new energy concepts and as a hub for power grid stabilization and greater price stability in the electricity market.
This article was originally published in German.

articles.title: Mata Hari: Celebrated dancer turns WWI spy
articles.summary: Mata Hari enthralled Europe's elite with her beauty and performances. Accused of spying during World War I, she faced a French firing squad in 1917.

image.caption: Mata Hari's life story has been adapted for the screen several times and continues to fascinate people to this dayImage: Darchivio/opale.photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: Mata Hari was already a legend in her own lifetime. When she stepped into the Parisian limelight in 1905, she swept high society off its feet.

"She danced with veils and jewel-encrusted bustiers and almost nothing else," the Parisian press reported. "Never had anyone dared to appear unveiled before the gods with such trembling ecstasy. And what wonderful movements she made — both daring and demure at the same time."
Mata Hari had convinced audiences and the press that she was an exotic temple dancer — but the dark-haired performer was actually Dutch.

One of the hallmarks of the Belle Epoque era was a heightened fascination with cultures the Parisians deemed to be exotic. Driven by financial desperation, she exploited this demand by pretending to be Indian. To make her act more credible, she fabricated a backstory claiming to be the daughter of a highly esteemed Brahmin.

blocks.caption: Mata Hari's sensual dance was her own creationImage: Scherl/SZ Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: "My mother, first bayadere [dancer] of the Ranganathaswamy Temple, died at the age of fourteen, on the day I was born. After the temple priests cremated her body, they adopted me and named me Mata Hari, which means 'Eye of the Day [a Malay word, Hari means sun]."

She claimed to have learned the sacred temple dances from a young age. During her performances, one veil after another would fall away. Later, she said, "I never danced well. The only reason people came to see me was that I was the first to dare to present myself naked to the public."
From Dutch hatmaker's daughter to Mata Hari
High society couldn't get enough of Mata Hari, unaware that her real name was Margaretha Geertruida Zelle and that she came from the small Dutch town of Leeuwarden.

Born on August 7, 1876, Mata Hari was the daughter of a hatmaker who had become wealthy through stock market speculation. He often spoiled his daughter with lavish gifts. For her sixth birthday, he gave her a carriage drawn by goats.

At the age of 13, Mata Hari's life of luxury ended abruptly. Her father went bankrupt and abandoned the family. Two years later, when her mother passed away, she moved in with relatives. Eventually, she met her husband through a newspaper ad: "An officer from the Dutch East Indies [now Indonesia], currently on home leave, seeks the company of a nice young woman with potential for future marriage. Financial circumstances irrelevant."

blocks.caption: The MacLeods around 1900Image: akg-images/picture alliance

blocks.text: Mata Hari and John Rudolf MacLeod, a Dutch nobleman of Scottish descent who was 20 years her senior, quickly became a couple. In 1897, she accompanied her husband to the Dutch East Indies. But her dream of a happy life never materialized. Frequent arguments strained their relationship.
