Then, their two-year-old son was tragically poisoned to death. When the MacLeods returned to Europe in 1902, their marriage fell apart. MacLeod left Mata Hari, taking their daughter with him and refusing to pay any alimony, leaving her to fend for herself.

She began her career in Paris as a model for painters and tried her luck at the circus. But it was her creation of the exotic stage persona Mata Hari that ultimately made her famous. She performed at prestigious venues across Europe, including Vienna and Monte Carlo, staying in luxurious hotels. She danced at soirées hosted by the Rothschild banking family and entertained Crown Prince Wilhelm, the son of the German Emperor Wilhelm II. Her success gave her access to the highest social circles, where she formed relationships with diplomats and high-ranking military officers who paid generously for her company.

blocks.caption: Mata Hari around 1906: All of Paris wanted to see herImage: akg-images/picture alliance

blocks.text: World War I agent driven by financial hardship

Eventually, Mata Hari's popularity began to wane. Younger dancers began imitating her, and thrill-seeking audiences in Paris moved on to the next sensation. When World War I broke out in 1914, Mata Hari could no longer sustain her luxurious lifestyle.

She accepted an offer from the German consul in the Netherlands to help pay off her debts. She was promised even more money for gathering intelligence from influential figures on the opposing side of the war. Her initial fee was 20,000 francs, a substantial sum at the time. And just like that, she became Agent H 21.

Then, when the French intelligence service approached her and offered her even more money, Mata Hari became a double agent. But she miscalculated the situation. The French had enlisted her so they could catch her spying for the Germans. At the same time, due to increasing suspicion of her activities, the British intelligence service also monitored Mata Hari as she traveled through Europe. On February 13, 1917, she was arrested.

blocks.caption: Official photograph of the defendant Margaretha Geertruida MacLeod from 1917Image: akg-images/picture alliance

blocks.text: On October 15, at the age of 41, Mata Hari was executed for high treason in the moat of the Château de Vincennes, near Paris. Eyewitnesses reported that she faced the 12-man firing squad with her head held high and even blew them a kiss. She refused to wear a blindfold and instead addressed her final words to the commander who gave the order to fire: "Thank you, monsieur!"

Mata Hari's status as a so-called master spy remains questionable. According to documents from the British intelligence service — which remained classified for several decades — any information she may have shared likely did not impact the course of World War I.

It seems that Mata Hari was used as a convenient scapegoat at a time when public enthusiasm for the war had significantly waned. And the French military court needed someone to blame. She herself denied having spied until the very end. Regardless of whether or not she was a master spy, she was undoubtedly a master of self-promotion until her last breath.
This article was originally published in German.

articles.title: AfD threatens to cut funding for 'modern-thinking' culture
articles.summary: The far-right party could win an absolute majority in Saxony-Anhalt's state election in September. Their cultural program denigrates Bauhaus, Holocaust remembrance culture and diversity in theater.

image.caption: Germany's far right is waging a culture war against the iconic Bauhaus school of architectureImage: Stiftung Bauhaus Dessau/Thomas Meyer/OSTKREUZ

blocks.text: In upcoming state elections to be held on September 6, polls suggest the Alternative for Germany (AfD) could win an absolute majority in the eastern German state of Saxony-Anhalt.
Based on the far-right's cultural policy program, museums, theaters and cultural institutions in the region say that artistic freedom is one of the far-right party's targets.

The AfD has announced that artists and institutions would be required to sign a declaration pledging "not to hold in contempt Germany and its culture" if they want to obtain state funding. Many of these organizations and individuals heavily rely on these subsidies.
The AfD's interpretation of disrespect to German culture also ambiguously includes what the party calls "anti-German art."

blocks.caption: Hans-Thomas Tillschneider is the cultural policy spokesperson for the AfD in Saxony-AnhaltImage: Heiko Rebsch/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: "We declared in our government program that we no longer intend to spend public funds on promoting anti-German art," said Hans-Thomas Tillschneider, cultural policy spokesperson for the AfD parliamentary group in the state legislature, in a speech held in Saxony-Anhalt's parliament in late June.

Asked by other members of parliament to specify what that meant exactly, Tillschneider said, "Anti-German art is German art that doesn't want to be German." He mentioned as an example an opera production he had seen some years ago; the classical German composer's work was revisited through a "feminist deconstructivist" lens that didn't please him and corresponds to what he sees as "anti-German art."
"This anti-German aversion is still considered de rigueur in large parts of the theater world," he said. "We will no longer support this attitude — let me state that quite clearly."
Bauhaus, a direct target — like in the 1930s

Bauhaus, Germany's iconic architecture, art and design school founded in 1919, was forced to close under the Nazis, who considered their avant-garde ideas and their open-minded attitude to be "un-German." Bauhaus nevertheless went on to become one of design's most important movements of the 20th century; its influence is still felt worldwide. Today, the AfD once again sees Bauhaus as too modernist and globalist for the "patriotic cultural policy" the party envisions.
100 years of this iconic German design school
To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video
"The AfD's criticism of Bauhaus picks up on criticism from 100 years ago; their wording is similar," Barbara Steiner, director of the Bauhaus Foundation, told DW.

The AfD Saxony-Anhalt's program describes Bauhaus as "a controversial school of architecture" and criticizes the current state government for putting too much emphasis on this landmark attraction in their current image campaign, titled "moderndenken" (thinking modern).

The AfD aims to adopt instead a campaign called "deutschdenken" (thinking German), which would downplay the role of Bauhaus and instead "highlight the state's significant contributions to the development of the German nation — from Henry I and Otto I to Luther, Bismarck and Nietzsche."
Historically loaded language
The Alternative for Germany (AfD) strongly rejects comparisons to the Nazi party and Adolf Hitler, often dismissing them as trivializations of Nazi crimes.

Yet in its cultural policy program, the far-right party regularly adopts the language used in Hitler's propaganda, downplays Nazi-era atrocities, challenges Germany's culture of remembrance and uses historically loaded language.
The proposed "deutschdenken" slogan is one example of this: "'Deutsch denken' refers to a speech Adolf Hitler made in 1938" — the "Reichenberger Rede," noted Steiner.

blocks.caption: Barbara Steiner, director of the Bauhaus Foundation in DessauImage: Jörg Linke/DW

blocks.text: Culture needs state support to thrive

The Bauhaus is not the only cultural organization that feels threatened in Saxony-Anhalt. "As cultural practitioners, cultural initiators and artists, we can say that we are now genuinely afraid, because what's being triggered there is, in fact, the idea that art and culture must be 'German,'" Annegret Laabs, director of the Kunstmuseum Magdeburg told DW.

Laabs is a spokesperson for the initiative Kultur ist Vielfalt und Heimat, which roughly translates as "Culture is diversity and home." The initiative brings together a wide range of cultural institutions and artists from the region; they are warning in a joint statement that the AfD's plans could have far-reaching consequences for artistic freedom, historical memory, and public cultural life.

blocks.caption: Annegret Laabs, director of the Kunstmuseum MagdeburgImage: Jörg Linke/DW

blocks.text: "We all know that what we do — from theaters to museums to libraries — is paid for with taxpayer money. It wouldn't exist otherwise," said Laabs.

Restricting funding based on an arbitrary definition of what constitutes "German" art basically equates to culture's demise, explains Laabs: "If we look at the bigger picture, we see that culture and art have been free for centuries and have known no boundaries — not even national ones. Wherever there are national boundaries, there is no longer any art or culture worthy of that name."
'Resist the beginnings'

Along with threats to funding, the AfD's program also describes Germany's existing culture of Holocaust remembrance as the "perpetuation of a guilt complex" that has "blocked the possibilities for forming a stable national identity." It sees this as an "identity disorder" that needs to be "healed," by focusing on the "positive aspects of German history."

blocks.caption: Sabine Schramm, director of the Puppentheater MagdeburgImage: Jörg Linke/DW

blocks.text: Sabine Schramm, director of Magdeburg's puppet theater, finds "it regrettable that we humans are not willing to draw conclusions from a complex history — conclusions that matter both to us as individuals and to us as a society."
She notes that throughout her 30-year career in theater, she has dealt with Germany's culture of remembrance, grappling with the horrors of Nazism on stage.

"It has always been important to me — especially in productions for young people — to tell stories that address precisely this issue: National Socialism, how it begins, and how the various elements interlock," she points out.

"I can still see myself standing on stage talking about 'resisting the beginnings' — that phrase, 'resisting the beginnings,' has become such a cliché," she says, referring to an idea Germans are deeply familiar with; after the horrors of the Nazi era, the generations that followed were urged to speak out against threats to democracy — before it's too late.
"But where, exactly, are the beginnings?" Schramm asks. "Is this the beginning, or are we still before the beginning? Are we right in the middle of it? What must I do to resist the beginnings?"
New report backs ban of German far-right party
Edited by: Brenda Haas

articles.title: How Gianni Infantino rose to rule football
articles.summary: Gianni Infantino is staying on as FIFA president despite growing pressure to step down. So who is football's most powerful man, why did UEFA and others turn against him, and how did he reassert his…

image.caption: Gianni Infantino was a surprise choice as FIFA president but has certainly made his markImage: Markus Ulmer/Pressefoto Ulmer/picture alliance

blocks.text: Despite strong pressure for him to resign, particularly from UEFA, Gianni Infantino convinced FIFA's Board of Management to express their full support for him following a crisis meeting in Rabat on Wednesday. It was the latest development in a crisis that began with news last week of a FIFA plan to create a subsidiary, FIFA Forward Enterprise (FFE), to run the men's World Cup and its other events, with a stake of up to 20% to be offered to external investors.
Where did Gianni Infantino come from?

Giovanni Vincenzo Infantino was born on March 23, 1970, in the southwestern Swiss town of Brig to Italian parents. Many years later, as FIFA president, he would speak of the discrimination he said he experienced as he grew up for being of Italian heritage in Switzerland. Infantino studied law at the University of Fribourg, before becoming the general secretary of the International Centre for Sports Studies at the University of Neuchatel in 1997. The foundation had been established two years earlier by FIFA in partnership with the university and the city and canton of Neuchatel.
What did Infantino do before FIFA?

Infantino, who speaks six languages, first gained notoriety beyond Switzerland after joining UEFA, football's European governing body, in 2000. There, he would climb the corporate ladder to become the organization's general secretary in 2009. Serving under former UEFA President Michel Platini, Infantino's position kept him largely out of the public eye, but during this time his face became a familiar one to European football fans, as one of his roles was hosting the Champions League and Euros draws, broadcast live on TV.
How did Infantino become FIFA president?

The door to the FIFA presidency was knocked open by the 2015 FIFA corruption scandal in which several officials were indicted, seven of whom were arrested at a Zurich hotel. This came just ahead of a FIFA Congress to elect a new president. Although Sepp Blatter won reelection for a fifth term, he announced his resignation just days later. An extraordinary FIFA Congress was called for February 2016.

blocks.caption: Sepp Blatter, who left FIFA under a corruption cloud, has been a critic of InfantinoImage: Stefan Wermuth/REUTERS

blocks.text: Infantino looked a rank outsider when he threw his hat into the ring. Platini, his boss at UEFA, was the favorite, but he withdrew his candidacy a month before the election, after both he and Blatter had been banned over ethics violations involving a dubious payment.

In the days leading up to the vote, Sheik Salman bin Ibrahim al Khalifa of Bahrain emerged as the frontrunner among the seven candidates. However, Infantino, running on a pledge to clean up what was a scandal-ridden organization, won the presidency in the second round of voting. He'd also promised to increase FIFA payments to every member association.

"We will restore the image of FIFA and the respect of FIFA, and everyone in the world will applaud us and will applaud all of you for what we'll do in FIFA in the future," Infantino told the delegates in Zurich's Hallenstadion.
What has Infantino done in power?

Gianni Infantino has presided over a decade of unprecedented growth in revenue for FIFA, culminating in the 2026 World Cup — the first to feature 48 teams and 104 games — compared to 32 teams and 64 games in Qatar four years earlier. This was bound to generate higher revenue, but it was compounded by the dynamic pricing system FIFA introduced for the tournament. This led to sky-high prices for tickets — and FIFA went one better by getting into the secondary market and taking a 15% cut from both buyer and seller on every transaction.

While the final revenue numbers won't be announced until FIFA publishes its annual report for 2026, the figures are expected to smash the almost $5.8 billion (€5.03 billion) the organization earned in 2022, largely from the Qatar World Cup. Infantino has spoken of a figure around double that. Others believe it could be far higher.
What controversies has he been involved in?

He says he wasn't to blame for a major talking point at the World Cup — the suspension of USA forward Folarin Balogun's red-card ban following his sending off against Bosnia in the round of 32. This followed a call by US President Donald Trump to Infantino to request a "review." Infantino insisted that an independent FIFA body had made the decision.
FIFA under fire for World Cup red card retraction
To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The hydration breaks, which effectively split games into four quarters, also didn't go over well with many football fans. Others were angry at his refusal to step in on rows over visas for traveling fans, officials and a referee from Somalia and the treatment of the Iran team in the US during the tournament.
Prior to the World Cup 2026, Infantino had made the headlines for the wrong reasons on several occasions. Among his more notable controversies were:

items: Ahead of the 2017 FIFA Congress in Bahrain, Infantino removed the chairmen of the Ethics Committee, Hans-Joachim Eckert and Cornel Borbely, without giving reasons.

A year later he agreed in principle to a deal that would have seen a financial consortium from the Middle East and Asia acquire the rights to the Club World Cup and a global Nations League for a reported $25 billion. The deal never happened.

In July 2020, the Swiss public prosecutor's office accused Infantino of inciting abuse of office by meeting secretly with the head of the Office of the Attorney General of Switzerland, Michael Lauber. Three years later the case was dropped due to a lack of evidence.

In a ceremony at the World Cup draw in December 2025, Infantino presented US President Donald Trump with the newly created FIFA Peace Prize. This could be seen as the culmination of a widely criticized "bromance" between the FIFA boss and Trump.

blocks.text: Why has Infantino been under such intense pressure to resign?

His problems began with the World Cup sell-off plan. UEFA sharply condemned the news within minutes — before threatening to boycott all FIFA events, including the men's and women's World Cups. After Infantino backed off the plan, UEFA doubled down, saying it had lost confidence in the "current FIFA leadership" and the "task of rebuilding trust in FIFA" had just begun. Football's European governing body also threatened action through its US lawyers over what it termed a "shabby, backroom, opaque deal."
How did he reassert himself?

The FIFA boss summoned senior staff members to an emergency meeting in Rabat on Wednesday. A statement issued after that meeting conceded that "mistakes made were acknowledged" in connection with the private investment plan and that the "process should have been handled differently."

It also said those present had "reaffirmed their full support" for the president and stressed that FIFA would "no longer tolerate any attacks on its integrity, good governance and due process and will take all necessary measures to protect and safeguard its name and reputation."
Edited by: Matt Pearson

articles.title: Why is Russia selling its gold?
articles.summary: Russia has become one of the world's biggest sellers of gold over the past 12 months. It's an attempt to raise cash in the face of budget issues, but not necessarily a sign of a looming financial…

image.caption: Russia has become one of the biggest sellers of gold as it attempts to prop up its war economyImage: Angelika Warmuth/REUTERS

blocks.text: Russia has sold significant volumes of its gold reserves so far in 2026 as the Kremlin seeks to raise cash to offset a big budget deficit.

The Russian Central Bank announced recently that its gold reserves stood at 73.4 million troy ounces, or 2,282 metric tons, as of the start of July. That represents a decline of around 43.5 metric tonnes since the start of 2026.
It means Russia's gold reserves are now at their lowest level since before the full-scale invasion of Ukraine began in February 2022.

Gold prices hit record levels earlier this year, with prices averaging around $4,800 (€4,210) per ounce in the first four months before falling back to a current level of around $4,000 per ounce. Moscow's sell-off is likely to have raised more than $5 billion.

"The fact that they're selling gold means that they're running out of other more liquid assets," Elina Ribakova, an economist with the Peterson Institute for International Economics, told DW. "So there is pressure on the deficit and also pressure on the sources to finance this deficit."
Budget problems
Russia's budget has been under serious strain in recent years due to its massively increased defense spending, which funds the war in Ukraine.

Earlier this year, the Financial Times reported that the country's finance ministry had warned the cabinet in a letter that overspending on the war would be at least $28 billion in 2026, with further overspends expected in 2027 and 2028. Defense spending has more than quadrupled since 2021. It totalled around 16 trillion rubles in 2025 ($204 billion; €178 billion).
Chris Weafer, a Moscow-based financial analyst with the consulting firm Macro-Advisory, says that while the Russian gold sell-off is significant, it is not a case of panic selling.

"It's an extraordinary situation, but it's a relatively normal trend," he told DW. "It doesn't represent any element of Russia going broke, running out of money, not having anything else and literally selling the household silver."
He says that the gold Russia has offloaded has mostly been sold by the country's finance ministry, via its National Welfare Fund (NWF), rather than the Russian Central Bank.

"Since early 2022, gold was one of the assets that the National Welfare Fund could buy, because US treasuries and bunds weren't available to them (as a result of sanctions following the invasion of Ukraine)."

Weafer pointed out that the asset had become a key liquid component of the fund, which, he said, was precisely what a national welfare fund is intended for: to be sold when funds are needed, particularly during difficult times. "To that extent, one can argue it is serving the intended purpose."

The fund's gold sale is intended to replenish its so-called liquid assets. Weafer estimates that the fund is worth approximately $150 billion, with around $50 billion of that being described as "liquid."

"The Kremlin doesn't want that buffer to go down because that would lead to maybe more speculation about financial crisis or economic difficulties, and it would undermine the Kremlin's geopolitical position," said Weafer.
"It likes to portray the country as being very stable and very strong, and that $50 billion of cash is an important part of that."

He says another important factor to consider is that as one of the world's biggest producers of gold, Russia can replenish stocks it has sold relatively quickly by buying from its domestic producers. Russia holds the fifth-largest reserves in the world, around the same level as China, France and Italy, and significantly behind the top two, Germany and the US.
Ribakova agrees that this offers Russia a significant buffer.

"Russia has an advantage," she said. "It does produce gold itself. So when it was worried about sanctions, it allocated part of the money into the gold purchases, which they were buying from the domestic producers."
Funding the war for the foreseeable future
The fact that Russia has become one of the biggest sellers of gold has raised further questions about its budget deficit and what that says about wider economic stability.

blocks.caption: Russia's defence budget has increased dramatically Image: Vyacheslav Prokofyev/Sputnik/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: Russia's federal budget spending and deficit could exceed official plans by more than 1 trillion roubles ($12.85 billion) in 2026, according to ​recent government data. The budget deficit is currently projected to be 1.6% of GDP for 2026, which is approximately $40 billion, and could yet grow.
However, improved revenues from oil and gas, boosted by higher oil prices due to the war in Iran, has helped Moscow to offset the budget difficulties so far in 2026.

Ribakova says everything comes back to the prices and revenues Russia gets from its oil and gas, calling it the "real limit" on Moscow's capacity to finance the four-and-a-half-year-long war in Ukraine.

"Everything hinges on that," she noted. "When the oil price is high, Russia gets revenues. It's easier to borrow, its domestic financial system is healthier. If the oil price drops, say, to sixty or forty, then you immediately have a crisis."

Both she and Weafer caution that despite the obvious economic difficulties the Russian economy has at present, it can continue to fund the war for the foreseeable future by cutting back on non-defense spending.

"Putin can continue going for years in the current environment," said Ribakova. "Maybe not making any progress on the front line, which we haven't seen any progress for the last couple of years, but still being able to throw resources at the war with Ukraine."
Could Russia save the global economy?
To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

"Even if the deficit continues as is, Russia can still find the money and really won't be in any sort of a financial crisis or a weak geopolitical position over the next 12 to 24 months," said Weafer.
Yet he points to obvious longer-term damage being done to the economy and the trouble that may bring further down the tracks.
"It is creating this huge distortion in the economy and creating this longer-term negative picture that's now creating divisions in government," he said.

He added that the situation had a divide between those responsible for economic growth and the Kremlin. Their message, he said, is that the current approach could not be sustained, "if you want the economy to go back to a more normal trajectory after peace. That's the bottom line."
Edited by: Rob Mudge

articles.title: The hidden problem with small modular nuclear reactors
articles.summary: Mini nuclear reactors are seen as a flexible energy source. Their promise: abundant energy, cheap, clean and climate-friendly with lower water use. But do the numbers add up? We look at what's behind…

image.caption: The core module of the world's first commercial small modular reactor was installed in China in 2023Image: Luo Yunfei/VCG/IMAGO

blocks.text: Many politicians and tech companies are now pushing to build new nuclear power plants to meet the world's rapidly growing energy demands. Small reactors — known as Small Modular Reactors, or SMRs — are gaining momentum.

They could be built in less time and come online faster than conventional nuclear power plants. Originally developed to power submarines and aircraft carriers, SMRs largely work the same way as larger reactors.

They contain a nuclear reactor fueled by uranium, which releases enormous amounts of heat through nuclear fission. That heat turns water into steam, and the steam pressure drives turbines that generate electricity.
Companies and startups are working on a wide variety of SMR designs and concepts, but the underlying principle is similar across all of them.

One advantage over conventional nuclear stations is that mini reactors require a maximum of two hectares (around five acres) of land — roughly the size of two soccer fields. By comparison, conventional plants require up to 280 soccer fields, according to the industry.

blocks.caption: The Linglong One small modular pressurized water reactor after completing its factory testImage: Zhang Boqun/Xinhua/picture alliance

blocks.text: Why use a modular design for mini nuclear plants?

What makes SMRs particularly attractive is their modular construction. Individual components can be mass-produced as prefabricated modules and pre-assembled off-site — much like a prefab house that simply needs to be put together once it arrives at its location.
Manufacturers promise an extremely short construction time of between one and a half to six years. Large reactors in the US can take anywhere from seven to 10 years to build.

Proponents also argue that modular units could deliver low-emission power to remote regions, where grid infrastructure is often not developed enough to handle the enormous energy output of a large conventional plant.
Those advantages are also shared by renewable energy sources like solar panels and wind turbines — without the risks that come with nuclear power.
The hidden cost of nuclear power
To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video
Why less radiation can mean greater risk

The output of mini nuclear reactors is significantly lower than that of conventional nuclear power plants. Depending on the design, SMRs can deliver between 10 and around 200 megawatts of power, while a conventional plant generates between 1,000 and 1,600 MW.
To produce the same amount of energy as the roughly 400 high-capacity reactors currently operating worldwide, tens of thousands of small reactors would need to be built.

SMRs could offer some safety advantages: they contain less radioactive material than large reactors and would be distributed across multiple sites. This means that an accident or military strike resulting in a meltdown would not be as catastrophic as a worst-case scenario at a large reactor. Nevertheless, the consequences of an SMR accident could still be severe.

Germany's Federal Office for Radiation Protection points out that despite lower radiation levels per reactor, the overall risk posed by mini reactors could be many times higher. Replacing the output of existing nuclear plants with large numbers of smaller ones would require an enormous number of reactors worldwide — and that increases the likelihood that at least one of them will eventually suffer a serious incident.

Nuclear accidents and radiation leaks are extremely rare — but the consequences can be catastrophic. The last major nuclear accident occurred in 2011 at the Fukushima power plant in Japan, following a tsunami. Parts of the region have been contaminated for generations to come, and nearly 170,000 people were forced to flee their homes.

blocks.caption: The core module of the Linglong One SMR being assembled at its construction site in Hainan Province, ChinaImage: China National Nuclear Corporation/Handout via Xinhua/picture alliance

blocks.text: Extreme efficiency and the dream of radioactive recycling

Part of the hype around some new mini reactors rests on the hope of extracting significantly more energy from the same amount of uranium. Some SMR models — known as "fast reactors" — could theoretically yield 60 to 70 times more energy from uranium than conventional technology, according to the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA).

But the technology is still in the early stages of development and has so far played only a limited role in IAEA projections. In practice, it has barely been proven in SMRs at all. Only two SMR facilities are currently in operation worldwide — one in China and one in Russia.
Work is also underway on recycling SMR fuel rods, but that process remains largely untested. Most SMR projects continue to rely on the same conventional technology used in traditional reactors.

And the problem of radioactive waste remains unsolved — for both conventional and fast reactors. The risks this poses are already visible: at the Asse facility in Lower Saxony, Germany, a temporary storage site built in the 1970s, hundreds of barrels of intermediate-level radioactive waste are now rusting and beginning to leak. Germany has yet to establish a permanent disposal site.

In fact, no permanent repository for spent fuel or highly radioactive reactor waste is currently in operation anywhere in the world. After 20 years of construction, the Onkalo facility in Finland is set to become the first when it opens in 2026.
Another problem for nuclear power is growing water scarcity. Recent heat and drought have already forced European nations to curb nuclear output due to for cooling due to low river levels.

Because SMRs are mainly just smaller, simplified versions conventional reactors, they still use water to run and for cooling. While individual units use less water than traditional plants, clustering units could increase overall use, warn experts. Researchers are investigating the use of alternative coolants like molten salts and helium gas for newer designs.

blocks.caption: Underground tunnels of the Onkalo spent nuclear fuel repository in Finland, set to open in 2026Image: Roni Rekomaa/Lehtikuva/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: When would SMRs make a climate impact — and at what cost?
Enthusiasm for small reactors runs high in the nuclear community. But what may look promising at first glance is, in many respects, difficult or impossible to back up with solid evidence.

Calculating the costs of a technology still in development is no easy task. Nevertheless, the German Institute for Economic Research estimates that electricity from new mini nuclear plants — even accounting for economies of scale, including construction and manufacturing — will cost at least twice as much per megawatt-hour as the already very affordable electricity generated by solar or wind power. In a worst-case scenario, the cost could be nearly eight times higher.

Adding up all the announcements, plans and strategies of major nations, a few hundred SMRs could come online in China, the US, Europe and India by 2050. But according to Germany's Federal Office for Nuclear Safety and Radiation Protection, citing figures from the nuclear industry, production would only become economically viable at a threshold of 3,000 reactors.

The international community has committed to limiting global warmingto well below 2 degrees Celsius (3.6 degrees Fahrenheit) by the end of the century. Meeting that target requires large parts of the global economy to become climate-neutral by 2050. The EU aims to reach zero emissions by then; Germany is even targeting net negative CO2 emissions by 2050.
That means climate-friendly nuclear technology would arrive too late to meaningfully limit global warming — and its advantages would be significantly diminished as a result.
What would remain: the radiation risk, and the question of what to do with the radioactive waste.
The toll of nuclear power on generations to come
This article was originally published in German.

articles.title: My sleep deprivation is your natural short sleep
articles.summary: Every so often we hear of high-ranking politicians or CEOs claiming to get by on very little sleep — some as little as three hours a night. If they're not natural short sleepers, chances are they're…

image.caption: Our bodies have a way of telling us when it's time for sleep. We just have to learn to listen and restImage: Adnan Abidi/REUTERS

blocks.text: I've been having trouble sleeping — for as long as forever. Sometimes it's just a feeling. Other times, it's a fact (I know because my watch tells me). But then my watch may be part of the problem. It's constantly reminding me to get to bed on time and accosting me with poor sleep scores. It drives my anxiety through the roof, my heart races and I feel like I can't sleep. But then I still feel fine the next day. Weird.
"When you're sleep deprived, you have poor judgment," said Catia Reis, a sleep researcher at the University of Lisbon, when we spoke.
That might explain my predicament. Because even when I feel fine during the week, I oversleep at the weekend, which is a sure sign of sleep debt, she said.
Reis has studied a variety of sleep-related conditions, including the effects of jet lag and sleep deprivation among athletes.

One investigation compared levels of sleepiness among patients with sleep apnea — a condition where you stop breathing intermittently through the night — and shift workers, who work against their natural, circadian rhythm. That's our inner clock that tells us when we're wakeful or sleepy.

She compared the results from both subjective assessments made by participants and objective, clinical tests, and found a "mismatch" in people's ability to assess their own levels of sleepiness the more they were exposed to that very thing: sleepiness.
Basically, the brain stops working. And that should be concerning, given that the brain plays a central role in sleep.
Sleep or die
When we sleep, the body performs several restorative functions: It removes toxins we have ingested through food or the atmosphere, generates new energy, and is essential for our learning and memory.

"Sleep involves many parts of the brain," said Ying-Hui Fu, a sleep researcher at the University of California San Franscisco. "Almost every disease of the brain, including neurological and psychiatric, [can be linked to] sleep problems."
On average, people need about 7.5-8.5 hours' sleep per night.

But every so often we hear about people in demanding jobs, usually politicians, boasting — or claiming credibility — by saying they rarely sleep more than a few hours; like they're ALWAYS WORKING FOR THE PEOPLE.
Most recently, it was Japan's Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi who reminded us she's slept between zero and three hours per night while in office.

As a former heavy metal drummer, you might expect a certain level of stamina from the Japanese PM. But while voluntary, habitual (or trained) sleep deprivation — if that's what it is in Takaichi's case — may be an impressive sleep-work-no-life-balance ethic, it's not a good, long-term strategy.
In the best-case scenario, a long-term "sleep debt" can cause your body to accumulate toxins, risking heart or brain disease. In the worst-case scenario, it can be fatal.
Why sleep is so important for your immune system
To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

"There are only two things more important than sleep for our total health," Fu told DW. "One is air. If we don't have air, we die in a few minutes. The other is water. If we don't have water, we die in a few days. If you don't eat, you can live a couple of months. But if you don't sleep, you can probably only live for a couple of weeks."
And that goes for all animals — "if we don't sleep, we die," she said.
The exception: natural short sleepers

Natural short sleepers are the exception to the rule. They can sleep fewer than six hours per night and not only feel fine, but also actually are fine — healthy, happy and energetic. They appear to have genetic variations that allow them to thrive. Fu cited an 80-year-old natural short sleeper who competed in triathlons.

Fu and her lab found the first of these variations in the gene DEC2 and published their findings in 2009. Ten years later, they published a paper suggesting that the gene ADRB1 was also linked to Natural Short Sleeper Syndrome. Findings into the genes NPSR1, GRM1, SIK3 followed, and there are others in the pipeline.

We're calling them gene "variations" rather than "mutations" because mutations are often associated with negative health effects. But it appears that Natural Short Sleep does not risk the health issues that habitual short sleepers or sleep deprived people face.
The genes show a range of functions that sleep effects:

items: DEC2: helps regulate sleep/wake duration
ADRB1: mediates cardiac and neuronal signaling
NPSR1: helps modulate arousal and anxiety
GRM1: involved in brain function; may be linked to depression
SIK3: plays a role in cell cycle-, metabolic and inflammatory- regulation

blocks.text: Each has taken years of painstaking basic — foundational — research to find and test.
"Every one of us has between 500 to 1,000 unique mutations in our genome. To know which one is causal is very difficult," said Fu.
Sleep smarter: How your body clock shapes your health
The impact of better sleep on humanity
The number of known natural short sleepers is small, but Fu says the condition is likely to be more common than research currently suggests.

Most of Fu's findings are limited families that share a gene variation. That's been for a practical, methodological reason: If three members of a family have the same variation and they all appear to be healthy on only four to six hours' sleep, then that gene variation may well be responsible, especially if it's in a gene that is known to be important for healthy sleep function. But it's early days.
"We just know that they perform better and they're healthier. And the most logical explanation for me is that their sleep function is better," said Fu.
Reis is also cautious about the state of research in this area, saying there are still too few studies into natural short sleepers.

"When we objectively test [habitual short sleepers] and we expand their sleep, we know they improve," said Reis. "But the problem is we don't have enough longitudinal studies with [natural short sleepers]."
Fu would agree. But she said it was a struggle to get the research financed.

"My goal is to help everybody get good sleep. Because if we can help everybody get good sleep, all diseases will drop," said Fu. "The entire spectrum of disease incidence would drop. Can you imagine the impact on humanity?"
Edited by: Carla Bleiker

articles.title: AI ecosystem's 'circular' investment: risk or advantage?
articles.summary: Amid talk of an AI sector bubble, one aspect is under scrutiny. Many big AI players are invested in smaller ones, who then buy the bigger firm's products. This brings risks and advantages.

image.caption: The "circular financing" investment system in the AI world creates risk of a domino effect should the AI bubble burstImage: Jaque Silva/NurPhoto/picture alliance

blocks.text: Reports that Nvidia is in talks to give financial guarantees of almost $250 billion (€217 billion) to OpenAI for a massive data center project show two sides of the artificial intelligence boom.

On one level, it shows the monumental scale of AI's financial muscle and potential. On another, it shows the risks of a so-called "circular" financing system at the core of the AI ecosystem. If one domino falls, would others fall with it?

"The interconnected nature of the AI ecosystem is real," Gary Tan, portfolio manager at Allspring Global Investments, told DW. "But near term risks are mitigated by the strong balance sheets, cash flows and credit quality of the major providers funding the buildout."

Jan Frederik Slijkerman, a tech sector strategist at ING, agrees that the exceptionally strong financial positions of big tech companies such as Nvidia, Microsoft, Amazon and Alphabet (Google parent company) mitigate against the risks.
He says the degree of collaboration regarding AI is "fascinating" but does not see a "a systemic industry-wide risk arising from the observed interdependencies".
The circular model

Circular financing typically works as follows: A company pays another for a product or deal, or invests in that company or provides a loan or lease. Then that company purchases the first company's products or services.
It can be seen across the spectrum of AI deals.

blocks.caption: The emergence of OpenAI's ChatGPT kickstarted the AI boomImage: Matteo Della Torre/NurPhoto/picture alliance

blocks.text: For many, the moment the AI revolution began was when ChatGPT, developed by OpenAI, was launched in November 2022. The chatbot's capabilities brought AI into the mainstream. Its success quickly attracted a massive $10 billion investment from software giant Microsoft, enabling it to develop more powerful models.
In return, OpenAI became a key customer for Microsoft's cloud services, which it is investing ever more heavily into as the AI boom gathers momentum.

It set the template for future deals. Amazon and Alphabet began investing billions into OpenAI's rival Anthropic, which has built the hugely successful Claude chatbot. In return, Anthropic uses Amazon's web services and Google's cloud services as well as buying its chips.
Nvidia: King of the Jungle
Yet that is all relatively small potatoes compared with what AI computing giant Nvidia has brought to the table.
"Nvidia sits at the center of the AI ecosystem, acting not only as a technology supplier but also as a strategic investor helping accelerate adoption of its platform," says Tan.

Slijkerman says Nvidia plays a vital role, as it contributes to the development of a variety of new businesses, from healthcare to autonomous driving. "Its investments help support the growth of the broader AI ecosystem while also facilitating the deployment of AI infrastructure," he says.
The story that Nvidia is in talks to provide $250 billion to OpenAI, first reported by The Wall Street Journal, would be just the latest megadeal the $4.6 trillion company has bankrolled.

blocks.caption: Nvidia's chips are at the center of the AI ecosystemImage: Ina Fassbender/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: Jensen Huang's company is at the center of the artificial intelligence boom thanks to its industry-leading chips. Since 2024, it has invested heavily in multiple AI start-ups, including OpenAI, Mistral and Elon Musk's SpaceX. In turn, these companies are all committed users of Nvidia's chips.

It has also begun to invest heavily in so-called neocloud providers, such as CoreWeave and Nebius. These start-ups rent out cloud space for AI computing. As well as investing, Nvidia itself is also purchasing cloud space from the firms.
Nvidia is stepping up its spending and dealmaking in 2026 too. It struck a partnership with South Korean conglomerate SK Group recently, worth potentially $500 billion in business.

Throughout 2026, such circular dealmaking has become even more pronounced across the sector. OpenAI has struck close to $1 trillion worth of deals with the likes of Microsoft and Advanced Micro Devices (AMD) agreeing to become one of AMD's biggest shareholders.
Microsoft and Nvidia have also invested heavily in Anthropic, with Anthropic in turn agreeing to step up its purchases of cloud capacity and chips from both.
Advantages and risks

The scale of the cross-pollination can bring advantages. "Interconnected ecosystems can accelerate innovation by aligning incentives across infrastructure providers, model developers, application companies and end users, helping new technologies scale faster," says Gary Tan.

Slijkerman says he does not see the circular trend as a form of "financial engineering". "These relationships make strategic sense because they help participants expand their market reach and accelerate adoption," he says. "They can also create mutual financial benefits."

Yet there are risks. Fears of an AI 'bubble' continue to stalk global markets. Tech and semiconductor stocks fell sharply last week amid doubts over profitability in the sector, relative to the vast sums being invested in data centers and other AI-related spending.
AI bubble incoming?
To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

If AI revenues do not grow sufficiently, companies that have received funding from bigger players might face financial challenges. In turn, they may stop buying the bigger company's products and their valuations will fall.

Some analysts have drawn comparisons to the dot-com bubble and subsequent crash, which happened after valuations surged in the early days of the internet. Circular financing was a factor in that crisis, too, but many observers reckon the AI boom is ultimately built on more solid foundations.

"While some individual companies or business models may ultimately disappoint, the broader investment cycle appears to be supported by genuine demand and real economic value creation," says Slijkerman.

Tan agrees and says a bigger risk in future problems is interest rates. He thinks if interest rates rise, it could have a significant impact on many AI companies as they will be penalized by the time they become profitable.
"AI cash flows are long dated, so the direction of the yield curve may ultimately matter more than the availability of capital," he says.
Edited by: Kristie Pladson

articles.title: South Sudan: How climate change can result in toxic water
articles.summary: Years of flooding have resulted in disastrous water pollution in South Sudan's main oil region. As communities, scientists and health workers scramble for solutions, the long-term impacts of the…

image.caption: Despite much of the region around Bentiu remaining submerged for years, there is hardly any access to clean water for the town's growing population of IDPsImage: Marco Simoncelli

blocks.text: The village of Bentiu has seen it all: Located in the north of South Sudan near the border with Sudan, the capital of Unity State used to have a population of merely several thousand people.

But war, violence and other crisis have resulted in an additional 140,000 displaced persons seeking shelter there since 2013, resulting in the establishment of a massive camp for internally displaced persons (IDPs).

Several UN bodies including the International Organization for Migration (IOM), the UN Refugee Agency (UNHCR) and the United Nations Children's Fund (UNICEF) are active on the ground, running what is known as the Protection of Civilians (POC) camp, which by now feels more like a permanent structure.

blocks.caption: In South Sudan, usable water is increasingly becoming a rare commodityImage: UIG/IMAGO

blocks.text: At a makeshift pier, children are seen playing, countless canoes bring in fish to feed scores of people at the camp, where food insecurity remains a chief concern.
Immediately, each day's yield is separated into two categories: One stock with fresh, healthy fish, and another for those believed to be contaminated.

Simon Gatkuoth, a camp resident in his early forties, lifts a fish from a wheelbarrow, explaining that fish that are caught near the oil fields are contaminated: "When we cook them, the soup sometimes smells like penicillin," he says.
"But there is no option. We have to eat. We cannot stop eating because there is no alternative."

blocks.caption: Fish in the polluted waters are often discarded if they show signs of contaminationImage: Marco Simoncelli

blocks.text: Flood waters that just won't recede
Viewed from the sky, the POC Camp resembles an artificial island in the midst of a region that has been transformed into what appears to be a gigantic lake.

Here, the largely nomadic communities of South Sudan's Unity State have long adapted their lives to the seasonal floods that shape life in what is one of the world's largest wetlands known as the Sudd.
But in 2021, and unprecedented deluge of floods linked to climate change submerged farmland across the region, destroying livelihoods and killing thousands of cattle.

Just one year earlier, authorities in neighboring Uganda had issued a warning that rising levels in Lake Victoria, situated roughly 1,000 kilometers (650 miles) to the south, would require the release of large volumes of water into the White Nile river, which flows past Bentiu.

But South Sudan, one of the poorest countries, lacked the dams, flood-control systems and water-management infrastructure needed to cope with the flooding, leaving many communities highly vulnerable to flooding.
To this day, the waters from that flood are yet to recede.
Oil and water do not mix
Maintained by the IOM, a simple levee is all that separates the POC Camp from the flooded plain; without constant maintenance, it would give way to the water.
The people here appear weary: First displaced by war and later hit by floods, most now depend on humanitarian aid, trapped somewhere between continuously rising water levels and unresolved conflict.

Yet in recent years, another disaster has slowly emerged, linking the devastating 2021 flooding to a major environmental hazard: Unity State, where the Bentiu POC Camp is located, is the South Sudan's biggest oil producing region.

Oil makes up more than 90% of state revenue, and accounts for nearly all of the country's exports. It is a vital sector for the country's battling economy, which has been severely limited in recent years by the war in Sudan to its north, with pipelines limited to a trickle, and many reserves sitting untapped or unused.

A geospatial analysis found that during the devastating 2021 floods, 159 out of over 400 oil wells in the region were submerged under water, amounting to around 41% of oil extraction infrastructure in the area.

blocks.caption: Water levels around Bentiu do not seem to want to subside, even years after the devastating floodsImage: Marco Simoncelli

blocks.text: In a joint effort with PlaceMarks Africa — an organization which makes of satellite imagery to help "design solutions for contemporary challenges" on the continent, DW has found that more than 50 of these wells continue to be submerged to this day — a growing cause for concern.

The rivers and lakes that hundreds of thousands depend on for drinking water, cooking and fishing appear to have been contaminated by the oil fields, with could carry potentially long-term consequences for both local ecosystems and human health.

"Many animals are dying because of this pollution, and people are also suffering from symptoms they attribute to it. All of this is visible, but we do not yet have sufficient evidence or epidemiological studies to state it with certainty," explains researcher Marko Gatkuoth, who is attached to the Rift Valley Institute — an independent research organization operating primarily in Central and Eastern Africa.
"The flood that began more than four years ago has become a vector of pollution. It has made the contaminants mobile."
'Deliberate negligence'
Bul Duot Kuer, a South Sudanese researcher at Kenyatta University in Kenya, has conducted extensive research on the environmental impact of oil production in Unity State.

In a recent study, he identified lead concentrations of up to 18 micrograms per liter in the rivers around Bentiu and nearby Rotriak — nearly double the guideline value set by the World Health Organization (WHO). He also found hydrocarbon concentrations in the water at more than five times above the recommended limits.

blocks.caption: Bul Duot Kuer blames the government for remaining inactive duing the growing water crisisImage: Marco Simoncelli

blocks.text: "Water is the most polluted element," says Kuer. "There is no control. The environmental laws are there on paper, but they are simply not being enforced. This is negligence. The government and the oil companies do not care about people's health."

Waters around the settlement of Rotriak are particularly affect by this oil contamination: Satellite imagery analysed by PlaceMarks exposed pipelines, wells and abandoned facilities scattered across the settlement.

This is an area were children play among rusty pipes and women wash laundry at a former retention pond for oil production wastewater — albeit typically not by choice: Local resident Anna Nyashing Bul told DW that she and her family had to evacuate to Rotriak "because it was the only place that remained dry" after the 2021 flooding.
The untreated water they rely on often has "black film on the surface," she explains, which has repeatedly made her family fall sick.
"But we had nothing else to drink."
Birth defects and miscarriages
Meanwhile at Bentiu State Hospital, staff have noticed an increase of children born with deformities and other birth defects.

Midwives interviewed by DW also describe an apparent increase in miscarriages, complicated deliveries and congenital anomalies in recent years — especially with mothers who come from areas located in and around the oil fields.
19-year-old Nyapuka Nios from Rotriak just gave birth days ago; her newborn presents visible malformations to the hands and upper lip.
"I don't know what will happen to him," she whispers. "It is God's will. God gave him to me this way."
In another room, Nyekal Nuok watches over her baby girl, who was born with spina bifida five days earlier. She also lived in Rotriak during most of her pregnancy.
Floodwaters, oil and health fears in South Sudan
To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video
Research has shown that women living near oil wells are more likely to give birth to children with congenital anomalies.

Dorgan Patai, Director of Health Services in Rubkona County agrees that "since the floods, we are seeing more miscarriages and more children born with malformations," adding that "in the long term, this could even lead to infertility."
However, there has been no comprehensive investigation to establish whether these cases are indeed linked to environmental contamination.

The WHO says that a review of routine health surveillance data failed to present any statistically relevant increase in miscarriages, complications or other anomalies in Unity State, stressing that anecdotal reports should be interpreted cautiously.

blocks.caption: Health workers in the region worry about a rise in birth defects, which is believed to be linked to oil pollution in the waterImage: Antonio Lacerda/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Dead in the water

There are few people who have done more to hold South Sudanese authorities accountable for the environmental consequences of oil production than Ayen Mijok Kiir, First Deputy Speaker of the Council of States, which is South Sudan's upper house of parliament.

blocks.caption: Ayen Mijok Kiir keeps fighting for justice for the thousands of people who have no access to clean waterImage: Marco Simoncelli

blocks.text: She believes that years of conflict and insecurity have pushed issues like environmental protection and public health down the list of national priorities.

"We are not a stable country," Kiir highlights. "There are challenges in allocating resources to different sectors. We are under pressure to prioritise security. But yes, even with these challenges, we should have done more."

With her tireless campaigning, she succeeded in encouraging President Salva Kiir to further investigate the potential link between deformities at birth and oil-related pollution in 2024 despite many other ongoing crises in the region.
But despite numerous ministerial meetings being held, nothing seems to change.
"What difference will it make if I talk about this yet again?" she s ays quietly. "I have spoken about it so much, given so many interviews, and nothing has happened."
Ultimately, South Sudan still lacks effective environmental monitoring and public health standard in its oil producing areas — 15 years after gaining independence.

With conflict and suffering remaining rife throughout the region, addressing the affects of global warming might remain an elusive goal, as South Sudan struggles on many fronts to keep its head above water.
South Sudan: Lack of access to safe drinking water
Edited by: Sertan Sanderson
This project was supported by the Pulitzer Center on Crisis Reporting

articles.title: Tennis star Sabalenka supports sport's new sex test policy
articles.summary: The world number one women's tennis player supports the WTA's new sex testing rules. Others are more critical of the policy.

image.caption: Aryna Sabalenka is supportive of tennis' new sex testing rulesImage: Mark Avellino/Anadolu/picture alliance

blocks.text: "I think it's really important to keep the fairness in our tour," said Sabalenka on Monday. "Obviously, biologically, men are way stronger than women, so I feel like it would not be really fair for a woman to compete against a biological man.

"I believe it took them a little while to make this decision and I support it," the Belarussian continued. "If they want to test us all, I'm happy to do that; it's pretty fair, and let's keep it that way."
Fact check: Trans athlete ban — fair or not?
To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video
WTA introduces genetic testing

In July 2026, the WTA (Women's Tennis Association) introduced a one-time, mandatory genetic test for all players. As part of the protocol, players will be tested for the SRY gene, a segment of DNA typically found on the Y chromosome. The test can be conducted by a cheek swab or a blood test.
The new policy also includes a document players must sign highlighting disciplinary action is possible if testing is refused.

The previous WTA policy allowed transgender women to compete if their testosterone levels had been lowered to below 2.5 nmol/L continuously for the previous two years. There are no known transgender women currently playing on the WTA Tour.
Sabalenka is currently the best female tennis player in the world, and has been ranked number 1 for 92 consecutive weeks, so her endorsement carries a lot of weight.

On top of that, she competed in the modern edition of Battle of the Sexes in Dubai in 2025 — a match she lost to Nick Kyrgios, a male Australian player. While billed as a way to generate interest in tennis, some were critical of the match-up.

blocks.caption: Imane Khelif was the subject of great debate after her gold medal in ParisImage: Jiang Wenyao/Xinhua/picture alliance

blocks.text: World Boxing introduced it in May 2025 after a lengthy and controversial debate around gold medal winner Imane Khelif at the 2024 Paris Olympics.
World Athletics did similarly in September 2025. Then, in the decision likely to have the most far-reaching impacts, the International Olympic Committee updated their guidelines in early 2026.
How has this new policy been received?
Trans athletes have long been politicized.

Riley Gaines, a former swimmer at the US collegiate level, has become a conservative political activist who is known for campaigning against the participation of trans women in women's sports. Recently, Gaines was seen supporting WNBA star Sophie Cunningham, who had said in an ESPN feature that "biological men" should not compete in female sports in order to protect young girls.

Maria Jose Martinez-Patino, whose personal experience with gender verification dramatically impacted sporting policy on the matter in the 1980s, believes new genetic testing for women at elite level is "a setback of several decades."

"It takes me back to the 1950s and 1960s, when women practically had to go through a series of controls, had to undress in front of a panel of doctors," Martinez-Patino told DW in an interview in 2025. "I get the impression that we haven't advanced from a scientific point of view. We've made practically no progress if it's now categorically said that women with X and Y chromosomes are not women."

World Athletics argues that the SRY gene — present in people with a Y chromosome, usually men — "is a reliable indicator for determining biological sex." Martinez-Patino believes, though, that determining someone's sex is not as simple as that.

"It's not black or white. There are more than 60 genetic mutations which I think are not all that complicated to study. Something that I've always said is that it should be done case by case," the Spanish former hurdler said.
Edited by: Matt Pearson

articles.title: More cancer-prone? Why younger generations may be at risk
articles.summary: Researchers are observing certain age-related types of cancer more frequently in younger people. A new study suggests this could be because younger generations are aging faster than their parents or…

image.caption: Lung, gastrointestinal and uterine cancers are becoming more prevalent among younger generations. A new study shows one explanation as to whyImage: CDC/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: Susanna was just 28 years old when she was diagnosed with bowel cancer. Andre developed lung cancer when he was only 34. Both of them have turned to social media to talk about their fight against the disease. Neither of them are medical outliers — not anymore.

The German Cancer Research Center (DKFZ) has reported a sharp increase in gastrointestinal cancer cases for patients between the ages of 20 and 39. In the US, researchers have observed a similar development, with an even higher disease ratio than in Germany. Younger people are also increasingly being diagnosed with other types of cancers, including those that affect patients' bone marrow or uterus.

Cancer is usually regarded as an age-related disease. According to the German Cancer Aid non-profit, the average age for men and women with cancer is around 69. Cancer cells form when certain sections of the genetic sequence mutate and can no longer be repaired. The older we get, the less reliable our repair system becomes.
Making cancer cell therapy affordable
To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video
Gap between chronologal and biological gap increasing

A study by researchers at Washington University School of Medicine, US, has now found a link that could help explain why an increasing number of people under 50 are developing early-onset cancer. The reason, they suggest, is that younger generations are displaying a wider gap between their biological and their chronological ages. In short, they are aging faster.

While the chronological age counts how many years have passed since a person's birth, their biological age describes how much their body has aged, based on the cellular damage accumulated. Individual organs and tissues can age at varying speeds.
In other words, the same person's liver, heart and brain could each have different biological ages, all of which could differ still from the person's actual age.

The recent study has now for the first time established a link between the increasing gap between biological and chronological ages in younger generations on the one hand, and the risk of early-onset cancer on the other, Ron Jachimowicz explains. He's an attending physician and hematologist at the University Hospital Cologne, as well as head of the Max Planck Research Group for Biology of Aging.
"Don't forget, this is a correlative study," Jachomowicz cautions.
Correlation refers to two things appearing in concert, so it looks like they are related. It does not prove causation, which we speak of when one factor causes another.

While results can provide certain indications that seem quite plausible, researchers were already well aware of the fact "that there is an association between biological age and the risk of developing cancer," Jachomowicz says.
Here's what you need to know about breast cancer
DNA, bloodmarkers and telomeres: How to determine one's biological age

It's not easy to determine a person's biological age. Calculating it requires a number of parameters — there is no single, precise test. Instead, epigenetic tests are used to determine chemical alterations of DNA sequences, evaluating certain blood values and measuring the length of so-called telomeres — that is, the repetitive DNA sequence located at the end of chromosomes that function as protective caps.
There are also physiological tests, to monitor various body and organ functions, as well as cognitive evaluations.

Researchers in the study at hand applied a combination of these various measurement techniques to analyze the data of more than 150,000 individuals drawn from the UK Biobank, a British biometric dataset.

They found that people born between 1965 and 1974 had a significantly higher gap between their chronological and biological ages than people born between 1950 and 1954. The younger the cohort examined, the wider that gap appeared to grow.
An investigation involving more than 10,000 US individuals revealed an even higher deviation for participants born between 1990 and 1999, compared to a cohort born between 1965 and 1969.

"In Australia, Canada, the United Kingdom (UK) and the US, people born in the 1990s face at least fourfold higher risk of early-onset colorectal cancer compared with those in the 1960s," the authors write in the study.
Prostate cancer: The shift in early detection
Can I improve my biological age?
We used to assume that a healthy lifestyle could make up 75% to 90% of one's biological age. Now we know that's not true, Jachimowicz explains.
"We can influence about 50% of it," he says, "while the other 50% are genetically predetermined."
To help slow the aging process, he recommends "typical lifestyle interventions," such as working out regularly, eating a balanced diet, getting enough sleep, and avoiding drugs and alcohol.
And the value of social contacts should not be underestimated, he adds.
It's not easy to say why, on a biological level, younger generations are aging faster than their parents and grandparents. But there are a few hypotheses.
"Younger people are being exposed to earlier and longer obesity," says Tanwei Yuan, an epidemiologist in the Department of Clinical Epidemiology and Aging Research of the DKFZ in Heidelberg.

Other contributing factors are a sedentary lifestyle, and poor sleep quality due to extended periods of time in front of a screen, Yuan adds. She says the current study delivers valuable insights that confirm hypotheses long held by cancer researchers.
She also stresses the value of a healthy lifestyle to help reduce the risk of early-onset cancer.
"If you feel unwell, go to a doctor and ask for the screening," Yuan recommends.
Could microrobots be used to zap cancer cells?

Yuan knows what she's talking about. The 32-year-old researcher says she had felt unwell for quite some time before being diagnosed with intestinal polyps last year. While these can start out benign, if left untreated, polyps can become cancerous. That's why it's important to listen closely to your body and take measures early, she says.
Can my doctor determine my biological age?
In a word: no, says Jachimowicz.
Determining an individual's biological age is the "subject of current scientific research, but in no way a practical routine or part of everyday clinical work."

However, he believes it should be, especially when it comes to initiating early cancer interventions. He believes this current study is particularly valuable because it highlights this path forward for future studies.
"It's still far off in the future," he says, "but it's very exciting."
This article was originally published in German.

articles.title: Binging on cringe: It's as addictive as 'eating junk food'
articles.summary: Flexing achievements? Cringe. Expressing genuine emotions? Cringe. You want to look away, but you can’t. Cringe. It's so addictive, people have built social media careers by monetizing other people's…

image.caption: Five years ago 'cringe' was Youth Word of the Year in Germany. Today, it's just cringeworthyImage: picture alliance/dpa

blocks.text: I feel it. You probably do, too. Someone posts a crying selfie, proposes at a wedding, or confidently sings off-key at karaoke and we cringe.
We cringe when we see something so awkward, embarrassing, or painfully lacking in self-awareness that it makes us recoil.
But we're attracted to it at the same time because — perhaps — we've experienced similar situations ourselves or we know and care about people who have embarrassed themselves and we felt empathy.

And that's why cringe is also known in psychology as secondhand or vicarious embarrassment. We feel it on behalf of other people as well as their feeling it themselves. And sometimes we just enjoy watching other people suffer in a socially awkward situation.
Cringe has an online community: There are cringe compilations, reaction channels on cringe, comedy and other formats built on people's most cringeworthy moments. And people appear to be hooked.

Stefan Hofmann, a clinical psychologist specializing in social anxiety disorder at Marburg University, Germany, says cringe videos are as addictive as junk food: "If you eat junk food, you want more of it [or] even more outrageous stuff," Hofmann said.
Why we can't we look away from cringe moments

Embarrassment is subjective. A bad grade won't embarrass a person who doesn't care about school, but it can trigger real embarrassment in a person for whom academic success is central to their sense of self, their identity.
"If you see a complete stranger misbehaving in public, you might get angry," said Frieder Paulus, a psychologist and neuroscientist at the University of Lübeck, Germany.
"But if your kid is doing the same stuff, you might feel embarrassed, not only for the kid, but also for yourself," said Paulus, "because [you feel] the behavior of the kid reflects [on] you."
Virtual people: Why you can't always trust what you see
To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Embarrassment belongs to a class of emotions psychologists call 'self-conscious emotions,' alongside shame, pride, and guilt. Within that class, embarrassment functions as a kind of emotional barometer that signals how well you're living up to social norms, and whether you're presenting yourself the way you want to be seen.

For people to feel embarrassment, they need a sense of self, as in some capacity for self-reflection, plus awareness of the social norms and context involved, and to be aware that there is an audience.
Our reactions to embarrassing situations are visible on a brain scan.
"We see failure ... the arousal region [lights] up because something is not okay," said Paulus.
Why cringe is a useful reaction
Matthew Feinberg, a social psychologist at the University of Toronto in Canada, has found that people understand displays of embarrassment as a signal of prosocial behavior.
And that prosocial behavior creates a feeling of trust in the observer — they see that the person who is embarrassed knows they have done something socially awkward or wrong.
The message is: "I did something silly and I want to signal that it wasn't intentional and that I am a good member of society," said Feinberg.

On whether the same logic applies to the person observing someone else's mishap, Feinberg said witnessing embarrassment "triggers a natural response. My mind tells me to respond to that person with sympathy."

Feinberg said vicarious embarrassment may even be a stronger trust signal than being embarrassed yourself: "Possibly … because you're experiencing it even though you didn't do anything. It's an interesting research question that as far as I know hasn't been explored."
Millions followed her — then fake nudes appeared
Exclusion: The cost of too much cringe

Embarrassment is also an expression of our fear that we may be excluded from a group when we do something embarrassing. For a social species such as that of humans and other animals, that can be dangerous.

"Fear of exclusion and fear of negative evaluation by others is painful psychologically as well as physically," said Hofmann. "It is certainly not the same quality of pain [as physical pain], but it's pain nonetheless."

In Hofmann's clinical work, he has tested so-called "social mishap exposures" in which patients embarrass themselves in an intentional and engineered way in an attempt to disprove the beliefs driving their fear or anxiety.

But cringe isn't something we can simply stop feeling. The emotion, researchers suggest, is involuntary and develops from an early age. And that also goes for associated emotions, such as empathy and trust, but also schadenfreude — not all of our addiction to cringe can be explained as an expression of positive emotion.

Hofmann says some people do experience pleasure when they see other people in embarrassing situations. And this distinction between empathy and schadenfreude also matters. If the pull toward cringe content was only about empathy, watching more of it would make us feel worse over time. But people keep watching cringe videos online.
Edited by: Zulfikar Abbany

articles.title: What happens next for Infantino and FIFA?
articles.summary: FIFA President Gianni Infantino is under pressure after the failure of his plan to create a commercial subsidiary for the World Cup. But will he be ousted? And what is needed for that to happen?

image.caption: Gianni Infantino is under pressure to keep his seat as FIFA PresidentImage: Harry Langer/DeFodi Images/IMAGO

blocks.text: Now that Gianno Infantino has shelved his plans to create a commercial subsidiary for the World Cup and other FIFA events, UEFA's boycott of FIFA events is over and matches now appear less in danger. Nevertheless, the European governing body says it is now "rebuilding trust" with FIFA — and the story continues to develop rapidly.

As a result, increased focus will be put on women's football when the U20 World Cup starts on September 5 in Poland, and when the U17 World Cup starts in October in Morocco. There are also matches around the world that will decide the qualifiers for next summer's World Cup in Brazil in the same month. Despite there being scant mention in FIFA's subsidiary proposal of the women's game, it will be the first test of life after it.

While a boycott is now off the table, the games will be harder to navigate given the current chaos around the sport's governing body. This is far from ideal for the teams competing, particularly given the tournament's importance.
FIFA revolt: Can Infantino's Trump connection save him?
To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video
Football associations have pulled support for Infantino
With UEFA, Europe's football governors, forming a united front, it is assumed that most, if not all, football associations on the continent will withdraw their support in the coming days.

The first nation to publicly drop their support for Gianni Infantino was Finland, last week. Wales followed on Monday, saying in a statement that "failing to put the best interests of football first is a failure we cannot accept," before England followed suit later in the day.

On Tuesday, Jordan FA President Ali bin Hussein accused Infantino of "blackmail", claiming FIFA offered to help solve the kingdom's problems in exchange for his endorsement. This is in stark contrast to some of the other Asian associations, such as Qatar, the UAE and Sri Lanka, who have publicly supported Infantino.

Germany's FA (DFB) is the biggest sports association in the world, but has yet to officially withdraw its support. It is expected to though, especially when considering the recent words of DFB Director Andreas Rettig. The 63-year-old recently told Stern magazine in an interview that Infantino's recent actions have led to "an irreparable loss of trust" and that football needs to "hit the reset button. We need a different culture. Because trust is the hardest currency."

"From my perspective, Mr. Infantino has invested a great deal of time, money, and energy into maintaining his power structure. Clearly, many decisions served primarily to consolidate his own position," added Retting.
FIFA presidential election next year
The election for Infantino's post is on March 18, 2027, at the 77th FIFA Congress in Rabat, Morocco.

He will run for re-election as president for a final four-year term, looking to gain 106 votes from FIFA's 211 member states (Uefa has 55 votes, Africa 54, Asia 46, Concacaf 35, Oceania 11 and Conmebol 10) to win. Each state gets a vote and voting is done in a secret ballot, which takes time.

However, it seems as though Infantino is increasingly under pressure. Following the resignation of Infantino's senior adviser Carlos Cordeiro last week, reports indicate that the FIFA President has called an emergency meeting on Wednesday.

If 19 of the 37 members of the FIFA Council, the organization's main executive body, vote in favor of his resignation then Infantino may well be out of office sooner rather than later. Several members of the council, including Germany's Bernd Neuendorf, have publicly crititcized Infantino for failing to consult them about his latest plans.

There might also be an Extraordinary FIFA Congress if 43 associations formally request it. Given that UEFA has 55 members, it holds the power to request it at any time. For Infantino to be voted out through a vote of no confidence, 106 votes would be required.

Before his venture to sell stakes in FIFA competitions to private investors ended in chaos after widespread condemnation, Infantino looked almost certain to win re-election.
