The reported revenues from this summer's World Cup were $15 billion (€13 billion), a significantly higher number than expected and one that would have strengthened his position in the organization, given that much of it would be redistibuted among the member organizations.
No clear candidates to succeed Infantino

There has been a lot of speculation about who might succeed Infantino since his position has come under threat in the last week, but it is too soon to really know the legitimacy of any claims. In any case, any potential challengers must declare their candidacy by 18 November.

Nasser Al-Khelaifi, the Paris Saint-Germain chairman, had been touted as a potential candidate given his increasingly influential position in world football. However, the Qatari recently ruled himself out, with a representative for the executive reportedly saying via Politico: "Nasser has absolutely no ambition, no intention, no interest in the Fifa role." Qatar is one of the few federations to have publicly backed Infantino in recent days.
The most obvious candidate is the current UEFA President, Alexander Ceferin, but the Slovenian lawyer is reportedly also not interested in the role.

Concacaf (the confederation of North and Central America and the Caribbean) president Victor Montagliani is one of the few candidates who has expressed interest in the role in the past, but it is unclear whether the man who speaks English, French, Italian and Spanish is ready to challenge now.

Outspoken Norwegian FA President Lise Klaveness has supporters, and, after an initial failure, reached the UEFA Executive Committee in 2025. But the outspoken style that has won her admirers is thought not to have the broad appeal needed in a FIFA candidate. Some also believe her gender may count against her.

Finally, AFC chief, Salman bin Ibrahim Al Khalifa, who lost out to Infantino in the 2016 election, could be a contender if the AFC breaks ranks from FIFA in the way UEFA have. A member of Bahrain’s ruling House of Khalifa, the 60-year-old called Infantino's actions "totally unacceptable" and may be tempted to go against him again, though human rights questions contributed to his previous defeat.
Edited by: Matt Pearson

articles.title: The economic toll of Spain's wildfires
articles.summary: Devastating wildfires are ravaging Spain's tourism, economy and nature. Could the country have done more to prevent them?

image.caption: In recent years, Spain has slashed investments in measures to prevent wildfiresImage: Cesar Manso/AFP

blocks.text: Charred tree stumps, melted asphalt, burned-out cars and destroyed buildings: The wildfires in southern Europe are leaving a trail of devastation and causing billions of euros in damage.

Spain's economy in particular is at risk of being choked by clouds of ash. According to the EU's Copernicus Earth observation system, around 206,000 hectares of forest in Spain have already gone up in flames this year.

"According to the European Commission, the economic impact of wildfires in Spain in 2022 amounted to approximately €7.1 billion ($8.1 billion), representing around 4.5% of the country's GDP. This figure reflects not only the direct costs of firefighting but also the long-term economic consequences of recovering the affected areas," Emilio Vizuete Luciano, an economist at the University of Barcelona, told DW.

The fires often devastate the local economy and disrupt trade in the affected regions, Luciano says. "Tourism is also severely affected. Given Spain's strong dependence on tourism, the disappearance of this activity in fire-affected regions has particularly significant economic repercussions."
Has Europe lost control of its wildfires?
To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video
Wildfires slow economic growth

Climate economist Sarah Meier of Swiss public research university ETH Zurich has taken a closer look at the economic losses caused by wildfires in southern Europe. Her findings show that in regions affected by at least one wildfire, the growth rate fell by between 0.11% and 0.18%.

According to a 2023 study she co-authored, the decline in growth was even greater when several wildfires occurred simultaneously, rising to as much as 4.5% depending on the extent of the fires. "Our calculations are an average for the period from 2011 to 2018," she explains.
And she issues a stark warning: "The costs become particularly high when wildfires reach larger cities, something that has so far been very rare in southern Europe."

The European Environment Agency (EEA) has also calculated the economic losses caused by wildfires in previous years. In 2017, when nearly 990,000 hectares burned across southern Europe, the losses amounted to almost €10 billion.
Europe is burning
According to the European Commission, the EU loses around 500,000 hectares of land to wildfires every year. Spain, Greece and France are among the countries where wildfires are most widespread.

The economic damage goes far beyond losses to tourism. It also includes the loss of biodiversity, declining forestry revenues, soil erosion, destroyed infrastructure and property, as well as the costs of fighting the fires.

A heated debate has erupted in Spain over the cost of fighting wildfires. Since 2009, investment in prevention has actually been declining — even though the number and scale of wildfires have reached alarming levels over the past decade.

According to official figures, spending on wildfire prevention in Spain fell from €364 million in 2009 to €144 million in 2024. Over the same period, annual spending on actually fighting and extinguishing fires remained stable at around €417 million.

For economist Luciano, there is "a certain irony" to this because prevention has been proven to be the best long-term investment. "It is far cheaper than fighting wildfires once they have already broken out."
Spain's high cost of firefighting

The Spanish forestry services company Forescat has estimated that fighting and extinguishing wildfires costs around €19,000 per hectare. Nearly 400,000 hectares of forest went up in flames in Spain in 2025, amounting to costs of around €7.6 billion.

It's still too early to say how much fighting this year's fires will cost Spain; however, Maria Inmaculada Marmol Tardaguila of MATS, a social organization representing public-sector healthcare workers, says things cannot continue this way.

"Continuing to rely on the heroic efforts of firefighting crews to keep our forests safe is both ecological recklessness and fiscal irresponsibility," she notes on the organization's platform, which has also warned of an increase in respiratory illnesses caused by wildfire smoke.

"The solution is not to keep buying more and more firefighting aircraft, but, for example, to remove combustible material such as deadwood from forests before the first spark catches," she points out.
Unless public officials understand this, she warns, Spain will continue to "burn through its budget at the same rate as its forests burn."
This piece was originally published in German.
Spain turns to grazing to curb wildfires

articles.title: Germany: As temperatures rise, so does climate skepticism
articles.summary: Some 98% of active climate scientists say climate change is happening, and is man-made. Nonetheless, a new study shows the number of climate-change skeptics in Germany has increased. Why is that?

image.caption: The heatwave in Germany is thought to have killed 10,000 people alreadyImage: Jochen Tack/picture alliance

blocks.text: Climate skeptics are no longer a small but noisy minority. They are now "a mass phenomenon," according to researchers at Flensburg University.

In a study published in the scientific journal Global Environmental Change, authors Katharina Gies and Emanuel Deutschmann reported that between 2022 and 2023 there was a big jump in skeptical attitudes to climate change among the majority of the 3,074 people surveyed. Some 59% said they had more doubts about climate change in 2023 than they had had in the previous year.

The researchers wrote that the respondents' individual economic situations could not be considered the primary explanation for the increase in skepticism. Other factors, they said, were much more decisive: A right-leaning political orientation, distrust of state institutions, and dissatisfaction with democracy.

Social psychologist Marlene Altenmüller said the Flensburg publication is important and fascinating, though she has doubts about its alarming tone. Other studies show that "the number of people who have doubts is still very small," she says. Altenmüller, a junior professor at the Leibniz Institute for Psychology in Trier, conducts research into science reception: How people perceive scientific evidence, and what they think about the scientific system and its researchers.

Altenmüller's research indicates that people in Germany do not have fundamental doubts about scientific evidence. Rather, it varies depending on the topic, and the view the group to which people feel they belong has of the topic.
Extreme heat: Can Europe adapt to climate change?
To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video
If a group has doubts about climate change, so do its members
Her work, and that of many other researchers, also shows that politically right-leaning people express more skepticism about climate change.

"If right-wing parties were suddenly to discover that we should in fact take action against climate change, my assumption is that the followers of these parties would also believe in climate change and would support political measures," Altenmüller said.

Nor does she believe that climate skeptics have a different personality structure. Instead, climate skepticism is more likely to be down to the fact that "people orientate themselves according to their group and its identity." The credo for most people is that content is secondary, or, as Altenmüller calls it, "Party over policy."

Underlying this is something psychologists call motivated reception. People always see the world through the lens of their own desires, ideas, values, and political ideologies, and anything that cannot be squared with their own ideas and values tends to be disparaged. Altenmüller's research demonstrates that all of us are predisposed to seeing the world through our own filters.
From climate skepticism to conspiracy theories

Both Altenmüller and the Flensburg researchers emphasize that climate change skepticism comes in different guises. One form is the rejection of climate policy measures. The basis for this may be the assumption that it won't be all that bad, or doubt that human activity is the cause. Another is the belief that all the talk about climate change is simply a con, a conspiracy.

This is the focus of research of Stephan Lewandowsky, a professor of cognitive science at the universities of Bristol and Potsdam. Among other things, he examines the persistence of misinformation and conspiracy theories, and is interested in the parameters that determine whether people reject or accept scientific proofs, especially in connection with vaccines and climate change. "Certain people are more susceptible to conspiracy theories than others," he said.

The COVID-19 pandemic made this very apparent. Lewandowsky argues that for some people, conspiracy theories that apportion blame for a particular situation provide a welcome opportunity to escape from feelings like fear and loss of control. "That offers some brief psychological comfort to people," Lewandowsky says.

However, he goes on to explain that the comfort they derive from assigning blame does not last long. "There's good evidence to suggest that people who do fall into that rabbit hole over time are suffering," he said. "They're less likely to hold their jobs. They lose social contacts. They become mentally challenged."
How climate change forces Indian farmers to stay single
Why climate skepticism is hardly an issue in India

Climate skepticism and conspiracy theories are mostly a Western phenomenon. Researchers observe them the most in the US, Europe, and Australia. In India and other countries of the global south, climate change is already a question of daily survival, and has been for some time. "In India, a lot of people still suffer from [not] getting access to clean drinking water," says Jagadish Thaker, senior lecturer at the University of Queensland, Australia, and an expert in climate change communication.
For years now, he says, people in the global south have been experiencing first-hand the ways that climate change is exacerbating problems through rising temperatures and extreme weather events.

Consequently, measures to reduce emissions and adapt to changing living conditions are not seen as a matter of political ideology. According to Thaker, people in India are trying to counteract their own vulnerability to climate change while still trying to develop economically.
Countering climate skepticism with respect

Heatwaves and other extreme weather events are a direct threat to human life in Germany, as has become apparent during this summer's heatwaves, which are reported to have killed as many as 10,000 people already.
This is why the authors of the Flensburg study are urging people to take climate change skepticism seriously if they are to successfully anchor climate protection measures in society.

Thaker believes the media plays a decisive role. He believes there is still a general lack of information and understanding of the effects of climate change. "The media coverage of extreme weather events, while it's a lot, it is dramatic, and unfortunately doesn't mention climate change."

Altenmüller says it's important to keep emphasizing that there is a scientific consensus that climate change is anthropogenic, or, caused by human activity. Sometimes, she says, it does matter who says it. Research shows that some scientific disciplines are perceived as more biased than others. Consequently, economists have a better chance of their message reaching a wide audience than sociologists.

Taking the values of people who express skepticism into account could also help to communicate a different point of view to them, says Altenmüller. Communication must emphasize not only the restrictions that need to be imposed through political measures, but also the opportunities arising from this.

People who have themselves experienced extreme weather events probably find it easier to shift their perspective. This is why Lewandowsky is hopeful that the this year's heatwaves and wildfires will make a difference. "At some point, people's personal experiences matter," he says.
This article has been translated from German.

articles.title: More women die in heatwaves, but biology 'isn't main cause'
articles.summary: In country after country, more women are dying from the heat than men. But researchers say biology isn't the main reason. Age, working conditions, and unequal access to rest may drive the gap.

image.caption: Exposure and working conditions play a larger role in women's heat risk than biology or geneticsImage: CRISTINA QUICLER/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: Observing recent heatwaves in Europe, one pattern has often been remarked on: More women appear to be dying than men. During Europe's then-record summer of 2022, a study found 56% more heat-related deaths among women than men, drawing on mortality data from 35 countries.

Germany, which has just logged its deadliest heat season since 2016, with close to 9,800 heat-related deaths by mid-July, according to the Robert Koch Institute, is seeing the same pattern again this year.
Are hormones making heatwaves more dangerous for women?
Some of the recent coverage has leaned on the hormonal reading that women's bodies simply aren't equipped for heat. They sweat less, carry more body fat, and progesterone nudges core temperature up.

But scientists who study the effect of heat on the human body say that's largely incorrect. "Overall, studies usually show only slightly more vulnerability to heat in women compared to men," saidAlexandra Schneider, an environmental epidemiologist and deputy director of the Institute of Epidemiology at Helmholtz Munich. "It's not really a very strong signal."

The small differences that do exist are real: Women do have a lower sweat rate, less skin area relative to body size, and fat distribution that affects thermoregulation. Hormones play a role too, but unevenly across a lifetime.
Schneider points to one group in particular: Women past menopause, when cardiovascular risk climbs. Older women with existing heart disease, she says, are probably at the highest risk of all.

But even in those cases, she doesn't think biology is the main cause for the extra deaths during a heatwave. "The living conditions, the social environment where women live, makes probably even more of a risk than just the differences in hormone status."
How to survive heat waves in the city
To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video
A research gap, not a biological difference

Toby Mündel, a kinesiology professor at Brock University in Canada, who studies extreme human environments, says that the impact is "overstated," when asked whether there's a real biological basis for the claim that women are more likely to die in heatwaves.
The factors that most determine how a person copes with a heatwave, Mündel says, are age, body size, fitness and habitual activity, and not biological sex.

Sweating is one example. Even though women do sweat less, that doesn't make them more vulnerable, because they compensate in another way. "They send blood flow to the skin, vasodilation, much better than males do," Mündel says, meaning their blood vessels widen more efficiently, moving heat to the surface where it can escape.

Pregnancy, which many assume must be dangerous, is another example. "As a woman progresses through pregnancy, she actually becomes better at handling heat," Mündel says. He draws a clear line between physiology and circumstance: There are good reasons not to have pregnant women doing heavy outdoor labor in extreme heat. But their bodies aren't the reason.
Why does the data suggest otherwise?

Partly, Mündel's argument is based on what gets measured. Studies often count hospital and emergency admissions, and women are far more likely than men to seek medical help. "That is not a physiological thing," he says. "Are they actually struggling, or have they just sought help earlier?"
Underneath it all sits a research gap. "We have about a hundred times as much data and evidence on men. We have nearly zero on women," Mündel says. "It's like comparing cats and dogs."

Numbers from Germany point in the same direction. The Robert Koch Institute attributes the higher female death toll to the fact that women make up a larger share of the oldest age groups. Its estimates also break down deaths per 100,000 people, and by that measure, the picture flips.
In every older age band this summer, the male death rate is higher than the female one. In other words, more women are dying in heatwaves only because more very old women are alive.
In scorching Taipei, locals seek ways to survive urban heat
The real risk is exposure for women, not biology
If the gap isn't physiological, where does it come from?
Laurie Parsons, a researcher at Royal Holloway, University of London, studies how heat stress moves through the global economy in construction, garment factories, farming, driving, street vending.

Across the board, he says, women spend 30% to 50% more of their working time above heat-stress thresholds than men. In construction, when comparing men and women doing the same job, the figure rises to around 50%.

The reasons, he says, are structural. Women often wear more clothing for the same job. Men are more confident asking for breaks. And where men's work is visibly strenuous, it's recognized as a heat risk and rewarded with rest. But women's work is steadier, less obviously punishing, and gets no such relief.

Parsons compares it to the difference between a plane crash and asbestos exposure: One is a sudden, visible catastrophe, the other a slow, constant harm that's easy to miss. "Male heat stress tends to be this taller risk, where you get relatively visible moments of physical distress that can be managed," he says. "Female heat stress is constantly there, but much less visible, because it doesn't have those same obvious peaks in the working day."

blocks.caption: Long working hours, limited breaks, and repeated exposure to heat - women often face greater burdens under these conditionsImage: Aaron Favila/AP/dpa

blocks.text: Then the shift ends, he says. Men rest, but women cook, clean and care for children.
Heat also cuts into pay. Parsons says workers under heat stress are around 30% less productive in the garment sector, which he says is the easiest to quantify.

In formal jobs, workers make up for it with longer hours during the hottest part of the day, feeding what he calls "a vicious cycle" of worsening health and falling output. The self-employed have no such buffer. For them, heat stress just means less income, which ripples the wider family over time.
For Parsons, the starting premise is flawed. "Heat stress is not an atmospheric condition," he says. "It is a social condition, which happens within particular atmospheric circumstances."
Edited by Ben Knight

articles.title: What's really causing Europe's wildfires
articles.summary: From Greece to France, Europe is burning. But what's the real reason for the historic blazes ripping through the continent and why are they getting harder to stop?

image.caption: Firefighters battle a wildfire in the Landes de Gascogne, a vast pine forest planted as a single-species monoculture in the 1800sImage: Manon Cruz/REUTERS

blocks.text: Wildfires almost always need a spark to ignite, whether it's lightning, arson, or a car's hot exhaust pipe touching dry vegetation.

In France's historic summer wildfires, authorities blamed a brush-clearing machine being operated around a high-voltage power line. Spanish investigators concluded that sparks from heavy machinery were behind major blazes there.
But scientists say those findings only explain how Europe's historic wildfires began, not why they grew into the megafires that have devastated the continent this summer.
Across Europe, a combination of human-caused climate change, insufficient planning and forests planted in ways that allow flames to spread quickly are fueling fires, say experts.
"It's not that wildfires are magic and just start. You have to have the right climatic conditions," said Silvia Abruscato, coordinator of FoRISK, a pan-European forest risk management hub.
Has Europe lost control of its wildfires?
To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video
Climate change is loading forests with fuel

Scientists point to three ingredients that determine whether a wildfire will spread rapidly: the amount of vegetation available to burn, how dry that vegetation is, and the weather conditions around a fire.

"When all three of these conditions are very much fire-prone and they align, then you have this kind of fire event," said Francesca Di Giuseppe, a fire forecast project coordinator at the European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts.

Climate change is making these conditions more common and intense. A rapid analysisfrom World Weather Attribution found global warming made the extreme weather behind Spain and France's summer wildfires much more likely.

blocks.caption: Residents watch smoke rise near Lege-Cap-Ferret, one of many towns caught in a summer of 'hydroclimatic whiplash'Image: Julien De Rosa/AFP

blocks.text: One reason is a phenomenon called hydroclimatic whiplash, where ecosystems suddenly swing between wet and dry conditions.
Essentially, as the planet warms, the atmosphere holds more moisture, intensifying rainfall that fuels plant growth.
"This has created an abundance of biomass that then has rapidly dried during a sequence of heat waves," Di Giuseppe said.

In spring, a warmer atmosphere draws water from soil and plants. Drought worsens, vegetation dries out, and landscapes become far easier to ignite. In simple terms, wet winters grow fuel, and dry springs turn that fuel into perfect kindling.
This summer, that's meant fires breaking out almost simultaneously in France, Spain, Greece, and Turkey — all driven by the same broad pattern of heat and drought.
Making matters worse, the fires themselves add to the problem. This year's blazes have already emitted nearly 18 million tons of planet-warming CO2, according to EU figures.
Spain turns to grazing to curb wildfires
Some forests are built to burn

Once a fire begins, it can take thousands of firefighters days or weeks of effort to contain the flames. That's partly due to the way forests have been managed over decades. Across parts of Europe, large areas have been planted as monocultures, dominated by a single species grown for quick timber.

"Some of the fires we've been seeing in France and Spain are in places where you have these very flammable trees which are quite fine and they often are growing close together so fire spreads really easily," Doug Kelley, a land surface modeler at the UK Centre for Ecology and Hydrology, told DW.

More than three-quarters of the Landes de Gascogne forest in southwestern France, which is currently ablaze, contains maritime pine. Created after Napoleon III ordered the region's marshes to be drained and planted with pine in 1857, it became Europe's largest man-made forest.

But the pine species sheds coarse needles that blanket the forest floor, providing bountiful fuel for fires. Because the trees are of similar age and height across vast areas, they are particularly vulnerable to fast-moving fire.

Another fast-growing timber tree is the eucalyptus. In Portugal the oily species — which represents more than a quarter of the country's forestland — burned far and wide in 2017's deadly wildfire season.

"In some regions of Europe, farmland and lower-biomass shrubland were replaced by fire-prone conifer or eucalyptus species of higher economic profitability, increasing the risk of fire," the European Commission wrote in a case study reporton the 2017 Portuguese wildfires.

That includes Spain, where some 3 million hectares (7.4 million acres) of former farmland and pasture were planted with pine and eucalyptus during and after the Franco dictatorship, which lasted from 1939 to 1975.

blocks.caption: Helicopters drop water over Spain's Avila province, where scientists say this year's extreme fire weather was made much more likely by climate changeImage: Miguel Riopa/AFP

blocks.text: Preventing the next disaster

Firefighters will always play a crucial role in suppressing wildfires. But experts say reducing risk before fires start is just as important. That starts with tackling the greenhouse gas emissions driving climate change and intensifying weather extremes.
"Trying to prevent in the first place the landscape becoming so flammable is one of the most effective ways to try to avoid this kind of extreme fire behavior," said Di Giuseppe.

Replacing monocultures with mixed forests would also go a long way. Forests with a wider variety of species are generally better able to withstand drought, windstorms, insect outbreaks, and fires, because different trees respond differently to environmental stresses.

Germany offers an instructive case for forest management. Demand for timber after World War II led to spruce being planted across mountain ranges like the Harz in former East Germany. But these monocultures proved vulnerable to drought and bark beetle infestation. Foresters are now working to convert them into mixed forests to improve resilience.

Planting broadleaf, deciduous trees — such as oak, beech, or maple — can help, as they typically store more moisture than conifers. Trees with thick bark, fewer low-hanging branches, and a higher moisture content tend to be more fire-resistant.

A post-event simulation studyof Portugal's 2017 blazes found fires that overwhelmed firefighters in pine and eucalyptus stands, with flames over four meters tall, could be contained in broadleaf forest, where flame heights dropped to under a meter and a half.

Forestry experts also recommend creating breaks between rows of trees to slow fire spread as well as pruning lower branches so flames can't jump quickly to the canopy. Clearing the forest floor of incendiary leaf litter and dead wood, and using controlled burns to reduce underbrush prior to wildfire season helps too.
"We need to manage our forest well in order to avoid such big disasters from happening. So prevention, prevention, prevention," Abruscato said.
Wildfires: Why mismanagement is the real enemy
Edited by: Jennifer Collins

articles.title: From petitions to memes: How students made dissent visible
articles.summary: From imperial China to present-day India, student movements have repeatedly adapted the tools and symbols of their age to challenge authority.

image.caption: One of the defining visuals of the recent Cockroach Protests in IndiaImage: Ashish Vaishnav/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: It was a clip destined to go viral.

On July 22, 2026, in rainy Mumbai, India, a casually dressed young woman stepped in front of a slow-moving police van carrying detained students. She placed her palm on the hood, forcing the vehicle to stop.
Mobile phones captured the moment from every angle. She too, raised her own phone and recorded the encounter. Within hours, the clip spread across India and beyond.
It became one of the defining visuals of the Cockroach Janta Party protests, a movement in which students demanded transparency and accountability, following leaks in India's medical entrance exams.
But the power of the moment lay not only in what she did, but in how quickly it was seen. A single gesture, a young woman confronting authority, became a symbol shared across millions of screens.
While the clip belongs to a generation raised on social media, the impulse behind it is much older.

From court petitions and revolutionary posters to photographs, umbrellas and memes, student movements have repeatedly adapted the tools and symbols available to them, turning them into vehicles for dissent.
India's Cockroach movement — and why it matters
To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video
Communicating dissent at court
Long before television or social media carried dissent across borders, students still found ways to make their grievances heard.

In Eastern Han China, for instance, scholars at the Imperial Academy (Taixue) aligned with reform-minded officials in opposing powerful eunuchs at court, whom many viewed as corrupt and politically overbearing.
They voiced their objections through public criticism, political networks and petitions.

In an era when political communication moved through official channels, petitions were among the established ways of bringing grievances before the throne. Written in formal language and delivered through the bureaucracy, they carried student concerns directly into the state's communication system.
Multiplying dissent through posters
Centuries later, communication and protest mechanisms evolved.

In Paris in 1968, students challenged university authorities and a conservative postwar social order. As demonstrations spread across the French capital and drew in workers, one of the movement's most enduring contributions emerged from a basement workshop at the Ecole des Beaux-Arts.

blocks.caption: The posters of the Paris 1968 protests were collectively created without credit to any one personImage: Philippe Gras/IMAGO

blocks.text: The Atelier Populaire ("People's Workshop") printed thousands of posters during the protests, many of them overnight. Their bold graphics, silhouettes and slogans became the visual language of the movement. Produced collectively, many carried no individual author's name, helping transform protest into a shared public voice.
The posters and their messages could appear in dozens of places overnight, giving the protest a wide local visual presence.
When a photograph became global witness
Protests also became more impactful when images could be transmitted across borders.

In Soweto in June 1976, Black South African students marched against the apartheid system's education policies, rejecting Afrikaans as a compulsory medium of instruction in Black schools. Many saw it as the language of an oppressive state and a barrier to equal education.

As thousands of students took to the streets, police opened fire. Amid the chaos, South African photographer Sam Nzima captured the image that would travel the world: 13-year-old Hector Pieterson being carried away from the scene after he was fatally shot.

blocks.caption: The iconic photograph of the fatally wounded Hector Pieterson being carried by a classmate highlighted apartheid's atrocitiesImage: ZUMA/IMAGO

blocks.text: The photograph became one of the defining images of apartheid. For many outside South Africa, it served as the lens through which the students' protest was seen and understood, helping build international awareness of and opposition to apartheid.
When images become iconic

In the spring of 1989, students gathered in Beijing's Tiananmen Square demanding democratic reforms, freedom of expression and an end to corruption. As the protests grew, so did the need for symbols that could communicate their message beyond the square.
In the final weeks of the occupation of Tiananmen Square, students built the Goddess of Democracy. Facing Mao Zedong's portrait, the 10-meter statue became a powerful symbol of the movement.

blocks.caption: Students had positioned the Goddess of Democracy opposite the poster of Mao Zedong in Tiananmen SquareImage: 64memo

blocks.text: But while the students created one icon, history would produce another. After the brutal military crackdown on the protesters, a photograph of a lone man, later known as "Tank Man," standing facing a column of tanks traveled around the world.
Global media did not create these symbols, but amplified them. Cameras, newspapers and broadcasters transformed these local acts of defiance into enduring images of resistance.
From organizers to participants
Over time, protest communication no longer flowed only from organizers outward. Crowds and bystanders increasingly helped shape it.

In Chile in 2011, students demanding education reform used flash mobs, performances and public spectacle to draw attention to their cause. Protest was no longer just something people watched. It became something they could join.

In Hong Kong in 2014, students protesting Beijing's plans for electoral reform transformed everyday objects into political symbols. And what began as a practical response to pepper spray and tear gas soon became the defining image of the Umbrella Movement.

blocks.caption: Umbrellas were both practical and symbolic during the 2014 Hong Kong student protestsImage: Philip Fong/AFP

blocks.text: Modeled on Prague's original John Lennon Wall that was created after his murder in 1988 and went on to provide a space for people to express irritation with the communist regime, Lennon Walls in Hong Kong also became hubs of public expression, attracting thousands of people who left messages of support and protest on sticky notes attached to walls around the city.
From slur to symbol
And then there are the political platforms that shape which symbols become widely seen, as is the case in India recently.
Students protesting exam irregularities took an insult aimed at them and made it their own: "Cockroach" quickly became one of the movement's most recognizable symbols online.

blocks.caption: A protester in New Delhi holds up a sign that reads ' I am a cockroach' Image: Adnan Abidi/REUTERS

blocks.text: Memes and reels often spread faster than official statements, with students using them to respond to criticism, mock their opponents and rally support.
Like posters in Paris or umbrellas in Hong Kong, this particular instance shows how memes can transform a disparaging label into a powerful protest symbol.
Edited by: Elizabeth Grenier

articles.title: Humanoid robots: Trump's latest China trade battle?
articles.summary: The US has banned foreign-made humanoid robots, a market Chinese tech firms dominate. Although Washington cited national security risks, analysts think Donald Trump is buying time for US robot makers…

image.caption: Chinese humanoid robots have shown they can talk, win half marathons and enjoy martial artsImage: Ying Tang/NurPhoto/picture alliance

blocks.text: In the latest sign of China's threat to the United States's tech dominance, the Trump administration on Tuesday banned new foreign-made humanoid and four-legged robotsfrom entering the country.
The Federal Communications Commission (FCC) cited "unacceptable risks" to national security for the decision.

The FCC noted how the robots "collect data that could be leveraged by malign actors to surveil Americans, enhance the capabilities of foreign intelligence services, or to remotely commandeer the robots."
The move is widely seen as aimed squarely at China, which accounted for 85% of humanoid robot deployments last year, according to British bank Barclays.
Humanoid robots steal the show at German trade fair
To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video
How serious is the security threat from Chinese robots?

US officials warn that Chinese humanoid and quadruped (four-legged) robots can collect detailed location and personal data, be controlled remotely and pose risks for critical US infrastructure. Specific concerns center on the robots' potential dual-use — civilian and military purposes.
Unitree Robotics, a leading Chinese robot maker, appears on the Pentagon's list of firms with links to the Chinese military. Its robots have been used in army exercises.
Researchers have also shown that Unitree robots have security flaws that let attackers take control with a voice command and then use one robot to control others.

Washington is also concerned that a large cohort of low-cost Chinese robots could feed real-world data back to Chinese artificial intelligence (AI) systems, which are fast catching up with their US rivals.
The threat, however, is largely theoretical as most commercial humanoid robots are in early stages of development.

blocks.caption: China has the edge over the US in humanoid robot deploymentImage: Imaginechina/Sipa USA/picture alliance

blocks.text: China has rejected the accusations, insisting the US is using national security as a pretext for protectionism to suppress Chinese technology. Beijing is expected to impose countermeasures, which could include curbs on the raw materials US robotics firms urgently need to scale up production.

The Trump administration has made no secret of its desire to help the domestic US robotics industry, which in turn supports the country's nearly trillion-dollar AI buildout. According to industry watchers, US President Donald Trump wants to ensure the likes of Figure AI, Tesla Optimus and Agility Robotics are protected from high-volume Chinese producers, whose robots often cost half the price or less of their US rivals.
Washington has put similar curbs on Chinese drones and solar panels and now levies a 100% tariff on Chinese electric vehicles.
Will the ban help US robot makers catch up?
The ban is widely seen as Trump's attempt to buy time, having been caught off guard by how quickly China scaled robotics production.
According to Omdia, a tech research house, China has six firms in the Top 10 robotics rankings. Those firms shipped nearly 11,600 humanoids last year, versus a few hundred by US firms.
In March, Bank of America forecast around 90,000 shipments by the end of this year.

blocks.caption: Elon Musk has big plans for Tesla's Optimus humanoid robotImage: CFOTO/picture alliance

blocks.text: The US is widely seen as stronger at making a robot's brain smart through advanced AI, while China leads at mass-producing cheaper robots with bodies that move better thanks to high-performance actuators or robotic muscles.

Rush Doshi, director of the Initiative on China Strategy at the Council on Foreign Relations, described the ban as "one of the most significant actions taken so far in support of the US robotics ecosystem."
Evan Beard, CEO of Standard Bots, a maker of robot arms, thinks the Trump administration is sending an "unambiguous" message to China.
"Robotics is a technology America must lead and own — and foreign-subsidized robots will not be allowed to unfairly dominate US robotics..." Beard wrote on X.
Critics, however, think the ban could slow US AI innovation as researchers currently benefit from being able to run tests on budget-friendly Chinese robots.
"Restrictions can reduce security exposure, but they do not by themselves create a competitive domestic ecosystem," Georg Stieler, an advisor to the robotics industry, wrote on X.

CNBC, a US business television channel, cited Marc Einstein, a research director at Counterpoint Research, as saying the ban was "bad news for Chinese humanoid producers planning their IPOs in the coming months."
Einstein warned that Beijing could now "further restrict rare earth sales to American companies and … Chinese market access for American companies like Tesla and Nvidia."
Drones, robots and the race to save lives
How big could humanoid robots become?

Barclays estimates the market, currently worth just $2 to 3 billion (€1.7 to 2.6 billion), could reach $200 billion by 2035 in the most optimistic scenario, if the robot's brains, brawn and batteries can be improved.
Elon Musk is even more bullish, saying Tesla's Optimus could become "the biggest product ever" with long-term sales potentially reaching $10 trillion.
At scale, he believes the robots, which currently sell for about $100,000, could eventually cost $20,000 to $30,000 each — cheap enough for factories, warehouses and later homes.
Combining Barclays' forecast with Musk's target price points to roughly 7 to 10 million humanoid robots being sold each year by 2035.
In the near term, humanoids are expected to take on repetitive and physically demanding jobs in warehouses and factories. Later, they could expand into health, elderly care and household chores.
Edited by: Rob Mudge

articles.title: Eco wins: From death strip to nature haven and other green surprises
articles.summary: A Cold War relic becomes a biodiversity haven, a Pokemon Go for trees and seagrass gets a second life. This week's eco wins come from some unexpected places.

image.caption: The former inner-German border death strip is now a thriving nature corridor open to allImage: MDR

blocks.text: After the fall of the Berlin Wall in 1989, the border zone that divided West and East Germany was left largely untouched. Today, the nearly 1,400-kilometer (870 miles) stretch, once known as the death strip, is a "green belt." It's home to around 7,500 species of insects and spiders, hundreds of them endangered, as well as otters, wildcats and birds on the brink of extinction.

Because the military zone was sealed off for decades, species that have vanished elsewhere in Germany were able to take hold here. Now 88% of the area is under protection, and cycle paths and information panels allow visitors to explore what was once completely off-limits.
Read the full story here: East-West border death zone now Germany's biodiversity oasis
An urban tree database

Not all heroes wear capes, but some do form a canopy. Urban trees quietly cool neighborhoods, reduce flooding and improve our wellbeing. But in many cities, trees are under pressure from heat, drought, traffic and too much concrete.
Now, a citizen-science project in Germany is helping people map and monitor the trees around them. Think Pokemon Go, but for urban nature and with real-world benefits for the climate.
Seagrass goes from beach nuisance to building material
On Poel, a German island in the Baltic Sea, washed-up seagrass is being turned into sustainable insulation for homes, while helping clean local beaches in the process.
As demand for eco-friendly construction materials grows, the project is attracting interest from across Europe and could give new value to a resource that was previously viewed as waste.
How seagrass is becoming a green building material

articles.title: German court rules that AI music firm Suno violated copyrights
articles.summary: Germany's state-mandated licensing agency, GEMA, says the verdict has "global significance," as Suno is also directed to pay yet-to-be-quantified damages.

image.caption: Founded in 1974 in West Germany, disco music group Boney M. remains popular — but would they have had a chance in today's market?Image: Hardy Schiffler/jazzarchiv/picture-alliance

blocks.text: The Munich Regional Court ruled on Friday that Suno AI, a US-based company, which generates songs from text prompts. has violated copyrights and has to disclose illicit revenues.

The lawsuit initiated in January 2025 by GEMA, Germany's state-mandated licensing agency, argued that Suno trained its AI models on copyrighted music without obtaining licences or compensating its rights holders.
According to the ‌verdict, Suno will have to pay damages that have yet to be quantified. Suno has disagreed with the ruling and said it would evaluate all available options, including an appeal.
"This is a verdict of global significance," Gema CEO Tobias Holzmueller told Reuters.
A closely watched case

The lawsuit has been closely watched, as it is one of the first major cases anywhere in the world to test how traditional copyright law applies to AI music training and AI-generated music outputs. Among Suno's arguments was the fact that the German court does not have proper jurisdiction to rule on AI model training activities that occurred exclusively inside the United States.
Paul McCartney & Rosalia: Strategies for surviving AI music
To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The proceedings could help determine whether AI music companies must obtain licenses before training their models on copyrighted songs, and whether AI-generated music that closely resembles existing songs constitutes copyright infringement.

"Our goal is not to clear Suno from the face of the earth, but obviously to get into licensing negotiations on an eye-to-eye level, which was not possible with Suno so far," explains GEMA CEO Tobias Holzmüller, who describes the company as "by far the largest and commercially most successful of all AI music models." He believes Suno pursues a much more aggressive business strategy than its competitors.

blocks.caption: Tobias Holzmüller, CEO of GEMAImage: Sebastian Linder

blocks.text: The outcome of this case is also linked to another central question: How should creators be compensated when their music is used to train generative AI systems?
At the forefront of the battle to protect artists' rights

Last year, GEMA won a related case against OpenAI before the same court. It found that OpenAI unlawfully trained its AI models on copyrighted song lyrics and reproduced them via ChatGPT without authorization.
OpenAI was ordered to cease and desist from reproducing the works in the model, to disclose information and pay damages. But as the company pursues an appeal, the ruling remains non-final.
In contrast to that decision, the current lawsuit does not focus on song lyrics, but on entire music pieces.

One of the aspects that makes this lawsuit important is that it has not been initiated by a private company or record label, but rather by a music collecting society, notes Martin Senftleben, professor of intellectual property law at the Amsterdam Law School.

Such initiatives "are particularly important because, by definition, you could say that they're more inclusive," Senftleben tells DW. "You can become a GEMA member even if you're not a very well-known high-profile artist or composer. And that means there's a chance of bringing remuneration for AI users to a much broader group of rights holders."
GEMA represents more than 95,000 composers, songwriters and music publishers in Germany, along with over 2 million rights holders worldwide.
How did GEMA present its case?

GEMA claims that Suno trained its AI on copyrighted music without permission or payment to songwriters, composers and publishers represented by the German music collecting society. GEMA also says that the US-based company is commercially benefiting from those works without compensating the artists.

Suno's music creation platform generates songs through simple text prompts. Users can describe the mood, style or genre they desire and the system synthesizes a structured track — complete with lyrics, vocals and instrumentation — in under a minute.
The songs that are produced by the AI system can be very similar to copyrighted songs.

During the court proceedings, GEMA demonstrated this by prompting Suno AI to create tracks with the original lyrics of different popular songs in its repertoire, including "Forever Young" by Alphaville, "Mambo No. 5" by Lou Bega, "Daddy Cool" by Boney M., "Cheri Cheri Lady" by Modern Talking and "Atemlos durch die Nacht," written by Kristina Bach and popularized by Helene Fischer.
Along with the lyrics, the plaintiffs prompted the desired musical style and the title of the work, without specifying any melody, rhythm, harmony or arrangement.
Yet the resulting AI songs are very similar to the original works.
German music: From 'Schlager' to 'Deutschrap'
Suno admits that the original songs at the center of GEMA's lawsuit are among the numerous pieces that were used to train the AI model.

AI companies such as Suno claim that the ingestion of data for AI training can be done freely on the basis of what is known as "fair use" in the US and the "text and data mining exception" rule in the EU.

But whether such licence-free AI training is allowed under copyright law remains heavily contested globally. In different lawsuits around the world, courts are now examining whether such uses harm the economic market of the original creators through unfair competition.

"The novelty in the lawsuit is that GEMA does not focus on the AI training stage," explains Senftleben. By basing their claim on tests that demonstrate that these AI systems generate songs that have similarities with copyright-protected works from their repertoire, "they bridge this gap between relevant use now taking place in AI training, and the market harm done at AI output level," he adds.
Why AI shouldn't be compared to human brains
Anyone who wants to become a good musician needs to listen to and learn from existing music.
Similarly, the AI industry claims this analogy applies to how their models are trained — by absorbing countless creative works in order to generate new ones.
But from the rights holders' perspective, AI models are rather copying and commercially exploiting their works.

This argument that an AI learns from music and is inspired by it like a human being is "completely ridiculous," notes Tobias Holzmüller. "These are concepts that come from the human brain and have been designed for the human brain, and not for a machine that is able to digest millions of sound files in split seconds. I mean, just the amount of sheer data — they say it's data; for us, it's music — that these machines have swallowed up and then digested and are now spitting out, this is completely incomparable to what's happening in a human brain.
"To humanize these machines by using these concepts is not logical — and it's certainly not moral."

blocks.caption: Suno users generate around 7 million tracks every dayImage: Samuel Boivin/NurPhoto/picture alliance

blocks.text: Across Suno's platform globally, users collectively generate roughly 7 million songs per day. Around 75,000 of them end up on streaming services daily, adds Holzmüller. "This is definitely where it's not sustainable anymore, but really toxic for the music ecosystem."

"If you want to create a sustainable model where you accept that AI music is here to stay, but at the same time, that it shouldn't push human-created music out of the market, the only way to tackle this is to put a price tag on the output," says the CEO of GEMA. "Because otherwise you will have free-of-charge AI sounds that will outcompete human music in a lot of circumstances."

For example, music in movie scores or social media has until recently allowed various songwriters to make a living. For Holzmüller, if licences lead to an increase in costs in AI-created sounds to a point that they are as expensive as human-created songs, it could provide a level playing field. "Then — it's my firm belief — people will continue to use human music, because it has this additional element."
This article was originally published on July 30, 2026 and was updated on July 31, 2026 to reflect the court's ruling.
Edited by: Brenda Haas

articles.title: BMW to Volkswagen: How deep is Germany's auto industry cull?
articles.summary: BMW joins VW, Porsche and Mercedes-Benz in cutting thousands of jobs, as Chinese rivals erode their market share. DW recaps the major reforms German automakers are pursuing to safeguard their future.

image.caption: German auto workers have been protesting against plans to cut jobsImage: Jens Schlüter/AFP

blocks.text: BMW makes five
BMW on Wednesday became the fifth German carmaker to announce major job cuts, as the country's auto sector seeks to tackle rising competition from China.
The Munich-based firm said it would cut up to 8,000 jobs globally, representing about 5% of its 154,000-strong workforce.

BMW, which also owns the Mini and Rolls-Royce brands, said the job losses would primarily affect operations in Germany and be achieved through natural staff turnover and a voluntary redundancy program.
Although BMW was seen as more resilient to Chinese competition, the company warned last month that its sales in China were falling sharply.
Chinese rivals have intensified competition for electric vehicles (EV), which has crushed BMW's sales volumes and pricing power.
Last year, BMW's vehicle deliveries in China dropped to their lowest level since 2017 and in the three months to June, they fell 30% year-on-year.

US PresidentDonald Trump's tariffs have also contributed to BMW's woes, along with higher energy prices from the Iran war and the growth of Chinese EV-makers in other major markets, including Europe, Asia Pacific and Latin America.

blocks.caption: BMW joins other German automakers in announcing large job cutsImage: Jade Gao/AFP

blocks.text: On Thursday, the company disclosed that second-quarter net profit dropped 35% to €1.2 billion ($1.4 billion), while revenue fell to €31 billion from €34 billion.
BMW has adjusted its guidance for the rest of the year, warning of a "significant decline" in profit.
Are AI-powered robots German carmaker BMW's future?
To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video
Even Porsche isn't immune
Two days earlier, Porsche announced plans to cut an additional 5,000 jobs in Germany by the end of 2035. The figure represents about 1 in 5 workers
The sports performance brand said the new measures would hit Porsche's main production plant in Stuttgart-Zuffenhausen and its research and development (R&D) center in nearby Weissach.
Last year, Porsche announced a restructuring program to cut 1,900 jobs in the Stuttgart region by 2029 and allow 2,000 fixed-term contracts to expire.
The company will also defer wage increases, while performance bonuses will be more closely linked to profits.
Porsche, which is owned by Volkswagen Group but run with a high degree of independence, has also reduced jobs at its Leipzig plant and is closing three subsidiaries that employ about 500 people.
At the end of last year, Porsche employed nearly 41,800 people, with about 85% of them in Germany.
Volkswagen plans the deepest cuts
Volkswagen, Europe’s largest carmaker, last month doubled its job-cull program, announcing plans to slash up to 100,000 jobs.
The company also wants to close four German factories.
Unions and the German state of Lower Saxony, which holds a 20% voting stake and can veto major decisions, have rejected the latest plans. VW had originally stated it would cut 50,000 positions.
VW is well-known for its oversized headcount of 630,000 globally — 680,000 including Chinese joint ventures.
The Wolfsburg-based giant employs around 60% more workers than Toyota, despite producing a similar number of vehicles.
Once a sign of German industrial strength, the huge workforce has become a costly burden amid intensifying competition from Chinese EV-makers.
VW controls more stages of production in-house than rivals, driving up labor demand, while German factory costs are often twice those of rivals.
Slow progress on electric vehicles further eroded sales in China, which once accounted for a third of VW’s total, as well as Europe.
VW is bringing out the axe
Mercedes trims without mass firings
In March last year, Mercedes-Benz agreed with its works council plans to deliver €5 billion in savings by 2027.
However, the company ruled out compulsory redundancies at German plants, insisting that voluntary departures could achieve the reforms.
Until March this year, around 5,500 administration, R&D and IT workers accepted severance packages and left. Production workers remained protected.
Additional headcount reductions have been reported in the firm's China operations.
Last month, Mercedes postponed a bonus payment for nearly three-quarters of its German workforce until 2027 and proposed extending the work week from 35 to 40 hours without extra pay.
Mercedes bosses also indicated that some jobs could be moved abroad.
On Tuesday (July 28), Mercedes said it had written off more than €700 million due to fierce competition in China.
Although second-quarter net profit grew 13.5% to €1.09 billion, core earnings at its key cars division fell by a quarter to €909 million.
Audi's premium brand under pressure
VW-owned Audi last year announced plans to cut up to 7,500 jobs in Germany by the end of 2029.
The company has ruled out compulsory redundancies and said the job losses in administration and R&D would be achieved through voluntary schemes and early retirement.
Last month, however, Audi's Neckarsulm plant was listed for possible closure in 2030 by parent company VW. This could impact about 15,000 workers.
The site, which makes the A5, A6 and A8, has already cut production from 300,000 to 225,000 vehicles a year.
Edited by: Rob Mudge

articles.title: 'Rienzi': Why this Wagner opera is so relevant today
articles.summary: The opera sparked controversy long before its Bayreuth Festival premiere, and the debate hasn't died down since it came to the stage. Now, another controversy surrounds the new AI-generated Ring…

image.caption: A new production of Hitler's favorite opera, 'Rienzi' opened the 150th Bayreuth FestivalImage: Enrico Nawrath

blocks.text: Even before opening night, expectations of how the themes of Richard Wagner's "Rienzi" would be handled were running high — not least because the opera had never been staged at the Bayreuth Festival. Now it has opened the festival's 150th anniversary. One aspect that fueled the debate: The close relationship between Wagner's descendants and Adolf Hitler — "Rienzi" was one of Hitler's favorite operas.

"It's a piece that's highly contaminated," director Alexandra Szemerédy told DW. "When Katharina Wagner [the festival's director] first approached us, my initial excitement was definitely a bit dampened." Nonetheless, the production received enthusiastic applause at its premiere — conductor Nathalie Stutzmann and the Bayreuth Festival Orchestra were given standing ovations, and Hungarian directors Alexandra Szemerédy and Magdolna Parditka were warmly celebrated for their interpretation of the work.

The directors tell the tale of the rise and fall of the 14th-century Roman tribune Rienzi in the present day. Rienzi, who initially seeks to free the people of Rome from aristocratic rule, is ultimately consumed by power and becomes a dictator himself.

blocks.caption: A glimpse of the surveillance state: Everyone knows everything about everyone elseImage: Enrico Nawrath

blocks.text: The production opens with a stark landscape of identical concrete apartment blocks that later break off into individual units. Through the windows, neighbors watch each other's lives unfold. Every apartment contains screens broadcasting the same news. Whatever can't be seen through the windows is shared through smartphones, social media and omnipresent screens.
From utopia to dystopia

In this new production, Rienzi initially doesn't defeat the aristocracy with violence. He calls for democratic elections — and wins. Afterward, he lavishly celebrates with the elites. But that changes when the same aristocrats attempt to assassinate him. Rienzi survives, imposes a military dictatorship and begins executing his enemies in the streets. Increasingly consumed by paranoia and delusion, he loses his grip on power and ultimately dies.

The directors said they were particularly interested in how someone can inspire the masses and, fueled by populism, become an authoritarian ruler. "He's considered a reference figure in the study of populism because of this first major citizens' uprising in Rome," Szemerédy said. The charisma of the real historical figure Cola di Rienzo, who lived in the 14th century, had also fascinated Adolf Hitler.
A controversial choice

Musicologist and theater scholar Anno Mungen criticized the decision to stage "Rienzi" for the first time during the Bayreuth Festival's 150th anniversary, calling it "historically tone-deaf." Wagner himself chose not to include "Rienzi" in the repertoire of his new Festspielhaus in Bayreuth in the 1870s, citing musical considerations.

In his book on the intersections between the festival and the Holocaust, Mungen writes about the deportations from Bayreuth to Auschwitz, which included Jewish members of the Bayreuth Festival Orchestra. "When we look at 'Rienzi,' it would have been both meaningful and necessary to place the production within the context of a major academic conference," Mungen said. "The University of Bayreuth would have been very willing to participate."

blocks.caption: The path to the Kingdom of Heaven: a favorite theme of Wagner's. But just before reaching his destination, Rienzi collapsesImage: Enrico Nawrath

blocks.text: From 1940 to 1944, in what are now known as the "Wartime Festivals," Bayreuth kept running thanks to Hitler's financial support. Performances were held for selected audiences only, including wounded soldiers and workers from the arms industry. History students are currently exploring that period in an exhibition at the Steingraeber piano factory in Bayreuth. "These wartime festivals became a cultural showcase, intended to project the message that 'things aren't really so bad in Germany'," Mungen said. He chose not to attend the "Rienzi" premiere because the subject remains too personal.

The opera's dramaturge Markus Kiesel also believes it's essential to confront the controvery surrounding the piece. "Not performing the opera — or even banning it — would achieve nothing," Kiesel said. "On the contrary, we need to face these issues openly, creatively and honestly, and discuss them critically. If not in Bayreuth, then where?" Szemerédy added: "We have to build a bridge from the past to the future, especially at a time when right-wing populism is once again gaining strength and becoming a threat. That's exactly why this work needs to be performed today."
At the end of the opera, Rienzi dies, new elections are held, and two candidates emerge victorious.

blocks.caption: AI images from decades of opera history form the concept for the production of this years Ring CycleImage: Enrico Nawrath

blocks.text: Throughout Richard Wagner's operas, power, greed, cruelty, love until death and the destruction of the world are recurring themes. His 16-hour cycle "The Ring of the Nibelung," written for the Bayreuth Festspielhaus that he built specifically for it, explores these human impulses. The Rhine gold guarded by the Rhinemaidens becomes an object of universal desire — and ultimately brings catastrophe.

The piece has been reinterpreted in Bayreuth many times. Patrice Chéreau's landmark 1976 production presented "The Ring" as a parable about greed and the decline of capitalism. Frank Castorf later replaced the symbolism of gold with oil as the true source of capitalist power.
An AI reinvention

The festival's interpretation curated by Marcus Lobbes, has no stage director. Instead, Lobbes and his team developed a new AI-based imaging system in which the singers perform inside a holographic three-dimensional environment. "What appears on stage is a unified audiovisual image," Lobbes explained. "We create a visual landscape for both the singers and the orchestral performance." To generate the projections, the team trained the AI using archival material from previous Ring productions spanning from 1876 to 2024.

In "Das Rheingold," the first installment of the cycle, viewers see Rhinemaidens in bathtubs, lakes and streams, along with forests of trees, vines and vegetation alternating with wood and metal structures, creating shifting worlds between nature and industrial romanticism. Images crack apart, dissolve into one another and morph continuously. At times, the visuals are mesmerizing; at others, human faces become distorted beyond recognition.

blocks.caption: 'Das Rheingold' used a Neo-Romantic style generated by AI Image: Enrico Nawrath

blocks.text: Whether the technology can sustain audience interest over the entire 16-hour cycle remains to be seen. While the imagery is constantly in motion, the singers often stand almost motionless so as not to disrupt the projections. "The singers' positions are predetermined, but they can still interact with one another," Lobbes said. After the performance, one audience member joked that perhaps Siegfried and Sieglinde would eventually be blowing kisses at each other. Musically, however, the production boasts an outstanding cast, including Klaus Florian Vogt, Jochen Schmeckenbecher and Evelin Novak, with Christian Thielemann conducting. As one audience member put it: "If the AI becomes too much for me, I'll simply close my eyes and enjoy the music."
This article was originally written in German and edited by Tenzin Sekhon.
